docs.research_question: Is China's policy-bank finance to Latin American sovereign governments primarily motivated by soft power, by extractive (resource-security) diplomacy, or by the commercial objectives of a neo-developmental state?
docs.methodology: Descriptive comparison of loan characteristics: size, interest rate/spread, sector, recipient country, tying conditions and maturity. The authors compile Chinese loans from government, bank and press reports in China and the borrowing countries, keeping only loans confirmed on both sides of the Pacific and generally excluding loans under US$50m. They compare these with World Bank, IDB, CAF and US Ex-Im loans and with private sovereign bond coupons (Bloomberg) and JP Morgan EMBI+ spreads. US Ex-Im and China Ex-Im rates are compared after adjusting for OECD country-risk premiums. The authors also use case comparisons (Argentina, Brazil/Petrobras, Ecuador, Venezuela). There is no regression analysis.
docs.summary: Gallagher and Irwin test three explanations for China's lending to Latin American sovereign governments: soft power (subsidised credit to political allies), extractive diplomacy (subsidised credit to lock up natural resources), and a neo-developmental state looking for commercial profit for national champions. They compile loan-by-loan data on China Development Bank (CDB) and China Ex-Im Bank loans for 2005–2011 (from Chinese and Latin American government, bank, SEC and press sources, later the Inter-American Dialogue database) and compare it with World Bank, IDB, CAF, US Ex-Im and private bond-market finance. Chinese commitments rose from under $1bn a year before 2008 to $37bn in 2010, more than the World Bank and IDB combined. docs.stance_on_premise: qualifies — The paper supports the premise that China expanded its economic relationships quickly: Chinese lending exceeded the World Bank and IDB combined by 2010. It attributes this to commercial, risk-reducing statecraft and to a gap in Western finance, not to ideological alignment or subsidies. This qualifies purely geopolitical explanations. It also implies that Chinese finance was concentrated in a few high-risk, often leftist states (Venezuela and Ecuador took 60%) and was marginal in US-aligned Mexico, Colombia and Peru, so China's financial position was not region-wide.

docs.harvard_reference: Urdinez, F., Mouron, F., Schenoni, L.L. and de Oliveira, A.J. (2016) 'Chinese Economic Statecraft and U.S. Hegemony in Latin America: An Empirical Analysis, 2003–2014', Latin American Politics and Society, 58(4), pp. 3–30. doi:10.1111/laps.12000.
docs.research_question: Is Chinese economic statecraft in Latin America (SOE FDI, bank loans, manufacturing exports) related to declining US hegemonic influence in the region, and if so, through which mechanism: Chinese contestation, Chinese accommodation, or Latin American diversification?
docs.methodology: Cross-national time-series regression for 21 Latin American countries, 2003–2014. All dependent variables are per capita. OLS with panel-corrected standard errors, a lagged dependent variable and an AR1 autocorrelation structure (Beck & Katz 1995). The key regressor is a US hegemonic influence index built by dynamic PCA (Kaiser rule, scree plot, KMO test), rescaled 0–1. Six models: (1) SOE FDI, (2) private FDI as a control group, (3) Chinese bank loans, (4) IBRD/IDA loans as a control group, (5) Chinese manufacturing exports, (6) Chinese commodity imports as a control group. Each model has 11–18 controls, including TAIWAN, STRATEGIC PARTNERSHIP and COMMODITY BOOM. Multicollinearity was checked by correlation matrices and VIF. Statistical simulations (King et al. 2000) were used for expected values.
docs.summary: Urdinez, Mouron, Schenoni and de Oliveira draw on hegemonic stability theory to ask whether China's economic penetration of Latin America, 2003–2014, is related to declining US hegemonic influence. They build a US-influence index for 21 Latin American countries with dynamic principal components analysis of five proxies: US economic aid and military aid per capita, UNGA vote convergence with the US, exports to the US as a share of total exports, and US FDI relative to GDP. The index is rescaled 0–1. All five proxies fell between 2003 and 2014. Using OLS with panel-corrected standard errors, a lagged dependent variable and AR1 correction (Beck–Katz), they regress per-capita Chinese SOE FDI, private FDI, Chinese bank loans (Inter-American Dialogue data), IBRD/IDA loans, Chinese manufacturing exports and Chinese commodity imports on the index plus controls, including Taiwan recognition and s
docs.stance_on_premise: supports — The paper finds that Chinese state-linked finance and investment expanded fastest where US hegemonic influence was declining or weak, and all US-influence proxies fell over 2003–2014. This is consistent with China consolidating relationships independently of, and in the gaps left by, US engagement. It qualifies the premise in two ways: the main trade flow (commodities) is apolitical demand-pull, and the period predates the rise in US strategic discourse that the central question emphasises. Its political reading (contestation) also conflicts with D01's commercial reading of the same loan patterns.

docs.summary: Albright looks at the demand side of Chinese development finance. She asks when Latin American and Caribbean governments choose to borrow from Chinese policy banks (CDB, CHEXIM) rather than the US-backed World Bank. She uses mixed-effects (multilevel) logistic regressions on 518 sovereign loans in 18 countries between 2008 and 2019: 443 from the World Bank and 75 from Chinese banks. The dependent variable is lender choice (China = 1). She adds 19 interviews with Ecuadorian policymakers from January to March 2024. docs.stance_on_premise: qualifies — The paper supports the idea that China consolidated its position as a development lender. Even when Ecuador regained access to Western finance, it chose China for over half its loans, and China dominates very large infrastructure loans. But China's share is sensitive to borrower politics: right-leaning parties have near-zero predicted probability of choosing China. China's share also fell once Western alternatives returned, from more than 80% to 53% in Ecuador. So China's expansion depends on demand-side ideology and on gaps in Western finance, not only on structural forces, and US-aligned governments substitute away from China.

docs.summary: This econometric study asks how geopolitical risk (GPR) originating in the US and in China spills over to inward FDI in Latin America (LATAM). It also tests whether bilateral trade and US–China tensions (UCT) moderate these effects. The sample is a fixed-effects panel of seven large economies (ARG, BRA, CHL, COL, MEX, PER, VEN) for 2000–2022, using the Caldara & Iacoviello GPR index and the Rogers et al. (2024) UCT index. Dependent variables are the log of total inward FDI (World Bank net inflows), FDI from the US (BEA) and FDI from China (patchy national, ECLAC and Statista data). US GPR is associated with lower total FDI (−0.010), while China GPR is associated with higher total FDI (0.400), which the authors read as risk-diversification inflows. GPR reduces US FDI but increases Chinese FDI. Chinese FDI is also positively associated with BRI membership and negatively with host governanc
docs.stance_on_premise: mixed — The finding that GPR deters US FDI but not Chinese FDI, together with BRI-linked and weak-governance-linked Chinese FDI, supports a state-backed resilience explanation for continued Chinese economic consolidation. It also suggests rivalry itself tilts relative flows toward China. However, BRI membership is associated with lower total FDI, high US–China tension makes both GPR spillovers negative, and USMCA and friendshoring channel FDI to Mexico. These point to a bifurcated picture rather than uniform Chinese expansion. Serious reporting anomalies (N, SEs, sign inconsistencies) mean the findings should be treated as suggestive.

LAC exports to China (~US$26bn in 2005) are overwhelmingly primary commodities: iron ore, soy, base-metal ores and copper. docs.stance_on_premise: mixed — It supports the premise that China's economic position expanded through market-driven complementarity: Chinese demand significantly boosted South American commodity exports, independent of any US discourse. But it qualifies the premise geographically and in kind. For Mexico, and to some extent Central America and Colombia, China is a competitor that displaced exports and FDI, not a partner. Region-wide, the relationship involved large and growing deficits rather than broad gains, so 'expansion' means both deeper commodity sales and Chinese manufacturing penetration.

docs.summary: Stallings argues that the comparative-political-economy 'growth model' (GM) literature (Baccaro, Blyth & Pontusson 2022) neglects the international context facing peripheral countries and should incorporate theories of hegemony and dependency. Dependency operates through three mechanisms: markets (trade and finance access), leverage (direct political/economic pressure) and linkage (ideas, education, elite identification). Applying this to Latin America, she distinguishes a consumption-led ISI model (1950–80, ending in the debt crisis) and an export-led model after 1990 with two variants. In the 1990s, under US/European hegemony, the 'north' (Mexico, Central America) won through NAFTA/CAFTA and integration into US value chains, though Mexico's gains were enclave-like. docs.harvard_reference: ECLAC (2018) Exploring New Forms of Cooperation between China and Latin America and the Caribbean. LC/TS.2018/6. Santiago: Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean. (Prepared for the Second Ministerial Meeting of the CELAC–China Forum, January 2018.)
docs.research_question: How can China-LAC cooperation be renewed and diversified across trade, finance, investment, infrastructure, environment, STI and social development? (Pages 1-52: what are the macro, financial, social and trade bases of the relationship?)
docs.methodology: Descriptive statistical overview using COMTRADE, UNCTAD, IMF, World Bank, ILO, UNESCO, OECD PISA and national customs data, plus unpublished estimates of Chinese development finance (Gallagher and Cipoletta 2017); charts and tables with brief bullet commentary; 2017 trade values are ECLAC projections.
docs.summary: ECLAC's background document for the Second Ministerial Meeting of the China-CELAC Forum (Santiago, January 2018). Pages 1-52 cover the global and Chinese macro context, Chinese finance in LAC, a social comparison, LAC-China trade and the opening of the FDI chapter. ECLAC presents China as a key engine of global growth that is shortening its value chains (Made in China 2025) while US trade policy turns protectionist under 'America First'. Chinese policy banks (CDB, China Exim) committed over US$141 billion to LAC governments in 2005-2016, more than the IDB, World Bank or CAF. The lending is concentrated in Venezuela, Brazil, Ecuador and Argentina (93%), goes mostly to infrastructure (52%) and energy (31%), and about half is loan-for-oil. ECLAC attributes it to Chinese strategy, including renminbi internationalisation, natural-resource access, geopolitics and 'consolidating allegiances'. T

It qualifies the picture: trade value is commodity-price-driven, LAC's share in China's trade fell after 2011, and Mexico/Central America experience China mainly as a manufacturing competitor.

docs.harvard_reference: Zhou, J. (2023) 'A double-edged sword: Chinese direct investment in Latin America', Structural Change and Economic Dynamics, 67, pp. 234–249. doi:10.1016/j.strueco.2023.07.010.
docs.research_question: What are the macroeconomic and sectoral effects of the stock of Chinese direct investment on Latin American host economies (GDP, trade, factor prices, sectoral output and bilateral trade), and does it produce a 'hollowing-out' of LAC manufactures?
docs.methodology: Static multi-region CGE model (GTAPinGAMS, after Rutherford 2005 and Lanz & Rutherford 2016, extended by the author to introduce FDI shocks simultaneously in several regions). Assumptions: perfect competition, full employment, Arrow–Debreu static equilibrium; Leontief top-level production nest; value added as a CES combination of sector-specific capital and mobile labour; Armington-type composite of imported and domestic intermediates. The shock is a sector- and country-specific increase in capital stock, computed from firm-level Chinese ODI stock (to 2019) relative to GTAP sectoral capital stocks (new parameter FDIK in the capital-market clearing equation). Three private-consumption specifications (Cobb–Douglas, LES, CDE) give a range of results. Aggregation: 3 factors (labour, capital, land/natural resources as described in the results), 19 regions (10 LAC hosts, China, US, rest of LAC
docs.summary: Zhou (Xiangtan University) estimates the economy-wide effects of Chinese direct investment on ten Latin American host economies (Brazil, Peru, Argentina, Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Panama, Bolivia, Chile, Mexico) with a static, perfectly competitive, full-employment CGE model (GTAPinGAMS, GTAP 10 database, reference year 2014; 3 factors, 19 regions, 21 sectors). Because official Chinese statistics route about 90% of ODI to LAC through the Cayman Islands and British Virgin Islands, the author maps firm-level project data from RED ALC–China and the China Global Investment Tracker (stock to 2019) into GTAP sectors and introduces it as a sector-specific increase in host capital stocks. Descriptively, Chinese ODI is concentrated in Mining and Electricity-Gas-Water everywhere except Mexico (48.23% manufactures), and GTAP data show complementary structures: LAC exports minerals, agriculture
docs.stance_on_premise: supports — The paper documents China's concentrated and growing investment footprint (ODI stock to 2019 across ten major economies) and models large host gains, consistent with M1 complementarity as a driver of consolidation. It qualifies the premise by showing (in-model) that consolidation is concentrated in mining/energy and deepens dependence and deindustrialisation risks, especially for small resource economies. It does not test US discourse or instruments, so it explains the Chinese side only.
docs.themes: FDI; trade; mining; energy-transition; manufacturing-competition; political-economy-models; China-policy; infrastructure
docs.limitations_analyst: Results are comparative-static simulations, not observed outcomes. The shock treats the entire 2019 ODI stock as an addition to the 2014 benchmark capital stock (a timing mismatch) under full employment and perfect competition, which mechanically yields large GDP and wage gains.; The text does not say how foreign ownership is handled (e.g. repatriation of profits to China), so GDP gains may overstate host national income gains; GNP/welfare (EV) results are not reported in the prose.; The ODI measure is the cumulative value of project records from RED ALC–China and the China Global Investment Tracker; the text does not say whether values are announced or completed, or whether CGIT construction contracts are excluded.; Tables 2–12 are images not available in the text, so the full sector-by-country results cannot be checked.; Internal inconsistencies: the conclusion gives US GDP +0.12% to 0

claims.t: Chinese policy banks now provide more finance to Latin American governments each year than the World Bank and IDB.
claims.q: Since 2009, the CDB and China Ex-Im have overtaken the World Bank and the IDB in finance to Latin America governments
claims.e: Authors' loan compilation compared with IFI annual reports (Figure 1).
claims.an: The figures measure commitments, not disbursements. 2011 lending fell back to $18bn, so the overtaking was driven by 2009–2010.

claims.t: Chinese finance appears primarily commercial: loan size, rates and sector focus resemble the private sovereign bond market more than IFIs.
claims.q: Chinese finance has much in common with the private sovereign debt market in terms of large loan siz
claims.e: Comparison of loan size, rates, sectors with IFIs and bond markets.
claims.an: The quote is truncated in the source ('siz') because of the scan margin.

claims.t: Chinese loans are much larger than IFI loans: 92% of funds came in packages of $1bn or more.
claims.q: Chinese banks lent 92 percent of their funds as packages of $1 billion or greater, compared to 20 percent for the World Bank, 11 percent for the IDB, and 8 percent for the US Ex-Im Bank.
claims.an: This is the scale gap that D03 later finds borrowers cite as a reason to choose China.

claims.t: Contrary to popular belief, CDB charges commercial rates well above World Bank, IDB and CAF rates (e.g. LIBOR+600bp to Argentina in 2010; LIBOR+280bp to Brazil in 2009).
claims.q: The CDB charges much higher interest rates than these IFIs, despite the prevailing conventional wisdom to the contrary.
claims.e: Rates from SEC filings and IFI posted rates.
claims.an: Undercuts the claim that China wins influence through cheap money.

claims.t: China Ex-Im subsidises only small loans framed as development aid (2% loans to Jamaica and Bolivia in 2010). These undercut US Ex-Im but make up just 1.2% of Chinese lending.
claims.q: In any case, these loans constitute only 1.2 percent of total Chinese lending to the region.
claims.e: OECD risk-premium-adjusted comparison of US Ex-Im and China Ex-Im rates.
claims.an: This is a niche where US Ex-Im saw Chinese deals as more competitive (US Ex-Im charged 1.5–2.5% above the OECD premium). It is an early sign of US concern about an unlevel export-credit playing field.

claims.t: China mixes export credits with development aid, which OECD countries prohibit, and budgets Ex-Im subsidies as official development aid.
claims.q: China budgets these subsidies as official development aid, although OECD countries prohibit mixing export credits with development aid.
claims.an: Relevant to the asymmetry in rules: US and OECD export credit agencies are bound by the OECD Arrangement.

claims.t: Even China Ex-Im's large loans carry commercial rates, e.g. 6.9% and 6.35% on Ecuador's two 2010 dam loans, about 2 percentage points above US Ex-Im even after adjusting for risk.
claims.q: China Ex-Im Bank is not undercutting US Ex-Im on these loans; it charged 6.9 and 6.35 percent interest on the Ecuador loans, about 2 percent higher than US Ex-Im rates even adjusting for Ecuador's high risk premium.
claims.e: Chinese embassy in Ecuador; OECD risk premiums.
claims.an: US Ex-Im did not lend to Ecuador at that scale. The comparison is hypothetical, based on its rate schedule.

claims.t: Ecuador's Foreign Debt Bulletin shows Chinese rates at the high end: in 2011 CDB and CHEXIM rates exceeded those of all lenders except Russia EXIM, and in 2013 CHEXIM's $312m loan was Ecuador's most expensive loan of the year.
claims.q: In 2013, CHEXIM's $312 million loan was Ecuador's most expensive loan of the year.
claims.e: Ecuador Foreign Debt Bulletin (Figure 4, illegible in extraction).
claims.an: Consistent with D03's regression finding that Chinese loans carry higher interest rates.

claims.t: Chinese lending is concentrated in Venezuela and Ecuador (60% of 2005–2011 lending), which have only 8% of the region's population and 7% of its GDP. IFIs and Western banks dominate lending to Mexico, Colombia and Peru.
claims.q: From 2005 to 2011, Chinese banks dedicated 60 percent of their lending to Venezuela and Ecuador.
claims.an: The financial division of labour follows political alignment and credit risk together. US-aligned states relied on IFIs, so Chinese finance was not region-wide.

claims.t: Large loans show the contrast most clearly: 93% of large IFI/US Ex-Im loans went to Brazil and Mexico, while 64% of large Chinese loans went to high-risk Ecuador and Venezuela, which received no large IFI or US Ex-Im loans.
claims.q: Chinese banks, on the other hand, gave 64 percent of their large loans to high-risk Ecuador and Venezuela, which received no large loans from the IFIs or US Ex-Im.
claims.e: Loan data for loans of $1bn or more.
claims.an: Direct evidence of the US/IFI instrument gap with respect to high-risk sovereigns.

claims.t: Unlike IFIs, Chinese banks impose no policy-reform conditionality but almost always tie loans to purchases of Chinese goods (from 20% to 100% of loan value).
claims.q: Unlike the IFIs, they do not seek to reform their borrowers by making the loans conditional on internal policy changes. Instead, like ECAs, Chinese banks almost always tie their loans to the purchase of Chinese goods.
claims.e: Loan agreement conditions found in official gazettes, filings and the press.
claims.an: Matches D03's interviews ('there weren't policy conditionalities' but 'not free money').

claims.t: Loans-for-oil deals with Latin America reached $59bn in four years, more than two-thirds of China's total commitments to the region. Venezuela signed six (totalling $44bn), Brazil one ($10bn, 2009), and Ecuador four (2009–2011).
claims.q: deals with Latin America have reached $59 billion in only four years
claims.an: Shows Chinese finance tied to commodity flows, a key point of state-coordinated M2 interacting with M1 demand.

claims.t: In the loans-for-oil structure, CDB withdraws interest and principal directly from the borrower's oil-sales account, up to about 30% of oil revenue, and the rest returns to the borrower.
claims.q: amount that might reach 30 percent of the total oil revenue, directly from Petro Ecuador's account. The rest of the revenue returns to Ecuador.

claims.t: Chinese and IFI loans hardly overlap: Chinese loans are larger, carry higher rates, go to EMITH sectors and concentrate in Ecuador and Venezuela, while IFIs lend more to pro-US governments such as Mexico and Colombia.
claims.q: and they direct far more funding to pro-US governments like Mexico and Colombia
claims.an: Shows the complementarity, rather than direct competition, of Chinese and Western finance in this period.

claims.t: Chinese lending is comparable in volume to private-market lending: $15bn from China in 2013 against an estimated $17bn from private lenders. Chinese loans account for a large share of external public debt stocks (86.5% Venezuela, 72.1% Ecuador).
claims.q: While China lent the region $15 billion in 2013, private lenders lent an estimated $17 billion.
claims.an: Shows heavy financial dependence of Venezuela and Ecuador on China.

claims.t: Chinese loans are not ultra-long-term: average maturity is 10.7 years against 18.0 years for other foreign public loans, which contradicts the popular image (e.g. Pomfret, Washington Post).
claims.q: In fact, China's loans carry similar and often shorter maturities compared
claims.e: IAD data and WDI average maturity (Figure 9).
claims.an: Contradicts p.120, where the authors say Chinese finance is 'set at longer terms' than Western finance.

claims.t: Chinese rates are close to, but measurably below, private-market rates: e.g. Argentina paid about 6.5% on the CDB loan against 7.82–8.75% on sovereign debt, Petrobras paid about 3–4% against 5.75–6.875% on bonds, and Venezuela paid about 1–4% against 7.75–12.75%.
claims.q: Our comparison found that Chinese interest rates are closer to market rates than IFI rates, though measurably lower.
claims.an: The Venezuela differential is 'surprisingly large' even by the authors' account, which leaves room for a political subsidy reading.

claims.t: The lower rates come from risk reduction: purchase requirements mean that Chinese firms profit even if the borrower defaults (e.g. the $10bn 'loan' to Argentina is really a credit line for Chinese railway companies).
claims.q: Even if Argentina defaults on the loan, the Chinese government doesn't lose everything - the railway companies have still made billions of dollars worth of sales.

claims.t: Loans-for-oil let China lend to otherwise non-creditworthy borrowers by lowering default risk. There is no evidence that Chinese oil contracts exploit borrowers, since prices are in line with commercial deals.
claims.q: Some have suggested that China's oil contracts are exploiting the Latin American borrowers, but there is no evidence for this assertion.
claims.e: Chen Yuan quote; Ecuador published prices; reports on Venezuela and Brazil.
claims.an: This contested claim should be checked against later evidence on Ecuador and Venezuela oil-backed debt (see D03 on Coca-Codo Sinclair problems).

claims.t: China's willingness to retaliate across issue areas lowers default risk. When Argentina filed anti-dumping cases, China cut soy oil and beef imports until Argentina withdrew them.
claims.q: China is willing to retaliate across the economic spectrum using its wide array of government bodies and state-run enterprises.
claims.an: This is Chinese coercive economic statecraft. It is notable because Chinese 'sticks' are less often discussed than US ones (M8).

claims.t: Chinese banks lent disproportionately to high-risk countries shut out of capital markets (Argentina, Ecuador, Venezuela, which pay 8–12% over US Treasuries), acting as a 'lender of last resort'.
claims.q: Chinese banks have taken up lending to risky countries abandoned by conventional sovereign lenders.
claims.an: D03 confirms that sovereign credit risk is the most robust predictor of Chinese loans.

claims.t: Chinese 'surrogate sovereign lending' helped Ecuador recover after its default by covering the budget deficit. Spreads fell from over 40% to 10%.
claims.q: Indeed, China's surrogate sovereign lending has helped Ecuador heal after its default by covering its budget deficit.

claims.t: The focus on populist governments (Venezuela, Ecuador, Argentina) supports the commercial argument rather than the soft-power one. If China wanted to court populists, it would spread money to Bolivia, Cuba, El Salvador and others, and it has kept its distance from Venezuela's rhetoric.
claims.q: China's choice of borrowing countries may seem to support the soft power argument, but in fact it lends greater credence to the commercial argument.
claims.an: This is the key disagreement with D02 (political/contestation reading) and D03 (borrower ideology). Credit risk and ideology are confounded here.

claims.t: Loans to left-leaning governments are no more likely to be subsidised. Concessional loans go to low-income Jamaica and Bolivia, and resource-related loans are no more subsidised than others.
claims.q: In addition, the funding for left-leaning governments is no more likely to be subsidized than loans to other governments.
claims.an: Bolivia had a leftist government (Morales), so 'low-income' and 'left' are not fully separable here either.

claims.t: A globalizing developmental state projects soft power implicitly by demonstrating a different development and sovereign-finance model, with larger loans, no controversial conditionalities and more risk-taking.
claims.q: Moreover, Chinese loans have none of the controversial conditionalities inherent in Western finance.

claims.t: Going Global is mainly a neo-developmental strategy to support national champions in gaining global market share, not a political or resource grand strategy.
claims.q: We conclude that China's Go Global strategy is less a political or resource-grand strategy than has previously been suggested and more a neo-developmental state's strategy to support national champions in gaining global market share in order to benefit the Chinese political economy.
claims.an: Implies that Chinese expansion would continue regardless of US discourse wherever commercial opportunity exists, which bears on the central question.

claims.t: Chinese SOE investment, bank loans and manufacturing exports are inversely related to US hegemonic influence: Beijing filled the void left by diminished US presence.
claims.q: Beijing has filled the void left by a diminished U.S. presence in the latter's own backyard.
claims.an: This is the core claim. 'Filled the void' is the authors' interpretation of a negative correlation.

claims.t: Latin American political and economic alignment with the US has weakened in the twenty-first century, partly because of China. After 9/11, US attention shifted to the Middle East and Central Asia, downgrading Latin America.
claims.an: Evidence of US strategic inattention (M15) in the 2000s.

claims.t: By the mid-2010s China was the region's second-largest trade partner and third-largest investor (behind only the EU, per ECLAC) and was involved in its most ambitious infrastructure projects.
claims.q: The China-driven commodity boom became a long-term boon
claims.e: Trademap 2015; ECLAC 2015; project examples (Argentine nuclear plants and rail, Brazil–Peru rail line, Ecuador refinery, Toromocho, Nicaragua canal).
claims.an: The Nicaragua canal is flagged by the authors themselves as 'the most obscure and least viable', and the Brazil–Peru rail line was an MoU. These are announced projects.

claims.t: Hegemonic stability theory predicts that, under hegemonic competition, trade, FDI and bank loans follow political considerations about the influence of the hegemon and the challenger in specific countries.
Accommodation evidence: MOFCOM asks Chinese embassies and consulates to review whether proposed investments would harm the interests of a third country.
claims.an: Suggests Beijing may consciously avoid areas of strong US interest. This is relevant to whether US discourse deters China (it may, at the margin).

claims.t: The diversification mechanism gives agency to Latin American governments that opposed the FTAA and formed 'rentier-populist' coalitions financed by commodity rents from China.
claims.an: D02 tests and largely rejects this as the primary mechanism. D03 later supports it from the borrower side.

claims.t: Since 2005 China has provided more than $100bn in loans to Latin America. CDB and China Ex-Im became important financiers for Argentina, Ecuador and Venezuela, allowing them to minimise penalisation by capital markets and IFIs.
claims.an: Cumulative commitments, not disbursements.

claims.t: Mexico and Colombia are the countries most influenced by the US according to the index, and Cuba the least.
claims.q: According to our index, Mexico and Colombia are the two countries most influenced by the United States, while Cuba is the least influenced.
claims.an: Consistent with D01's finding that Mexico and Colombia received almost no Chinese loans.

claims.t: US influence proxies all declined between 2003 and 2014: economic aid per capita 5.46→5.24, US FDI/GDP 6.4%→0.23%, military aid 0.65→0.39, UNGA convergence 45%→26%, exports to US 34%→23%.
claims.an: Shows US economic and diplomatic linkages receding while China rose, before the later rise in US strategic discourse.

claims.t: In line with H1 and H2, entities closely related to the Chinese government targeted countries with strategic partnerships and low US influence and avoided countries with Taiwan ties and high US influence. Control groups (POE FDI, Western loans, commodity imports) were not affected.
claims.q: The interpretation of thes
claims.an: The quote field holds only a fragment, since the full sentence is cut by the margin. Better to cite the prose summary.

claims.t: Model 1: a one-unit increase in US influence is associated with an US$81 per capita decrease in Chinese SOE FDI, a standardised effect of 0.72 SD. With low US influence, expected SOE investment reaches US$60 per capita a year.
claims.an: Since the index runs 0–1, a 'one-unit increase' is the full range from least to most US-influenced country.

claims.t: Chinese SOEs invested on average US$15 less per person in countries with diplomatic ties to Taiwan, and US$53 more in countries with strategic partnerships, ceteris paribus. Strategic partnership status is 'not merely cheap talk'.
claims.q: showing that this status is not merely "cheap talk."
claims.e: Model 1 coefficients on TAIWAN and STRATEGIC PARTNERSHIP.
claims.an: Diplomatic recognition shapes the allocation of state-linked capital. Relevant to Central American and Caribbean switches after 2014 (outside this study period).

claims.t: SOE FDI was higher during periods of low commodity prices, and AGRIBUSINESS is related to SOE FDI despite domestic restrictions on land acquisition.
claims.q: the findings show that SOE FDI was higher during periods in which commodity prices were actually low.
claims.an: Counter-cyclical SOE investment suggests strategic or asset-buying behaviour rather than simple boom-chasing. That helps explain why China kept expanding after the commodity boom ended.

claims.t: Chinese investment in oil went mainly to Brazil, followed by Venezuela and Argentina (out of US$20.8bn invested in oil), and GAS endowment is negatively related to SOE FDI.
claims.an: The two gas-rich countries named are Bolivia (truncated) and Trinidad and Tobago.

claims.t: Private Chinese firms (POEs) were affected by US influence in an almost null way. They are driven by market size, commodity imports, education and openness to FDI.
claims.an: Shows the commercial (non-political) tier of Chinese engagement, which could continue regardless of US discourse.

claims.t: Model 3: Chinese bank loans are negatively related to US influence. A one-unit increase in the index means US$63 per capita less in loans, a standardised effect of 0.4 SD.
claims.q: Model 3 gives support to our hypothesis; namely, that Chinese bank loans were negatively related to U.S. influence within host countries. An increase of one unit in the index translates to a decrease of US$63 per capita in loans.
claims.an: The headline political-determinant finding for policy banks.

claims.t: With low US influence, loans are expected to be US$15–35 per capita per year larger. Above an index value of 0.5 the positive relationship disappears (the lower bound crosses zero).
claims.q: Above the threshold of 0.5 in the index, investments no longer maintain this positive relationship, as the lower bound crosses the threshold of zero loans.
claims.an: Implies a threshold: strongly US-linked countries received little Chinese policy-bank finance in 2003–2014.

claims.t: Taiwan recognition reduces Chinese loans by US$21 per capita, but Chinese banks lent indiscriminately with respect to strategic partnership status.
claims.q: However, Chinese banks seem to have lent indiscriminately to countries independently of whether they had strategic partnership status
claims.an: The null strategic-partnership effect on loans is somewhat at odds with a pure 'contestation' story for policy banks and is closer to D01's commercial reading.

claims.t: Chinese loans are probably an alternative source of capital for countries unable to obtain loans from Western agencies, so debt service and debt stock are controlled for. Chinese loans show higher tolerance of inflation and low financial freedom than IMF/World Bank lending.
claims.q: Chinese loans are probably an alternative source of capital for countrie

claims.t: Western (IBRD/IDA) loans are subjected to the foreign debt holdings of host countries and are 'immune' to US influence.
claims.an: Suggests that the US did not use World Bank lending to reward or punish alignment in this period. That is a missing 'carrot' (M3/M8).

claims.t: Model 5: Chinese manufacturing exports per capita are negatively affected by US influence. The gap between weak- and strong-influence countries is about US$10 per capita, much smaller than for investment and loans. Strategic partnerships are negatively related to manufacturing exports, perhaps because partners negotiated protection.
claims.an: The strategic-partnership result suggests Latin American bargaining (M4) over market access.

claims.t: Latin American commodity exports to China are not subject to US influence or the One China policy: China buys commodities from a purely economic standpoint, driven by agribusiness and minerals (soy, meat, iron ore, copper) and not oil.
claims.q: Latin American commodity exports are not subject to U.S. influence or to the One China Policy. In sum, this information gives credence to the argument that China has been buying commodities from a purely economic standpoint.
claims.an: The bulk of the economic relationship (commodity trade) is structural demand-pull that US discourse cannot easily alter.

claims.t: The diversification mechanism is less consistent with the evidence, because only Chinese state-influenced actors respond to US influence and commodity trade does not.
claims.q: it is still curious that only Chinese state-influenced actors - as op
claims.an: D03 contests this downplaying of Latin American agency.

claims.t: The evidence from US influence, the One China response and strategic partnerships suggests that China is pursuing contestation by actively engaging pro-Chinese domestic constituencies.
claims.q: suggest that China is putting forth a contesting policy by actively engaging with pro-Chinese domestic constituencies.
claims.an: Strong interpretive leap from correlations.

claims.t: There is a clear trade-off for Latin American countries between alignment with the US and attracting Chinese economic attention.
claims.q: a clear tradeoff for Latin America between being under the wing of the American eagle and attracting the attention of the Chinese dragon
claims.an: Later evidence of cross-ideological engagement with China (e.g. by right-leaning governments) would test whether this trade-off persisted.

claims.t: Between 2008 and 2019 LAC countries borrowed $132bn from Chinese DFIs and $155bn from the World Bank (IBRD + IDA).
claims.q: Between 2008 and 2019, Latin American (LAC) countries borrowed $132 billion from Chinese development finance institutions (DFIs) (Ray and Myers 2023) and $155 billion from the World Bank
claims.an: Over the full 2008–2019 period the World Bank still lent more in total than China, which tempers the 'China overtook IFIs' framing based on 2009–2010 peaks (D01).

claims.t: More than 20 LAC countries have signed on to the BRI. LAC was the first region the US visited to promote B3W in 2021 (Colombia, Ecuador, Panama).
claims.q: LAC was the first region the United States visited to promote its own infrastructure development program, Build Back Better World (B3W), in 2021, with stops in Colombia, Ecuador, and Panama
claims.an: This is the US response: an infrastructure initiative announced as a counter-offer. The paper gives no evidence of B3W financing actually delivered, which matters for M3 (rhetoric versus instruments).

claims.t: LAC has become a battleground in US–China competition, and development finance is a tool for great powers to exert influence or impose consequences. But borrowers' interests supplement lenders' preferences as explanations.
claims.q: However, interviews with policymakers and cross-national loan data show that LAC borrowers' interests supplement lenders' preferences as explanatory factors for China's development finance.
claims.e: Literature plus interviews and loan data.

claims.t: Ecuador financed seven hydroelectric facilities with Chinese loans, including the troubled flagship Coca-Codo Sinclair dam, completed in 2016 but since affected by degrading materials and environmental damage.
claims.q: This includes the troubled flagship project, the Coca-Codo Sinclair hydroelectric dam, completed in 2016 but which has since suffered from degrading materials and environmental damages
claims.e: Villavicencio Valencia et al. 2022 (National Assembly audit).
claims.an: Shows quality and governance problems with Chinese-financed infrastructure. These are reputational costs that could limit expansion.

claims.t: Ecuador and China set up a discretionary loan facility for infrastructure in 2010, partly backed by oil export revenues and renewed in five phases, most recently in 2018. Xi Jinping's 2016 state visit was a highlight of close political relations.
claims.q: The two countries established a discretionary loan facility for infrastructure projects in 2010, backed in part by oil export revenues, which has since been renewed in five phases, most recently in 2018
claims.an: The 2018 renewal came under Lenín Moreno, who moved away from Correa's line. This is a sign that relations continued after the political turn.

claims.t: Prior literature finds that profit and commerce, the One China policy and reputation-building drive Chinese lending. Some see geopolitical motives, others argue China simply fills needs the US neglected. Evidence on support for authoritarian regimes is mixed.
claims.q: Some authors suggest that China has geopolitical motives for lending to LAC (Ellis 2011; Mendez and Alden 2021), but others argue that China is simply filling needs the United States has neglected (Urdinez et al. 2016).

claims.t: China is an exit option, but even countries with access to Western financing keep borrowing from China: after regaining market and World Bank access, 10 of Ecuador's 19 loans in 2014–2019 were from China.
claims.q: Between 2014–2019, after it regained access to bond markets and World Bank loans, 10 of Ecuador's 19 loans were from China, indicating that even when Western financing was available, Ecuador chose to borrow from China in over half the cases.
claims.an: Consolidation of Chinese finance even after the market-access constraint was lifted. Key evidence for the central question. Note that Correa was in office until May 2017.

claims.t: With Correa's election in 2007, Ecuador expelled its World Bank representative and ceased all World Bank operations. These resumed in 2013 through political will and World Bank activism via sub-national transport projects, with the Bank deliberately limiting its visibility.
claims.q: Ecuador expelled its World Bank representative and ceased all new and ongoing World Bank operations in the country
claims.an: This is the US-backed institution's response: quiet, low-visibility re-engagement. It is a case where a Western instrument partly recovered ground.

claims.t: World Bank staff reported that their re-engagement in Ecuador started with sub-national and informal meetings to meet the government's desire to limit the Bank's visibility, and that the Bank faced direct political constraints.
claims.q: meet the government's desire to limit the World Bank's visibility

claims.t: Ecuador is among the world's top ten borrowers from China and the third-largest in LAC after Venezuela and Brazil: over $18bn in 24 loans, against $2.3bn in 13 World Bank loans, 2008–2019.
claims.q: Across the study period, Ecuador borrowed over $18 billion from China in 24 specific loans.

claims.t: Several Chinese loans to Ecuador were backed by future oil shipments, which is often taken as evidence of Chinese pressure for unfavourable terms. Interviewees reject the 'pressure' narrative.
claims.q: Several were backed with future oil shipments to China, a characteristic frequently taken as evidence of China pressuring Ecuador to accept unfavorable loan terms to ensure access to key natural resources for China's own interests.

claims.t: Over 80% of Ecuador's loans in 2008–2013 were from China, but only 53% in 2014–2019, after it issued bonds (2014) and signed its first post-default World Bank loan (2013).
claims.q: Between 2008–2013, over 80% of Ecuador's loans were from China. Between 2014–2019, only 53% were from China.
claims.an: China's relative position declined when Western access was restored, which qualifies 'continued expansion'. The share is by loan count, and value shares may differ.

claims.t: Chinese loans are much larger: average $1,668m (median $300m) against World Bank average $342m (median $70m).
claims.q: For Chinese banks, the average size was $1,668 million with a median of $300 million
claims.an: Consistent with D01 (92% of Chinese funds in packages of $1bn or more).

claims.t: The economic model replicates earlier work: middle-income countries with poorer credit ratings tend to borrow from China. Higher GDP per capita and lower inflation, but poorer governance and creditworthiness, predict Chinese loans.
claims.q: namely that middle income countries with poorer credit ratings tend to borrow from China
claims.e: Table 4, column 1: log GDP pc 2.818*** (0.894); inflation −0.061* (0.036); governance −1.604* (0.854); trade with China −0.005 (0.121); sovereign credit risk 1.118*** (0.307); N = 514.
claims.an: Inflation and governance are significant only at p < .1.

claims.t: Ecuador's 2008 default limited its access to bond markets. Both deliberate exit from and externally limited access to traditional finance explain its borrowing.
claims.q: This suggests that a convergence of demand- and supply-side considerations, including both deliberate exit from and externally limited access to traditional finance, is responsible for Ecuador's borrowing patterns.

claims.t: Trade with China does not predict which lender a country chooses, contrary to earlier findings. No interviewee mentioned trade, and one argued that imports from the US (wheat, technology) were more influential.
claims.q: These findings suggest that trade may be a key predictor for the amounts that China decides to lend but is not a factor for countries in deciding which lender to use.
claims.e: Table 4 (trade coefficient insignificant in all models); interview ECU 5.
claims.an: Undercuts simple trade-dependency explanations of finance ties.

claims.t: The more leftist the governing party at the time of a loan, the more likely it is to come from China. Right-leaning parties have almost zero predicted probability of borrowing from China for a given project.
claims.q: parties have almost a zero percent probability of borrowing from China for a given project.
claims.e: Table 4, column 2: Party Left-Right Lean −0.733*** (0.251); Figure 3; interviews (ECU 1, 3, 5, 8, 16, 19, 20).
claims.an: Strong evidence that ideology matters for sovereign lender choice in 2008–2019. It challenges 'cross-ideological pragmatism' for sovereign loans specifically, though not necessarily for trade or FDI.

claims.t: Interviewees stressed the overwhelming influence of leftist ideology on Ecuador's borrowing under Correa ('stronger' than other factors; 'very, very political'; 'Correa's socialist government' was the primary reason).
claims.q: A member of the National Assembly concluded that "Correa's socialist government" was the primary reason for Ecuador's significant debt to China (ECU 16).
claims.an: The quoted sentence is on PDF p.14 (printed 91). The surrounding discussion continues to p.15.

claims.t: Change in public opinion of the US is not significantly related to borrowing decisions.
claims.q: Public opinion is not significantly related to borrowing, consistent with a former government official's statement that the public does not have much knowledge or influence in foreign policy (ECU 5).
claims.e: Table 4: Δ Opinion of US −0.109 (1.256), n.s.; interview ECU 5.
claims.an: Public opinion and soft power channels appear weak for sovereign lending choices.

claims.t: Both China's relative power and the year-on-year change in UN vote distance from the US are positive and significant. A one-unit increase in vote distance raises the probability of borrowing from China nearly fivefold.
claims.q: a one-unit increase (compared to zero change) in vote distance from the United States increases the probability of borrowing from China nearly fivefold
claims.e: Table 4, column 2: Δ UN Vote Distance–US 1.718** (0.855); China Relative Power 0.303** (0.137).
claims.an: Analyst check: the reported 'nearly fivefold' matches exp(1.718) ≈ 5.6 as an odds ratio rather than a probability ratio. Given the variable's range (SD 0.191), the realistic effect is much smaller.

claims.t: Borrowing from China was about distancing from the US rather than embracing China: 'resistance, antipathy towards the US'. China appeared as an 'exit from the international monetary funds'.
claims.q: it was not embracing or pursuing China, but resistance, antipathy towards the US
claims.an: Translated from Spanish by the author. The original Spanish wording is not provided in the document.

claims.t: Alignment with China is not the key factor. Borrowers seek to diversify both borrowing and international relations beyond the 'hegemony of the US'.
claims.q: These results indicate that alignment with China is not the key factor in borrowing decisions, but rather a desire to diversify both borrowing and international relations beyond the "hegemony of the US"
claims.an: US hegemonic discourse may itself feed diversification demand, which bears on the central question.

claims.t: For larger financing needs countries are more likely to borrow from China: a $10bn loan has even odds, a $20bn loan is nearly certain to be Chinese. Officials said traditional lenders 'are never going to give us financing of the same magnitude as China', and 'China was a cash machine'.
claims.q: a $10 billion loan has fairly even chances of coming from either lender, but a loan of $20 billion has a nearly 100% probability of coming from China
claims.e: Table 4, column 3: Loan Amount (scaled) 0.637*** (0.161); Figure 4; interviews ECU 20, ECU 27.
claims.an: Shows the scale gap in US-backed instruments (M3).

claims.t: Infrastructure projects are much more likely to be financed by China: 10% of non-infrastructure loans against 37% of infrastructure loans. Borrowers strategically allocated energy and hydro projects identified in national plans before China's growing role.
claims.q: While only 10% of non-infrastructure loans came from China, 37% of infrastructure loans did.

claims.t: The US and Europe no longer have the capacity to build projects such as dams, whereas 'China does do it, China is interested'. Borrowers see the package of financing plus contractors as an asset.
claims.q: where the United States and Europe no longer have the capacity to build projects such as dams, but "China does do it, China is interested" in these projects (ECU 4)
claims.an: Direct borrower testimony on the US instrument and capacity gap.

claims.t: Loans with shorter grace periods and higher interest rates are more likely to be Chinese, which reflects China's preferences. Countries accept these worse terms because political leaders prefer China, and terms are negotiated only after the lender is chosen.
claims.q: The negotiation of terms such as interest rates, grace periods, and maturities occurs only after political leaders have identified a preferred lender.
claims.e: Table 4: Grace Period −0.893*** (0.209); Interest Rate 0.821** (0.355); interviews ECU 5, 18, 20, 28.
claims.an: Confirms D01: Chinese loans are not cheaper than World Bank loans.

claims.t: Chinese loans carry no policy conditionality but are 'not free money', since they come with commercial conditions (buying Chinese products, using Chinese technology). Policymakers judged commercial conditionality more favourable for domestic politics.
claims.q: one interviewee explained that one of the advantages of Chinese loans is that "there weren't policy conditionalities" associated with them (ECU 20).

claims.t: Accessing Chinese credit was 'very difficult' (insurance requirements, commercial interests, high rates calibrated to repayment capacity). Ecuador insisted that no more than 20–25% of a project workforce could come from China, which frustrated Chinese negotiators.
claims.q: Ecuador insisted that a "limit of 20–25%" of any project workforce could come from China, with most jobs reserved for the local labor force
claims.an: Shows borrower bargaining power (M4) and that China is not an indiscriminate lender.

claims.t: Great powers do not dictate terms to borrowers. Interviewees denied Chinese pressure, said China was 'very receptive to our requests', and said the 'US did not abandon us … Correa threw them out'. The strategy was described as 'diversification to achieve our objectives'.
claims.q: Finally, the results demonstrate that in development finance, great powers do not dictate terms to their borrowers.
claims.e: Interviews ECU 1, ECU 3, ECU 4, ECU 16, ECU 5, ECU 19.
claims.an: Interviewee ECU 16's claim that the 'US did not abandon us' runs against a pure US-inattention (M15) narrative for Ecuador. The rupture was initiated by the borrower.

claims.t: After the 2008 financial crisis 'slammed the capitalist-Western world', China could offer not just capital but 'technology and companies' for Ecuador's national energy plan.
claims.q: In that moment, when Ecuador needed financing for its national energy plan, China was able to not only offer capital, but also "technology and companies."
claims.an: Links the global financial crisis to the shift to China (M13).

claims.t: Leftist parties are more likely to finance projects with Chinese loans, and beyond bandwagoning with China, countries seek to diversify beyond US-led financial institutions. Loan amount and sector are very strong predictors.
claims.q: Beyond simply bandwagoning with China, countries seek to diversify beyond United States-led financial institutions.
claims.e: Conclusion synthesising the regressions and interviews.

claims.t: US perception of Chinese economic presence in Latin America shifted from indifference (seen as part of US-led globalisation; Obama focused on the Pacific) to a threat to US interests under Trump.
claims.q: Initially, the expansion of China’s economic and political engagement in Latin America went unnoticed by the US and was rather seen as “another piece in the US-led globalization process”
claims.e: Speeches and documents: Tillerson's Monroe Doctrine declaration, Trump's UNGA speech (Sept 2018), USCC 2021 Annual Report; Clinton (2011); Cordeiro Pires and do Nascimento (2020).
claims.an: Supports the idea that US strategic discourse rose after China's economic position was already established (late reaction).

claims.t: The US framed BRI, Chinese influence over critical trade routes, dominance in critical technologies such as lithium, and Chinese 'predatory loans' as threats to US strategic interests and to democracy and open markets in the region.
claims.q: the United States warned against Chinese “predatory loans” that burden countries “with unsustainable debts and threats to national security and sovereignty”
claims.an: Shows the discursive escalation that the central question refers to.

claims.t: Carrots will prevail when the challenge threatens a strategic US interest, the challenger is a non-revisionist democracy, and sanctions are unlikely to succeed because of the target's power or an outside option. Sticks will prevail for short-term specific policy changes.
claims.q: we hypothesize that positive economic statecraft—carrots—will be the prevailing answer when three conditions are met: the challenge threats a strategic American interest, the challenger is a non-revisionist democratic state, and sanctions are unlikely to succeed
claims.e: Synthesis of the economic statecraft literature (Drezner, Mastanduno, Baldwin, Peksen & Peterson).
claims.an: A useful framework for explaining why US 'sticks' have been rare in Latin America.

claims.t: As a target's investment and economic ties with third countries such as China increase, punitive economic measures become less effective because the target can mitigate their impact.
claims.q: the effectiveness of punitive economic measures diminishes, as the targeted country has alternative options to mitigate the impact.
claims.an: This is a reason China's presence is self-reinforcing: once it exists, coercion against it becomes less credible.

claims.t: Panama's recognition of the PRC on 12 June 2017 was unexpected by Washington. The US ambassador reportedly learned of it an hour before the announcement.
claims.q: the American ambassador to Panama at the time, John Feeley, learned about the switch only an hour before it was announced
claims.an: Points to a US intelligence and attention gap in a core ally.

claims.t: Before the switch, Panama's budget under the US Strategy for Engagement in Central America had been reduced because of the focus on the Northern Triangle and Panama's improved economic performance. Bilateral relations were affected by Martinelli's US asylum and the Panama Papers.
claims.q: Panama’s budget in the US Strategy for Engagement in Central America was reduced due to the growing focus on the “Northern Triangle” of Central America
claims.an: US security and migration priorities (Northern Triangle) diverted resources from Panama before it turned to China.

claims.t: After the switch, Panama's trade with China grew exponentially while the US share of Panama's exports fell. By end-2018 Panama had signed 47 bilateral agreements with China.
claims.q: By the end of 2018, Panama had signed 47 bilateral agreements with China
claims.e: ITC trade data (Figs 1–2); Marra de Souza et al. 2023.

claims.t: The US position evolved from treating the switch as a bilateral matter to a more interventionist stance, including State Department warnings and Pompeo's visit. The later switches of the Dominican Republic and El Salvador heightened US concern.
claims.q: Washington began cautioning Panama, stating that “Chinese practices are not always beneficial to governments in the region”
claims.e: State Department briefings (13 June 2017; 17 October 2018); Wong 2018.

claims.t: US aid to El Salvador fell 14% in 2019 after its Taiwan switch but rose 77% above 2018 levels by 2022. Aid to the Dominican Republic was unchanged after its switch and was 59% higher than 2018 by 2022. Coercion via aid cuts was therefore short-lived or absent.
claims.q: In 2019, US foreign assistance disbursements to El Salvador experienced a reduction of 14%, but it began to increase the following year.
claims.an: Weak and temporary sticks, consistent with a US instrument gap.

claims.t: The TAIPEI Act proposed by Marco Rubio, aimed at downgrading relations with governments moving away from Taiwan, was the main threat of a stick. The US nonetheless refrained from coercive economic measures toward Panama.
claims.q: despite the concerns raised, the United States has refrained from implementing coercive measures involving negative economic statecraft towards Panama.
claims.e: Congressional proposal; Table 1 codes it as a 'threat' (regional, financial aid).

claims.t: The 2018 Growth in the Americas Initiative and the renewed US Strategy for Central America were carrots meant to counter Chinese expansion, but many remained promises. Under USAID fiscal limits, disbursements to Panama decreased in 2017–2020 even though obligations were maintained.
claims.q: These were “carrots” looking to counter the Chinese expansion, although many of them remained only promises.
claims.an: Direct evidence for M3: rhetoric and announced initiatives were not matched by disbursements. The 'Growth in the Americas Initiative' corresponds to what is elsewhere called America Crece, though the paper does not use that name.

claims.t: The Trump administration's FY2019 request cut USAID's LAC budget by 34% relative to estimated 2018 assistance.
claims.q: In 2019 the Trump Administration requested that the USAID budget for Latin American and the Caribbean region was 34% less than the estimated assistance to the region in 2018
claims.an: Shows the gap between anti-China rhetoric and the resources requested.

claims.t: After the pro-US Cortizo won in 2019, US engagement grew (Kozak's first trip abroad to Panama with promises on infrastructure and investment). Closer ties with the US did not reverse economic engagement with China, and Panama's exports to China rose to 8% of total exports in 2021.
claims.q: These closer ties with the United States did not result in a reversal of the economic engagement with China.
claims.an: Core evidence for the central question: even a pro-US government with expanding US aid kept growing trade with China. Infrastructure contracts 'cooled down', so trade expansion and infrastructure need to be distinguished.

claims.t: On 5G, the US combined State Department warnings with an invitation to join the Clean Network (alongside Brazil, Ecuador, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica). Panama did not join but soon backpedaled on its 5G announcement.
claims.q: Panama did not join the network but backpedaled the 5G announcement soon after
claims.e: Carreño 2020 (DPL News); US Embassy Panama 2020; Bnamericas 2021.
claims.an: A case where US pressure coincided with a halt in a Chinese-linked technology process. This qualifies the premise in the tech sector.

claims.t: The Biden administration continued the carrots approach while reframing China as a strategic rival. The 2022 NSS calls the PRC America's most consequential geopolitical challenge, and officials proposed EXIM trade finance, DFC financing and USAID assistance to counter PRC influence.
claims.q: will continue to explore the use of bilateral tools, such as (the) US Export-Import Bank trade financing, US International Development Finance Corporation financing, and assistance through USAID, to provide needed economic and technical support.
claims.e: 2022 NSS; statement by Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary Laura Lochman (2021).
claims.an: The language is 'explore the use of' the tools, which signals intent rather than committed finance.

claims.t: The Americas Partnership for Economic Prosperity (APEP), announced in 2022 as part of Build Back Better World, was explicitly presented as an alternative to Chinese economic engagement. Panama is among the partner countries and the initiative 'promises' more assistance and investment.
claims.q: This project was explicitly presented as “a viable alternative to Chinese economic engagement”
claims.an: No amounts are given. APEP is coded as a promise, not a disbursement.

claims.t: The State Department announced a partnership with Panama to explore growing and diversifying the global semiconductor ecosystem under the ITSI Fund created by the CHIPS Act of 2022.
claims.q: exploring opportunities to grow and diversify the global semiconductor ecosystem under the International Technology Security and Innovation Fund (‘ITSI’ Fund), created by the CHIPS Act of 2022
claims.an: A supply-chain or nearshoring carrot, not a counter-offer in infrastructure finance.

claims.t: Beyond economic tools, the US increased political oversight of Panama. SOUTHCOM visits expressed concern about Chinese presence near the Canal, and the US pressed on Chinese investment and the planned Chinese embassy near the Canal. There is little evidence of sanctions or threats of economic coercion.
claims.q: However, there is little evidence of sanctions or economic coercion threats.
claims.e: Reports and press releases. Footnote 5 notes China has not signed the 1977 Canal Neutrality Treaty.
claims.an: Security-channel pressure concentrated on the Canal. The sectors where China retreated (port, embassy site) match where this pressure was focused.

claims.t: There was no US trade coercion against Panama. Of 225 US measures affecting Panama's trade in 2016–2023, only 36 could relate to weaponised trade, and none targeted Panama specifically.
claims.q: the United States implemented 225 measures between 2016 and 2023 that affected Panama’s trade. From those measures, only 36 measures involved a kind of policy that could be related to a weaponized use of trade flows against Panama.
claims.e: Global Trade Alert database; footnote 7 on the measure types included.

claims.t: Panama's 2022 intention to reopen FTA negotiations with China met disapproval in Washington. The authors do not code this as negative statecraft, because the demand came from Panama and the US did not sign or revise any FTA in the region in the period.
claims.q: A contested situation took place in 2022 when President Cortizo expressed his intention to reopen negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement with China
claims.an: Panama used the China FTA as leverage to seek a better US deal (hedging). The US offered no new market access, which fits M3.

claims.t: Outcome in Panama: Cortizo suspended many Chinese investment projects (the PCCP container port and northern railway were delayed or cancelled, and the Amador site for the Chinese embassy was discarded). Panama did not reverse BRI membership or restore ties with Taiwan, and Chinese companies remained in charge of the fourth Canal bridge and a Panama City subway.
claims.q: while Cortizo suspended many Chinese investment projects, it did not reverse its
claims.an: The key nuance: China's position was checked in strategic infrastructure near the Canal but continued in trade and in some construction contracts. Partisan change (Varela to Cortizo) also matters (M5).

claims.t: In LAC panel regressions (2012–2021), when a country with zero alignment with the US increases Chinese FDI and construction (as % of GDP), next-year US economic aid falls significantly. Chinese development assistance has a weaker negative effect, and export variation has none.
claims.q: Predictably, all coefficients are negative, suggesting a decrease in US foreign assistance when a non-aligned country moves closer to Beijing.
claims.e: Table 2, Model 1: Chinese investment −10.56*** (SE 3.272); Chinese assistance −2.400* (1.421); exports to China −4.403 (3.392), not significant.
claims.an: There is mild 'stick' behaviour via aid toward non-aligned engagers such as Venezuela and Nicaragua (the countries are not named in the results).

claims.t: All interactions between engagement with China and alignment with the US are positive and significant and larger in absolute value than the main effects. Aligned countries can therefore expect more US aid when they move economically closer to China.
claims.q: Countries that are aligned with the United States, consequently, can expect an increase in its foreign assistance when moving economically closer to China.
claims.e: Table 2: interactions exports 12.82** (5.267), investment 18.31*** (5.678), assistance 10.31*** (3.603), robust across Models 2–6; AME plot (Fig. 5).
claims.an: This implies an incentive for aligned LAC states to hedge: engaging China draws more US attention and money, which helps explain why engagement with China persists alongside US ties.

claims.t: CGIT data overestimates Chinese investment because it relies on announcements and planned projects, but announcements can themselves trigger US political responses.
claims.q: CGIT tends to overestimate figures since it is based on public announcements or planned projects
claims.an: Relevant to the project's announced-versus-realised distinction. The perceived threat may run ahead of realised Chinese investment.

claims.t: Sticks were seldom used and appeared mainly as threats aimed at specific policy changes, while carrots, both promises and payments, were the predominant instrument for countering Chinese presence.
claims.q: “Sticks” were seldom employed and primarily manifested as threats rather than actual disruptions of economic flows.
claims.e: Synthesis of the case study and regressions.

claims.t: Twenty LAC countries had joined the BRI by the end of 2022, following Beijing's 2018 invitation to CELAC. The China–CELAC Forum (2014) expanded the channels for China's presence.
claims.q: By the end of 2022, 20 countries from the region had already become members.

claims.t: US GPR negatively affects FDI in LATAM because of geographic proximity, while China GPR positively affects it through risk-diversification-driven inflows.
claims.q: US GPR negatively impacts FDI in LATAM due to geographic proximity, while the positive impact of China GPR suggests a dynamic of risk-diversification-driven FDI inflows to LATAM.
claims.an: If valid, this means Chinese instability does not make LATAM less attractive, while US instability does.

claims.t: Geopolitical risk deters US FDI but not Chinese FDI, reflecting differences in strategic priorities, risk tolerance and state involvement.
claims.q: Furthermore, GPR deters US FDI but not Chinese FDI, highlighting how firms’ responses to geopolitical risk vary based on strategic priorities, risk tolerance, and state involvement.
claims.e: Table 3, Sub-models 5–8: US GPR on US FDI −0.010***, China GPR on US FDI −0.029***; US GPR on China FDI 0.090***, China GPR on China FDI 1.499***, host GPR on China FDI 4.001***/0.553***.
claims.an: The most directly relevant finding for the central question. Heightened risk and rivalry do not deter Chinese FDI.

claims.t: Sub-models 5–8 show that US GPR, China GPR and host-country GPR all increase Chinese FDI, whereas US FDI declines with higher GPR.
claims.q: Sub-models 5–8 reveal that US GPR, China GPR, and host country … GPR increase Chinese FDI, whereas US FDI declines with higher GPR.
claims.an: Host GPR raising Chinese FDI matches the view that Chinese capital enters where Western capital is hesitant.

claims.t: Host-country governance positively affects US FDI and total FDI but negatively affects Chinese FDI, suggesting Chinese investment is more prominent in countries with weaker governance.
claims.e: Table 3: governance on total FDI 0.311–0.721***; on US FDI 0.147***/0.453***; on China FDI −1.086***/−1.606***.
claims.an: Consistent with the BRI exploiting 'institutional voids' (Enderwick 2020). Venezuela likely drives this association, but there are no country-level results.

claims.t: BRI membership is associated with lower total FDI inflows to LATAM, possibly reflecting investor concern about dependency on China.
claims.q: the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) variable is … consistently negative and significant (-0.247 to − 0.179, p < 0.01), … suggesting that LATAM countries involved in the BRI experience lower
claims.an: BRI participation is not associated with a broad FDI boom. It may displace or deter non-Chinese FDI. Which sample countries are coded BRI is not listed.

claims.t: BRI membership has a positive effect on Chinese FDI, so the BRI operates as a strategic mechanism for redirecting China's outward investment toward regions aligned with its geopolitical objectives.
claims.e: Table 3: BRI on China FDI 0.308***, 0.233*** (Sub-models 7, 8); BRI on US FDI −0.048*** (Sub-model 5).

claims.t: Brazil is an outlier: it remains the largest recipient of Chinese FDI in LATAM despite not being a BRI participant.
claims.q: Notably, Brazil stands out as an outlier, remaining the largest recipient … of Chinese FDI in LATAM despite not being a BRI participant.
claims.e: Authors' statement in conclusions. No table breakdown is given.
claims.an: Shows that Chinese FDI follows market size and resources (M1) independently of formal BRI alignment. Ideology and BRI membership are not necessary conditions.

claims.t: The negative influence of BRI on total FDI suggests that Chinese infrastructure investments may substitute for FDI within the region.
claims.q: negative influence of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) suggests that … infrastructure investments from China may serve as substitutes for FDI … within the region.
claims.an: Chinese loan- or contract-financed infrastructure is not counted as FDI. The project should keep FDI separate from construction and finance.

claims.t: Bilateral trade with China is positively associated with total FDI (0.395***), whereas trade with the US is negatively associated (−0.097***) once both are included.
claims.e: Table 3 Sub-model 4. Quantile regressions show trade with China significant across multiple quantiles.
claims.an: Trade-led integration with China co-moves with FDI. Correlations: China trade with total FDI 0.710; with China FDI 0.740.

claims.t: Countries more economically aligned with the US receive less FDI from China. FDI from China has a weak negative correlation with trade with the US (−0.024), and USMCA correlates negatively with China FDI (−0.361) and positively with US FDI (0.613).
claims.an: Mexico appears as a case where US economic integration limits Chinese FDI, a counterexample to uniform Chinese expansion.

claims.t: Higher bilateral trade with China turns the impact of Chinese GPR on FDI negative, while trade with the US amplifies the negative effect of US GPR.
claims.q: Higher bilateral trade with China turns the impact of Chinese GPR on FDI negative, while trade with the US amplifies the negative effect of US GPR.
claims.e: Table 5 conditional effects at −1 SD, mean, +1 SD of trade.
claims.an: Implies that deepening trade dependence on China increases LATAM's exposure to China-originated shocks, a cost of China's consolidation.

claims.t: H2b (trade with China increases the positive effect of China GPR) is refuted. At high China trade the China GPR effect is −0.214, and China and LATAM may be perceived as competitors for FDI.
claims.q: These results refute hypothesis H2b,

claims.t: At high US–China tension both US and Chinese GPR reduce FDI in LATAM, whereas at low tension both have positive effects.
claims.q: At high UCT levels, both US and Chinese GPR reduce FDI in LATAM, whereas at low UCT levels, their impact turns positive
claims.an: Escalating rivalry (the setting of intensified US discourse) erodes LATAM's attractiveness for FDI overall. It does not by itself favour the US.

claims.t: Under high US–China conflict the China GPR effect on LATAM FDI turns negative.
claims.q: and ultimately turns negative under high US-China conflict … (China GPR coefficient=-0.035, p < 0.05).

claims.t: Forbes–Rigobon tests show no contagion of US GPR via US–LATAM trade, but contagion via China–LATAM trade and via high UCT for both US and China GPR.
claims.q: The test results … indicate that higher bilateral trade between LATAM countries and China … does result in contagion effects of Chinese GPR on FDI inflows.
claims.e: Table 4: US trade Z=0.46 p=0.64; China trade Z=2.47 p=0.01; UCT US Z=2.52 p=0.01, China Z=2.85 p=0.00.
claims.an: The contagion test for the US is described oddly ('high bilateral trade between the US and China does not significantly cause contagion').

claims.t: Chinese firms, often state-backed or supported by the BRI, are more inclined to maintain or expand FDI in high-risk environments as part of broader geopolitical and economic strategies. During heightened GPR, Chinese investment in LATAM will likely outpace US investment.
claims.q: In contrast, … Chinese firms, many of which are state-backed or benefit from … government-led initiatives like the Belt and Road Initiative, may be … more inclined to maintain or expand their FDI in high-risk environments … as part of broader geopolitical and economic strategies.
claims.e: Interpretation of the investor-origin asymmetry, with institutional theory.
claims.an: This offers a direct explanation for the central puzzle: rivalry-induced risk weighs on US private capital more than on Chinese state-linked capital.

claims.t: US MNCs may be more sensitive to GPR because of stricter regulatory constraints, investor scrutiny and market-driven decision-making.
claims.q: From an institutional theory perspective, US MNCs may exhibit
claims.an: Related to M3: US reliance on private, shareholder-driven capital is a structural weakness in a high-risk competition.

claims.t: Higher Chinese GPR leads Western countries, especially the US and Europe, to impose trade restrictions, investment screening and sanctions on Chinese firms, pushing Chinese MNEs toward alternative regions with fewer restrictions such as LATAM.
claims.q: Higher GPR in China often leads Western countries—especially the … US and Europe—to impose restrictions and barriers on Chinese firms, … such as trade restrictions, investment screening, and sanctions, which … limit their access to key markets.
claims.e: Literature-based argument (Li, Shapiro & Ufimtseva 2024; Caldara & Iacoviello 2022).
claims.an: This suggests US screening and coercion can unintentionally divert Chinese capital toward Latin America.

claims.t: The US has broadened national-security regulation to scrutinise Chinese investments across strategic industries and encouraged allied nations to adopt similar measures, contributing to an unstable business environment.
claims.an: No LATAM-specific screening cases are given.

claims.t: Mexico has reaped early benefits from friendshoring because of its manufacturing base and proximity to the US. Tesla's planned Nuevo León facility exemplifies US firms realigning supply chains.
claims.q: Mexico, in particular, has reaped early benefits from this shift in FDI.
claims.e: Anecdotal example. Yellen's late-2023 friendshoring remarks (WEF 2024).
claims.an: Evidence that a US instrument (USMCA plus friendshoring) can redirect investment in at least one country. The Tesla facility is an announced project; check its status externally.

claims.t: USMCA participation is positively associated with total FDI and US FDI and initially negatively with Chinese FDI (Sub-model 7: −0.065***). The sign turns positive (0.024***) when trade with China is controlled.
The model explains 58% of total FDI determinants and 76% of US FDI but only 50% of Chinese FDI, suggesting other factors influence China's regional investment.
claims.an: Chinese FDI is less explained by market fundamentals, which is consistent with strategic or state drivers but not proof of them.

claims.t: The GPR index is built from text searches of predominantly US-based publications and may carry a Western bias in perceptions of GPR.
claims.q: Moreover, the … GPR index utilized in this study uses text searches from predominantly … US-based publications, which may introduce a Western bias in the … perception of GPR.

claims.t: LATAM countries should adopt an open and balanced strategy, using USMCA for supply-chain integration and engaging selectively in BRI infrastructure to attract diversified FDI and reduce over-reliance on a single partner.
claims.q: LATAM countries should adopt an open … and balanced strategy that remains receptive to diverse economic
claims.an: This is a hedging prescription consistent with M4.

claims.t: Most LATAM nations have maintained balanced relationships with both Western and Eastern powers, which sustains the region's status as a relatively neutral investment context.
claims.e: Discursive conclusion (Aguinis et al. 2020; Bartesaghi et al. 2024).

claims.t: A bilateral trade surplus with China has a positive, statistically significant effect on public favourability toward China.
claims.q: Model 5 shows that trade surplus against China has a positive and statistically significant effect on opinion of China.
claims.e: Random-effects panel regressions on Latinobarómetro favourability 2001–2016, 17 countries, N=236 (Table 2 Models 5 and 7). Robust in random effects/OLS in Tables 4–6, not significant in fixed effects.
claims.an: Implies commodity exporters running surpluses (e.g. CHL, PER, BRA, ARG at times) provide a more receptive public environment for China.

claims.t: Chinese FDI inflows have a statistically significant negative effect on China's public image in Latin America.
claims.q: The statistics show that Chinese FDI imposes a statistically significant and negative effect on the public image of China, while contracts have no clear impact on public opinion of China
claims.e: Table 3 Model 1 (random effects, N=127) and Table 4 fixed-effects models; Tables 5–6 (p=0.053 in Table 5 Model 3).
claims.an: This is a potential source of friction for China's expansion through investment rather than trade.

claims.t: Imports from China and exports to China, taken separately, have no statistically significant effect on favourability.
claims.q: Models 1 and 3 of Table 2 indicate that the effects of import and of export on opinion of China are not statistically significant.
