claims.an: Opinion is correlated negatively with imports (-0.355) at bivariate level, but this is not significant once GDP and HDI are controlled for.

claims.t: Less developed Latin American countries (lower HDI, lower GDP per capita) view China more favourably than richer ones.
claims.q: Latin American countries with lower income and education attainment and shorter life expectancies have a better impression of China's image
claims.e: HDI negative and highly significant across Table 2–4 models; GDP per capita negative in Table 5; confirms Xie & Page (2013).

claims.t: Countries under a left-wing president have favourability toward China about 12–13 percentage points higher than countries under non-left presidents.
claims.q: When the country is under a left-wing president, the nation's aggregate positive rating on China stands 12–13% higher than that if the country is under a president with non-left-wing ideology
claims.e: Table 5 Models 3–4 (random effects) and Models 5–6 (OLS), president ideology coefficient ~12–13, significant at 1%; Table 6 ~7.6–8.0.
claims.an: The authors write '%' but the dependent variable is in percentage points.

claims.t: Presidential ideology is the most important political source of public opinion of China, whereas diplomatic relations with the PRC and Confucius Institutes have weak or insignificant effects.
claims.q: Diplomatic relations with China and the presence of the Confucius Institute both take the expected positive sign, but are statistically insignificant.
claims.e: Table 5 (diplomatic relations and Confucius Institute insignificant); Table 6 Model 2 (Confucius Institute significant in one specification).
claims.an: Suggests Chinese soft-power investments have limited payoff in public opinion compared with domestic politics.

claims.t: The country's dominant ideology, as represented by the president's ideology, is the most important political determinant of China's image.
claims.q: Among the political factors, the country's dominant ideology as represented by the president's ideology is the most important source of public opinion of China.

claims.t: Favourable opinion of China in Latin America was high and trendless over 2001–2016.
claims.q: percentages of the public with a favourable view of China in the 17 Latin American countries do not display a clear trend in the period
claims.e: Latinobarómetro: 237 country-year observations, mean 76.26%, SD 7.49, range 54.93–92.59; Figures 7–8.
claims.an: High baseline favourability means public opinion was not a barrier to China's economic expansion in this period.

claims.t: Fear of Chinese manufacturing competition is particularly salient in Mexico and Central America, which compete with China in supplying assembled goods to the US. Argentina's industry has repeatedly obtained anti-dumping measures, and Mexico filed its fourth WTO complaint against China in 2012.
claims.q: The fear of competition is particularly salient in Mexico and Central American countries, which see China as a competitor in terms of supplying assembled goods to the US market
claims.an: This is the manufacturing-competitor side of the regional divide and is consistent with D07's Mexico finding.

claims.t: LAC exports to China became increasingly concentrated in primary commodities: the top three categories (copper, oil seed, ores) rose from 50% to 72% of exports to China between 2000 and 2014, and medium- and high-tech goods were only about 5%.
claims.q: Latin America's top-three export categories to China – copper, oil seed, and ores – increased from 50% to 72% of total exports from 2000 to 2014.

claims.t: Trade with China helped many Latin American economies weather the 2009 global recession, because exports to China rose while exports to the US and EU fell sharply.
claims.q: Indeed, it was the trade with China that helped save the economy of many Latin American countries from the global recession in 2009.
claims.e: Saiz (2013, El País): 2009 exports to US -26%, EU -28%, China +5%.
claims.an: The 2008–09 crisis is a turning point when China's countercyclical demand and finance (cf. the 2009 spike in contracts) strengthened its position relative to the US/EU.

claims.t: China's policy banks became the largest annual public creditors to Latin American governments by 2015, and over the past decade China's two biggest development banks lent US$125bn, more than the World Bank and IDB combined.
claims.q: China's policy banks became the largest annual public creditors to Latin American governments as of 2015.
claims.an: The two banks are not named in the text; 'two biggest development banks' is the authors' wording.

claims.t: China has been a critical source of finance for Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador and Venezuela, which had limited access to international capital markets.
claims.q: China has been a critical source of finance for Latin America – especially for countries such as Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, and Venezuela, which have had relatively limited access to international capital markets in recent years
claims.an: Credit-constrained borrowers turn to China, which helps explain concentration of Chinese lending; these are also mostly left-governed states in the period.

claims.t: Chinese banks do not impose policy conditions but often tie finance to the use of Chinese construction firms and equipment, and the projects often import Chinese labour and management, limiting local employment.
claims.q: even though Chinese banks still refrain from imposing policy conditions on loan recipients, which is consistent with the 'no-strings-attached' principle, finance is often contingent on the use of Chinese construction firms and equipment makers.
claims.an: Non-conditionality as an attraction combined with bundled finance and construction.

claims.t: About 65% of Chinese investment in Latin America has been in mining and petroleum.
claims.q: some 65% of Chinese investment in the region has been in the mining and petroleum sectors

claims.t: Official Chinese FDI figures for Latin America may be significantly overstated because most flows go to Caribbean tax havens (Cayman Islands, BVI, Bermuda).
claims.q: Closer scrutiny of China's FDI data for countries in the region, however, shows that the overall level could be significantly overstated.
claims.e: Note 2, citing a 2017 CASS Institute of Latin American Studies study (Zhang, Wei & Zhu 2017).
claims.an: Relevant to data traceability: MOFCOM headline FDI overstates China's productive presence. Same point appears in D27 note 2 for 2006 data.

claims.t: China's state-dominated economy lets its contractors offer turnkey, packaged large-scale projects (e.g. the Brazil-Peru Interoceanic Highway and the Santa Cruz Dam in Argentina) aimed at moving Latin American resources to China.
claims.q: The omnipresence of the public sector enables China to design short-, medium-, and long-term development strategies, making it possible for China to offer turnkey projects
claims.e: Peters (2015); Szamosszegi & Kyle (2011); Feng, Gao & Jiang (2018).

claims.t: Growing trade with China has not produced political alignment in UN voting. Inter-American Dialogue found no discernible effect of trade for 1991–2003, and Latin American human-rights votes aligned increasingly with the US in 2005–2015. ALBA states such as Ecuador and Venezuela voted with Beijing.
claims.q: ideologically aligned states in the ALBA bloc, which have close economic ties with China, such as Ecuador and Venezuela, consistently voted in the past along with Beijing
claims.e: Domínguez et al. (2006); Flores-Macías & Kreps (2013) (contrary positive correlation 1992–2006); Piccone (2016).
claims.an: Economic consolidation does not imply diplomatic alignment, except where ideology coincides; consistent with hedging/calibration (M4).

claims.t: Although many Latin Americans see China as highly influential, China's development model has minority support (average 19.6% approval), and US and Japanese models are preferred.
claims.q: China's development model never received support by the majority of the respondents surveyed in each of these countries, with the approval rate averaging at 19.6%.
claims.an: Shows China's position is economic, not ideational, and that the US retains model legitimacy.

claims.t: As the commodity boom subsides, the negative aspects of ties with China (re-primarisation, erosion of the industrial base) may become more salient and fuel anti-Chinese sentiment.
claims.q: As the commodity boom subsides, the negative aspects of economic ties with China would have become more salient, harbingering a nationalistic surge with anti-Chinese sentiment.

claims.t: Exports to China support about 20% fewer jobs per US$1 million than overall LAC exports, and are twice as carbon-intensive and three times as water-intensive as average economic activity.
claims.q: Latin America's exports to China are twice as carbon intensive and three times as water intensive compared to the average economic activity in the region
claims.e: Peters (2015); Ray et al. (2015, Working Group on Development and Environment in the Americas).

claims.t: Chinese investors must adapt to Latin America's alternation in power, because policies change between parties (Argentina, Brazil, Mexico) and even between leaders of the same party (Ecuador). They should maintain relations with governments, opposition and interest groups.
claims.q: The governing party may change as a result of elections, and national economic policies may alter between different political parties (e.g. recently in Argentina, Brazil, and Mexico) or even between different leaders of the same party (e.g. in Ecuador).
claims.an: Political cycles create risk for Chinese projects. The Ecuador reference presumably concerns the Correa–Moreno shift, but the text does not name the leaders.

claims.t: Given the lack of historical, linguistic and social links, the sources of China's soft power in Latin America have been mainly economic.
claims.q: the sources of China's soft power in the region have primarily been economic in nature.

claims.t: Analysis of online discourse in five countries found widespread negative views of China, driven by cultural distance, poor product quality, unfair business practices, environmental concerns and fear of Chinese domination.
claims.q: negative views on China were widespread, driven by the language barrier and cultural differences, the poor quality of 'Made-in-China' products
claims.e: Armony & Velasquez (2015), Facebook comments on Spanish-language newspapers in ARG, CHL, COL, MEX, PER.

claims.t: Newly signed Chinese contracts in Latin America spiked in 2009, likely because the financial crisis weakened Western financial institutions. The main areas were electric power, telecoms, transport, construction and petrochemicals.
claims.q: A notable spike for newly-signed contracts happened in 2009, which was likely a result of the financial crisis that debilitated major Western financial institutions.
claims.an: Ties the post-2008 crisis to China's countercyclical expansion and Western retreat.

claims.t: China's demand has had a positive and significant impact on LAC export growth: China's GDP growth 2000–2004 explains about 7% of LAC's export growth in 2004.
claims.q: China's GDP growth from 2000 to 2004 explains approximately 7 percent of LAC's exports growth in 2004.
claims.e: World Bank (Lederman, Olarreaga & Perry 2006); authors' replication with 2001–2005 data (Table 1).

claims.t: The export boost from China is uneven: the Southern Cone and Andean countries benefit most (14% and 9% of total exports), and Central America (2%) and the Caribbean (1%) least.
claims.q: The World Bank study identifies the Southern Cone and Andean nations as those that have been most positively affected-with increases equivalent to 14 and 9 percent of their total exports, respectively.
claims.e: World Bank study; Table 1; Dussel Peters (2005).
claims.an: Shows a sub-regional divide in the gains from China.

claims.t: The vast majority of LAC exports to China are primary commodities. Of ~US$26bn in 2005, the top 20 products account for >90%.
claims.q: In 2005 there were approximately $26 billion in LAC exports to China. These top twenty account for more than 90 percent of those exports, or $24 billion.

claims.t: LAC moved from a trade surplus with China in 1993 to a deficit of over US$16bn in 2005. Only Brazil, Argentina, Chile and Peru ran surpluses (grains, beef, copper).
claims.q: the region had a trade surplus with China in 1993 of$158 million (2005 U.S. dollars). but posted a trade deficit with China in 2005 to the tune of over $16billion.
claims.an: Shows that China's expansion includes manufacturing import penetration, not only commodity purchases.

claims.t: For deficit countries, the deficit with China is a large share of their total trade deficit: ten times the total in Colombia, twice in Mexico, 25% in Uruguay and 14% in Guatemala.
claims.q: In Colombia, the trade deficit with China is ten times the nation's entire trade deficit, and in Mexico, the China deficit is twice the entire deficit

claims.t: Because LAC and China have dissimilar export structures, LAC is not substantially threatened by China's penetration of world markets, at least in the short and intermediate term.
claims.q: Therefore, LAC is not as threatened by China's rapid penetration of world markets as one might think.
claims.e: OECD (Blázquez-Lidoy et al. 2006), World Bank, Lall & Weiss (2005).
claims.an: Complementarity rather than competition underpins acceptance of China in South America.

claims.t: Mexico is the exception: its export profile resembles China's, and there is near-unanimous consensus that it is losing competitiveness and FDI to China.
claims.q: The one exception to this is Mexico, which has a similar export profile to China. There is near unanimous consensus that Mexico is losing competitiveness and foreign investment to China.
claims.e: Synthesis of OECD, World Bank, Lall & Weiss, Dussel Peters, Bank of Spain, Gallagher & Porzecanski (2007).
claims.an: Mexico's integration with the US market makes China a rival there, so Mexico is a case where China's economic relationship is competitive rather than complementary.

claims.t: World Bank estimates suggest Chinese and LAC exports are complements in third markets: Chinese export growth is associated with an increase in LAC exports equal to 32% of LAC exports in 2004, and cheaper Chinese inputs boost LAC competitiveness.
claims.q: the growth in Chinese exports to third markets leads to an increase in LAC exports to these markets equivalent to 32 percent of LAC exports in 2004

claims.t: The IDB warns that LAC's, and especially Mexico's, export baskets are converging with China's in manufacturing, intensifying direct competition.
claims.q: As China and Latin America-and Mexico in.particular-have converged toward increasingly similar export baskets, especially in manufacturing industries, direct competition has intensified

claims.t: Lall and Weiss find the share of LAC exports under 'threat' from China stable or falling (45.1% in 1990, 39.4% in 2002), with only 11% under 'direct threat' in 2002.
claims.q: the average weighted share of 'threatened exports'-under direct plus partial threat-is surprisingly stable at 45.1% in 1990 and 39.4% in 2002.
claims.e: Lall & Weiss (2005), market-share method, 18 LAC countries.

claims.t: In manufacturing, LAC either lost world-market share or grew slowly while China made large gains in 2000–2004. Resource-based and agricultural products were not under threat.
claims.q: However, in every case, for manufacturing, LAC either declined in share or grew slowly while China made significant changes.
claims.e: Authors' Table 4 (percentage-point change in world-market penetration).

claims.t: LAC manufacturing export losses attributable to China were relatively small (1.7% of manufacturing exports, US$5.5bn, in 2004) but growing (0.7% in the 1990–2002 version), and spanned the whole factor-intensity spectrum.
claims.q: reaching 1.7% of the region's total manufacturing exports in 2004 (US$ 5.5 billion).

claims.t: There is no evidence that China diverts FDI from LAC in aggregate. Investment flows to China and LAC show synergy, and China and LAC largely draw on different FDI source countries.
claims.q: the threat from China and India in terms of FDI might be the dog that did not bark.
claims.e: World Bank; Cravino, Lederman & Olarreaga (2006); Chantasasawat et al. (2004); IDB.

claims.t: The emerging consensus is that China is not diverting FDI from Latin America in absolute terms and may be contributing to its increase.
claims.q: in terms of absolute levels, China is not diverting FDI flows to Latin America and, if anything, is contributing to their increase.

claims.t: Dussel Peters finds strong competition between China and Mexico/Central America in the US market (clothing, electronics, auto parts, furniture, optical instruments), with China displacing competitors since 2000.
claims.q: the dynamic growth of Chinese exports and their increasing share of the U.S. market seems to have initiated a deep going process that began in 2000 of Beijing displacing its main competitors.
claims.e: Dussel Peters (2005), top US-market export categories 1990–2003.
claims.an: The competition takes place in the US market, so China competes with US-integrated LAC economies within the US's own trade space.

claims.t: With data through 2004, after China's WTO entry, Mexico was losing US-market share or growing more slowly than China in resource-based and all technology categories of exports to the US.
claims.q: in resource-based and all levels of technological exports to the United States, Mexico is either losing shares of the U.S. market where China is gaining, or gaining in cases where China is gaining much faster

claims.t: Mexico and Colombia lost FDI to China in 1995–2001: each US$100m increase in Chinese inward FDI reduced Colombian and Mexican inward FDI by US$84m and US$29m. Both have a high manufacturing share of FDI (59% Mexico, 21% Colombia).
claims.q: when Chinese inward FDI increases by $100 million, Colombian and Mexican inward FDI is reduced by $84 and $29 million, respectively.
claims.e: Bank of Spain econometrics (Santabárbara & García-Herrero 2005); no substitution in 1984–2001.

claims.t: US$514m of electronics FDI was diverted from Guadalajara, and Mexico should be concerned about export-led growth despite proximity to and NAFTA access to the US market.
claims.q: In the electronics sector, he finds that $514 million in FDI was diverted from the hi-tech hub of Guadalajara, Mexico, alone
claims.an: US preferential access (NAFTA) did not shield Mexico from Chinese competition; this is relevant to later nearshoring debates.

claims.t: China accentuates LAC's dependence on primary commodities and its persistent trade deficits, exacerbating long-held concerns about commodity dependence and terms-of-trade vulnerability.
claims.q: China is accentuating LAC's dependence on primary commodities and its persistent trade deficits.
claims.e: Synthesis; World Bank; Lall & Weiss (2005); Mesquita Moreira (2004).
claims.an: Documents the dependency risk; it supports the premise that China's position consolidated through commodity specialisation.

claims.t: Responding requires industrial policy to diversify into higher-value manufacturing, but LAC lacks the financing, political will and policy space under current trade agreements to use East Asian-style policies.
claims.q: must confront the fact that LAC lacks the financing, political will, and policy space under current trade agreements to engage in many of the policies that its East Asian counterparts have practiced in the past.
claims.an: Trade agreements, many with the US, constrain policy space. This is an indirect US-related constraint, not explicitly framed as US policy.

claims.t: China's rise as a net creditor lowered the cost of capital for LAC net debtors, and as China grows it will invest in LAC to secure raw materials.
claims.q: their growth accompanied by an increase in net foreign lending has contributed to lowering thecost of capital for LAC net debtors.
claims.an: Anticipates resource-seeking Chinese FDI.

claims.t: Since 2003 China has been second only to the US as a source of Mexican imports and Mexico's principal deficit partner; Chinese import penetration is rising across LAC subregions.
claims.q: since 2003,China has become second only to the United States in Mexican imports.
claims.an: China expands as an import supplier even in US-integrated Mexico.

claims.t: In the short term, China's demand for raw materials benefits LAC both through export volumes and by driving up commodity prices.
claims.q: China's demand for raw materials is positive not only because it may increase direct exports from LAC but also because it may help to drive the prices of these exports higher

claims.t: Shrinking development space may push countries most hit by Chinese light-manufacturing competition toward labour export and remittance-based development.
claims.q: a move toward a remittance-based model of development, particularly in the countries most affected by China's competition in light manufacturing.
claims.an: Links Chinese competition to migration, a US security-agenda issue (M12).

claims.t: The principal explanation for the early-2000s boom in Sino-Latin American relations ('China fever') is the growth of China's own economy and of its worldwide trade, which 'finally reached Latin American shores'; there is 'no sinister mystery'.
claims.q: worldwide growth of China's trade explains
claims.e: IMF Direction of Trade data for nine LAC countries (Tables 1-8), China Customs yearbook (Fig. 1); restated in Conclusions (p.47).
claims.an: Supports the 'China expands for structural/market reasons' strand (M1) rather than a deliberate political preference for LAC; note this is pre-policy-bank era (pre-2007) so it says nothing about M2 finance.

claims.t: China made no political decision to privilege Latin American trade: LAC's share of China's imports rose only from 2% (1990) to 4% (2004) and of its exports from 1% to 3%; only Brazil reached 1% of China's world imports and only Mexico and Brazil 1% of its exports in 2004. The uptick in LAC's relative share is 'insignificant'.
claims.q: China has not made a political decision to
claims.e: Tables 1-2 (IMF DOTS); Figure 1 (China Customs Statistics Yearbook 1998-2003) showing LAC trade share similar to Africa and Oceania.
claims.an: Qualifies any premise that China 'targets' LAC economically in this period: LAC mattered far more to China's growth narrative in LAC than to China.

claims.t: Gains are shared but hopes are asymmetric: China has disproportionate leverage over Latin America in trade negotiations because LAC depends much more on China than vice versa; LAC will likely remain a minor player in China's growth while China has become a major factor in LAC growth (e.g. 2004, best LAC GDP growth since 1997, driven by Chinese commodity demand lifting prices and output).
claims.q: growth in 2004 was China's demand for
claims.e: Trade-dependence asymmetry from tables; CEPAL 2004 regional growth assessment.
claims.an: Commodity-demand-pull (M1) with an asymmetric dependence dimension (M10). The 'asymmetric hopes' frame is the document's core thesis.

claims.t: Ideology and regime type do not explain trends in Sino-Latin American relations: China built ties with anti-communist military dictatorships in the 1970s (Chile under Pinochet, Argentina's 1976 junta, Brazil's military regime), while relations between communist China and Cuba were hostile for most of the 1960s-80s.
claims.q: regimist factors do not explain trends in
claims.e: Historical narrative of diplomatic recognitions and agreements 1970-1990 (pp.3-6).
claims.an: Strong historical evidence against a purely ideological (Pink Tide) explanation of China ties (M5). Useful for the brief's warning not to assume ideology explains alignment.

claims.t: Cross-ideological and multi-partisan support for ties with China long predates the left-wing governments of the 2000s; the political foundations were laid under right-wing military dictatorships in the 1970s. Latin American right-wing politicians and armed forces 'do not fear China', and by the late 1990s business firms were the principal advocates of closer ties.
claims.q: politicians do not fear China.
claims.e: Historical narrative; country sections for Brazil, Argentina, Chile.
claims.an: Directly relevant to the project: it explains why China ties survived 'right turns' (later cycles) — a structural cross-ideological base (M5 pragmatism).

claims.t: Across the ideological spectrum, South American governments have used relations with China partly to provide some balance to U.S. power; in the 1970s the military governments of Argentina, Brazil and Chile developed ties with China to counter U.S. human-rights pressure and welcomed China's defence of non-intervention.
claims.q: well as on the left, to use such relations to
claims.e: Historical narrative (Carter-era deterioration of U.S.-Argentine relations; Brazil-U.S. tensions in late 1970s).
claims.an: Early evidence for M4 (hedging/autonomy) and M6 (non-intervention norm) operating independently of commodity trade.

claims.t: Military relations are an effect, not a cause, of improved Sino-Latin American relations; they remain modest (visits, attachés, training) and there is little evidence of a military dimension that should worry other countries. Exceptions are indirect benefits from high-tech cooperation (nuclear, space satellites) with Brazil and Argentina.
claims.q: are not the cause that propels Sino-Latin
claims.e: Review of military visits, agreements (e.g. Oct 2004 Brazil-China Defense Cooperation Accord), U.S. DoD annual reports 2003-05, Venezuela's arms purchases from Russia, Brazil, Spain but not China.
claims.an: Contrasts with Gen. Craddock's 2005 testimony framing PRC presence as an 'emerging dynamic'. Relevant to how US security discourse may overstate the military dimension relative to the economic one.

claims.t: In 2005 U.S. Southern Command (Gen. Bantz Craddock) told the House Armed Services Committee that the PRC's growing presence in the region was an 'emerging dynamic', citing 20 visits by PRC national-level defence officials to LAC in 2004 and visits by defence ministers/chiefs from nine LAC countries to the PRC.
claims.q: An increasing presence of the People's
claims.an: Early instance of US strategic discourse on China in LAC; the authors judge the military concern overstated.

claims.t: U.S. concern was limited as of 2006: China's engagement was 'not yet a major concern' for the U.S., with few real frictions; U.S. policymakers saw little need to respond to China's effort to win over Taiwan's 12 LAC allies, although some officials and members of Congress already saw China as the most serious challenge to U.S. interests in the region since the Cold War (Panama Canal, Haitian peacekeepers, Cuba, Venezuelan oil).
claims.q: China's engagement in Latin America is not yet a major concern for the United States, and there are few signs of any real frictions between the two countries on that score.
claims.e: Foreword by Daniel P. Erikson (Inter-American Dialogue).
claims.an: Baseline for the 'US strategic discourse' half of the central question: in 2006 discourse was divided and largely not alarmed (M15 strategic inattention).

claims.t: At the November 2004 APEC summit in Santiago, U.S. Secretary of State Colin Powell said he was pleased that President Hu Jintao was having good visits in the hemisphere — a response the authors say was no doubt a relief to Chinese officials.
claims.q: pleased that President Hu Jintao is having
claims.e: U.S. State Department transcript, joint press conference, Santiago, 20 Nov 2004.
claims.an: Evidence of a non-confrontational US stance in 2004 (M15).

claims.t: China pledged (as reported) to raise its investment in Latin America to US$100 billion by 2014, while actual Chinese investment through 2004 was only about US$6.5 billion (though half of China's overseas investment); there was already concern that several investment pledges were falling short in Brazil, Argentina and elsewhere.
claims.q: China has promised to increase its investments in Latin America to $100 billion by 2014, although there is concern that several investment pledges are already showing signs of falling short in Brazil, Argentina, and elsewhere.
claims.e: Foreword (Erikson); no source cited for the pledge figure.
claims.an: Central to announced-vs-realised distinction. The US$100bn appears only in the Foreword, not in Domínguez's analysis. The commonly cited ~US$20bn Argentina pledge from Hu's 2004 visit is NOT mentioned anywhere in D08 (checked full text); verify externally.

claims.t: In Argentina, Chinese investments in railways, ports, forestry, energy and mining were welcomed but few had been realised; the Kirchner presidency's support team even indicated China would fund Argentina's exit from debt default, which Chinese officials had to deny.
claims.q: energy, and mining but few of these investments have been realized.
claims.e: Argentina country section, based on Argentine official sources and interviews.
claims.an: Key announced-vs-realised evidence: expectations created around the 2004 Hu visit outran actual Chinese commitments; Argentine officials themselves inflated expectations.

claims.t: Argentine hopes for gains from China outrun the capacity of its government and firms to deliver; Argentina lacks a China policy as well defined as Brazil's, its policy process under Kirchner was personalist and poorly coordinated (e.g. market-economy recognition decided without the Economy Ministry), and Argentina recognised China as a market economy in Nov 2004 for only a symbolic upgrade to 'strategic partner'.
claims.q: namely, China upgraded Argentina from "cooperative partner" to "strategic partner."
claims.an: Shows limits of LAC agency (M4): weak state capacity reduced bargaining returns. Relevant to whether LAC 'hedging' actually extracts gains.

claims.t: During Hu Jintao's 2004 tour China sought formal recognition as a 'market economy' before the Doha Round concluded (making anti-dumping duties harder); Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Peru conceded, got little in return, and highlighted asymmetric bargaining power.
claims.q: concession, got little in return, and called attention to asymmetric bargaining power
claims.e: Account of Hu visit from People's Daily (13-25 Nov 2004); Kennedy (2005) on anti-dumping.
claims.an: Example of coordinated Chinese diplomatic-economic strategy (M2 in a broad sense) extracting concessions; LAC governments traded trade-defence policy space for symbolic/political goods.

claims.t: China has a systematic long-term strategy to engage Latin America: retaining ties with 1970s right-wing regimes, training cadres (110 officials at El Colegio de México), professional ambassadors, investment in think-tanks (CASS Institute of Latin American Studies), high-level visits at key junctures, and a graded labelling scheme (strategic partner / cooperative partner / friendly cooperative relations).
claims.q: systematic long-term strategy to engage
claims.e: Section 'A View from China' (pp.21-27) using Chinese sources and academic literature.
claims.an: Supports a state-coordinated, long-horizon Chinese approach (diplomatic statecraft version of M2), contrasted implicitly with episodic US attention.

claims.t: Chinese academics and officials stress that China does not intend to balance or reduce U.S. influence in Latin America (China 'has no need and no capability' to do so) and that China depends on the U.S. market far more than it could gain from contesting U.S. power; discussion of the Panama Canal is 'limited and demure'.
claims.q: China has no need and no
claims.e: Chinese academic writings (Jiang Shixue, Xu Shicheng, CASS); Chinese technical press on the canal.
claims.an: Relevant to discourse: China's own framing (South-South, anti-hegemonism without confronting the US) — compare D21/D22 on Chinese normative diplomacy.

claims.t: China's Latin American partners want China to 'balance' the U.S. to differing degrees: Brazil and Argentina seek a 'soft balancer' offering new political-economic options without confronting the U.S.; Cuba and Venezuela seek a 'hard balance' alliance; Chile and Mexico do not use China to balance the U.S.
claims.q: In effect, Brazil and Argentina want China
claims.an: Typology of LAC hedging (M4). Notably China rewarded economic salience, not balancing ardour (see C18).

claims.t: The countries that matter least to China are those whose China policy is driven mainly by political motives (Venezuela, Cuba); the best relationship is with Brazil, combining economic salience, strategic political design and professional policy execution. Chávez's courtship is disproportionate to Venezuela's economic weight.
claims.q: The countries that matter the least for
claims.an: Challenges an ideology-driven explanation of China's economic engagement (M5): ideological affinity did not translate into proportional economic engagement in 2000-2005.

claims.t: Latin America plays a trivial role in China's energy supply: Venezuela, China's largest LAC energy partner, supplied only 1.1% of China's oil imports in 2003 (about 1% of petroleum imports). Sinopec-Petrobras deals (US$1bn pipeline; US$7bn exploration/production/refining), a Cuban offshore contract and Venezuelan JVs were 'medium-term prospects at best'.
claims.q: In short, Latin America has a trivial role in
claims.e: Trade data; reports of signed deals.
claims.an: Pre-2007 baseline: oil-backed loans to Venezuela (later the largest Chinese finance) had not yet started; contrast with later literature (e.g. D01/D03).

claims.t: China was strikingly slow and risk-averse in Venezuela: Hu skipped Venezuela on his 2004 tour as conditions were 'too unstable'; Chinese officials said there was 'too much risk for little return', declined an offer of 120,000 b/d of fuel oil, and saw U.S. deals as more lucrative given heavy-crude refining and transport costs. China needs a benign U.S. more than a strategic partnership with Venezuela.
claims.q: benign United States far more than it needs
claims.e: Confidential interview (22 Feb 2005) with Chinese official; technical analysis of heavy crude and shipping.
claims.an: Important for timing: pre-2007 China avoided being drawn into US-Venezuela disputes; contrast with later China Development Bank loans-for-oil to Venezuela (to verify externally).

claims.t: The U.S. vetoed a proposed sale of PDVSA's CITGO to China National Offshore Oil Company (CNOOC).
claims.q: the United States vetoed
claims.e: Venezuelan press sources (El Universal, 2005); no further detail.
claims.an: Early instance of US investment-screening/blocking (M8); verify externally what instrument was used.

claims.t: The U.S. government expressed little interest in financing the Panama Canal expansion, giving China an opening to express interest in participating; China was the third most frequent canal user and Hutchison Whampoa (Hong Kong) had operated ports at both ends of the canal since 2000.
claims.q: has expressed little interest in financing the
claims.e: Narrative on Panama, citing Santoli (1999) for alarmist view.
claims.an: Early, concrete instance of the US instrument gap (M3) in infrastructure finance — the US declined to finance while China expressed interest.

claims.t: Trade growth did not shift Latin American UN General Assembly voting toward China (1991/92-2002/03): Argentina, Brazil, Chile were equidistant or closer to Japan; Mexico and Venezuela agreed with China more often than not but stably; only Cuba adjusted (early 1990s) for political reasons; Chávez did not change Venezuela's voting.
claims.q: the major Latin American countries in the
claims.e: Voting-coincidence analysis of UNGA votes, Figures 3a-6c, calibrated against Japan.
claims.an: Economic ties did not buy political alignment in the UN in this period — complicates claims that China's economic expansion translates into diplomatic influence.

claims.t: The Taiwan question explains much of Beijing's behaviour in the hemisphere, including disproportionate expense courting micro-states; Beijing offers incentives but does not threaten harm, and is not punitive toward Taiwan's allies (e.g. booming trade with Panama). Countries recognising Taipei confine disagreement with the PRC to diplomatic status.
claims.q: does not threaten harm to induce
claims.e: Case narratives: Dominica 2004, Grenada 2005, Bahamas/St Lucia 1997, Honduras, Haiti, Panama.
claims.an: Shows aid-for-recognition as a distinct driver of Chinese finance commitments in the Caribbean/Central America (M14).

claims.t: Variation in the value of trade across Latin American partners is explained by economic factors — overall economic importance (non-petroleum exporters Brazil, Argentina, Chile), key commodities (copper, soy, iron ore) and trade-regime openness — so political explanations are unnecessary for the main outlines of trade variation.
claims.q: the main outlines of variation in the value of
claims.e: Comparison of CEPAL 2004 export rankings with China's import rankings; WDI trade-openness (Fig. 9).

claims.t: Argentina, Brazil and Chile retain some bargaining leverage because they export products important in proportion (Chilean copper ~one-fifth of China's copper imports) or sensitivity (soy: Brazil 30% of China's soybean imports) to China; petroleum exporters, especially Venezuela, lack leverage since China meets energy needs elsewhere.
claims.an: Commodity-specific leverage as a condition for LAC agency (M4).

claims.t: Brazil is China's most important LAC partner: strategic partner since 1994, bilateral trade >US$12bn in 2004 (quintupled 2000-04), a cross-ideological/multi-partisan coalition (PT through the armed forces) supports ties, Cardoso and Lula pursued diversification and political balancing of U.S. power, and Brazilian firms (Petrobras, CVRD, Embraco, Embraer) invested in China.
claims.q: in Brazil supports relations with China, encompassing the ruling left-wing Labor
claims.e: Brazil case study (pp.27-31) using Brazilian Ministry of Development, Industry and Trade data.
claims.an: Cross-partisan continuity in Brazil (Cardoso to Lula) supports a state-level, not cycle-level, explanation.

claims.t: Brazil and China share a 'strategic partnership' aimed at shared gains and a 'soft balance' to U.S. power, exemplified by joint G-20 action that helped derail U.S.-EU proposals at Cancún; but Brazil did not change its UN voting or weaken MERCOSUR for China, and Brazilian industry (footwear, toys, textiles, electronics) opposed concessions.
claims.q: a "soft
claims.an: Note: the text dates Cancún as 2003 (p.29) and 2002 (p.31); the 2003 date is correct.

claims.t: Chile is a 'trading state': it engages China for economic opportunity rather than to counter U.S. power, through professional, multilateral and multi-partisan diplomacy (first to sign a WTO bilateral with China in 1999; first in LAC to recognise China as a market economy; FTA signed Nov 2005). Policy toward China is the policy of the Chilean state.
claims.q: Chile is not keen on
claims.an: Shows that deep China ties need not involve balancing the US — relevant to explaining continuity under non-left or US-aligned governments.

claims.t: Mexico is the exception: its economy competes rather than complements China's. Under Fox the 'China threat' was real — China displaced Mexico as the No.2 source of U.S. imports in 2003, ~250,000 maquiladora jobs were lost 2000-04 as firms moved to China, and 85% of Mexican shoe manufacturers shifted operations to China by 2003; Mexico was the last of 141 WTO members to sign China's accession bilateral.
claims.q: government, the "China threat" was real.
claims.e: Mexico case study; CEPAL, Poder magazine, Mexican government sources.
claims.an: Counter-case to 'China expands everywhere': competition generated conflict with Mexico; useful for the challenges side of the central premise.

claims.t: China was a significant foreign direct investor in Mexico: in 2004 the stock of accumulated Chinese direct investment in Mexico reportedly exceeded US$28 billion (clothing manufacturing about one-third, plastics nearly one-fourth), much of it oriented to NAFTA markets.
claims.an: Internal inconsistency within the document — flag; do not use without external verification.

claims.t: Cuba's China ties are driven by ideology and political value rather than economics: China labels relations 'friendly cooperative' (lowest rung), Hu spent least time in Cuba and signed no high-value initiatives, though China deferred repayment of 1990-94 credits by ten years and opened a US$500m credit line for the Camariocas nickel deposit plus new nickel projects worth up to US$1.3bn.
claims.q: opened a line of credit of $500 million to exploit
claims.e: Cuba case study using Granma, Cuban statistical yearbook.
claims.an: Ideology produced closeness but limited economic weight (M5).

claims.t: Chávez's China policy was a personal innovation and politically motivated (seeking an 'alliance' to reduce dependence on the U.S. oil market), but the worth of Sino-Venezuelan economic relations lagged his hopes; Venezuela lacked capacity to raise oil exports (PDVSA purge of ~20,000 staff after the 2002-03 strike, no major investment since 2003, weak property rights).
claims.q: toward China, however, not much of material consequence would happen.
claims.an: Shows ideological courtship alone did not deliver Chinese economic commitment in 2001-2005.

claims.t: Chinese competition generated growing defensive reactions in LAC: Argentina opened 40 anti-dumping cases against China in 1995-2004 (about one-tenth of all WTO cases against China, nearly three times Brazil's 15), whereas China initiated only one anti-dumping case against a LAC country (Mexico) between 1997 and 2005.
claims.an: Early evidence of LAC protectionist pushback to Chinese manufactures; complements later deindustrialisation literature (D10).

claims.t: Public opinion (Nov-Dec 2004) in Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Mexico was on balance positive about China's world influence (Chile, Brazil by clear majorities), more benign than in the U.S. and Japan; views of China's economic power were more volatile (by Nov-Dec 2005, 52% of Mexicans saw China as a source of unfair competition).
claims.an: Soft-power baseline (M11) before the policy-bank era.

claims.t: Latin America opened the 21st century under two exogenous shocks: growing distance between the region's governments and the George W. Bush administration (ending the late-1980s/1990s 'era of good feeling'), and China's dramatic entrance as an economic and sometimes political partner.
claims.q: The first was the growing distance
claims.an: The authors pair US-LAC estrangement with China's arrival — useful for M15 (US inattention/distance) in the early 2000s.

claims.t: Latin American countries' China policies mostly transcend administrations and personalities (state policies), with exceptions: ideology in Sino-Cuban swings, Venezuela pre-Chávez lacking a China policy, and Fox's break with Mexico's prior state policy. Professionalism varies: Brazil, Chile and Cuba professional; Argentina, Mexico and Venezuela personalist.
claims.q: American relations have been pragmatic and
claims.an: Supports the idea that China ties are resilient to political cycles, a key part of the explanation for consolidation despite US discourse.

claims.t: The growth-model literature focuses on industrial countries and domestic drivers, neglecting the international political economy context crucial for peripheral countries.
claims.q: It focuses heavily on industrial countries, especially western Europe, and it concentrates on domestic aspects of growth while neglecting the international political economy (IPE) context in which growth occurs.
claims.e: Literature review of Baccaro et al. (2022) and Schwartz & Blyth (2022).
claims.an: Framing claim; useful as conceptual tool for linking external hegemon needs to domestic models.

claims.t: Western countries export capital to the periphery mainly via private channels, whereas China's finance comes from the public sector (SOE FDI and government bank loans).
claims.q: In the case of China, the public sector is the main source of finance for the periphery: FDI from state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and loans from government banks.
claims.e: Stylised comparison; later supported by IAD loan data and Dussel Peters FDI data.
claims.an: Instrument asymmetry relevant to M3: US relies on private capital, China on state-directed capital.

claims.t: Dependency functions through three mechanisms—markets, leverage and linkage—with market access dominant and leverage/linkage complementary.
claims.q: Stallings, (2020) suggests three mechanisms that characterize a dependent relationship: markets, leverage, and linkage.
claims.an: Conceptual toolkit for coding US vs China channels.

claims.t: The US shifted from leverage toward linkage as norms made force less acceptable; for China, leverage was never viable in Latin America, so it relied on markets and linkage.
claims.q: For China, leverage was never viable in Latin America for geographical and historical reasons, so markets and linkage were used.
claims.e: Historical interpretation; US interventions (Guatemala 1954, Cuba 1960, DR 1965, Chile 1973) as leverage examples.
claims.an: Implies China's expansion depends on market attraction rather than coercion—consistent with expansion despite US discourse.

claims.t: In the 1990s, the northern-tier countries were locked into US-based value chains via NAFTA (1994) and CAFTA-DR, with the US market absorbing 89% of Mexican and 65% of Central American exports (2000).
claims.q: the US market was critical for exports from Mexico (89% of total Mexican sales were in the United States in 2000) and from Central America (65%)
claims.an: Shows where US instruments (FTAs, GVC integration) do bind—an important counterweight to China's expansion narrative.

claims.t: Mexico's export success under NAFTA produced enclaves with limited value added and few backward/forward linkages.
claims.q: It mainly assembled imported inputs, which limited the impact on the rest of the economy due to the absence of backward and forward linkages.

claims.t: China entered Latin America in a major way around 2000 to obtain minerals and agricultural goods and markets for its manufactures; trade rose more than 20-fold 2000–2019 and China became the largest export market for five South American countries.
claims.q: trade between Latin America and China increased more than 20-fold, with China replacing the United States as the largest export market for five South American countries and becoming a major source of finance for the subregion.
claims.an: Core demand-pull evidence.

claims.t: The China Boom (2004–13) accelerated growth, raised employment and lowered poverty; after 2013 the old stop-go pattern returned. China's trade arguably kept the region from another lost decade.
claims.q: The impact of the new relationship showed up in a particularly dramatic way during the so-called China Boom in 2004-13. Latin America's growth accelerated, employment increased, and the poverty rate fell.
claims.e: World Bank growth data (Figure 3); Stallings (2020); Myers & Gallagher (2020).
claims.an: Material benefits give LAC governments incentives to keep engaging China regardless of US messaging.

claims.t: Mexico and Central America lost out from China's rise: they compete with China's industrial products, run large deficits with China and lost US market share to it.
claims.q: Mexico's deficit with China in 2015 was US$55 billion or 4.7% of its GDP (IMF, 2016). Another problem was even more damaging—China began to displace Mexico in the US market.
claims.e: IMF (2016); Stallings (2023): Mexico's US import share 11%→13% (2000–2015) vs China's 8%→22%; Mexico deficit with China US$55bn (2015).
claims.an: Shows China's 'expansion' in the north is via import penetration and competition, not complementarity—a different relationship type than in South America.

claims.t: Most Chinese FDI is carried out by SOEs, which prioritise short-term profits less and receive state financial support.
claims.q: Unlike US and European firms, which are private entities although they can call on their governments for limited support, most Chinese FDI is carried out by SOEs.
claims.an: Explains why Chinese capital can persist where private Western capital would not.

claims.t: Chinese FDI inflows 2005–2019 totalled about US$150bn, only ~5% of FDI from all sources, highly concentrated (over half to Brazil, then Peru and Argentina), diversifying toward energy and some manufacturing.
claims.q: From 2005 to 2019, total FDI inflows from China were about US$150 billion (around 5% of FDI from all sources).
claims.e: Dussel Peters (2023) Monitor of Chinese OFDI.
claims.an: Important qualifier: China's FDI weight is modest relative to Western FDI.

claims.t: Chinese policy-bank loans (often placed under the BRI after 2013) totalled US$138bn gross 2005–2019; four borrowers took 92% (Venezuela 45%, Brazil, Argentina, Ecuador), mostly for energy, mining and transport infrastructure.
claims.q: Between 2005 and 2019, gross loan volume totaled US$138 billion (Inter-American Dialogue, online), slightly less than FDI inflows.
claims.e: Inter-American Dialogue China-Latin America Finance Database.
claims.an: Document does not name the banks. Extreme concentration qualifies 'region-wide' expansion claims.

claims.t: The main Chinese loan recipients (except partly Brazil) could not access international capital markets because of high risk and anti-western policies; China became their lender of last resort.
claims.q: With the partial exception of Brazil, the main recipients could not access international capital markets because of their high risk and anti-western policies; China became their lender of last resort.
claims.e: Author's interpretation of IAD loan concentration.
claims.an: Links ideology/market exclusion to Chinese lending; cf. D11 on Ecuador's 2008 default.

claims.t: Chinese loans lack macroeconomic conditions but impose commercial conditions (Chinese companies and equipment) and are often commodity-backed, especially oil-backed.
claims.q: While Chinese officials insist their loans do not have macroeconomic conditions as western loans often do, they have commercial conditions such as requiring use of Chinese companies and Chinese equipment.
claims.an: Non-conditionality is relative: commercial conditionality substitutes for policy conditionality.

claims.t: Several Central American countries switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China and were 'amply rewarded'.
claims.q: several Central America countries have switched diplomatic relations from Taiwan to China and been amply rewarded.
claims.e: Assertion without specific data or country names.
claims.an: Document names no countries or dates; 'amply rewarded' is unquantified. Identify switchers externally.

claims.t: China's increased role let countries diversify political and economic linkages, partly loosening dependency; Chinese policy banks' 'patient capital' may counter financialization.
claims.q: China's increased role enabled countries in the region to diversify their political and economic linkages, which can provide some loosening of dependency relations.
claims.an: Diversification motive = LAC agency explanation for continued engagement.

claims.t: The China relationship caused deindustrialization and reprimarization in South America, commodity-price volatility, and worse environmental and labour/indigenous-rights outcomes than FDI generally.
claims.q: South American governments worry about deindustrialization and the reprimarization of their economies, as the industries they struggled to create have been undermined by industrial imports from China
claims.e: Cooney (2021); Ray et al. (2017); Sanborn & Chonn (2017); Rodrik (2016).
claims.an: Costs that could fuel political backlash, but the doc does not show they reversed engagement.

claims.t: Mexico has received little Chinese investment and continues to rely on the US for finance and trade.
claims.q: Unlike its southern neighbors, Mexico has received little Chinese investment, so it continues to rely on the United States for finance as well as trade.
claims.e: Table 2: China's share of Mexico's FDI 2.6% and of exports 0.015% (2000–19).
claims.an: Counter-case: China's economic position in Mexico (other than imports) is not expanding much through 2019.

claims.t: China–LAC trade is inter-industry (commodities for manufactures) while US–LAC trade is more intra-industry, making the China relationship more problematic.
claims.q: In the case of China, trade is mainly of the inter-industry type—involving commodity exports from Latin America in exchange for industrial goods from China.

claims.t: China has more state-controlled money to invest and lend than the West, but FDI stocks remain strongly in US and European favour.
claims.q: With respect to financial flows, China has more state-controlled money to invest and lend in Latin America than does the west, although FDI stocks remain strongly in US and European favor.
claims.e: Comparison drawing on Table 2 FDI shares.
claims.an: Key nuance: stock vs flow; China's advantage is in state-directed flows, not accumulated presence.

claims.t: 'Dependency with Chinese characteristics': both US and Chinese power rest on markets supplemented by linkage; China builds linkage via high-level visits, media, scholarships and exchanges.
claims.q: it has sought to construct linkages with governments and private actors in the region through high-level visits, media, scholarships, and other exchanges.

claims.t: China made weak attempts at institutionalisation (FTAs with Chile and Peru; China-CELAC Forum), but the forum is a pale shadow of US FTAs with Mexico and Central America.
claims.q: But this forum was a pale shadow compared to the FTAs that united Mexico and Central America with the United States.
claims.an: US institutional lock-in remains stronger in the north.

claims.t: Latin America was invited into the BRI at the 2016 China-CELAC meeting; 20 Latin American countries have signed BRI agreements; BRI loans shrank after 2019.
claims.q: Latin America was not initially meant to be part of the BRI, but it was invited at the 2016 China-CELAC meeting; 20 Latin American countries have now signed agreements with the BRI.
claims.an: Shrinking loans after 2019 is evidence of Chinese retrenchment in one channel.

claims.t: In the 1990s, linkage (US-trained economists, guidance from IFIs) reduced the need for US leverage.
claims.q: US-trained economists assumed important roles in their countries, and they sought guidance from international financial institutions in implementing the new model; consequently, the use of leverage was less often needed.
claims.an: US soft-power linkage historically deep—relevant to why US retains influence despite weaker finance.

claims.t: US–China rivalry has become very intense and Latin American countries may be able to exploit it for development objectives.
claims.q: The US–China rivalry has become very intense, and Latin American countries may be able to take advantage in pursuit of development objectives.

claims.t: Under China's influence (2000–19), Brazil out-grew Mexico (2.4% vs 2.0%; 4.0% vs 2.3% during the boom), reversing the 1990s pattern when Mexico (3.5%) outgrew Brazil (1.6%).

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 470)
claims.t: Subordinated integration of Latin America into international trade and a US-dollar market-based system shapes political cycles, creating constraints and opportunities for domestic actors.
claims.q: This paper argues that the region's integration into international trade and global finance has also shaped and subordinated political cycles, introducing varied constraints and opportunities for domestic political actors.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 471)
claims.t: The 2000s–mid-2010s commodity supercycle, driven by Chinese demand, improved terms of trade, trade and current-account balances, and attracted FDI mainly into the primary sector.
claims.q: the supercycle commodities boom significantly improved the region's terms of trade, as trade (TB) and current account (CA) balances surged due to a heightened demand for commodities from China
claims.e: Gottschalk & Prates (2005); CEPAL (2015); IMF BoP data.
claims.an: Only explicit China mechanism in the paper: demand-pull.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 471)
claims.t: Pink Tide governments had more space for progressive policies because they relied on more stable capital from the commodity boom and rising FDI; from the late 2010s left governments relied on unstable inflows.
claims.q: the Pink Tide governments during the 2000s and early 2010s had more space to implement progressive policies as they relied on a more stable source of capital due to the supercycle commodities boom and increasing FDI inflows
claims.e: IMF BoP data on FDI vs FFFs; case narratives.
claims.an: Economic resources condition ideological projects, not vice versa.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 472)
claims.t: The shift toward volatile inflows has been driven by consistent neoliberal policies since the 1980s, reinforced by recent conservative ('Blue Tide') governments.
claims.q: these more volatile inflows has been driven by the consistent adoption of neoliberal policies since the 1980s
claims.e: Policy narratives (e.g. Brazil's Law 14,286 in 2021; capital-control relaxations).

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 475)
claims.t: The research design is a descriptive, exploratory three-case study with diverse case selection; the authors explicitly disclaim a causal relationship.
claims.q: While we do not suggest a causal relationship, we leave this open for future research.
claims.an: Important for weighting the paper's causal claims.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 473)
claims.t: Lower position in the international currency hierarchy forces developing economies to offer higher interest rates, making their assets targets for unstable carry-trade operations.
claims.q: forces DEEs to offer higher interest rates to attract cross-border capital flows
claims.e: De Paula et al. (2025); Bonizzi & Kaltenbrunner (2019).
claims.an: US structural financial power (dollar) as a constraint distinct from US diplomacy.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 477)
claims.t: Despite generally positive net trade (avg 0.85% of GDP, 1980–2022), current accounts were negative (avg −2.86%; −1.78% since 2000s) because primary-income outflows outweighed trade surpluses.
claims.q: In particular, negative primary income values have continued to outweigh trade balance and secondary income positivity, dragging down the overall CA.
claims.an: Profit repatriation by foreign (incl. mining) investors as structural drain.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 478)
claims.t: Brazil underwent reprimarisation: raw materials rose from about 20% to about 55% of exports and capital goods halved from 20% to 10%.
claims.q: The exports composition has been characterized by an increase in raw materials from about 20% to about 55% during the period under examination
claims.an: Main exports named: iron, crude oil, soybeans, raw sugar—China-relevant commodities, though the paper does not break down by destination.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 479)
claims.t: PT industrial plans (2003, 2008, 2011) expanded sectors and local-content requirements but were reversed by Temer and Bolsonaro; the current PT industrial policy is constrained by limited fiscal space.
claims.q: However, those policies were reversed under the right-wing administrations led by Temer and Bolsonaro.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 480)
claims.t: Peru shifted to a mining export economy with copper over 60% of exports; raw materials rose from 15% to 50% of exports in 2000–2020; Humala's diversification policy was limited and kept by right-wing successors who redirected tools to extractives.
claims.q: Peru also faced a strong reprimarisation process with values of raw materials passing from 15% to 50% during the 2000-2020 decade.
claims.an: Extractive orientation continuous across left and right—cross-ideological continuity.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 481)
claims.t: Chile's net goods exports reached up to 15% of GDP during the copper surge but primary-income outflows reached 12% of GDP in 2006; Chile had the lightest tax and royalty burden of the three.
claims.q: The strongest structural negative component of the CA consisted also in this case by its primary income which increased further during the supercycle commodity boom, reaching 12% of GDP in 2006

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 482)
claims.t: Chile's Pink Tide industrial policies were horizontal due to the mining lobby; Piñera weakened diversification; Boric changed little except steps to strengthen national control over lithium.
claims.q: except for taking steps to strengthen national control over lithium production, Boric did not alter the orientation of industrial policies under previous left-wing governments.
claims.an: Only lithium mention; no detail on Chinese/US lithium actors.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 482)
claims.t: In 2003–2011 FDI was more significant relative to GDP than foreign financial flows in all three countries; in the late 2010s FFFs to Chile and Peru surpassed FDI considerably, with growing volatility.
claims.q: during the initial phase of the 2000s Pink Tide—from 2003 to 2011—FDI appears to hold greater significance relative to GDP than FFFs in Brazil, Peru, and Chile. However, this trend reverses in the late 2010s
claims.an: FDI not disaggregated by origin, so cannot assess Chinese vs US FDI.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 483)
claims.t: Brazil's FDI was 2–4% of GDP (2002–2009) and ~4% (2010–2019), attributed to financial deregulation and privatisation-driven M&A; Lula introduced selective capital controls; temporary controls 2009–2011.
claims.q: This consistent pattern in FDI inflows can be attributed to the increasing deregulation of the financial account and the privatization wave initiated in the 1990s

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 484)
claims.t: In 2021 FFFs to Brazil rose almost 6% of GDP in a year, attributed to Global North QE; Bolsonaro's Law No. 14,286 liberalised FX and capital rules.
claims.q: What is particularly noteworthy here is the exponential recovery of FFFs in 2021, which saw an increase of almost 6% within a single year.
claims.e: IMF BoP; CEPAL (2020); Banco Central do Brasil (2024).

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 485)
claims.t: Peru's FFFs were highly volatile; under Castillo in 2021 they surged from nearly zero to 6% of GDP, then fell back to zero in 2022 amid political deterioration.
claims.q: In 2021, under President Pedro Castillo, FFFs unexpectedly surged from nearly zero to 6% of GDP within a single year.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 487)
claims.t: Chile's FFFs reached 10% of GDP in 2021, surpassing FDI, then plummeted to nearly zero in 2022 as Boric was elected; Chile kept its liberalised financial structure.
claims.q: accounting for 10% of Chilean GDP and significantly surpassing FDI inflows. However, this surge was short-lived as these inflows plummeted to nearly zero by 2022 coinciding with the election of President Gabriel Boric.
claims.an: Possible investor reaction to left election; authors don't establish causality.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 488)
claims.t: The 2000s left turn cannot be understood without the late-1990s financial instability, the commodity boom and post-2008 capital inflows; its end combined corruption scandals and the populist right with the end of the boom and the Fed's Taper Tantrum.
claims.q: these domestic drivers interacted with external shocks, like the end of the commodity boom and the Federal Reserve's Taper Tantrum
claims.e: Secondary literature (Kapiszewski et al. 2021; Gallagher 2014; Grugel & Riggirozzi 2018).
claims.an: US monetary policy as structural channel of US influence over LAC political cycles.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 489)
claims.t: PT's 2016 demise stemmed partly from economic deterioration after the commodity boom and the 2013 reversal of the global financial cycle, which caused devaluation and inflation; this coincided with peak anti-government protests.
claims.q: leading to a currency devaluation that deepened inflationary pressures, hurting the party's popular support
claims.e: Fritz & Prates (2018); Araujo et al. (2020); Martínez (2021) protest data (Figure 9).

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 489)
claims.t: Brazil's Pink Tide was most ambitious because of PT's ties with social movements, a larger manufacturing base, and being in power from the start of the boom and during the post-crisis capital surge.
claims.q: the party was in power since the beginning of the commodity boom, and its bolder initiatives were taken during the post-crisis surge of capital inflows, benefitting from an expanded policy space
claims.an: Timing relative to commodity cycle is a key variable.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 491)
claims.t: Peru's left (Humala) won only in 2011, after the boom's peak, and faced declining capital inflows; its weak party institutionalisation and primary-sector-dependent economy made it the least ambitious case.
claims.q: left-wing forces experienced unstable capital flows and were not in power since the beginning of the commodity boom, lacking policy space to implement a bolder agenda

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 495)
claims.t: Castillo pledged to renegotiate mining contracts, raise corporate taxes and even nationalise mines.
claims.q: Castillo declared his plans to renegotiate mining contracts, raise corporate taxes, and even nationalize mines
claims.an: Relevant to Chinese-owned mining assets in Peru, though not discussed.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 496)
claims.t: Recent left governments are politically more fragile and their policy reorientation more homogeneous, reflecting convergence through deindustrialisation, regressive specialisation and financial subordination.
claims.q: This shared fragility and moderation reflects the fact that Latin American economies became more similar in the last decades, experiencing converging processes of deindustrialization, regressive specialization, and financial subordination.
claims.an: Suggests ideology matters less than structural constraints for economic orientation—cautions against ideological explanations of alignment with China.

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 496)
claims.t: Without high commodity prices and stable FDI, governments became more dependent on short-term, unstable capital flows; financial channels opened by the Blue Tide were hard to restrain.
claims.q: without high commodity prices and stable FDI inflows, the governments became more dependent on short-term, unstable capital flows (FFFs).
claims.an: Implies demand for stable, long-term external finance—potentially a pull factor for Chinese FDI/loans (analyst inference, not in doc).

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 497)
claims.t: Economic and political waves interact to produce a hysteresis effect that progressively reduces the space for progressive policies.
claims.q: The result of that process has hence been (and would be) a longer-term hysteresis effect reduction of the policy space for progressive policies due to the interaction between the economic and political waves

claims.c: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 498)
claims.t: A temporary trade boom adds policy space, but it shrinks once the boom ends, forcing reliance on unstable financial flows that cannot fund structural change.
claims.q: a momentaneous trade boom might add policy space to left-wing governments, but new opportunities shrink as waves as soon as the boom ends

claims.t: China's trade with Ecuador is market-driven: its pattern (2008 spike, post-2010 increase) is almost identical to China–Latin America trade, and composition (over 80% oil and raw materials) matches broader trends.
claims.q: Ecuador trade is market-driven, and exploring its links to Ecuadorean politics is unlikely to yield insightful conclusions
claims.e: Comparison of Figures 1 and 2 (Banco Central del Ecuador; Bárcena et al. 2015).
claims.an: Trade channel independent of ideology.

claims.t: Chinese FDI in Ecuador diverges from Chinese global OFDI and China–LAC FDI trends, spiking in 2007 and 2011 and stabilising afterwards, all related to Correa's election wins and consolidation of power.
claims.q: Figure 5 illustrates three major trends of Chinese FDI into Ecuador after 2006: a spike in 2007, a spike in 2011, and post-2011 stabilization. All three are related to Correa's election wins and his consolidation of power
claims.e: Figures 3–5 (MOFCOM; Avedano et al. 2017; Banco Central del Ecuador 2020c).
claims.an: Political alignment as accelerator of FDI.

claims.t: Correa's agenda was almost entirely spending-focused except for developing new oil extraction projects and refineries, which matched China's economic interests.
claims.q: His agenda was almost entirely focused on spending, except in two areas: developing new oil extraction projects and constructing new refineries, both of which matched China's economic interests.
claims.an: Complementarity of extractive-led spending model with Chinese demand.

claims.t: China's energy demand will exceed domestic supply; the 2007 investment spike in Ecuador was a natural match between China's supply diversification and Correa's plan to intensify oil extraction.
claims.q: the 2007 spike in investment into Ecuador is a natural match between the projected increase in its energy needs and Correa's plan to intensify oil extraction.

claims.t: After 2007 Chinese investment in Ecuador concentrated in energy; in 2014 China invested US$74.5m in mines and quarries versus at most US$4m in any non-energy sector (manufacturing).
claims.q: in 2014 alone China invested US$74.5 million in developing Ecuadorian mines and quarries, while the largest amount it ever invested in a non-energy sector was US$4 million
claims.e: Banco Central del Ecuador (2020d) FDI by sector.
claims.an: Realised FDI per Central Bank (BoP-type data), small in absolute terms.

claims.t: Escalating tensions with the US (Manta base withdrawal, 30-S coup attempt, Snowden-related disputes, alleged trade-negotiation pressure) led Correa to promote decoupling from the US, a turning point spurring lasting opening to Chinese investment from 2011 through 2014.
claims.q: This served as a turning point, spurring a lasting opening toward Chinese foreign investment which started in 2011 and continued through 2014.
claims.an: US–Ecuador friction as push factor toward China.

claims.t: Ecuador's 2014 debt to China was between US$6.6bn and US$13.8bn (about 10–20% of external debt); discrepancies stem from uncertainty over which deals materialised and Central Bank loan definitions.
claims.q: Discrepancies stem from a lack of clarity on the number of reported deals which in fact materialized and the criteria used by the Central Bank of Ecuador to define loans as opposed to investment or transaction deals.
claims.e: Banco Central del Ecuador (2020a); Araujo (2016); The Dialogue (2018).
claims.an: Directly illustrates announced/signed vs materialised gap central to the project.

claims.t: Chinese loans to Ecuador began in 2009 after Correa's reelection, driven by the GFC stifling Western lenders, the 2009 oil price drop, and Correa's December 2008 default on a US$31m bond interest payment ('odious debt'), which excluded Ecuador from global finance until 2014.
claims.q: This was a de facto payment refusal to the United States and it led to Ecuador's temporary exclusion from the global financial system which lasted until 2014.
claims.an: Market exclusion → China as lender of last resort (cf. D09).

claims.t: Correa's pivot to Chinese development loans was motivated by his alienation of US and international institutions and Ecuador's need to diversify funding amid market instability.
claims.q: Compiling these factors reveals that Correa's pivot to Chinese development loans was motivated by his alienation of U.S. and international institutions and by Ecuador's need to diversify its funding sources during a period of global market instability.
claims.e: Synthesis of preceding factors; 2009–2010 energy crisis prompting energy projects (e.g. Coca Codo Sinclair).

claims.t: China–Bolivia trade is market-driven (nearly 99% of Bolivian exports to China are raw materials; imports from China were over four times exports by 2014), but tin—almost half of China's global tin purchases—gives it a strategic aspect.
claims.q: Although tin takes up a relatively small portion of Bolivian exports (fluctuating around 15% during the 2009–2014 period), it represents almost half of China's total global tin purchases.
claims.e: Banco Central de Bolivia (2020a, 2020b); Agramont & Bonifaz (2018).
claims.an: Early example of strategic-minerals logic (tin) beyond oil.

claims.t: Chinese FDI in Bolivia is negligible (<1% of total FDI), but Morales' nationalisation campaign deterred Western investors and opened space for investors less sensitive to anti-liberalisation reforms, including Chinese ones.
claims.q: Western investors interpreted it as a sign of market uncertainty, opening an opportunity for those who are less sensitive to anti-liberalization reforms, including Chinese investors.
claims.an: Risk tolerance of Chinese capital as a niche-filling mechanism, but with very small volumes.

claims.t: Post-2007 fluctuations in Chinese FDI in Bolivia are unexplained by markets or politics; e.g. after 2008 commodity price falls (zinc −52%, tin −26%, silver −32%) no surge occurred.
claims.q: In other words, post-2007 fluctuations do not reveal any substantial political insight.
claims.an: Honest null finding that limits the ideology argument for FDI.

claims.t: Morales cut Bolivia's World Bank debt share from over 34% to nearly 10% in his first term and 8.7% by 2014, shifting to Latin American lenders (IDB, CAF at 30.9% in 2014) and China (9% by 2014), so Chinese loans surpassed World Bank loans.
claims.q: Before and during Morales' first term, Chinese lending was virtually nonexistent, but it gradually rose to reach 9 percent of the country's total external debt by 2014.
claims.an: Note: regional lenders (CAF, IDB) remained more important than China—China is an alternative, not the dominant lender.

claims.t: US–Bolivia strain (coca disputes, Morales' claim the CIA orchestrated an assassination attempt, secret US indictments, the Snowden-related forced landing in Austria) accompanied Bolivia's reduced reliance on Western institutions.
claims.q: Overall, the decrease in Bolivia's financial dependence on Western institutions has been paired with continuous strain on its relations with the United States.
claims.an: US counter-narcotics-driven friction (M12) as contributor to Chinese opening.

claims.t: Chinese banks established themselves as key alternative lenders counterbalancing Western institutions, though Bolivia's most important financial ties remain with Latin American institutions.
claims.q: while Bolivia's most important financial ties are with Latin American institutions, Chinese banks successfully established themselves as key alternative lenders, counterbalancing Western institutions.

claims.t: Four factors produced cyclic reinforcement of China's interests and Pink Tide agendas: mutually beneficial resource-for-funding deals; geopolitical competition encouraging hedging; China's solidarity diplomacy; and anti-Americanism in national identity.
claims.q: a combination of four factors led to the development of a cyclic reinforcement of China's interests and leftist Pink Tide agendas
claims.an: Core two-way mechanism: economic interest ↔ ideology.

claims.t: China pursues energy security through improving relations and signing long-term deals with oil and gas exporters, seeking comprehensive strategic partnerships rather than short-term profit; rapprochement with Ecuador and Bolivia is part of this strategy.
claims.q: China is interested in developing comprehensive strategic partnerships, rather than seeking short-term profit from deals with natural resource exporters.
claims.an: Long-horizon state strategy explains persistence beyond political cycles.

claims.t: Correa's loan-for-oil deals gave immediate funding at the cost of future production; repayments are linked to WTI prices, with Ecuador receiving advance payment and committing to China as a single buyer—'a gambler's bet on a bullish oil market'.
claims.q: the deals could be more accurately understood as a gambler's bet on a bullish oil market. China–Ecuador loan-for-oil repayment agreements are linked to the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) index
claims.e: Author's analysis of deal structure (no specific deal cited).
claims.an: Oil-backed finance; post-2014 oil collapse implications not analysed.

claims.t: Chinese funding helped Correa pursue his spending-heavy agenda and sustain popular support for three consecutive terms, though it was only a small part of Ecuador's political landscape.
claims.q: While Chinese funding to Ecuador is only a small part of the latter's complex political landscape, it helped Correa to pursue his spending-heavy agenda and sustain popular support for three consecutive terms.
claims.an: China → ideology direction of causation.

claims.t: Ecuador and Bolivia hedged rather than bandwagoned: they maintained economic partnerships with the US while deepening ties with China, gaining negotiating leverage from US–China competition.
claims.q: Ecuador and Bolivia have opted not to bandwagon with either one great power but seem to have been hedging between the two.

claims.t: US–China competition for influence in Latin America is a self-reinforcing 'vicious cycle' akin to an arms race, in which Chinese moves respond to quasi-containment of China.
claims.q: the more assertive each great power becomes, the stronger the response from its counterpart, triggering a vicious cycle of escalating competition for influence in Latin America.

claims.t: China presents itself as a historically credible alternative to the West through solidarity rhetoric and non-interference, contrasting with Western political conditionalities; the CCP International Liaison Department legacy gives a marginal preference for leftist governments.
claims.q: Such a marginal and unofficial preference cannot be seen as a major driving factor for China's rapprochement with Ecuador and Bolivia.
claims.an: Author himself downgrades ideological affinity on China's side.
