claims.t: Correa and Morales built national identity around anti-Americanism; having damaged economic relations with the US, they filled financial gaps through alternative channels (China).
claims.q: After damaging the economic aspect of these relations, Ecuador and Bolivia sought to fill in financial gaps through alternative channels.
claims.e: Rimassa (2008); MAS (2004); Conaghan & de la Torre (2008).

claims.t: From China's perspective the cyclic relationship may not be deliberate; Chinese banks often legitimately target profits or follow energy-security policy, though they indirectly aided leftist leaders.
claims.q: Chinese banks are in many cases legitimately targeting profits or acting in line with Beijing's energy security policy by seeking diversification of natural resource suppliers.
claims.an: Pragmatic, non-ideological Chinese motives.

claims.t: Aside from market-driven trade, non-leftist governments would have been unlikely to engage with China.
claims.q: aside from market-driven increases in trade, non-leftist governments would have been unlikely to engage with China.
claims.an: Key contestable claim; cross-ideological pragmatism evidence elsewhere in corpus should be checked.

claims.t: Economic engagement and geographic proximity to the US still outweigh Chinese economic influence on Latin American domestic politics over the long term; the Pink Tide was followed by a conservative wave.
claims.q: economic engagement and geographical proximity to the United States still outweigh Chinese economic influence on domestic politics in Latin America over the long term.
claims.e: Post-2014 political developments (Moreno, Morales' fall, Macri, Piñera, Bolsonaro).
claims.an: US retains political influence even as Chinese economic ties persist—separating political and economic influence.

claims.t: Chinese investment and loans continued after the Pink Tide ended: Ecuador's Chinese FDI averaged US$81.8m/yr in 2015–2018 (vs US$85.5m in 2011–2014) and Bolivia's debt to China held at ~9%; China thus emerged as the realist 'winner'.
claims.q: This means that what started as a cyclic relationship ultimately resulted in the fall of the Pink Tide and the sustenance of Chinese economic engagement with Ecuador and Bolivia.
claims.e: Banco Central del Ecuador (2020c); Banco Central de Bolivia (2020c).
claims.an: Strongest evidence for central premise: Chinese economic presence persists across political turnover, including Moreno's rapprochement with the US.

claims.t: Some Chinese funding harmed local communities through environmental damage and use of Chinese workers on construction projects (Ecuador since at least 2013; minor criticisms in Bolivia).
claims.q: some Chinese funding to Ecuador and Bolivia has impacted local communities negatively. This includes environmental damage and undermining the local
claims.e: Gallagher et al. (2017); González-Vicente (2013); Hill (2014); Nathanson (2017); Praeli (2018).
claims.an: Sentence continues onto PDF p.17 ('labor market by employing Chinese workers to complete construction projects').

claims.t: China now rivals or overtakes the US as a trade and investment partner in much of LAC, while the US still supplies unsurpassed security guarantees and agenda-setting power.
claims.q: China now rivals or overtakes it as a trade and investment partner in much of the region.
claims.e: Introductory framing; no data cited at this point.

claims.t: Some LAC governments 'hedge': they accept Chinese economic opportunities while quietly maintaining security, diplomatic or normative alignment with Washington. Others double down on the US or lean more openly to Beijing.
claims.q: they accept Chinese economic opportunities while quietly maintaining security, diplomatic or normative alignment with Washington.
claims.e: Conceptual framing, developed through the Hedging Index.
claims.an: This is the core mechanism by which Chinese economic ties persist despite US strategic discourse: economics and security are compartmentalised.

claims.t: Typology of hedging: (i) economic returns-maximisation via simultaneous engagement with several great powers, (ii) security risk-management without formal alliances, (iii) preservation of strategic flexibility ('deferred bandwagoning'). Operationally, the raw index gives >0.66 = pronounced US alignment, <0.33 = pronounced China alignment, 0.33–0.66 = dual engagement. Fuzzy membership then sorts countries into true hedgers (≥0.70), moderate hedgers, US-leaning and US-aligned.
claims.e: Literature synthesis (Kuik, Jackson, Wang, Wu) and index construction (Tables 3, 7–10).
claims.an: Thresholds appear on p.07 (index bands) and pp.11–12 (Tables 7–10). The authors also use Kuik's 'asymmetric hedging' for Uruguay (p.09).

claims.t: Hedging under hegemony is a measurement-oriented gloss on familiar Latin American traditions: relational autonomy, autonomy through diversification and Active Non-Alignment.
claims.e: Literature review linking Russell & Tokatlian, Vigevani & Cepaluni, and Fortin et al. (2023).
claims.an: Useful bridge between the M4 agency literature and Asian hedging theory.

claims.t: Explanations based on declining US engagement (e.g. first Trump administration isolationism) are insufficient, because hedging patterns persisted across multiple US administrations with varying levels of regional engagement.
claims.q: insufficient, as hedging patterns have persisted across multiple
claims.e: Literature review (citing Grass 2022), supported by index stability across the 2013–2017 and 2019–2023 sub-periods.
claims.an: Weighs against M15 (US inattention) as a sufficient explanation for continued Chinese economic ties.

claims.t: China's expanding footprint in Latin America across trade, finance, infrastructure and telecoms is widening policy space even under a persistent US security ceiling.
claims.q: is widening policy space even under a persistent US
claims.e: Citations to Borquez et al. 2023, Jenkins 2021, Lee & Sims 2024, Sims et al. 2023.

claims.t: Because US suppliers dominate the regional arms market, procurement of major Chinese weapons systems is less a strategic choice than a foreclosed option. Hedging scores must therefore be read relatively, as distance from a hegemonic baseline.
claims.q: is less a strategic choice than a foreclosed option.
claims.e: Reasoning about the structure of the arms market (O'Keefe 2020; Santa-Cruz 2019).
claims.an: The US retains a structural security instrument even if its economic instruments lag.

claims.t: Where state capacity is weak, infrastructure deals with Beijing are prone to rent-seeking and defence understandings with Washington become muddled, eroding the ambiguity that hedging depends on.
claims.q: Beijing are prone to rent-seeking and defence understandings with
claims.e: Theoretical argument (Lyu & Singh 2023); no case data given.

claims.t: Fragile macro-fundamentals turn external shocks into domestic crises, forcing leaders to rely on whichever patron can offer the fastest relief and collapsing room for balanced engagement.
claims.q: rely on whichever patron can offer the fastest relief
claims.an: Implies that crisis-hit states (e.g. Argentina, Ecuador) may lean on Chinese finance or on US/IMF support depending on who offers faster relief. This is relevant to swap lines and loans-for-oil, but the paper does not test it.

claims.t: Ideology and governing coalitions mediate rather than cause hedging. Conservative or market-oriented coalitions often privilege US security ties and trade regimes, while left or nationalist coalitions sometimes push diversification, but both patterns vary with domestic incentives. Political projects do not on their own generate room for manoeuvre.
claims.q: they do not, on their own, generate that room.
claims.e: Literature (Gardini & Lambert; Neto & Malamud; Wehner & Thies); Costa Rica, Mexico and Colombia discussion.
claims.an: Supports the brief's caution that ideology alone does not explain alignment.

claims.t: Venezuela and Cuba are excluded because sweeping US sanctions drive Venezuelan oil into opaque swap deals and black-market routes and leave Cuba with virtually no option but Chinese alignment. Their behaviour reflects coercion rather than strategic choice.
claims.q: sweeping US sanctions drive Venezuelan oil into opaque swap deals
claims.an: Evidence that US sticks can push targets towards China, i.e. coercive statecraft is counter-productive for US aims in these cases.

claims.t: Twelve of the 14 cases sit above the 0.66 cut-off, signalling a 'hegemonic ceiling' on policy autonomy. Mexico, Honduras and Nicaragua (index >0.94) pair overwhelming US trade shares with complete military dependence.
claims.q: signalling a “hegemonic ceiling” on policy autonomy
claims.e: Hedging Index, Table 3 (UN Comtrade + SIPRI TIV, 2013–2023 sums).
claims.an: Nicaragua scoring 0.946 (US-aligned) despite its political hostility to Washington is driven by trade and arms composition. This shows how far the index diverges from political alignment.

claims.t: Even the commodity giants Brazil, Chile and Peru, whose exports are now majority-China, stay in the 'weak-to-moderate US alignment' band because their hard-security links are still monopolised by the US. Defence ties weigh more heavily than commerce.
claims.q: stay in the “weak-to-moderate US alignment” band
claims.e: Table 3 index values (BRA 0.691, CHL 0.691, PER 0.698); Medeiros 2005.
claims.an: Key evidence of compartmentalisation: China wins the trade leg in commodity exporters while the US keeps the security leg.

claims.t: Only Panama (0.490), with a near-even trade split and no meaningful arms deals with either power, and Uruguay (0.654), which leverages China's agricultural demand while anchoring security in long-standing US ties ('asymmetric hedging'), fall in the 0.33–0.66 hedging window.
claims.q: practises what Kuik calls “asymmetric hedging,” leveraging China’s

claims.t: Brazil shows that one strong bureaucratic pillar can offset political volatility: Brasília negotiated Chinese investment in the Porto do Açu while conducting AMAZONLOG joint exercises with the US Army.
claims.q: US Army illustrates how one strong bureaucratic pillar can offset
claims.e: fsQCA truth-table row SC=1, PS=0, EF=0 (Brazil); illustrative example without citation.
claims.an: Brazil is inconsistently classified (true hedger in Table 7 vs 'just outside the hedging band' on p.13).

claims.t: Honduras is locked into US alignment by hosting US Joint Task Force Bravo at Soto Cano Air Base and receiving almost all its Foreign Military Financing from Washington.
claims.e: Illustrative case for the 0-0-0 truth-table row.
claims.an: The index does not register Honduras's 2023 switch of diplomatic recognition to Beijing. This is my external knowledge, not stated in the document; see gaps.

claims.t: Chile's bureaucratic heft (Dirección de Presupuestos, CORFO) lets Santiago juggle Chinese lithium deals and US F-16 upgrades despite middling growth.
claims.q: juggle Chinese lithium deals and US F-16 upgrades
claims.e: Illustrative example for Paths 4–5; no citation.
claims.an: Links critical-minerals engagement with China (M7) to domestic agency (M4).

claims.t: Panama leverages the Colón Container Port concession to China while keeping US Southern Command at hand through the 1977 Torrijos–Carter Treaties. It also hosted the 2023 US–Panama 'Panamax' naval exercise alongside the inauguration of China-funded cruise-terminal facilities at Amador Causeway, making it the 'ideal-type hedger'.
claims.q: Port concession to China while keeping the US. Southern Command
claims.an: Panama is a key case where US pressure intensified after the study window. The index ends in 2023, so the classification predates US pressure on Panama's ports and BRI membership from 2025; external check needed.

claims.t: The high-high-high recipe covers barely 40% of successful hedgers, tempering any notion of an 'institutional golden ticket'. Six equifinal pathways exist.
claims.q: tempering any notion of an “institutional golden ticket.”

claims.t: Colombia's 2018 accession to NATO 'global partner' status tilted it towards Washington despite booming Chinese coal purchases (raw 0.840, membership 0.397). It drifts modestly towards balance in Period 2 (Δ −0.040).
claims.q: NATO’s “global partner” status tilted it towards Washington despite

claims.t: In 2013–2023 Latin America obtained more than 99% of its major weapons from Washington or allied suppliers, so complete equidistance is implausible.
claims.q: more than 99 per cent of its major weapons from Washington or allied
claims.e: SIPRI TIV aggregates (attributed to Table 3, which does not show it).

claims.t: The longitudinal split shows only modest late-decade movement towards balance after the 2017–2018 inflection in US–China competition. Period 1 has no true hedgers; Period 2 has five true and three moderate hedgers. The causal architecture is unchanged.
claims.e: Re-computed index and fsQCA per sub-period (Supplementary Tables 19–24).
claims.an: Suggests the intensification of US–China rivalry coincided with slightly more, not less, hedging.

claims.t: Costa Rica is the puzzle case. Despite a 1-1-1 configuration, its hedging membership is only 0.276. Its 2007 diplomatic switch from Taipei to Beijing was followed by swift ratification of CAFTA with the US and a US-funded counter-narcotics radar upgrade. Ideological affinity with Washington, a demilitarised security identity and elite scepticism towards Chinese finance outweigh structural permissiveness.
claims.q: with Washington, a demilitarised security identity and elite scepticism
claims.an: Shows that diplomatic recognition of Beijing (M14) need not produce economic or security realignment.

claims.t: Mexico (raw 0.954, membership 0.192) is locked into alignment by deep rules-based USMCA integration and long-standing US security reliance, even as trade with China grows at the margin. It shows virtually no movement between sub-periods (Δ −0.003).
claims.q: narrow the scope for dual-track signalling, even as trade
claims.an: Index uses bilateral trade (exports+imports), so it may understate Mexico's import dependence on China.

claims.t: For the US, punitive measures aimed at minimal diversification could prove counter-productive, hardening the very behaviour they seek to deter. Governments should build bureaucratic coherence or macro resilience to widen options.
claims.q: diversification could prove counter-productive, hardening the very
claims.e: Policy implication drawn from the findings.

claims.t: For China, commercial engagement alone is insufficient. Without complementary moves in the security domain, which face strong structural obstacles, Beijing's influence will remain capped.
claims.q: commercial engagement alone is insufficient; without complementary
claims.an: Challenges any reading of China's economic expansion as strategic displacement of the US. China consolidates economically but does not translate this into security influence.

claims.t: Hedging is not mechanically produced by favourable structures; it is chosen. Ideology, normative identity and elite world-views can override structural incentives.
claims.q: mechanically produced by favourable structures; it is chosen.

claims.t: Bolsonaro's government cannot be adequately characterised as neofascist because it did not initiate a radical transformation of the state form or political regime in a fascist direction.
claims.q: En la medida en que el gobierno de Bolsonaro no inició posteriormente un proceso de transformación radical de la forma de Estado ni del régimen político vigentes en un sentido fascista, el concepto de neofascismo se vuelve inadecuado para su caracterización.
claims.e: Conceptual argument drawing on Poulantzas and Boron; critique of Boito Jr., Mattos and Melo.

claims.t: Bolsonarista mass mobilisations, organised through social networks and evangelical churches, are not comparable to fascist masses organised in parties and paramilitary organisations.
claims.q: Las masas reaccionarias movilizadas a través de las redes sociales o las iglesias evangélicas no son comparables con las masas fascistas encuadradas en partidos y organizaciones militares y paramilitares
claims.e: Comparison with classical fascism; cites Filgueiras and Druck.

claims.t: Bolsonaro maintained market-oriented economic and social policy and alignment with the United States in foreign policy throughout his term.
claims.q: Bolsonaro mantuvo, en efecto, esas orientaciones de mercado en su política económica (así como social) y de alineamiento con los Estados Unidos en su política exterior durante el resto de su mandato.
claims.e: Assertion in the context of Boito Jr.'s characterisation (Guedes as economy minister; Ernesto Araújo as foreign minister).
claims.an: The only foreign-policy statement in the article; China is not mentioned. To test cross-ideological pragmatism (M5), compare with data on Brazil–China trade and investment during 2019–2022 from other corpus documents.

claims.t: Boito Jr. defines Bolsonaro's 'neofascism' as neoliberal (because of Paulo Guedes's appointment as economy minister) and neocolonial (because of the appointment of Ernesto Araújo, a disciple of Olavo de Carvalho, as foreign minister). Bonnet argues these orientations are radically opposed to classical fascism's.
claims.q: La noción de un neofascismo neoliberal es, en este sentido, muy problemática.
claims.an: 'Neocolonial' here refers to subordination to the US in foreign policy.

claims.t: The new far-right forces combine neoliberal economic and social policies with conservative and even authoritarian positions on democratic rights and freedoms. The Trump government was the most significant example.
claims.q: Estas fuerzas y gobiernos combinan posiciones neoliberales en materia de políticas económicas y sociales con posiciones conservadoras e incluso autoritarias en materia de derechos y libertades democráticas.
claims.an: Core definition of the new right in the article.

claims.t: The 2007–08 financial crisis and the policies used to exit it caused a severe legitimacy crisis of neoliberalism. Because neoliberal policies were maintained or intensified, the response in some cases was a kind of authoritarian neoliberalism.
claims.q: la respuesta a esa crisis de legitimidad resultó en algunos casos en la emergencia de una suerte de neoliberalismo autoritario

claims.t: After the 2007–08 crisis Latin America entered a decade of mediocre growth, averaging only 1.75% a year in 2011–2019, which eroded the economic conditions that had fuelled the progressive cycle.
claims.q: El PBI latinoamericano promedio aumentó apenas un 1,75% anual entre 2011 y 2019
claims.an: Coincides with the end of the China-driven commodity super-cycle, though the article does not make that link.

claims.t: Progressive governments' policies varied but regularly involved greater state interventionism and social policies financed by surpluses from the commodity-export boom.
claims.q: involucraron regularmente un mayor intervencionismo del Estado y, en particular, la implementación de políticas sociales […] a partir de los excedentes provenientes del boom registrado por la exportación de commodities
claims.e: Cites Grugel and Riggirozzi (2009, 2012); Weyland, Madrid and Hunter (2010).
claims.an: The elided word is 'financiadas' (financed), which is rendered with a corrupted ligature glyph in the text file. China is not named as the source of the commodity boom.

claims.t: The progressive orientation was 'economic growth with social inclusion': growth based on commodity exports at favourable international prices replaced post-war import-substitution development, and assistance-based redistribution of export surpluses to the excluded replaced social justice for the included.
claims.q: el crecimiento económico, sustentado en aquella exportación de commodities en un contexto de precios internacionales favorables, reemplaza el desarrollo sustitutivo de importaciones del capitalismo de posguerra
claims.an: Relevant to reprimarisation and dependency (M10), but no reference to trading partners.

claims.t: The closure of the progressive cycle almost invariably followed a neoliberal course and in some cases adopted conservative and authoritarian traits (Bolsonaro in Brazil, Áñez in Bolivia, Duque in Colombia), as the future Milei government might.
claims.q: En ambos casos, la clausura del ciclo progresista siguió casi invariablemente un curso neoliberal y, en algunos casos, adoptó (como en los gobiernos de Bolsonaro en Brasil, de Áñez en Bolivia o de Duque en Colombia) o puede adoptar (en el futuro gobierno de Milei en Argentina) rasgos conservadores y autoritarios.
claims.an: Identifies the right-turn cases. Their US/China economic policy should be checked in other documents.

claims.t: The political crises accompanying the closure of the progressive cycle are crises of party systems and pre-existing leaderships, not organic crises or crises of representative democracy. Such crises favour outsider leaders of different ideological orientations (Bolsonaro, Kast, López Aliaga and Milei, but also Castillo, Giammattei, Boric and Bukele).
claims.q: No se trata de crisis orgánicas, tampoco de crisis de la democracia representativa (que se encuentra consolidada en la región), ni de crisis de representación (que no es impugnada en su conjunto), sino más bien de crisis del sistema de partidos y liderazgos preexistentes.

claims.t: Milei's neoliberal positions are more radical than those of other Latin American far-right figures. He proposes currency competition ('dollarisation'), abolition of the Central Bank (replaced by segmented 100%-reserve transactional banks and investment banks) and vouchers for education and possibly health.
claims.q: Por una parte, sus posiciones neoliberales son aún más radicales que las de otros exponentes de esa extrema derecha latinoamericana.
claims.e: Milei's books and campaign statements; Austrian School influences (note 12).
claims.an: Programmatic economic content only; nothing on trade partners.

claims.t: Judging by his post-election statements, Milei is unlikely to implement his most radical measures in the short term.
claims.q: Aunque, según indican sus declaraciones posteriores a las elecciones, es poco probable que las implemente en el corto plazo.
claims.an: Illustrates gap between campaign ideology and governing pragmatism.

claims.t: Milei does not appear to maintain relations with the armed forces as close as Bolsonaro's, and the Argentine armed forces are far more discredited than Brazil's. His traits do not allow one to anticipate a neofascist government.
claims.q: Milei no parece mantener relaciones tan estrechas con las fuerzas armadas locales como las que mantuvo su par, el excapitán Bolsonaro.
claims.e: Comparison of the Brazilian and Argentine dictatorship legacies; Villarruel's statements (note 13).

claims.t: Milei won the runoff with 55.65% (14,550,000 votes), 6,520,000 more than in the first round. Massa's 44.35% was 11,600,000 votes.
claims.q: Milei se impuso, entonces, en la segunda vuelta, con un 55,65%, 14.550.000 votos

claims.t: The transformative option prevailed because Argentine society already carried a new 'lost decade' of economic stagnation and social degradation. The turning point was 2008–2009; the lost decade began around 2011–2012 and erupted in 2020–2023 because of the pandemic and a severe drought.
claims.q: la sociedad argentina ya cargaba sobre sus espaldas con una nueva década perdida, es decir, con unos diez años de estancamiento económico y de degradación social.
claims.an: The drought reference points to agro-export dependence, but no trade-partner analysis is offered.

claims.t: There was no polarisation between reactionary and progressive exits from the crisis. The only alternative was conserving the status quo through ongoing adjustment or transforming it through even more severe adjustment.
claims.q: no se registró en absoluto una polarización entre salidas reaccionarias y progresistas a la crisis, sino un escenario regido exclusivamente por la alternativa entre conservar lo existente a través de las políticas de ajuste en curso o transformarlo a través de políticas de ajuste aún más severas.

claims.t: Kirchnerism's repeated concealment behind right-leaning candidates (Scioli 2015, Fernández 2019, Massa 2023) indicates that the conditions for progressivism's survival were exhausted a decade earlier. Milei's rise is the end product of that exhaustion.
claims.q: indica insistentemente que las condiciones para la supervivencia del progresismo se agotaron hace ya una década.

claims.t: The March–July 2008 'conflicto del campo' over export taxes on agro-commodities was Kirchnerism's most serious street challenge. It organised a right-wing opposition, produced the kirchnerismo/anti-kirchnerismo divide ('la grieta'), and began the conversion of rebelliousness into a right-wing cause that ultimately fed Milei's rise.
claims.q: a partir del mismo se inició una suerte de proceso de conversión de la rebeldía en un asunto de la derecha
claims.e: Historical interpretation; cites Bonnet (2010) and Stefanoni (2021) (note 20).
claims.an: Links distributional conflict over commodity export rents (M10) to Argentina's political cycle.

claims.t: Milei's vote is transversal but seems to come especially from the social sectors hardest hit by stagnation and social degradation. The young–male–poor–interior bias reported by some polls does not appear very significant.
claims.q: El voto a Milei es transversal, pero parece provenir especialmente de los sectores sociales más golpeados por ese estancamiento económico y esa degradación social
claims.e: Electoral geography (poor districts of Greater Buenos Aires, Rosario, Resistencia, Salta); polls (Balsa and Liaudat; Pagni).

claims.t: Following Mises, Milei excludes democracy from his 'fundamental institutions of capitalism'. The Austrian tradition has shown little commitment to democratic institutions (Mises and Dollfuss; Hayek and Pinochet).
claims.q: Milei, siguiendo a Mises, excluya de sus “instituciones fundamentales del capitalismo” (la propiedad privada, los mercados, la competencia, la división del trabajo y la cooperación) a la democracia

claims.t: The progressivism-versus-neofascism (or democracy-versus-fascism) dichotomy simultaneously distorts the nature of both poles. Progressivism acted as a 'vanishing mediator' of reaction.
claims.q: La alternativa progresismo versus neofascismo (o cualquier otra variante de democracia versus fascismo) distorsiona simultáneamente la naturaleza de ambos polos.

claims.t: The Lithium Triangle holds 56% of world lithium resources, 52% of reserves and one-third of 2021 production, making it a site of competition among actors seeking to extract lithium.
claims.q: It is estimated that the so-called “lithium triangle” in the salt flats of Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina accounted for 56% of the world resources, 52% of world reserves, and one-third of the world production in 2021
claims.an: Resource endowment explains why the region matters to all powers; it does not by itself explain Chinese advantage.

claims.t: Lithium processing/refining capacity (into hydroxide and carbonate), the key upstream value-capture stage, is mostly concentrated in China, with Ganfeng Lithium as the most important vertically integrated player; SQM's Chilean facilities supply a small share.
claims.q: Today, most of the capacity is concentrated in China. Ganfeng Lithium is the most important stakeholder; as a vertically integrated company, it operates in several stages of the supply chain
claims.e: Automotive Manufacturing Solutions (2021) data; Figure 2; industry sources.
claims.an: Core M7 mechanism: processing dominance makes China the default buyer and partner.

claims.t: China dominates downstream: >65% of battery component capacity, 75% of battery manufacturing capacity (South Korea 15%), 60% of battery assembly and 43% of EV/hybrid production.
claims.q: The battery manufacturing capacity is even more concentrated in China (75%), followed by South Korea (15%).

claims.t: Value in the LIB chain is concentrated downstream: mining and refining capture only 2% (US$3.8bn), cells/components/assembly 46%, EV manufacturing 54%; this sets a difficult scenario for Bolivia and Argentina, which seek to industrialise lithium.
claims.q: The upstream stages (mining and refining processes) represent only 2% of the value
claims.an: Explains why producer states court downstream partners (mostly Chinese) through JV/industrialisation clauses.

claims.t: Gigafactory capacity is heavily concentrated in Asia/China; CATL alone held 22% of the world's 500 GWh gigafactory capacity in 2021; Europe and the US plan to double capacity but remain well behind China.
claims.q: Chinese Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) not only has 22% of the world's total of 500 GWh Gigafactory capacity in 2021

claims.t: BYD and CATL benefited from past supportive policies of the Chinese government; since 2019 subsidies to automotive companies changed and the sector opened to foreign competition.
claims.q: Both BYD and CATL have benefited from past supportive policies of the Chinese government.
claims.an: State industrial policy is the root of the downstream dominance that then shapes LAC relationships.

claims.t: In March 2022 the US government announced it would invoke the Defense Production Act to support production and processing of battery minerals (lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, manganese); over-reliance on China is now seen as a national-security concern.
claims.q: the overreliance on China and other perceived hostile trading countries for key materials is now seen as a national security concern that requires direct economic incentives and policies
claims.an: The only US instrument named in the document; it is domestic industrial policy, not an offer to Lithium Triangle countries. The IRA (Aug 2022), the MSP and FTA-sourcing rules are NOT mentioned. M15 tag is the analyst's interpretation (late response).

claims.t: In 2020 the European Commission added lithium to its Critical Raw Materials list because of EV/storage relevance, demand growth (up to 18x by 2030, 60x by 2050) and high import dependence on South America.
claims.q: In 2020, the European Commission finally included lithium among the Critical Raw Materials (CRM)
claims.an: Shows a third competitor (EU) in the region.

claims.t: China's economic weight differs across the three countries: it is the largest bilateral creditor for Argentina and Bolivia, while in Chile China has pursued a trade strategy rather than loans, so structural contexts create variable degrees of dependency.
claims.q: In Chile, by contrast, China has taken on a trade strategy rather than foreign loans
claims.e: OEC 2019 trade data; Inter-American Dialogue (2020) finance database; Agramont & Bonifaz (2018); Table 3.

claims.t: Since 2005 China has lent about US$86bn to Latin America, more than the World Bank and IDB combined.
claims.q: since 2005, China has granted approximately US$86 billion in loans to Latin American countries, an amount greater than the World Bank (WB) and the Inter‐American Development Bank combined
claims.an: Figure appears low relative to IAD totals cited elsewhere (~US$137bn by 2019); verify definition and comparison period.

claims.t: Through the market mechanism China has high influence: it is the main market and manufacturing hub for lithium and sets the LCE spot price; Bolivia and Argentina are highly market-dependent on China, Chile much less so.
claims.q: China has a high level of influence since it is the main market and manufacturing hub of lithium, and it determines the spot price of Lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE)
claims.e: CHRTD (2022) 2018 export data; Figure 7; interviews; Table 5.
claims.an: Market power, not ideology, is the channel.

claims.t: Chile exports only 15% of its lithium to China (60% to other Asian countries, 19% to Europe), so it has a lesser degree of market dependence.
claims.q: Chile, on the other hand, produced 77 thousand tons, with approximately 60% of the exports destined to Asian countries (excluding China), 19% to Europe, and only in third place, China, with 15% of exports.
claims.an: Counter-evidence: Chinese market dominance does not translate uniformly into bilateral export dependence.

claims.t: From 2017 to 2020 China increased its presence in Australia, DRC, Argentina, Bolivia and Chile; one-third of these investments took place in Argentina, where Ganfeng (with Lithium Americas) is developing Cauchari-Olaroz and signed a 2021 MoU for an LIB factory.
claims.q: Of the investments over this period, one‐third took place in Argentina

claims.t: Argentina's decentralised governance allows Chinese firms to negotiate directly with provincial governments; China is gaining ground despite other foreign investors.
claims.q: In Argentina, the decentralized governance allows the direct negotiation of Chinese companies with the provincial governments.
claims.an: Emergent explanation: subnational/federal institutional design as an enabling condition for Chinese entry.

claims.t: Tianqi Lithium bought 24% of SQM for US$4.1bn in 2018, an unprecedented cross-ownership strategy that illustrates China's growing power in the region.
claims.q: In Chile, China's Tianqi Lithium Corp bought a 24% share in the competitor Chilean lithium company SQM for US $4.1 billion in 2018
claims.an: Completed acquisition (not merely announced).

claims.t: Chile's lower dependency reflects the presence of US company Albemarle and Chilean SQM, which determine a different dynamic despite Chinese penetration.
claims.q: the presence of US companies such as Albemarle or the Chilean SQM determines a different dynamic for lithium mining in the country, with less dependence than their neighbors have
claims.an: Evidence that incumbent US private capital (not US state instruments) limits Chinese penetration in one case.

claims.t: Bolivia has the world's largest lithium deposit but has not entered the global market meaningfully; about US$1bn of public investment over a decade produced ~666 tonnes of lithium carbonate (2017–2019, pilot scale).
claims.q: Bolivia is a peculiar case; although it has the world's largest deposit of lithium, it has not entered the global lithium market in any meaningful way.
claims.an: State-led resource nationalism has limited everyone's (including China's) extraction gains.

claims.t: Bolivia's December 2018 JV with German ACI Systems (YLB–ACISA) for a lithium hydroxide complex was rescinded by the Morales government amid Potosí protests and the 2019 political crisis; in early 2019 Bolivia signed a JV with Chinese consortium Xinjiang TBEA Group-Baocheng for Coipasa and Pastos Grandes.
claims.q: Early that year, Morales' government also signed a joint venture with the Chinese consortium Xinjiang TBEA Group‐Baocheng for exploring and extracting resources from the Coipasa and Pastos Grandes salt flats
claims.an: The Western (German) alternative failed for domestic political reasons, not because of Chinese competition; the Chinese JV remained. Bolivia is high-dependence per Table 5.

claims.t: China played a key role providing construction services for Uyuni salt-flat infrastructure over the past decade, and a Chinese consortium will partner with YLB despite constitutional bars on foreign participation in extraction.
claims.q: has played a key role providing construction services for the infrastructure developed in the Uyuni salt flat over the past decade

claims.t: Joint ventures are an important strategy for Chinese firms to combine extraction, manufacturing and consumption, especially with 'newcomers' such as YLB or the Ganfeng–Jujuy alliance; whether they will foster a lithium-based industry is yet to be seen.
claims.q: It is yet to be seen how effective and beneficial these types of alliances will prove to be to foster a lithium‐based industry in these countries.
claims.an: Industrialisation promises are part of China's offer to resource states seeking value capture.

claims.t: Chinese ownership of many lithium projects in the region will not necessarily secure China's future dominance; the US–China trade war creates an uncertain scenario of rivalry in the Lithium Triangle.
claims.q: Although Chinese companies have a significant number of projects in the region, this ownership will not necessarily secure the country's future dominance.
claims.e: Literature review citing Heredia et al. (2020).

claims.t: China's position derives from three factors: dominance in the LIB value chain, expansive state policies for renewable technologies, and concentration of strategic materials; China produces cobalt (6%), natural graphite (66%), silicon metal (68%) and lithium (7%) and has influence in resource-rich countries like the DRC.
claims.q: with China emerging as a powerful player for three main reasons—its dominance in the LIB value chain, the expansive state policies to foster renewable technologies for the low‐carbon energy transition, and the concentration of strategic materials for key technologies

claims.t: Since 2000 China has become the biggest raw-material consumer (49% of steel, 46% copper, 45% zinc, 53% nickel), and its demand plus protectionist measures and overseas resource strategies have raised concerns among other industrial nations.
claims.q: the biggest raw‐material consumer in the world—49% of steel, 46% cooper, 45% zinc, and 53% of nickel
claims.an: Demand-pull basis of LAC relations.

claims.t: China may simply be acting as any other state would, and demonising narratives about China may be ideologically situated.
claims.q: China could also be seen as simply acting as any other state is (and would), and demonizing narratives may be ideologically situated.
claims.an: Useful caution against securitised US framings.

claims.t: China's influence has deepened Latin America's role as a raw-material provider, diversified funding sources, and its state-led model is praised by some; unequal trade conditions point to a reloaded neo-dependency.
claims.q: At the same time, the unequal trade conditions point to a reloaded version of neo dependency.

claims.t: China secures resources through a flexible approach of negotiations and alliances; whether lithium enables a just transition or reproduces dependence depends on how power imbalances are addressed.
claims.q: In this scenario, China has a strategy of securitization of resources via a flexible approach of negotiations and alliances.
claims.an: Adaptability to host regimes (state-led, provincial, private) is an explanation for consolidation across ideologically different governments.

claims.t: Lithium Triangle countries (and Australia) are seeking to expand domestic processing capacity to capture more value.
claims.q: the increasing interest of different countries including Australia, Chile, Bolivia, and Argentina to expand the domestic processing capacity
claims.an: Host agency: value-added demands are a bargaining lever toward any partner.

claims.t: Western automakers themselves ally with Asian battery makers (e.g., Tesla with Panasonic, LG Chem and CATL), creating a contradiction in which Western and Asian manufacturers collaborate while competing for the EV market.
claims.q: vertical integration of automotive manufacturers with Asia‐based LIB counterparts creates an interesting contradiction
claims.an: Private Western capital's interdependence with Chinese suppliers dilutes state-level rivalry.

claims.t: Chinese policy-bank finance (CDB, China Eximbank) was predominantly for infrastructure and fossil fuels, about two-thirds of loans from 2005 to 2022; since 2019 direct investments by these banks have declined while SOE mergers and acquisitions surged.
claims.q: with approximately two-thirds of loans allocated to this conventional energy sector from 2005 to 2022, as per data sourced from the Inter-American Dialogue
claims.e: Inter-American Dialogue data; Becard et al. (2020).
claims.an: Decline of policy-bank lending did not mean Chinese retreat; instruments changed.

claims.t: China's expansion in Latin America can be interpreted, from a neorealist view, as a rational response to pressures of the US-led order and a strategy to guarantee energy security and critical raw materials.
claims.q: can be interpreted as a rational response to the pressures of the U.S.-led international order, as well as a strategy to guarantee energy security and access to critical raw materials

claims.t: China institutionalises its presence through the China–CELAC Forum (Joint Plan of Action covering energy policy, renewables and efficiency) and BRICS/New Development Bank, building a parallel governance framework to Western-dominated institutions.
claims.q: China uses BRICS as an institutional mechanism to construct a parallel governance framework that challenges Western dominance in setting global energy norms and financing rules
claims.e: China–CELAC Joint Plan of Action; BRICS Energy Research Cooperation Platform; literature.
claims.an: Emergent explanation: multilateral/normative institution-building as a channel of consolidation.

claims.t: China directed 68% of its overseas energy investments in 2022–2023 to solar and wind, fuelling concerns about 'monopolization of electricity markets' and technological dependence of Latin America.
claims.q: directing 68% of its overseas energy investments (2022–2023) toward these sectors
claims.e: Morro et al. (2025) Boston University GDP Center.
claims.an: Global figure, not LAC-specific.

claims.t: China prefers direct physical control over strategic resources: oil through oil-backed loans and direct investments; minerals like iron, copper and lithium mostly through asset acquisitions and supply-chain control via FDI.
claims.q: As for critical minerals like iron, copper, or lithium, the most frequent pattern has been the acquisition of assets and control over key segments of the supply chain through foreign direct investment
claims.e: Gallagher et al. (2012); Freitas da Rocha & Bielschowsky (2019).

claims.t: US–China rivalry forces Latin American states to balance the economic benefits of cooperation with China against historical dependence on US hegemony; partnering with China offers infrastructure and partner diversification but entails debt and political-leverage risks.
claims.q: forcing them to maintain a delicate balance between the economic benefits derived from cooperation with China and their historical dependence on US hegemony
claims.an: Hedging explanation; no case evidence.

claims.t: Energy's share of Chinese infrastructure finance in the region rose sharply from 2013, exceeding 80% in 2016; finance for traditional energy rose from 2009, peaked around 2014 at over US$35bn annually (50% to oil), then declined markedly.
claims.q: peaking around 2014 with amounts exceeding $35 billion annually
claims.e: AidData Geospatial Global Chinese Development Finance Dataset; Fig. 1.
claims.an: Shows retreat of fossil finance, i.e., Chinese finance is not expanding in every segment.

claims.t: China's 2021 pledge to stop financing new overseas coal plants signals a strategic reorientation, using the energy transition as an instrument to expand its global sphere of influence.
claims.q: China's 2021 pledge to stop financing new overseas coal-fired power projects was an unequivocal political signal of this strategic reorientation

claims.t: Chinese companies have been key players in large hydro projects (Patuca III, Honduras, 104 MW; Coca Codo Sinclair, Ecuador, 1,500 MW), but socio-environmental scrutiny led China to shift to smaller projects.
claims.q: Faced with increasing international scrutiny, China has begun to adjust its foreign investment strategy, focusing on smaller-scale projects with more manageable socio-environmental impacts.
claims.e: Ecuador Ministry of Energy; literature on hydro conflicts.
claims.an: Adaptation to criticism helps sustain presence.

claims.t: From 2018 hydro investment drops sharply while solar and wind gain prominence, with small or medium concessional projects ('small is beautiful') responding to BRI sustainability demands and sovereign over-indebtedness risks.
claims.q: a drastic turning point is observed from 2018 onwards: investment in hydroelectric power drops sharply, while solar and wind initiatives gain prominence
claims.e: BU China's Global Power Database; Fig. 2; Ray (2023).

claims.t: Latin America is structurally inserted as a key supplier to China's energy-transition supply chains: 72% of China's copper imports (2021), 95% of silver (2018 peak) and 98% of lithium imports (2022) came from the region.
claims.q: in 2022, 98% of the lithium imported by China, an irreplaceable mineral for battery manufacturing, originated from Latin America
claims.an: Mutual dependence: China is also dependent on LAC — a potential bargaining lever (M4).

claims.t: China pursues a vertically integrated model; BYD, Great Wall and Changan are establishing EV and battery assembly plants in Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador and Paraguay, aiming to supply regional and even US markets.
claims.q: Chinese companies like BYD, Great Wall, and Changan are establishing assembly plants for electric vehicles and batteries in countries such as Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, and Paraguay
claims.an: Targeting the US market via LAC plants is relevant to USMCA/IRA rules-of-origin debates (not discussed by author).

claims.t: In the foundational phase (c.2010–2019) CDB and China Eximbank channelled sovereign loans for megaprojects under an 'infrastructure-for-resources' model, presented as an alternative to Washington Consensus conditionalities and granting leaders fiscal autonomy.
claims.q: Chinese financing was presented as a direct alternative to the strict conditionalities of the Washington Consensus

claims.t: In 2016, the average installed capacity per project financed by policy banks exceeded 800 MW, the peak of the megaproject model; average project scale fell thereafter.
claims.q: the average installed capacity per project financed by policy banks exceeded 800 MW
claims.e: BU China's Global Power Database; Fig. 3.

claims.t: Between 2015 and 2021, SOE mergers and acquisitions (SGCC, China Southern Power Grid, CTGC) of transmission and distribution assets replaced sovereign lending, marking a shift in 'Going Out' from construction to ownership and long-term operational control.
claims.q: This shift from financing new megaprojects to acquiring operational infrastructure reflects a broader process of consolidation and entrenchment of Chinese influence across the Latin American energy value chain.
claims.an: Key evidence of consolidation after the lending peak.

claims.t: Since 2017, Chinese private companies (Goldwind, LONGi, Trina Solar) have led greenfield wind and PV investment in Chile, Argentina and Brazil; private firms with strong international competitiveness are playing a leading role.
claims.q: Chinese private companies, represented by Goldwind, LONGi, and Trina Solar, are consolidating their presence in Latin America through the investment and development of large wind and photovoltaic projects in countries like Chile, Argentina, and Brazil.
claims.an: Market-competitive private firms complicate a purely state-coordinated (M2) explanation.

claims.t: The 'debt-trap diplomacy' narrative is less applicable to the evolving model, but asymmetry persists in trade flows, FDI balances and influence over capital, technology standards and expertise.
claims.q: appears less applicable under this evolving approach, the underlying structure of the relationship continues to be characterized by asymmetry

claims.t: Several countries switched recognition from Taiwan to China, showing how economic dependence can be translated into political realignment; Paraguay remains an exception, with President Peña reaffirming the Taiwan alliance in July 2025.
claims.q: Paraguay remains a notable exception, with President Santiago Peña reaffirming in July 2025 the enduring alliance with Taiwan
claims.e: Rodriguez et al. (2025); Veney & Abidde (2024); Paraguay presidency (2025).
claims.an: Exception that tests the limits of economic leverage.

claims.t: In Lima, metropolitan distribution was split between ENEL and Luz del Sur until 2019, when China Yangtze Power (CTGC subsidiary) bought Luz del Sur; with ENEL's potential divestment to another Chinese company, Lima faces a de facto Chinese monopoly in electricity distribution.
claims.q: With the potential divestment of ENEL and the Likelihood of another Chinese company taking over its assets, the Peruvian capital faces the prospect of a de facto monopoly in electricity distribution.
claims.e: Author account (no source cited for the ENEL divestment).
claims.an: Verify the 2023–2024 sale of Enel Distribución Perú to China Southern Power Grid International.

claims.t: In 2020 SGCC acquired 97.3% of Chile's Compañía General de Electricidad for US$3bn, controlling distribution in 11 of 16 regions; such acquisitions create concentrated market structures and governance-centred dependency (reduced regulatory autonomy, energy sovereignty).
claims.q: Similarly, in 2020, the SGCC acquired 97.3% of Compañía General de Electricidad in Chile for $3 billion, thereby controlling electricity distribution in 11 of the country's 16 regions.
claims.an: Acquisition took place under a centre-right Chilean government (Piñera), which suggests cross-ideological pragmatism (analyst inference; not stated by author).

claims.t: In lithium, Chinese companies prioritise direct control of primary resources to supply domestic battery/EV industries; in Argentina Chinese firms accounted for 67.6% of lithium exports by 2024, more than five times the US share.
claims.q: In Argentina, for instance, Chinese firms accounted for 67.6% of Lithium exports by 2024, more than five times the share of the USA, the second-largest destination
claims.e: Argentine Ministry of Economy (2025); Shiquan & Deyi (2023).
claims.an: Compare with D14: 51% of Argentina's LCE exports to China in 2018, which suggests deepening concentration.

claims.t: Lithium industrialisation in Argentina faces weak infrastructure, insufficient technological capacity and pressures to export raw materials; Latin America remains locked in the lower rungs of value chains.
claims.q: The result is a structural asymmetry in which Latin American countries remain locked into the lower rungs of global value chains, exporting raw materials while importing high-value-added goods.

claims.t: Chinese-financed energy projects have been criticised for weak socio-environmental safeguards; the UN CESCR associated them with rights violations; Chinese trade and investment are drivers of environmental degradation and social conflict.
claims.q: several Chinese-financed energy projects have been criticized for insufficient commitment to environmental and social safeguards

claims.t: The turnkey model in BRI energy projects produces technological lock-in: Chinese firms oversee entire lifecycles while local involvement is limited, curtailing indigenous industrial capability.
claims.q: the heavy reliance on Chinese technology has significantly curtailed the ability of Latin American firms to cultivate an indigenous industrial base
claims.e: Literature on technology transfer and absorptive capacity.
claims.an: Low cost of turnkey delivery is part of the appeal (M1/M3 comparison).

claims.t: China's role is not a classical monopoly but a strategic concentration of control over infrastructures, technologies and resource flows; dependency now rests on strategic minerals and clean-energy technology standards rather than hydrocarbons or agriculture.
claims.q: Dependency is no longer primarily anchored in hydrocarbons or agricultural commodities, but increasingly in strategic minerals and in the technological standards that structure clean energy systems.

claims.t: Dependency varies: Brazil channels Chinese capital and technology into higher value-added sectors; Mexico, embedded in the US orbit under USMCA, faces tighter external restrictions limiting Chinese infrastructural penetration; Bolivia and Ecuador are most vulnerable.
claims.q: Mexico, constrained by its geopolitical position and its strategic embeddedness within the orbit of the USA under frameworks such as the USA–Mexico–Canada Agreement, faces tighter external restrictions
claims.e: Becard et al. (2020); Masiero et al. (2016); Peters (2016).
claims.an: The only US instrument in the document: trade-agreement embeddedness (USMCA) as a structural constraint. This is evidence that US frameworks can limit Chinese penetration where they bind.

claims.t: China has created alternative governance (China–CELAC, BRICS) while resisting existing norms such as IEA membership, yet its green policies positively affect global decarbonisation.
claims.q: it has also shown resistance to existing global energy governance norms, such as its non-participation in the IEA

claims.t: The new architecture of domination is less overtly coercive than earlier dependency but more deeply embedded in the technical, financial and institutional fabric of recipient economies, potentially circumscribing host autonomy.
claims.q: This emerging architecture of structural domination differs markedly from earlier models of dependency, which is less overtly coercive yet more deeply embedded within the technical, financial, and institutional fabric of recipient economies.
claims.an: Low coercion helps explain acceptance across governments.

claims.t: At the 2024 G20 Summit Xi Jinping highlighted clean-energy cooperation for the Global South, referencing the IEA roadmap (Brazil G20 presidency) calling for sixfold clean-energy investment in developing economies by 2035 and tripled concessional finance.
claims.q: This roadmap calls for a sixfold increase in clean energy investment in developing economies (excluding China) by 2035, a tripling of concessional financing

claims.t: In 2022 Chinese firms controlled 62% of cobalt mine materials used for chemical refining, 95% of refined commercial-grade cobalt chemicals, 92% of battery-grade tricobalt tetroxide, 85% of battery-grade cobalt sulphate and 91% of NCM cathode precursors.
claims.q: in 2022 Chinese firms had control over 62% of cobalt mine materials primarily used for cobalt chemical refining, 95% control of refined commercial-grade cobalt chemicals, 92% control of battery-grade tricobalt tetroxide, 85% control of battery-grade cobalt sulfate, and 91% control of nickel–cobalt-manganese cathode precursor materials
claims.an: Benchmark for the processing-dominance mechanism in battery minerals.

claims.t: In a 2010 diplomatic dispute China reportedly blocked rare-earth exports to Japan, leveraging its near-monopoly; this precipitated the current focus on non-fuel critical minerals.
claims.q: During a 2010 diplomatic dispute, China reportedly blocked exports of rare earth elements to Japan, thereby leveraging China's near-monopoly to threaten Japanese manufacturers of advanced technologies
claims.an: Precedent behind US securitisation of critical minerals.

claims.t: China's control over critical minerals other than rare earths has not been studied comprehensively; cobalt is the mineral with the most attention for supply risk after REEs, ranked in the top 3, 4 and 10 most critical by the US, China and EU respectively.
claims.q: Although this caused significant concern for manufacturers outside China, China's control over other critical minerals has yet to be studied comprehensively.
claims.e: Literature; Nassar & Fortier (2021); Blengini et al. (2020); Yan & Wang (2021).

claims.t: Cobalt became a critical defence mineral in WWI and the US Congress mandated stockpiling in 1946.
claims.an: Historical US concern with mineral security.

claims.t: Chinese control over the cobalt chain rose 2000–2022 from 0 to 62% for chemical refinery feedstock and from 10% to 95% for refined chemicals; in the LCO chain from 0 to 92% (battery-grade oxides) and 0 to 84% (LCO cathodes); in the NCM chain (2008–2022) from 0 to 85% (sulphate) and 0 to 91% (precursors).

China's government has increasingly focused on supply chokepoints to 'accelerate the leapfrog development of the new energy industry' and has recently imposed export controls on gallium, germanium, graphite and rare earths.
claims.q: to accelerate the leapfrog development of the new energy
claims.an: Shows explicit state strategy, not only market outcome.

claims.t: Chinese control is concentrated in strategic minerals rather than mining generally: Ericsson et al. (2020) estimated Chinese control at 3.4% of global mine production value, 6.4% for Africa and 24% for the DRC in 2018, but 28% of African copper and 41% of African cobalt; this study estimates 37% control of production, 56% including offtakes.
claims.an: Selective targeting: China's overall mining footprint is small but concentrated where strategic. This qualifies any claim of across-the-board expansion.

claims.t: Chinese foreign cobalt investments have targeted almost exclusively mine and intermediate (refinery-feedstock) assets in the DRC.

In the late 2000s the DRC required cobalt mined materials to be processed before export; crude cobalt hydroxide emerged as the lowest-cost input for chemical refining, and by 2022 copper-cobalt output flowed mainly to chemical refining for battery-grade chemicals.
claims.an: Host export-processing rules shaped the chain but intermediate processing did not prevent Chinese downstream dominance; relevant to Lithium Triangle value-added policies.

claims.t: Few governments have created more policies than China to advance domestic manufacturing and secure foreign mineral resources; it supported OFDI via the Going Out Strategy, BRI and the 2007 minerals-for-infrastructure agreement with the DRC.
claims.q: No government, perhaps, has created more policies to
claims.an: Minerals-for-infrastructure is analogous to the 'infrastructure-for-resources' model D15 describes for Latin America.

claims.t: Chinese control of mine/intermediate production in 2022 came almost entirely from OFDI in DRC facilities (remainder from Indonesian MHP); control of refining, battery chemicals, precursors and cathodes is limited almost exclusively to facilities in China.
claims.an: Pattern: extract abroad, process at home, which is the same structure D14/D15 describe for lithium.

claims.t: By contrast, Chinese control of the metal chain rose only from 0 to 5% (metal refinery feedstock) and 0 to 26% (metal refining), indicating Chinese investment targeted the battery-cathode portion of the chain.
claims.q: These results indicate that cobalt investments from Chinese
claims.an: Strategic targeting rather than generic market expansion.

claims.t: China expanded chemical refining rapidly from 2000, refining more cobalt chemicals than the rest of the world by 2008 and 95% of the world's cobalt chemicals in 2022; its chemical refinery production grew 109-fold.
claims.q: refining 95% of the world's cobalt chemicals in 2022

claims.t: After the purchase of majority shares of Tenke Fungurume in 2016–2017, Chinese-controlled production exceeded half of DRC and world chemical refinery feedstock production; the shift began after the 2007 minerals-for-infrastructure agreement.
claims.an: M&A of existing mines as a route to control, as with Tianqi–SQM (D14) and utility acquisitions (D15).

claims.t: China's share of world cobalt consumption grew in every application 2000–2022: batteries 3% to 87%, magnets 0 to 63%, hardmetals 23% to 58%, ceramics/pigments 15% to 35%, catalysts 7% to 34%, superalloys 0 to 21%; 89% of 43-fold battery-cobalt consumption growth occurred in China.
claims.an: Demand-pull side: control follows the location of manufacturing.

claims.t: Preliminary 2023 estimates show China's control of world cobalt metal production rose to 43%, mainly aerospace-grade metal, 93% of which was purchased by the State Reserve Bureau.
claims.q: the State Reserve Bureau (SRB), purchased 93%
claims.an: State stockpiling as an instrument.

claims.t: Chinese control of secondary production (recycling) also increased: batteries 0 to 75%, catalysts 0 to 67%, hardmetals 11% to 67%, superalloys and magnets 13% to 50%, though these numbers are uncertain.

World cobalt production has mostly exceeded consumption for 20 years; 2022 cumulative world stocks equalled 10 months of chemical-refinery consumption and 7 months of refined-chemical consumption, but 2020–2022 deficits show chemical refining not keeping pace with cathode production.
claims.an: Scarcity is not the issue; control/access is.

claims.t: In 2022 China held 31% of world chemical-refinery feedstock stocks, 35% of refined chemical stocks, 6% of metal feedstock and 62% of refined metal stocks; the SRB purchased 10,300 t of cobalt metal (2014–2022) and preliminarily 8,700 t of aerospace-grade metal in 2023.
claims.e: Fig. 4; Supplementary Table 10; Gulley et al. (2019); Darton (2021, 2024).

claims.t: China's large refined-chemical stocks may reflect the relative lack of pressure on Chinese firms to adjust production when prices decline.
claims.q: been due to the relative lack of pressure on Chinese firms
claims.an: Soft-budget/state-backed resilience lets Chinese processors outlast price downturns, which deters Western competitors.

claims.t: China's dominance extends to other critical minerals for strategic emerging industries: gallium share rose from 0 (2000) to 97% (2022); germanium similar; bismuth 42% to 82%; graphite 51% to 72%; an estimated 99% of spherical graphite for batteries.

As with rare earths in 2010, Chinese exports are virtually the only source of refined cobalt chemicals and cobalt-containing precursors, which could become unavailable through domestic absorption or withholding of exports during a dispute.
claims.q: China's monopoly over cobalt battery materials may imply a serious supply risk to non-Chinese battery producing and consuming industries
claims.an: Underpins US supply-chain policies that later target Latin American minerals (not discussed here).

claims.t: Mitigation options: build chemical refineries (supplied via open-market purchases, offtakes, controlling stakes in mines or new mining); buy cobalt metal to dissolve (e.g., Volkswagen offtake with a Moroccan producer); form JVs with Chinese firms (e.g., LG Chem–Huayou Cobalt); or shift to cobalt-free cathode chemistries.
claims.an: Even 'de-risking' options often route through Chinese partners (JVs), which reinforces Chinese centrality.

claims.t: Stakeholders should analyse each material at each stage; indirect import reliance (imports from adversaries via friendly intermediaries) may hide supply risks; research on Chinese control over lithium, nickel, graphite and manganese has become a priority for some governments (Trump 2020 executive order).
claims.e: Trump (2020) executive order on reliance on critical minerals from foreign adversaries.
claims.an: Only US policy instrument cited. The point about 'friendly intermediaries' is relevant to FTA/friend-shoring rules, e.g., Chinese-owned processing in FTA partners such as Chile and Peru (analyst inference).

claims.t: Artisanal cobalt mining (associated with child labour) represented an estimated 2% of world cobalt mine production in 2020.
Critical mineral supply chains cannot be secure, reliable and resilient unless they are also sustainable and responsible; ESG harms can disrupt supply of clean-energy technologies.
claims.q: Critical mineral supply chains cannot be truly secure, reliable and resilient unless they are also sustainable and responsible.
claims.e: Executive-summary framing; supported in Ch. 1 by listing how ESG failures limit market access, spur litigation and community opposition.
claims.an: Shows the Western multilateral framing that links security of supply to ESG standards — the basis on which traceability becomes a potential differentiator against less transparent supply chains.

claims.t: Mineral demand for clean energy technologies doubles between 2025 and 2030 in the IEA Stated Policies Scenario and nearly triples by 2030 in the Net Zero Scenario, implying about 150 new average-sized mines, processing facilities and refineries.
claims.q: In the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario, mineral demand for clean energy technologies doubles between 2025 and 2030.
claims.an: Demand-pull growth for minerals that LAC supplies (copper, lithium) underpins M1 explanations of continued Chinese engagement.

claims.t: Traceability can serve supply-chain security objectives beyond ESG, including diversification, supply chain dependencies, national security and trade sanctions.
claims.q: In addition to these, traceability is relevant to product safety, supply chain dependencies, national security and trade sanctions.
claims.an: Signals that traceability is dual-use: a responsible-sourcing tool and a geo-economic tool to identify/exclude supply from particular jurisdictions (e.g. China-linked FEOCs).

claims.t: Policy makers should avoid universally mandating immediate end-to-end traceability; aligning timelines with industry readiness prevents blanket disengagement from source countries and preserves emerging markets' market access.
claims.q: Aligning implementation timelines with industry needs and readiness would foster inclusive engagement with source countries, preventing blanket disengagement and ensuring that market access is not being denied to emerging market economies.
claims.e: Policy reasoning on market functioning and inclusiveness.
claims.an: Analyst interpretation: overly strict Western traceability rules could push LAC/emerging producers toward less demanding buyers (plausibly Chinese), which would reinforce China's position — the report does not say this explicitly.

claims.t: Major consumer markets (EU, US) have developed sophisticated traceability frameworks that primarily affect downstream companies; producer countries such as Colombia and the DRC have their own national frameworks, but limited direct regulation of upstream/midstream operators creates implementation gaps.
claims.q: while major consumer markets like the European Union and the United States have developed sophisticated frameworks, these primarily affect downstream companies through market requirements.
claims.e: Regulatory inventory in Table 3.1 (IEA Critical Minerals Policy Tracker 2025).
claims.an: US/EU leverage operates through access to their consumer markets rather than direct presence upstream — consistent with M3 (instrument gap) where upstream investment/finance is concerned.

claims.t: The 2024 US final rules on IRA clean-vehicle provisions require verification of non-Foreign Entity of Concern status throughout the supply chain (serial-number tracking), a Traced Qualifying Value Test for extraction/processing/recycling value-added, and a compliant-battery ledger verifying facility locations.
claims.q: Requires verification of non-Foreign Entity of Concern status throughout the supply chain through a serial number or other identification system to physically track compliant batteries to specific new clean vehicles.
claims.an: The report does not name China in connection with FEOC; analyst note: FEOC rules are widely understood to target Chinese-linked entities (external knowledge — verify). This is a US instrument that could advantage non-Chinese supply (including LAC minerals processed outside China) in the US market.

claims.t: The IRS 'impracticable-to-trace battery materials' rule temporarily exempts highly commingled low-value battery minerals (e.g. graphite in anodes, electrolyte minerals) from FEOC restrictions where tracing is infeasible, illustrating regulatory flexibility in the face of market realities.
claims.q: It temporarily exempts certain highly commingled low-value battery minerals from Foreign Entity of Concern restrictions when tracing would be infeasible, while still requiring manufacturers to document their traceability capabilities.
claims.e: Description of IRS rules on clean vehicle credits.
claims.an: Read together with p. 59 (China ~100% of graphite refining), this exemption is evidence that US de-risking instruments are constrained by China's processing dominance — a concrete limit on US counter-statecraft.

claims.t: The US uses two levers to drive traceability: market incentives via IRA tax credits and import restrictions via the UFLPA; UFLPA enforcement in solar shows focused enforcement can standardise traceability industry-wide without explicit requirements.
claims.q: The US approach illustrates two distinct policy levers: market incentives through the Inflation Reduction Act’s tax credits and import restrictions through the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA).
claims.an: Evidence that US instruments directed at China-linked supply (Xinjiang) do have market effects — a 'stick' with demonstrable impact.

claims.t: UFLPA's shift of the burden of proof to importers has imposed significant burdens and reportedly caused significant delays of large volumes of imports, even where no forced-labour connection may exist.
claims.q: Indications are that it has led to significant delays of large volumes of imports, even where there may be no connection to forced labour.
claims.e: Qualitative assessment; authors note empirical studies are scarce.
claims.an: Shows costs/collateral effects of US coercive trade instruments.

claims.t: Stringent traceability requirements can push artisanal miners and small-scale processors, who lack capacity and resources, into informal or opaque markets, undermining social goals and supply-chain integrity — especially where informal mining is already large.
claims.q: This regulatory burden risks pushing these actors into informal or markets with low levels of transparency, potentially undermining both the social development goals of traceability programmes and the integrity of mineral supply chains.
claims.e: Policy reasoning; no quantitative evidence offered.
claims.an: Relevant to Amazon illegal gold (D19) and Peruvian copper ASM (p. 55).

claims.t: China's Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law and Data Security Law (data localisation, transfer restrictions, countermeasures against entities complying with foreign sanctions) could obstruct foreign companies' global traceability systems and their ability to audit supply chains within China.
claims.q: The combination of China’s Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law and Data Security Law could also create obstacles for foreign companies implementing global traceability systems.
claims.an: Analyst interpretation: this cuts both ways — it may make Chinese-processed material harder to certify for US/EU markets (disadvantaging Chinese chains there), while shielding Chinese chains from Western scrutiny and raising compliance costs for Western firms reliant on Chinese midstream.

claims.t: China's dual role as world's largest producer and consumer of critical minerals is reflected in its own traceability regimes (Battery ID / 2018 battery recycling traceability provisions; Rare Earth Management Regulation in force October 2024), though data security laws may limit interoperability; the Battery ID system has difficulty mapping provenance to mine level.
claims.q: the dual role of the People’s Republic of China (hereafter, “China”) as both the world’s largest producer and consumer of critical minerals is reflected in its Battery ID system and Rare Earth Management Regulation
claims.an: China's state-administered tracing (REE flow records, export) reinforces state oversight of strategic minerals — consistent with M2 coordination.

claims.t: The CCCMC (overseen by China's Ministry of Commerce) issued Chinese Due Diligence Guidelines and an audit programme helping Chinese firms comply with London Metal Exchange responsible-sourcing requirements, assessed using the OECD Alignment Assessment Methodology — a common benchmark supporting consistency.
claims.q: has developed an audit programme to help Chinese companies comply with the London Metal Exchange’s responsible sourcing requirements.
claims.an: Chinese industry adapts to Western market-access standards rather than being excluded — suggests traceability regimes may not straightforwardly disadvantage Chinese supply.

claims.t: Copper production is among the least concentrated (mining in over 60 countries; Chile, China and Peru together less than half), but refining is more concentrated with China at 45%.
claims.q: Refining is more concentrated, with China accounting for 45% of global copper refining.
claims.an: Chile and Peru (top LAC copper producers) feed a refining stage where China holds 45% — structural basis for Chinese demand-pull and processing ties.

claims.t: Lithium is sourced primarily from Latin American brines (Argentina, Chile) and Australian hard rock (over 70% of 2023 production), but China accounted for nearly two-thirds of refined lithium production in 2023.
claims.q: This process largely occurs in China, which accounted for nearly two-thirds of refined production in 2023.
claims.an: Core evidence for M7: LAC lithium upstream is coupled to Chinese midstream processing.

claims.t: Low-grade nickel is processed into intermediates largely in Indonesia and then converted into battery-grade nickel sulphate in China, which hosts almost 75% of battery-sulphate production.
claims.q: Almost 75% of battery-sulphate production takes place in China.

claims.t: Graphite is the most geographically concentrated mineral (about 80% of mining and almost 100% of refining in China), with nearly 300 companies and low top-three concentration, making full traceability extremely difficult and costly.
claims.q: Graphite is the most geographically concentrated mineral, with about 80% of mining and almost 100% of refining occurring in China.
claims.an: Explains why US FEOC rules needed an 'impracticable-to-trace' exemption for graphite (p. 32).

claims.t: Cobalt mining is concentrated in the DRC (65%), with ASM 5–15%; China accounts for almost 80% of refining and smelting; disengaging from the informal sector is not responsible sourcing and may worsen child labour.
claims.q: At the midstream, cobalt refining mostly takes place in China, a market that accounts for almost 80% of refining and smelting operations.
claims.an: DRC is a useful comparator for LAC: upstream supplier with Chinese-dominated midstream.

claims.t: Rare earths: over 85% of mining in the top three producers and over 90% of refining in China; China has only two main refiners, making it hard for other supply-chain firms to exert leverage on responsible sourcing.
claims.q: China has only two main rare earth element refiners, making it potentially challenging for other companies in the supply chain to exert leverage on responsible sourcing issues.
claims.an: Concentration limits the efficacy of buyer-driven (Western) traceability leverage.

claims.t: Rare-earth supply chains face social/governance risks hard to trace in illegal mining, e.g. smuggling from Myanmar (Kachin State, KIO-controlled), Malaysia and Viet Nam into China, where processors combine diverse sources.
claims.q: may be particularly difficult to trace in cases of illegal mining, such as smuggling from Myanmar, Malaysia and Viet Nam to China.
claims.an: Comparative case of illicit mining feeding Chinese processing — analogous issue to illegal gold in the Amazon (D19), though D19 does not link Amazon gold to China.

claims.t: In Peru copper ASM employs an estimated 100,000 people in almost complete informality, entering legal chains via concentrators or 'invoicers'; Chile's state-owned ENAMI (since 1960) buys ASM copper and gold, smelts, and provides credit and capacity building.
claims.q: In Peru, it is estimated to employ 100 000 people working in almost complete informality.
claims.e: Country examples (source not specified in text).
claims.an: Chile's ENAMI is a LAC state-led model for formalising ASM — a contrast case to Peru's informality.

claims.t: Lack of FPIC and insufficient consultation have led to opposition to lithium projects in Argentina (as well as Portugal and the US); there have been governance issues over licence acquisition in Chile, the DRC and Namibia.
claims.q: Insufficient consultation with local communities and the absence of free, prior and informed consent from Indigenous Peoples have led to opposition to extraction projects, such as in Argentina, Portugal and the United States.
claims.an: Domestic political economy constraints on lithium development in LAC apply regardless of investor nationality.

claims.t: Legal artisanal gold supply chains cannot compete with informal or illegal buyers offering higher prices (because smuggled gold avoids taxes) and immediate payment; Brazil's Ouro Alvo project uses geochemical, morphological and isotopic signatures to verify chain of custody; Swiss Better Gold Association and Alliance for Responsible Mining run formalisation/closed-pipe traceability in South America.
claims.q: As a result, legal artisanal mining supply chains cannot compete with informal or illegal buyers who offer higher prices (as the material is subsequently smuggled without paying taxes) and immediate compensation.
claims.e: Box 6.1 lessons from gold traceability pilots.
claims.an: Direct bridge to D19 (illegal gold and organized crime in the Amazon).

claims.t: Colombia requires (since 2023) mining producers and traders to record mineral commercial transactions on a government platform via approved providers, operates a 2024 Mining Traceability and Transaction Control System with physical mine inspections, and called for an international agreement on mineral traceability at COP16.
claims.q: At the international level, Colombia’s call for an international agreement at the United Nations Biodiversity Conference of the Parties (COP16) signalled a growing recognition of the need for global co-ordination on mineral traceability.
claims.an: Example of LAC agency in shaping global mineral governance rules.

claims.t: Traceability used to avoid jurisdictions (trade sanctions, origin requirements, industrial policies disincentivising sourcing from specific jurisdictions) falls outside responsible business conduct; RBC-oriented policy should incentivise addressing risk rather than avoiding it.
claims.q: In some cases, traceability may support compliance with industrial policies that disincentivise sourcing from specific jurisdictions or with sanctions on entities within the supply chain. However, these policy objectives fall outside the scope of responsible business conduct.
claims.an: The closest the report comes to acknowledging the geo-economic (anti-China) use of traceability (e.g. FEOC), while distancing OECD RBC from it.

claims.t: Mineral-producing countries may use traceability for product differentiation supporting higher prices, while downstream countries can use tax credits for minerals sourced from designated countries to incentivise traceability.
claims.q: For example, mineral-producing countries may be interested in increasing traceability to enable product differentiation, potentially supporting higher prices for products with strong performance throughout the supply chain.
claims.an: Analyst: a channel through which LAC producers (e.g. Chile/Argentina lithium) could gain from Western 'designated country' incentives — a potential US/EU counterweight to Chinese demand, if premiums materialise.
