claims.t: Mandatory due-diligence pressures largely rely on downstream enforcement with requirements cascading slowly upstream; the Global Battery Alliance's 2024 Battery Passport pilots (10 consortia, 80% of global EV battery manufacturing, ~250 site-level reports) found firms limited disclosure over commercial sensitivity and comparability problems.
claims.q: Working with ten consortia representing 80% of global EV battery manufacturing, the pilots revealed several critical insights.
claims.an: Since much EV battery manufacturing is Chinese (external knowledge), participation of 80% of the industry suggests Chinese firms engage in Western-led passport schemes — not stated explicitly in the report.

claims.t: Over the past two decades Chinese criminal networks have expanded in LAC alongside China's legal trade and investment expansion.
claims.q: Chinese criminal networks have expanded in Latin America and the Caribbean, just like in other regions of the world, alongside China’s legal trade and investment expansion in the region.
claims.e: Author's synthesis of fieldwork and secondary sources (GAO, Ellis 2011, Brookings work).
claims.an: Implies the illicit footprint co-moves with legal economic expansion, i.e. it is a by-product rather than a driver of China's economic ties.

claims.t: Chinese legal businesses in ports, infrastructure, fisheries and extractive industries also sometimes violate regulations and engage in corruption and illicit practices.
claims.q: Crucially, however, Chinese legal businesses, such as some of those involved in ports, infrastructure, fisheries, and extractive industries, also sometimes violate regulatory measures and engage in corruption and nefarious and illicit practices.
claims.e: GAO report; examples in mining, logging, fishing sections.
claims.an: Only explicit reference to ports/infrastructure in the testimony; no specific port project is named.

claims.t: Chinese networks remain the principal suppliers of precursor chemicals for fentanyl and methamphetamine to Mexican cartels, also supply chemicals for cocaine processing, and pivot to non-scheduled precursors after each wave of Chinese scheduling.
claims.q: Chinese networks remain the principal suppliers for precursor chemicals for the production of fentanyl and methamphetamine for Mexican cartels.
claims.e: Author's prior research; US DOJ cases; Indian networks named as second most frequent supplier.
claims.an: This is the issue that most directly drives US security framing of China in the hemisphere.

claims.t: After China's 2019 class-wide scheduling of fentanyl-type substances (achieved through US diplomacy), Chinese suppliers shifted from shipping finished fentanyl to the US to supplying precursors to Mexican groups; Mexican cartels now synthesise most US-bound fentanyl and methamphetamine.
claims.q: After China scheduled the entire class of fentanyl-type substances in 2019 as a result of U.S. diplomacy, Chinese supply networks shifted from exporting finished fentanyl directly to the United States to supplying an expanding range of precursors and pre-precursor chemicals to Mexican criminal groups.
claims.an: Evidence that US diplomacy did produce a Chinese policy change (a 'US instrument worked' case), though with displacement effects.

claims.t: Chinese underground banking networks have become the top money launderers for Mexican cartels, displacing the Black Peso Exchange, because they pass costs onto Chinese citizens evading capital controls and so offer cheaper rates.
claims.q: Chinese underground banking networks have become the top money launders for Mexican cartels, displacing other long-established money laundering systems in the region and elsewhere in the world.
claims.e: Reuters (Jorgic 2020); US investigations and court cases; DOJ 2024 indictment.
claims.an: Bank of China named (p. 7) as among firms used per US investigations — a link between a state bank and illicit flows that feeds US securitised framing.

claims.t: The spread of Chinese underground banking could lead legal businesses and political actors to move funds outside regulated banks, reducing AML reach and central-bank visibility and creating a parallel financial system that undermines domestic policies.
claims.q: a parallel financial system could undermine domestic policies.

claims.t: US–China counternarcotics and AML cooperation, revived by the Biden administration in 2024 (working group, new scheduling, Treasury–PBoC platform, arrests of Chinese launderers), was disrupted by Trump's January 2025 fentanyl-linked tariffs; cooperation is contingent on broader strategic relations.
claims.q: Thus, the U.S.-China anti-money-laundering cooperation was disrupted when the Trump administration imposed fentanyl-linked tariffs on China in January 2025.
claims.e: Chronology of US–China fentanyl diplomacy 2019–2025; author's Brookings analyses; FinCEN advisory; DOJ indictment.
claims.an: Coercive US instrument (tariffs) undermined a cooperative instrument that was producing results.

claims.t: In 2025 China created counter-leverage against fentanyl tariffs (counter-tariffs, boycott of politically salient US exports like soybeans, restrictions on rare earths) and by October 2025 offered Trump essentially the same deliverables already agreed with Biden, double-counting them.
claims.q: It was essentially able to double-count the same deliverables to two different U.S. administrations.
claims.e: Chronology of 2025 US–China diplomacy; October 2025 Trump–Xi summit.
claims.an: Illustrates limits of US coercive statecraft against China; rare-earth export leverage links to M7. Soybean boycott implicitly benefits Latin American (e.g. Brazilian/Argentine) soy exporters, though the testimony does not say so.

claims.t: The Biden administration's 2023 Global Coalition to Address Synthetic Drug Threats was an important platform for engaging LAC; the Trump administration let it lapse and instead launched the 'Shield of the Americas', a small coalition aimed at drugs, migration and China's role in Latin America.
claims.q: the Trump administration has let the Global Coalition to Address Synthetic Drug Threats die on the vine.
claims.an: Shield of the Americas explicitly bundles China with drugs and migration — strong evidence of security framing of US China policy in the region.

claims.t: The Trump administration emphasises a highly militarised counternarcotics approach, urging Shield of the Americas members to adopt military rather than criminal-justice measures, and has deemphasised capacity building and anti-corruption by dismantling USAID and cutting INL.
claims.q: the Trump administration has further strongly deemphasized capacity building and institutional support for criminal justice systems and anti-corruption efforts as core tools against organized crime.
claims.an: Key evidence for the rhetoric–instrument gap: heightened China rhetoric paired with removal of non-coercive tools.

claims.t: Chinese intermediaries link LAC extractive sectors with Chinese demand, capital, logistics and markets; because China is the largest importer of many commodities, a few intermediaries can profoundly shape local markets and governance.
claims.q: Because China is the world’s largest importer of many of these commodities, even a relatively small number of Chinese intermediaries can profoundly shape local markets and distort governance incentives and systems.
claims.an: Demand-pull logic parallels the legal commodity relationship (M1).

claims.t: In illegal gold mining in Peru, Bolivia, Guyana, Venezuela and Ecuador, Chinese companies and brokers provide capital, heavy machinery, fuel, mercury/cyanide, often via 'partnerships' with local cooperatives or political patrons, then buy and launder the gold with falsified origin documents; pre-financing and guaranteed purchase have transformed artisanal mining into larger, more destructive operations.
claims.q: Chinese networks’ participation has at times transformed small-scale artisanal mining into far more extensive and environmentally detrimental operations.
claims.e: UNODC (2025) reports; Diálogo/The Watch (2025); investigative reporting.
claims.an: Rarely do Chinese actors appear as illegal miners themselves.

claims.t: In Peru, more than 70% of timber shipped to China from Callao in 2021 came from companies on the government's red list for suspected illegality, showing systemic illicit sourcing in China-bound exports; but illegal timber also flows to India, Europe and the US.
claims.q: more than 70% of timber shipped to China from the Port of Callao in 2021 came from companies that were on the Peruvian government’s “red list” for suspected illegality or ongoing legal proceedings

claims.t: Chinese wildlife traffickers organise poaching of jaguars, songbirds, parrots, reptiles, totoaba, shark fins, sea cucumbers and seahorses, using legal Chinese trade infrastructure, diaspora networks and Mexican criminal groups, and sometimes the same channels as for timber, minerals and drugs; wildlife and timber also serve as barter to pay for precursors.
claims.q: Thus, wildlife products and timber no longer function merely as direct illicit revenue sources, but also as commodities for value transfer and barter to pay for drug precursors.
claims.an: Species list on p. 11.

claims.t: Large Chinese fishing fleets engage in IUU fishing off Ecuador, Peru, Chile and Argentina (flotillas of 300–500 vessels), causing regional losses up to $2.3bn/yr; some vessels may double as maritime militia or carry spy equipment.
claims.q: Chinese flotillas of 300-500 vessels at a time have been documented operating off of Ecuador, Peru, Chile, and Argentina and in their exclusive economic zones
claims.e: ODI (2020); American University/InSight Crime (2022); The Economist (2023).
claims.an: Securitises a commercial activity (fishing).

claims.t: Facing international pressure, China has taken partial steps against IUU fishing: 2019 Fisheries Law revisions, June 2023 acceptance of WTO Fisheries Subsidies Agreement, 2022 fisheries Five-Year Plan to shrink fleet, 2025 ratification of the Port State Measures Agreement; enforcement remains limited.
claims.q: Facing international diplomatic pressure, China has begun cracking down on IUU fishing linked to Chinese vessels.
claims.an: Evidence that external (including US) pressure can modify Chinese behaviour at the margin.

claims.t: Illicit (and legal) resource extraction for export to China reinforces commodity dependence, skewing economies toward primary commodities with volatile prices and capturing value in criminal networks, deepening the resource curse.
claims.q: By privileging the rapid exploitation of natural resources for export to China, Chinese traders and their partners skew economies toward primary commodities with high environmental externalities and volatile prices, rather than toward higher value, more diversified sectors.
claims.e: CEPAL Review (Freitas da Rocha & Bielschowsky 2018); CFR (Lawson-Remer 2012).
claims.an: Converges with dependency/reprimarisation literature (M10).

claims.t: Mixed legal/illegal Chinese portfolios raise the political costs of enforcement because prosecutions can be framed as attacks on investment, jobs or bilateral ties; officials hesitate to confront China-linked actors.
claims.q: Such operations also raise the political costs of enforcement, since investigations and prosecution can easily be framed as attacks on investment, jobs, or bilateral economic ties.
claims.an: Mechanism by which economic interdependence with China generates domestic political constituencies that protect it — relevant to why relationships consolidate.

claims.t: Erosion of fiscal capacity from IUU fishing, illegal logging and mining increases dependence on short-term rents or external financing, strengthening leverage of domestic oligarchs and foreign state-linked investors.
claims.q: increase dependence on short-term rents or external financing, strengthening the leverage of domestic oligarchs and foreign state-linked investors.
claims.an: Suggests a feedback loop in which weakened fiscal capacity increases demand for (e.g. Chinese) external financing.

claims.t: Chinese state enforcement is selective and subordinated to geostrategic interests; some criminal groups (e.g. 14K Triad) provide services to the CCP and Chinese firms, including building influence networks that secure favourable business deals; China acts mainly when red lines are crossed (violence against Chinese, capital flight, opposition to CCP) or exposure becomes too costly.
claims.q: Such services include establishing networks of corruption and influence among foreign politicians and businesses that can be parlayed into securing favorable business deals for Chinese companies or extending China’s diplomatic and political influence in specific countries.
claims.e: Author's Brookings work; ProPublica; United Front literature.
claims.an: Author explicitly cautions against reading this as systematic state direction (p. 18–19).

claims.t: Beijing's management of criminal groups should not be interpreted as systematically directing all Chinese criminal networks; rather it selectively shields actors at the crime–business–state intersection.
claims.q: Cumulatively, China’s managed approached to criminal groups should not be interpreted as the Chinese government systematically directing all Chinese criminal networks.
claims.an: Important caveat against overstated 'state-directed crime' narratives in US discourse.

claims.t: China markets its surveillance/technology-driven policing model in LAC: Huawei Safe City bought by at least 35 major cities; ECU 911 financed by Chinese loans and built by Huawei and CEIEC; exports to Argentina and Bolivia; these lock in long-term vendor relationships and create asymmetric dependencies and espionage risks.
claims.q: They also lock governments into long-term relationships with Chinese firms for maintenance, software updates, and data management.
claims.e: NYT (2019), Reuters (2019), AidData, Ellis (2022), Security Boulevard (2025).
claims.an: An example of China's bundled finance + technology (loan-financed, Chinese-built) model extending into the security sector.

claims.t: Weakly governed, violent states seeking visible security gains are particularly susceptible to Chinese turnkey surveillance offers, which may enhance Beijing's leverage rather than strengthen rule of law.
claims.q: Weakly governed and highly violent environments where governments urgently seek visible security gains are particularly susceptible to Chinese offers of turnkey surveillance and policing systems.
claims.an: Demand-side explanation (LAC agency) of Chinese uptake; Chinese assistance described as unconstrained by human-rights safeguards (p. 20) — a non-conditionality attraction (M6).

claims.t: Reliance on Chinese surveillance/training could complicate US counternarcotics partnerships by constraining US intelligence sharing; when both China and the US underemphasise institutional impartiality, anti-crime efforts become a tool of geopolitical competition.
claims.q: Anti-crime and anti-corruption efforts become a narrow tool of political and geopolitical competition, where advantage can easily swing toward U.S. adversaries.
claims.an: Implicit critique of current US approach.

claims.t: To persuade LAC to eschew Chinese technology, the US must provide alternatives; Congress could authorise dedicated financing such as a regional security and governance facility for acquiring US/allied technology for anti-crime, port monitoring and customs.
claims.q: To be effective in persuading Latin American and Caribbean countries to eschew Chinese technologies, with their associated espionage and repression risks, the United States will need to provide them with technological alternatives for critical infrastructure and public safety systems.
claims.an: Implicit acknowledgment that warnings alone (sticks) do not work without affordable alternatives (carrots) — M3.

claims.t: US domestic capacity is inadequate: Coast Guard platforms tied up in counternarcotics; Fish and Wildlife inspectors flat since the 1970s; HSI capacity reoriented to undocumented migrants; OCDETF dismantled by Trump administration; FCPA prosecutions minimised.
claims.q: Before they were dismantled by the Trump administration, they were some of the world’s most effective law enforcement bodies.
claims.an: Shows US priorities (migration) crowding out other instruments.

claims.t: The US should treat China-linked criminal activity in LAC as a governance challenge rather than a drug-control problem, through multi-sectoral, rule-of-law approaches rather than narrowly militaristic ones.
claims.q: Overall, the United States should treat China-linked criminal activity in Latin America as a governance challenge, not merely a drug-control problem.

claims.t: Chinese migrant smuggling is small relative to intra-Latin American undocumented migration to the US.
claims.q: the scale of Chinese migrant smuggling pales in comparison to the scale of undocumented migration into the United States from within Latin America.
claims.an: A caveat against inflating the China–migration link that the Shield of the Americas framing implies.

claims.t: Illegal gold mining and drug trafficking in the Amazon operate within the same criminal ecosystem, marked by shared logistics, territorial control, illicit financial flows and operational cooperation.
claims.q: The findings suggest that illegal gold mining and drug trafficking operate within the same criminal ecosystem, characterized by shared logistics, territorial control, illicit financial flows, and operational cooperation.
claims.e: Content analysis of 41 investigative/institutional documents; VNSA mapping (Table 3).
claims.an: Core security-landscape evidence for M12.

claims.t: Criminal convergence is defined as a systemic interaction of criminal activities, actors and environments that creates a self-regulated, functional and resilient criminal ecosystem — a symbiosis sharing flows and infrastructures, not a simple overlap.
claims.q: “criminal convergence” is defined as a systemic interaction between criminal activities, actors and environments that creates a self-regulated, functional and resilient criminal ecosystem.
claims.e: Conceptual synthesis of GST, functional ecology and convergence literature.
claims.an: Conceptual tool; peripheral to central question.

claims.t: 34 organizations classified as Violent Non-State Actors operate in the Amazon's illegal gold trade chain, some originating outside the Americas (Asia, Europe), and many also run drug trafficking.
claims.q: In total, 34 organizations classified as Violent Non-State Actors were identified operating in the Amazon region participating in the illegal gold trade chain, some of them originating from other continents (such as Asia and Europe).
claims.e: VNSA inventory in Table 3 compiled from content analysis.
claims.an: Asian-origin groups in the table are Chinese criminal groups (Dragón Rojo; Chinese/Hong Kong groups) — criminal, not state, actors.

claims.t: Armed groups have transformed their operational capacity: FARC dissidents entered Brazilian territory in 2021 to collect fees from miners; Comandos de la Frontera compete for drug routes and gold areas with Brazilian and Ecuadorian factions and external cartels; the ELN uses illegal gold mining to finance operations.
claims.q: Recent episodes, such as the incursion of dissident groups from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia into Brazilian territory in 2021 to collect fees from miners
claims.e: Citations to GIATOC (2016) and InSight Crime (2024).
claims.an: Cross-border spillover of Colombian armed actors into Brazil is a security concern relevant to US/regional security agendas (analyst).

claims.t: Criminal systems can be analysed using four variables (Agent Networks, Levels and Scales, Behavioral Patterns, Illicit Niches), and state–crime relations follow Lupsha's phases of predation, parasitism and symbiosis.
claims.an: Table 2 on PDF p. 9 lists subclassifications.

claims.t: Lack of state control in remote areas enables illegal mining, and corruption — including direct participation of state agents — is a critical facilitating factor.
claims.q: Corruption is a critical facilitating factor: illegal mining frequently flourishes where enforcement is weak or where state agents themselves participate in the activity.

claims.t: Igarapé Institute data show violent crimes, slave labour, drug crimes or weapons possession in 29% of Brazilian Federal Police operations (2016–2021), with criminal-organization investigations in 51% overall and 47% of illegal-mining operations.
claims.q: violent crimes against the person, slave labor, drug-related crimes, or possession of weapons, ammunition and explosives were present in 29% of all Federal Police operations

claims.t: GIATOC (2016) linked illegal mining with paramilitarism and identified illegal mines as critical points for slavery in Colombia and Peru and rising human trafficking for illegal mining in Colombia.
Gold's portability and easy conversion into cash without traceability make it attractive for money laundering, and global demand for gold drives illegal exploration.
claims.q: Gold can be transported in small quantities and readily converted into cash without proper traceability, making it attractive for money laundering (asset laundering).
claims.an: Connects to D17 on gold traceability.

claims.t: Integration of mining and drug trafficking occurs mainly through drug-trafficking organizations' logistics (air and river transport operators serving both) and gold's money-laundering potential; gold can pay drug suppliers and drugs are sold to miners in mining zones.
claims.q: This integration occurs mainly through the structured logistical capabilities of drug trafficking organizations and the money laundering potential that gold offers to these same groups.
claims.e: FBSP (2024); Franchi and Rodrigues (2024); Amazônia Real (2025).

claims.t: Drug trafficking is not the most frequent crime associated with illegal gold mining: extortion/territorial control (22 VNSAs) and armed protection (20) exceed drug trafficking (18); firearms trafficking appears in 7.
claims.q: Although this article focuses on what has been called “narco-mining”, drug trafficking was not the most recurrent form of criminal activity associated with illegal gold mining.
claims.e: Coding of activities per VNSA (Table 4, image).
claims.se: gold; extortion; drug trafficking; arms trafficking
claims.an: Qualifies a drugs-centred framing of Amazon security: territorial control/extortion economies are more pervasive.

claims.t: Niche convergence is spatial: gold deposits cluster in zones crossed by consolidated drug-trafficking corridors, which supply mines, launder money and transport gold — the trafficking logistics network indicates the intra-regional distribution of illegal gold.
claims.q: Drug trafficking routes pass through several mineral exploration areas, and serving as a powerful vector of convergence.

claims.t: Lack of gold traceability allows illegally extracted gold to enter legal processes; Peru, officially South America's main gold producer/exporter, exports more gold than it produces and much of its legal gold exports are of unknown origin, suggesting it serves as a regional processing point for illicit gold.
claims.q: This supports the hypothesis that Peru functions as a contact and processing point for the region’s illicit gold destined for the rest of the world.
claims.e: Comparison of production vs exports (UN-Comtrade 2022; World Gold Council 2022; Figs. 5–6).
claims.an: Destination markets for Peru's gold are not stated in text (Fig. 5 image).

claims.t: Brazilian factions are central actors: the PCC provides weapons, machinery and protection and controls gold logistics in exchange for drugs (and partners with Tren de Aragua); Comando Vermelho finances and supplies illegal mines (including in Madre de Dios, Peru) and allies with Colombian dissidents to export illegal gold.
claims.q: Provides weapons and machinery, protects miners, and controls gold logistics
claims.e: Table 3 compiled from O Globo, Bloomberg Línea, Repórter Brasil, OjoPúblico, UOL, Pesquisa FAPESP, El País.
claims.an: PCC entry is on PDF p. 15; CV entry on p. 14.

claims.t: Tren de Aragua controls routes, airstrips and rivers, recruits migrants for forced labour, engages in extortion and partners with the PCC in illegal gold; Tren de Guayana runs a 'parallel government' in Bolívar mines; Venezuelan gold 'sindicatos' operate with authority connivance.
claims.q: Controls routes, airstrips, and rivers; recruits migrants for forced labor
claims.e: Table 3 (Castro et al. 2025; Bechara 2023; Pérez 2023; Unidad Investigativa de Venezuela 2024; Singer 2020; HRW 2020).
claims.an: Tren de Aragua is a focus of US security discourse (external knowledge); the article itself makes no US link.

claims.t: The ELN directly controls mines in Venezuela and along the Brazil–Colombia border, cooperates with the Venezuelan military and FARC dissidents, and derives up to 60% of its illicit income from gold; several FARC dissident fronts (Acácio Medina, Carolina Ramírez, Armando Ríos, Miguel Botache Santillana, Comandos de la Frontera) tax, protect or control gold/coltan mines.
claims.q: up to 60% of its illicit income comes from gold
claims.e: Table 3 (Castro et al. 2025; Tarazona and Guarnizo 2024; Sassine and Fernandes 2019; InSight Crime 2022, 2023; Vélez 2024).

claims.t: State-embedded criminal actors: Venezuela's Cartel de los Soles (military) collects bribes and sells protection at mining sites and smuggles gold into Brazil; in Brazil, police-run militias control mines in the Kayapó Indigenous Territory and 'legalise' gold, and a paramilitary militia linked to a Roraima politician supplied weapons to mines — illustrating parasitic/symbiotic relations.
claims.q: Collects bribes from mining unions; provides political/military protection for
claims.e: Table 3 and analysis section (Tabory 2015; Camargos and Junqueira 2024; Camargos and Harari 2024; Bispo 2022a/b).
claims.an: The text names 'Jalser Renier (Brazil)' in the militia entry; the reference title (Bispo 2022a) refers to a Roraima deputy.

claims.t: Chinese criminal groups appear among the VNSAs: the 'Dragón Rojo' (Chinese mafia) has operated clandestine dredges in Peruvian rivers since the 1990s with extortion, human trafficking and drug trade; Chinese/Hong Kong groups traffic forced labour to gold mines and smuggle gold through Guyana.
claims.q: Traffic forced labor to gold mines and smuggle the metal through Guyana
claims.an: These are non-state criminal actors; the article makes no connection to the Chinese state, Chinese investment, or Chinese gold demand. Only China-related content in the document.

claims.t: Extra-regional actors connect Amazon gold to global markets: the Sinaloa Cartel buys illegally mined gold (and coltan) from Colombian groups to launder drug money; the 'Ndrangheta buys smuggled Peruvian/Bolivian gold; Hezbollah allegedly smuggles gold to Turkey/Iran; 'Los Kilates' exported illegal gold bars to the UAE and India.
claims.q: Purchases/extracts gold illegally, smuggles it to Turkey/Iran, and launders it to
claims.an: Named destinations of illicit gold are the UAE, India, Turkey/Iran — not China or the US in this text. External note (verify): Diálogo Americas is a US Southern Command publication, so the Hezbollah claim carries a US-security framing.

claims.t: The Amazon criminal ecosystem includes 'legal' actors (mining companies, gold buyers, banks) who help legalise illegal gold and contribute indirectly to environmental damage, but the article leaves them outside its analysis.
claims.q: This includes mining companies, gold buyers, banks and many others who may contribute indirectly to environmental damage.
claims.e: Scope statement drawing on green criminology (Van Uhm and Nijman 2022).
claims.an: Demand-side/corporate links (where traceability regimes such as those in D17 would bite) are not analysed.

claims.t: Land-use 'gray zones' (PADDD — protected-area downgrading, downsizing and degazettement) and special mining zones, such as Venezuela's Orinoco Mining Arc (111,843.70 km²), blur legal/illegal boundaries and enable illegal operations.
claims.an: State policy (Orinoco Mining Arc) as an enabler of illicit extraction.

claims.t: Viewed through agent network and geographic level, drug trafficking has a commensal relationship with illegal mining, justifying the 'narco-mining' label; this understanding is crucial for public policy, regional cooperation and crime prevention.
claims.q: This understanding is crucial for the design of public policies, regional cooperation and crime prevention strategies.
claims.an: Calls for regional cooperation; no mention of US or extra-regional security partners.

claims.t: The Bush and Obama administrations did not strongly contest China's advances. Aside from Obama's 're-engagement' rhetoric and some late policies (the Cuba thaw), no major initiatives were promoted to strengthen US relations with Latin America.
claims.q: no major policies or initiatives were promoted to strengthen the United States’ relations with Latin America during this period
claims.e: Secondary literature (Santibañes; León-Manríquez; Wigell and Soliz Landivar; Randall; Saragoza; Creutzfeldt).

claims.t: No significant balancing countermeasures, traditional or non-traditional, to China's advances can be identified between 2001 and 2017. The US response has been described as 'relaxed' and 'slow'.
claims.q: Moreover, no significant balancing countermeasures ... to China’s advances can be identified between 2001 and 2017.
claims.e: Literature review; the author's document analysis.

claims.t: The belated response is explained by regional structural conditions (waning US influence, China's rise) together with an unprecedented policy window under Trump's first term.
claims.q: the belated US response to China’s actions in Latin America is explained by the interplay of regional structural conditions ... as well as by the emergence of an unprecedented ‘policy window’ during Trump’s first term, which enabled a change in 2017.
claims.e: Neo-classical realist framework with Kingdon's multiple streams; document analysis.
claims.an: Central thesis.

claims.t: The window opened when the problem (concerns about China's advances), the policy (sticks and carrots readily available) and the politics (anti-China national mood and turnover of key personnel) aligned.
claims.q: the ‘problem’ (concerns about China’s advances in the region) became aligned with the ‘policy’ (sticks and carrots readily available to counter Beijing) and ‘politics’ (an anti-China ‘national mood’ and the turnover of key personnel in the US)

claims.t: Latin America is a most-likely case for a US response because of its strategic importance as the US 'backyard' and the US record of contesting hegemonic challengers since the Monroe Doctrine (Britain, Nazi Germany, the USSR). The delay is therefore puzzling.
claims.q: I focus on Latin America, considering it is a most likely case for a US response
claims.an: Frames the puzzle.

claims.t: Structural realism can explain why the US responded (changing balance of power) but not when. Several Chinese milestones could have triggered an earlier response and did not.
claims.q: a structural realist explanation could explain why the US responded (i.e. changes in the balance of power), but it cannot explain the timing of the policy shift.
claims.e: Comparison of timing with milestones (2014 trade ranking, China–CELAC, etc.).

claims.t: The 2017 shift was not only rhetorical: it mobilised resources and policy instruments with enduring effects. Its maintenance under Biden shows the problem was real and structural, not personal to Trump.
claims.q: The foreign policy shift of 2017 was not only rhetorical; it involved policy change with enduring effects, mobilizing resources and policy instruments.
claims.e: Continuity of official threat perceptions and policies across administrations.
claims.an: This is the main point of friction with the 'rhetoric without commensurate instruments' hypothesis (M3). It should be checked against financing data (D04 and others).

claims.t: The 9/11 attacks shifted US priorities, producing a general lack of interest in Latin America. The region moved to lower-level officials and a militarised war-on-terror agenda.
claims.q: One of the main arguments is that the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US mainland dramatically shifted US foreign policy priorities, leading to a general lack of interest in relations with Latin America from that year on.
claims.e: Hakim 2006; Milani 2021; Emerson 2010; Riggirozzi and Tussie 2011.
claims.an: Security-agenda narrowing parallels the later securitised framing in D18.

claims.t: Washington's shift to the Middle East opened a window of opportunity for China. Urdinez et al. show an inverse relationship between Chinese economic expansion and US hegemonic influence in 21 countries (2003–2014): Beijing 'filled the void'.
claims.q: Washington’s foreign policy shift towards the Middle East opened a window of opportunity for Beijing to increase its presence in Latin America.
claims.e: Urdinez et al. 2016 dataset (Chinese SOE investment, bank loans, manufacturing exports vs US exports, FDI, aid, military aid and UNGA vote convergence).

claims.t: China's advances began in economics (second-largest trading partner by 2014; investment and funding) and moved into politics (diplomatic boost under Hu Jintao, strategic partnerships with almost every country, the 2014 China–CELAC forum) and the military domain (arms sales, personnel networks, the PLA-controlled Neuquén space station).
claims.q: the establishment of a space monitoring base in Neuquén, Argentinian Patagonia, controlled by China’s People’s Liberation Army.
claims.e: Ray and Batista Barbosa 2020; Myers et al. 2024; Ellis; Strüver 2014; Myers 2020.
claims.an: China's second-largest trading partner status is stated on p. 912.

claims.t: China's emergence (enabled by US waning) was a necessary but not sufficient condition. China became a problem in the early 2000s, but this does not explain the timing of the shift.
claims.q: For the US to respond, there needed to be a problem first, and China’s regional advances became a problem in the early 2000s. However, this was not a sufficient condition to explain the timing of the US foreign policy shift.

claims.t: Until 2005 US concerns were confined to specific issues such as the Panama Canal. The US–Panama Security Act bill of 1997 voiced concern that Hutchison Whampoa's management of the ports of Balboa and Cristóbal raised the specter of Chinese political influence.
claims.q: ‘raised the specter of the expansion of Chinese political influence in Panama’
claims.an: Ports-security concern dating to 1997; the author says it remained a recurrent topic in Congress.

claims.t: From 2005 Congress identified China's advances as a major problem in bipartisan hearings. It criticised US neglect and the lack of a policy beyond trade and counternarcotics, and by the late 2010s called urgently to 'counter' China.
claims.q: criticized the lack of a ‘real policy in the hemisphere outside of trade and counternarcotics’
claims.e: Six hearings (2005, 2005, 2008, 2015, 2019, 2022); named members of both parties.
claims.an: Shows legislative discourse running well ahead of executive action, a version of the premise's 'increasing prominence' of discourse.

claims.t: The executive first acknowledged the problem in 2005. SOUTHCOM's Craddock (2005) called China's presence an emerging dynamic that 'must not be ignored'; in 2006 he noted China's use of economic measures, diplomacy, infrastructure, trade deals and no-strings resources for militaries. The DIA threat assessments of 2006 and 2008 warned of resource access and image-building.
claims.q: offering resources to cash-strapped militaries and security forces with no strings attached
claims.an: Early US military recognition of China's no-conditions appeal (M6).

claims.t: Under Obama, SOUTHCOM commanders (Fraser, Kelly, Tidd, 2011–2016) warned of rising Chinese arms sales and visits, a 'partnership vacuum' due to reduced US engagement, and China pivoting to the Western Hemisphere as the US pivoted to the Pacific.
claims.q: as Washington ‘pivoted’ to the Pacific, China had ‘pivoted to the Western Hemisphere’

claims.t: Under Obama's second term, Latin America lost priority to East Asia; the Asia pivot meant Latin America was not discussed in the threat assessments.
claims.q: The decision to actively contest China with the ‘pivot’ to Asia was reflected in the assessments, in which Latin America was not discussed.
claims.an: Clear evidence of attention displacement.

claims.t: In 2017–2021 China in Latin America was a top priority. SOUTHCOM spoke of 'malign influence' and a 'threat'. The threat assessments from 2018 covered security influence in Venezuela, PLA logistics basing and COVID-19 assistance inroads. The 2017 NSS criticised state-led investments and loans.
claims.q: pull the region into its orbit through state-led investments and loans
claims.an: The US executive explicitly names Chinese state-led finance (M2) as the problem.

claims.t: The Biden 2022 NSS retained these concerns: China 'frequently uses its economic power to coerce countries', and the US committed to 'compete vigorously'.
claims.q: frequently uses its economic power to coerce countries
claims.an: The quoted NSS passage is global; the Latin America-specific Biden policy is not described.

claims.t: Since 2017 the US has used a wide range of coercive and non-coercive diplomatic and economic countermeasures to limit countries' relations with Beijing. Examples include Pompeo's 2018–2020 warnings of 'political costs', pressure against Huawei 5G, and warnings by Breier and Chung of 'risks' and 'hidden costs'.
claims.q: The US response to China’s advances in Latin America since 2017 has included a wide range of coercive and non-coercive diplomatic and economic countermeasures aimed at limiting or diminishing countries’ relations with Beijing and at dissuading further exchanges in future.
claims.an: Mostly warnings ('sticks' of a discursive kind).

claims.t: Pompeo's 2019 pressure on President Piñera succeeded: Chile ended negotiations with Huawei on the trans-Pacific submarine cable and opted for the US alternative with Google.
claims.q: The pressure was successful, as Chile decided to end negotiations with Huawei and opted for the US alternative.
claims.an: One documented case of US counter-statecraft working, and notably one where a US commercial alternative existed.

claims.t: The US implemented economic countermeasures including sanctions, threats to end financial aid, inducements and promises of benefits. The main promise was America Crece (supporting development and infrastructure partnerships to compete with China). In November 2020, OFAC sanctioned CEIEC for surveillance tools in Venezuela.
claims.q: One of the main such promises was the announcement of the América Crece (Growth in the Americas) initiative
claims.an: The article's own wording ('promises', 'announcement') is consistent with an announced-versus-delivered gap (M3), though the author does not draw that conclusion.

claims.t: These instruments were available throughout the period and had been used against China in Asia (the Obama pivot), but were not used in Latin America until the window opened in 2017.
claims.q: They were not actively used to counter China’s advances in Latin America until the policy window opened during Trump’s first term, even though Washington did use them to counter China in other regions of the world before.
claims.e: Historical availability of US statecraft since 1823; comparison with the Asia pivot.
claims.an: Implies the delay was a matter of will and attention, not capacity (contra M3). It does not consider whether the instruments were adequate in scale to match Chinese finance.

claims.t: US negative views of China rose from 2006 (above 50% in 2013, 55% in 2016) but were not a major domestic issue under Bush and Obama. In 2016 the mood reached critical mass and Trump mobilised it in his campaign.
claims.q: surpassing 50 per cent of respondents in 2013 and reaching 55 per cent in 2016
claims.an: Domestic-politics driver of US policy timing.

claims.t: Bush and Obama-era officials were heterogeneous, with mostly moderate and cooperative views of China. Examples: Powell ('positive', not 'confrontational'), Rice ('candid, cooperative and constructive'), Kerry ('not by strategic rivalry, but by practical cooperation'), and Valenzuela and Jacobson (China 'not a threat', 'extremely positive'). Exceptions were Rumsfeld, Gates, Noriega, Clinton ('disturbing') and Carter.
claims.q: not by strategic rivalry, but by practical cooperation
claims.an: Threat-perception variable: elite consensus was absent.

claims.t: From January 2017 all US foreign-policy institutions were headed by China hard-liners in an unprecedented consensus. Tillerson praised the Monroe Doctrine and Bolton urged sanctions.
claims.q: Since January 2017, when Trump’s first term began, all US foreign policy-making institutions were headed by individuals with hard-line views on China, in an unprecedented consensus.
claims.e: Personnel analysis (Ross, Lighthizer, Navarro, Bannon, Tillerson, Pompeo, Breier, McMaster, Bolton, O'Brien, Mattis, Esper).

claims.t: The consensus persisted under Biden (Blinken, Nichols, Sullivan, Austin), with China seen as a threat but the tone softened to 'competition' rather than confrontation.
claims.q: The tone of the messaging changed, with some of these officials using more moderate terms such as competition instead of confrontation or contestation at times
claims.an: Continuity is shown at the level of discourse, which fits the premise's 'increasing prominence of discourse'.

claims.t: Under Obama the problem and policy streams were aligned but the politics stream was not: anti-China sentiment was not mobilised as a national mood, and elites did not uniformly see China in Latin America as a threat.
claims.q: during Obama’s presidency, the problem and policy streams were aligned, but the politics one was not.

claims.t: Senator Marco Rubio, later secretary of state in the second Trump administration, said in 2022 that the US cannot let the CCP absorb Latin America into its political-economic bloc.
claims.q: cannot afford to let the Chinese Communist Party expand its influence and absorb Latin America and the Caribbean into its private political economic bloc
claims.an: Only reference to the Trump II personnel; it signals continuity into 2025 but is not analysed.

claims.t: The framework can be generalised to US responses to China in other historically prioritised regions (Asia, Oceania, Indo-Pacific).

Chinese state-bank loans are easier to obtain than IMF loans because they carry fewer strings, and China's non-interference discourse is credible in the global South because China lacks a colonial past.
claims.q: loans from Chinese state banks are easier to obtain than International Monetary Fund (IMF) loans because they have fewer strings attached.
claims.e: Argument citing Jenkins (2022, p. 144); no new data.
claims.an: Core statement of the non-conditionality mechanism; applicable to LAC by analogy (e.g. Venezuela/Ecuador CDB loans) but the article provides no LAC evidence.

claims.t: Chinese aid has 'different strings attached': non-recognition of Taiwan, support for China in UN votes, non-support for Tibetan/Uighur independence, and non-interference in China's internal affairs.
claims.q: However, Chinese aid has different strings attached: non-recognition of Taiwan, support for China in votes in the United Nations, non-support for Tibetan or Uighur independence, and non-interference in China's internal affairs
claims.e: Cites Raess, Ren & Wagner (2022) and Garlick (2023, p. 71).
claims.an: Important qualification for the project: Chinese 'non-conditionality' is non-conditionality on domestic governance, not absence of political conditions. Directly relevant to LAC where most of Taiwan's remaining allies are located (analyst's external knowledge, not stated in the article).

claims.t: Unlike the EU, which attaches democracy and human-rights requirements to aid (a form of coercion), China does not explicitly state that partners should adopt its norms; it relies on repeated exposure and mimicry, especially by elites.
claims.q: Unlike the EU, with its explicit democracy and human rights agendas—often presented as a set of requirements accompanying aid, which thus clearly constitute a form of coercion—China does not directly state that it wants partner countries to absorb and adopt Chinese norms of behaviour.
claims.e: Conceptual argument building on Garlick & Qin (2023), Manners (2002), Kavalski (2010).
claims.an: Usable as conceptual contrast with US conditionality in LAC (e.g. governance/anti-corruption conditions), but the authors do not analyse US practice specifically.

claims.t: China keeps coercion in reserve for when persuasion, education and mimicry fail (e.g. sanctions on Lithuania over the Taiwan Representative Office), and coercion is ineffective where Beijing lacks economic leverage.
claims.q: Coercion is kept in reserve for cases where the three more subtle means of norm diffusion have failed
claims.an: Implies Chinese Taiwan-related coercion works best where trade/investment dependence is high — a testable proposition for LAC/Caribbean Taiwan allies.

claims.t: Non-discursive practices (e.g. One China, non-interference, loan-for-infrastructure deals) are expected to gain more traction than discursive ones because compliance can be enforced through economic leverage.
claims.q: Compliance with non-discursive practices can be achieved through coercive enforcement (namely, economic leverage) which is lacking in discursive diplomacy.
claims.e: Theoretical expectation later supported by descriptive evidence on Taiwan recognition and platform participation.
claims.an: Suggests material leverage, not ideational appeal, is the operative channel — consistent with an economics-first explanation of China's LAC expansion.

claims.t: The negative norms of non-interference and non-recognition of Taiwan are expected to be adopted as conditions of cooperation with China.
claims.q: These include norms such as the principle of non-interference in domestic affairs by external actors and the non-recognition of Taiwan, both of which are expected to be adopted as conditions of cooperation with China.
claims.an: Explicitly frames One China as a condition — useful to nuance the 'no-strings' narrative in LAC debates.

claims.t: China does not necessarily cut off all cooperation with countries that do not respect non-interference or One China; it keeps promoting its normative diplomacy to win them back.
claims.q: the PRC government does not necessarily completely cut off all cooperation with countries which do not respect these norms
claims.e: Conceptual argument; no case evidence given.
claims.an: Relevant to LAC: China trades extensively with Taiwan allies (e.g. Paraguay, Guatemala — analyst's external knowledge), consistent with this claim; verify with trade data.

claims.t: China's investment deals — state-backed loans funding infrastructure built by Chinese commercial actors, use of Chinese labour, and resource access as part payment — are not typical of Western practice and constitute a distinct Chinese norm.
claims.q: In particular, the Chinese use of state-backed loans to fund infrastructure construction by Chinese commercial actors is not a common Western practice.
claims.an: Bundled finance+construction model (M2) presented as a normative practice, not only an economic instrument.

claims.t: N+1 regional cooperation platforms (SCO, FOCAC, CASCF, China-CELAC) with regular meetings are not a feature of US or European diplomacy in the global South and are a distinctive Chinese practice; bilateral ties are nested within them.
claims.q: Regional cooperation platforms of this type, with annual or bi-annual meetings, are not generally a feature of US or European diplomacy in the global South, so can be considered a distinctive feature of Chinese normative diplomacy
claims.an: China-CELAC is the LAC instance; the article notes CELAC pre-existed the N+1 grouping. Contrast with US hemispheric mechanisms (OAS, Summit of the Americas) is not addressed by the authors.

claims.t: The 'support/embrace multilateralism' slogan expresses opposition to perceived US hegemony and is intended to promote Chinese influence at the expense of the US, underpinning China-led forums that exclude the US.
claims.q: the 'support/embrace multilateralism' discursive practice is intended to promote Chinese influence at the expense of the US.
claims.an: Frames China's multilateral platforms (incl. China-CELAC) as explicitly competitive with US influence.

claims.t: Xi-era Chinese slogans made little or no impression on global South leaders: none of the three uniquely Chinese units appeared in 16 UNGA speeches by Central Asian and sub-Saharan African leaders (2022–2023).
claims.q: Based on this analysis, it would appear that the Xi era discursive practices have made little or no impression on global South leaders.
claims.e: Frequency search of six discursive units in 16 UNGA General Debate speeches (Table 2).
claims.an: Weak ideational/soft-power uptake suggests ideology/discourse is not what drives alignment with China — consistent with brief's caution not to assume ideology.

claims.t: Chinese discursive practices are reproduced only by some leaders and only when addressing Chinese interlocutors (e.g. Ramaphosa at FOCAC 2018).
claims.q: In short, we find that Chinese discursive practices were reproduced only by some global South leaders, and only when they knew they were addressing Chinese interlocutors.
claims.e: Ramaphosa FOCAC 2018 speech; Mulatu Teshome 2022 interview; Chinese media reports of Central Asian meetings.
claims.an: Indicates strategic, audience-specific rhetorical alignment — a form of hedging/agency (M4).

claims.t: The One China negative norm has been accepted by the vast majority of global South states: by 2022 only 13 economically developing nations still had full diplomatic relations with Taiwan; in Africa only 1 of 52 (down from as many as 19 in the mid-1960s).
claims.q: It is therefore clear that the 'One China' negative norm had been accepted by the vast majority of nations in the global South.
claims.e: Figure 2 based on Rich & Banerjee (2015) and Panda (2020).
claims.an: The article does not name the 13 states; per analyst's external knowledge most were in Latin America/Caribbean and the Pacific (e.g. Paraguay, Guatemala, Belize, Haiti, St Kitts & Nevis, St Lucia, St Vincent & the Grenadines; Honduras until March 2023) — verify. LAC thus is the main remaining arena

claims.t: The return of some African states to Taiwan in the 1990s was probably linked to reduced post-Mao aid levels; Beijing reversed the trend after 1997.
claims.q: A factor in this was probably the reduction in the levels of aid during the post-Mao era
claims.an: Supports a material-inducement reading of recognition switches (relevant to Central American switches 2017–2023, which the article does not cover).

claims.t: Participation of global South states in China-led platforms and summits (BRI Forum Oct 2023, BRICS expansion incl. Argentina) indicates general acceptance of Chinese practices, though it may reflect deference to obtain BRI benefits.
claims.q: Attendance at these meetings can be interpreted as showing deference to Beijing as a benefactor of the global South simply in order to obtain more BRI benefits.
claims.e: Membership counts; attendance at BRI Forum 2023; BRICS expansion; Xi's absence from G20.
claims.an: Only explicit LAC country evidence in D21. Argentina's later withdrawal illustrates that political cycles (M5) can reverse such 'acceptance'.

claims.t: China earns a high degree of recognition for its non-discursive practices without attaching explicit conditions in the Western manner, while expecting partners to follow its practice-based norms.
claims.q: The PRC has earned a high degree of recognition for this portion of its normative diplomacy without attaching explicit conditions to it in the way that the West tends to do.
claims.an: Key formulation of M6 for the project's synthesis.

claims.t: Western counter-initiatives (EU Global Gateway, US B3W) will succeed only if they diffuse Western norms effectively; understanding China's practice-based success is the first step.
claims.q: The success of the EU's Global Gateway and the USA's B3W initiatives will depends in large part on their ability to diffuse Western norms effectively.
claims.an: Only explicit reference to a US instrument (B3W). The article does not assess B3W's finance volume or results — relevant to M3 only as a pointer.

claims.t: China's 'community of shared destiny' framing promises respect to partners but implies that cooperation depends on recognition and acceptance of Chinese practices; official LAC-related documents (MFA 2014, 'Build a Community of Shared Destiny for Common Progress') use the slogan in their titles.
claims.q: However, such respect must be mutual, which implies that cooperation is also dependent on Chinese practices (norms) being recognised and accepted.
claims.an: The 2014 MFA URL points to an Aug 2014 speech; analyst believes it relates to Xi's July 2014 Brasília China–LAC leaders' meeting — verify externally.

claims.t: China propagates a new and distinctive, relative doctrine of non-intervention that changes depending on who is interfering with whom, in what context and for what purpose.
claims.q: It argues that China propagates a new and distinctive approach to the doctrine of non-intervention, by which the doctrine changes depending on who is interfering with whom, in what context and for what purpose.
claims.e: Analysis of Chinese State practice and Chinese legal literature.
claims.an: Core thesis; useful for interpreting China's 'non-interference' offer to LAC as selective rather than universal.

claims.t: Chinese uses of non-intervention reflect the original concerns that animated the doctrine in the Global South and NAM ideas held for at least 70 years.
claims.q: These uses arguably reflect the original concerns that animated the doctrine in the Global South, and are in line with ideas which have been advocated by the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) for at least 70 years.
claims.an: Explains why China's sovereignty discourse resonates with Global South (incl. LAC) governments independent of ideology.

claims.t: Before the 1933 Montevideo Convention the US had claimed a right to intervene in Latin American States to protect nationals and recover debts; by ratifying Montevideo it accepted a more restrictive view. The doctrine of non-intervention emerged to protect Global South choices of political, economic, social and cultural systems.
claims.q: Before signing the Montevideo Convention, the US had invoked a right to intervene in Latin American States to 'protect its nationals or national interest, to recover public debt and other pecuniary claims based on injuries suffered by its nationals'
claims.e: Becker Lorca (2015); Montevideo Convention art 8; example of 1854 US naval bombardment of a Nicaraguan town (footnote 39).
claims.an: Key LAC-specific historical root: non-intervention is a Latin American legal tradition directed against the US, which gives China's non-interference discourse a receptive regional audience. Analyst interpretation, not the authors' claim about contemporary LAC.

claims.t: The Friendly Relations Declaration and the OAS Charter set the bar for 'coercion' far lower than the Tallinn Manual, covering activity designed to obtain 'advantages of any kind'.
claims.q: the Friendly Relations Declaration and the Charter of the Organization of American States set the bar for what constitutes 'coercion' far lower than the Tallinn Manual.
claims.an: Inter-American law encodes a broad anti-coercion norm — relevant when assessing LAC reception of US 'sticks' (M8) vs Chinese non-conditionality.

claims.t: Under a baseline theory of coercion, even an invitation to accept a loan or join a free-trade zone could be coercive if the offer is good enough to bend a State's will; what counts as coercion depends on context.
claims.q: international lawyers might think that an invitation to accept a loan, or to join a free trade zone or non-aggression pact is coercive, provided that the offer is good enough to bend the State's will.
claims.an: Conceptual tool: 'carrots' (Chinese loans) and 'sticks' (US pressure) can both be read as coercion depending on baseline — useful for evaluating claims that Chinese finance is non-coercive.

claims.t: Chinese critiques of foreign interference rest on a broad understanding of 'internal' affairs (e.g. in the 1990s China called Rwanda's genocide and Srebrenica 'domestic affairs') and fail to explain what makes alleged interventions coercive.
claims.q: Chinese critiques of foreign interference are premised on a broad understanding of what sort of affairs are considered 'internal'.

claims.t: China's classical approach to sovereignty derives from the 'hundred years of humiliation', when its prescriptive jurisdiction was usurped by Western powers and international law served foreign domination.
claims.q: International law was one key mechanism for this foreign domination.
claims.e: Historical account (Treaty of Nanjing 1842; Convention of Peking 1860; Mitchell 2022; Cai 2019).
claims.an: Shared anti-colonial/anti-imperial narrative China can invoke with LAC (cf. Xi on Latin America, C08).

claims.t: Xi Jinping (2024) presented the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence as a rallying force for developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America to resist foreign interference and follow independent development paths.
claims.q: more and more countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America have … stood up against foreign interference, and embarked on an independent path of development.
claims.e: Xi speech at 70th anniversary of the Five Principles, 28 June 2024.
claims.an: Explicit Chinese framing of Latin America within the anti-interference/independent-development narrative.

claims.t: China's self-imposed 'Five Nos' in Africa include no interference in development paths or internal affairs, no impositions of will, no political conditions on aid, and no political self-interest in investment and financing.
claims.q: no interference with African countries' exploration of development paths … ; no interference in Africa's internal affairs; no impositions of one's will on others; no attachment of political conditions to aid to Africa; and no political self-interest in investments and financing in Africa
claims.e: China Society of Private International Law (2021); SCIO white paper (2021).
claims.an: Formal statement of non-conditionality; Africa-specific, but the same principles feature in China's LAC policy papers (analyst's external knowledge — verify).

claims.t: China generally refrains from criticising like-minded governments' human-rights records and accuses Western governments of using human rights as a pretext for selfish intervention; it also objects to economic sanctions and military interventions outside UN Chapter VII.
claims.q: The Chinese Government and international lawyers have generally refrained from criticising likeminded governments for human rights violations. Instead, China has accused Western governments of using human rights as a pretext to intervene in foreign States for selfish motives.
claims.e: Chinese legal literature (Zhu 1992; Li 2007; Shao & Zhao 2003).
claims.an: Opposition to unilateral sanctions is relevant to sanctioned LAC states (Venezuela, Cuba, Nicaragua) — not discussed by the authors.

claims.t: China does not invoke non-intervention against all foreign pressure: it did not call the 2019 US currency-manipulator designation or the 2022 US chip export controls 'intervention', and accepts WTO rulings on censorship while rejecting UPR recommendations.
claims.q: The point remains that the Chinese Government accepts some types of interference by some actors, but not by others.
claims.e: PBoC statement 2019; China's WTO request DS615 (2022); Chen (2014); Qin (2011).
claims.an: Shows China treats economic/trade disputes in legal-economic (WTO) rather than sovereignty terms — non-intervention is aimed at governance/human-rights criticism.

claims.t: China's 'core interests', initially referring exclusively to Taiwan, have been broadened to Tibet, Xinjiang and the Diaoyu/Senkaku Islands, and involvement in them is opposed as interference.
claims.q: Subsequently, the scope of the Chinese 'core interests' has been broadened to include other territorial issues, such as China's sovereignty over Tibet, Xinjiang and the Diaoyu/Senkaku Islands.
claims.an: Confirms Taiwan as the foundational red line behind China's non-interference demands of partners (cf. D21's One China 'string').

claims.t: China itself engages in economic pressure that could be seen as interference: after Liu Xiaobo's 2010 Nobel Prize it imposed controls on Norwegian salmon (share fell from over 80% to 25%); it later excised Lithuania from its customs list to influence Lithuanian policy; Glaser describes Chinese coercive economic diplomacy in Southeast Asia.
claims.q: The share of Norwegian salmon imports in the Chinese market fell from over 80 per cent to 25 per cent.
claims.an: Qualifies the 'non-coercive China' framing; relevant if testing whether China uses trade leverage on LAC states over Taiwan (none discussed here).

claims.t: Chinese scholars propose that China adopt Western-style interventionist tools: 'protective intervention' (incl. military force to protect Chinese personnel and investments in strategically important locations), flexible recognition of governments, sanctions to protect investments, and long-arm jurisdiction.
claims.q: In sufficiently important geographical locations, preparations should be made for using military force to ensure the safety of Chinese personnel and investments.
claims.e: Yang Zewei (2012); Li Ming (2016); Xiao Yongping (2019).
claims.an: As Chinese overseas assets grow (incl. in LAC), pressure to protect investments may erode strict non-intervention — a long-run qualification of M6.

claims.t: Li Ming observes that Western countries, especially the US, use recognition and non-recognition of foreign governments as a tool to pursue interests abroad, and argues China should keep flexibility in applying non-interference when recognising governments.
claims.q: Western countries, and the US in particular, use the recognition and non-recognition of foreign governments as a tool to pursue their interests abroad.
claims.an: Analyst link: relevant to contested recognition in LAC (e.g. Venezuela 2019 Guaidó recognition by US vs China's continued recognition of Maduro) — not discussed in the article.

claims.t: The authors believe the relativisation of Chinese non-interventionism is sanctioned by the party-state, given Party control over legal scholarship on sensitive issues.
claims.q: the authors believe that the relativisation of the Chinese non-interventionism is sanctioned by the Chinese party-state.
claims.e: Institutional analysis (Party committees in law schools; Shambaugh 2007; Roberts 2017).

claims.t: Several States have adopted Chinese language on intervention; at HRC50 (June 2022) Cuba delivered a joint statement on behalf of 69 States opposing interference in China's internal affairs under the pretext of human rights.
claims.q: the Cuban representative issued a joint statement on behalf of 69 States, opposing 'interference in China's internal affairs under the pretext of human rights'
claims.an: Only contemporary LAC State-behaviour evidence in D22: Cuba as China's lead voice in multilateral voting on non-interference. Which other LAC states signed must be verified externally.

claims.t: The new doctrine polices some actors more closely than others: it condemns intervention by the HRC while accommodating WTO interference, and validates widespread economic intervention to compel policy change while regulating diplomatic criticism of human rights — an agent-relative doctrine.
claims.q: It is a doctrine flexible enough to condemn intervention by the HRC, while accommodating interference by the WTO.
claims.an: Implies China's 'non-interference' offer to partners shields governance choices but not economic relationships from leverage.

claims.t: Faced with an increasingly interventionist China, Western governments may converge on Chinese-style arguments about intervention (e.g. against clandestine influence and electoral interference).
claims.q: Nevertheless, faced with an ever more interventionist China, Western governments may soon find themselves repeating Chinese arguments about intervention.
claims.an: Relevant to US framing of Chinese 'malign influence' in LAC, which invokes sovereignty language similar to China's.

claims.t: Respect for sovereignty is the hallmark norm of the PRC–Third World coalition, originating in Third World support for PRC representation at the UNGA.
claims.q: Respect for sovereignty is a hallmark norm for the coalition between the People's Republic of China (PRC) and the Third World/Global South countries since the latter supported the PRC to represent "China" at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
claims.e: Historical account; voting data on Resolution 2758.
claims.an: Historical root of M6/M14 linkage.

claims.t: When the PRC and a counterpart disagree on at least one of the two sovereignty questions, the PRC detaches Third World solidarity rhetoric to avoid appearing self-contradictory, emphasising it only when aligned on both.
claims.q: the PRC decides to detach its rhetoric on Third World solidarity regarding the respect for sovereignty from the context in order to avoid appearing as self-contradictory, and only emphasizes it when aligned on both points.
claims.e: Typology and archival speech analysis (Categories I–IV).
claims.an: Shows strategic, recognition-contingent use of South–South solidarity discourse.

claims.t: Original datasets on G77, NAM and PRC recognisers confirm PRC reliance on Third World support at the UNGA and the potential for dissonance over sovereignty.
claims.q: Using original datasets on the Group of 77, the Non-Aligned Movement, and PRC recognizers, the study confirms the PRC's reliance on Third World support and the potential for dissonance over sovereignty.
claims.e: Dataset of 479,158 observations matched to Voeten et al. (2009) UNGA voting data; Figures 1–4.
claims.an: Dataset (Harvard Dataverse KPI6YG) could be reused to examine LAC voting alignment with the PRC 1971–1990.

claims.t: Third World states provided the bulk of the votes restoring the PRC to the UN: of 76 votes for Resolution 2758, 47 came from G77 and 42 from NAM members.
claims.q: 76 members that voted in favor of Resolution 2758, which ... brought the PRC into the UN, and expelled the ROC, 47 ... members were affiliated to the G77, and 42 to NAM.
claims.an: The article does not break down LAC votes on Res. 2758.

claims.t: The share of G77/NAM members among states siding with the PRC tends to be higher than their share among all eligible UNGA voters.
claims.q: the PRC coalitions varies widely, it is true that the ratios tend ... to be higher than when randomly selecting its partners

claims.t: ROC recognisers voted on the same side as the PRC less than their share among all eligible voters, supporting the assumption that non-recognition can disrupt the coalition.
claims.q: that in figure 4 shows that the ratio of ROC-recognizers ... that vote on the same side with the PRC is smaller than ... the ratio of those countries within all eligible voters at the
claims.an: Historically, ROC recognisers (many in LAC/Caribbean) were less aligned with PRC in UNGA votes — relevant baseline for M14 tests of whether recognition switches shift UN voting.

claims.t: The PRC did not directly connect its Third World narratives to the One China question; the only direct Taiwan reference found was Zhao Weiguan's 1979 complaint that the World Bank and IMF upheld a 'Two China' policy.
claims.q: The PRC does not directly relate narratives on the Third World to the question of the One China Policy.
claims.an: Shows Taiwan linkage was kept implicit in solidarity rhetoric — consistent with D21's 'unstated strings'.

claims.t: On Saint Vincent and the Grenadines' UN admission (independent October 1979; recognised the ROC from August 1981 to the present), the PRC commended its independence and developing-country status but avoided linking it to the Third World coalition amid uncertainty about its recognition.
claims.q: The state became independent on October 1979
claims.an: LAC case: Eastern Caribbean microstates were recognition battlegrounds from independence; SVG remains a Taiwan ally (per the article, 'until today').

claims.t: The PRC upheld Argentina's sovereignty over the Malvinas against the British claim and twice invoked the Third World: NAM summits had supported Argentina, and the PRC upheld the Third World struggle to protect sovereignty and territorial integrity.
claims.q: To begin with, the PRC upheld Argentina's sovereignty ... over the "Malvinas Islands" against the British claim in the ... Falkland War, and touched upon the Third World concept
claims.e: D.C. 1978 July–December, 44–5 (as cited by the author).
claims.an: LAC case of China using sovereignty support against a Northern power to build ties with a Latin American state — an early instance of M6 in LAC (Argentina was then a military regime, indicating non-ideological alignment).

claims.t: Addressing UN membership of Dominica and the Solomon Islands (G77 members that recognised the PRC as of 1978), the PRC emphasised their common Third World affiliation and struggle for independence; both later switched to Taiwan in 1983 (Dominica returned to the PRC in 2004, Solomon Islands in 2019).
claims.q: that of Dominica, a G77 member ... who switched from recognizing the PRC to Taiwan in 1983, ... until this changed again in 2004.
claims.an: LAC/Caribbean case of recognition volatility; the 2004 Dominica switch back to the PRC falls within the project period (2001–2026).

claims.t: The PRC described Cuba and Vietnam — G77/NAM members and non-ROC recognisers — as Soviet 'Trojan horses' destroying NAM, and called Vietnam 'Asia's Cuba', rhetorically expelling them from the coalition rather than airing intra-coalition rifts.
claims.q: the PRC described Cuba and ... Vietnam as the "Trojan horse" of the superpower
claims.an: LAC case: China–Cuba relations were hostile in the Sino-Soviet split era despite shared socialism — evidence that ideological affinity (M5) did not determine alignment; contrast with Cuba leading the 2022 pro-China HRC statement (D22).

claims.t: UN representation is legally separate from recognition of governments; draft resolutions by Cuba and the United Kingdom on Chinese representation followed the same direction, endorsed by the UNGA (1950s documentation).
claims.e: Liang (1951); Japanese MFA International Cooperation Bureau (1955).
claims.an: Implies ROC-recognising states can cooperate with the PRC at the UNGA without legal contradiction — relevant to LAC Taiwan allies' multilateral behaviour.

claims.t: PRC officials framed the Third World as 'the main force' against imperialism, colonialism and hegemonism and for a New International Economic Order, noting Third World states amounted to over 80% of all states.
claims.q: the Third World countries amount to more than 80 percent ... of all the states on the globe
claims.e: D.C. 1978 July–December (Huang Hua, Lai Yali, Liang Yufan speeches).
claims.an: Early form of China's development-first South–South framing (NIEO).

claims.t: In the contemporary era, the PRC's position as a US rival, with the US taking sides in Ukraine and Israel–Hamas and becoming more confrontational about One China, makes the two questions of sovereignty directly related.
claims.q: as a rival of the United States, who take explicit sides in ... both cases, and has also started to be more confrontational ... about the One China Policy. In other words, the American ... factor seems to make the two questions directly related to ... each other.
claims.an: Directly relevant to LAC where most of Taiwan's remaining allies sit: US pressure to retain allies vs Chinese inducements — the article does not analyse LAC here.

claims.t: The number of sovereign wealth funds rose from 50 to 92 between 2005 and 2017, with assets under management above $7.5 trillion, more than hedge funds and private equity combined.
claims.q: the number of SWFs increased from 50 to 92 between 2005 and 2017, while assets under management grew to over $7.5 trillion

claims.t: SOEs generate about one-tenth of world GDP and about 20% of global equity market value. Three of the top five 2018 Fortune Global 500 companies are Chinese SOEs (State Grid, Sinopec, CNPC), and PetroChina leads with a market value above $1 trillion.
claims.q: Three of the top five companies in the 2018 Fortune Global 500 are Chinese SOEs (State Grid, Sinopec Group and China National Petroleum Corp).
claims.an: State Grid, Sinopec and CNPC are all major investors in LAC energy (my external knowledge; not discussed in D24).

claims.t: The term state capitalism lacks a unified definition. It variously designates a national variant of capitalism, a new brand of SOE or state investment fund, a type of state–business relation, a threat or alternative to Western liberal capitalism, a reconfiguration of the state–capital nexus, and the use of markets for geo-economic and geopolitical goals.
claims.q: the term not only lacks a unified definition, it refers to an extremely wide array of practices, policy instruments and vehicles, institutional forms, relations and networks that involve the state to different degrees
claims.an: Warns the project to specify which meaning of 'Chinese state capitalism' is invoked under M2.

claims.t: As currently deployed, the concept of state capitalism has weak analytical value. It describes much but explains little.
claims.q: we submit that, at this stage, the analytical value of the concept is weak.

claims.t: Strategic management literature: the 'new form' of state capitalism (hybrid SOEs, partial state ownership, marketised state ownership via holding companies, SWFs, pension funds and national development banks) is characterised by market orientation and globalisation.
claims.q: the ‘new form’ of state capitalism is characterized by ‘market orientation’ and by ‘increasing globalization’
claims.e: Review of Musacchio and Lazzarini; Bruton et al.; Grosman et al.; Li et al.
claims.an: Chinese policy banks (CDB, China Exim) would fall under 'marketized forms of state ownership' in this typology.

claims.t: The management literature's assumption that state influence is 'dysfunctional political interference' leaves no room for firms that are economically efficient while also serving state strategic interests, and precludes analysis of (geo)economic strategies involving both public and private actors.
claims.q: it does not leave room (if any) for scenarios where firms are efficient in economic terms and simultaneously perform functions that further the strategic interests of state actors.
claims.an: Useful for analysing Chinese SOEs in LAC as both commercial and strategic actors, instead of 'statecraft vs market'.

claims.t: Comparative capitalism has identified state-led varieties of capitalism beyond the CME/LME dichotomy. Examples are China and Malaysia (Walter and Zhang). Fainshmidt et al. also include Venezuela and Argentina alongside China, Russia, Vietnam, India and others in a state-capitalism variant with political networks as coordination mechanisms, though other CC studies dispute cross-regional grouping.
claims.an: Places Venezuela and Argentina (as classified by Fainshmidt et al. 2018) in the same institutional family as China. This may be relevant to ideological or institutional affinity arguments (M5/M13).

claims.t: 'State-permeated' capitalism, typical of large emerging markets such as Brazil, India and China, combines dense informal public–private relationships as the central coordination mechanism with deep immersion in global trade and production and a policy of selective, phased integration into the global economy aimed at catch-up.
claims.q: ‘dense informal relationships between public authorities and major domestic corporations, which function as the central coordination mechanism of the economic system’
claims.an: Brazil is placed in the same 'state-permeated' type as China.

claims.t: 'State capitalism 3.0' differs from earlier waves because third-generation late developers are not centrally planned and use sophisticated policies to improve their relative position in the world economy rather than merely shield themselves protectively.
claims.q: ‘third-generation late developers’ are not coherently directed by a central planning body, and they use sophisticated policies not simply to shield themselves from global competition in a protectionist fashion but to improve their relative position in the world economy

claims.t: The comparative-capitalism field is split between those who uphold state-led or state-permeated capitalism (with contested contours, so small methodological changes shift its geography dramatically) and those who reject the category ('strong capitalist states everywhere, state capitalism nowhere').
claims.q: strong capitalist states everywhere, state capitalism nowhere
claims.e: Critical assessment of the CC literature; Witt et al. (2018).

claims.t: Following Kaplan (2016), the longer-term horizons of Chinese state-to-state lending give Latin American debtors more fiscal space than market borrowing, affecting their policy choices and potentially triggering a move away from Western market-centric governance of sovereign borrowing.
claims.q: the longer-term horizons of Chinese state-to-state lending provides more fiscal space to Latin American debtors than when they borrow from financial markets, thereby affecting their policy choices.
claims.an: Directly relevant: explains the attractiveness of Chinese finance to LAC governments regardless of US discourse.

claims.t: Critical scholars doubt that state capitalism as a source of finance and investment will significantly alter South–South relations (Gonzalez-Vicente 2017 on China–Ecuador). Taylor (2014) argues that state capitalism exported to Africa serves externally oriented class fractions.
claims.q: state capitalism as a source of finance and investment is unlikely to significantly alter South–South relations.
claims.an: Counterweight to the South–South framing (M6): Chinese finance may reproduce dependency (M10).

claims.t: Asian and Middle Eastern SWFs helped recapitalise distressed Western banks and automotive firms after 2008, increasing state-controlled capital in the global network of corporate ownership.
claims.q: Asian and Middle Eastern SWFs helped recapitalize distressed banks and automotive firms in the West in the post-2008 crisis environment

claims.t: Debates on the internationalisation of state capital identify three perspectives (Meckling et al. 2015). Realist: national oil companies are 'arms of state power' and a threat.
