Commercial: firms lead and governments follow. Hybrid: cooperation and conflict between profit-driven NOCs and partially supportive home governments.
claims.q: National oil companies are typically seen as ‘arms of state power’.
claims.e: Review of Meckling et al.; Bremmer; Kurlantzick; Steinfeld; Victor et al.
claims.an: The realist 'arms of state power' framing is described as often 'alarmist and anxiogenic' and associated with Western corporate and policy circles, i.e. the framing common in US strategic discourse.

claims.t: Chinese energy SOEs play a 'dual role', following commercial principles abroad while retaining state responsibilities at home. Chinese transnationalising state-directed capital is therefore essentially contradictory.
claims.q: ‘dual role, adhering to commercial principles abroad (e.g. prioritizing profit-making) but retaining the responsibilities of a state-owned company at home (e.g. prioritizing energy security and social stability)’
claims.an: Qualifies M2: Chinese energy SOE activity in LAC may be more profit-driven abroad than statecraft accounts assume.

claims.t: Chinese SOEs have considerable power and autonomy to pursue profit-making and are very weakly regulated, owing to a fragmented, decentralised and internationalised party-state. Party-state/SOE relations are an evolving struggle within multi-level governance (Jones and Zou 2017, a case of a Chinese SOE in Myanmar hydropower).
claims.q: Chinese SOEs have ‘considerable power and autonomy to pursue profit-making activities and are very weakly regulated’
claims.an: Challenges assumptions of tight central coordination behind Chinese projects abroad.

claims.t: The GPE literature divides on state capitalism's relation to the liberal order. Bremmer sees it as antithetical to free markets. Kurlantzick distinguishes authoritarian types (China, Russia, Egypt, Vietnam) from democratic ones (Brazil, Indonesia) but sees serious threats overall. Nölke et al. foresee a 'State Capitalist Consensus' replacing the Post-Washington Consensus.
claims.q: ‘State Capitalist Consensus’, which could replace the ‘Post-Washington Consensus’
claims.e: Review of Bremmer (2010), Kurlantzick (2016), Nölke et al. (2015).
claims.an: Frames competing models: Chinese state-coordinated capitalism versus liberal market models.

claims.t: McNally argues that refurbished state capitalisms, especially China's, form a monumental alternate model distrustful of full liberalisation, yet are deeply enmeshed in the GPE (e.g. holding US Treasury debt), so the two models are co-dependent and in competition. De Graaff and van Apeldoorn envisage co-existence, with China partially adapting to liberal rules while retaining its distinctive model.
claims.q: Both models of capitalism are thus simultaneously co-dependent and in competition
claims.e: McNally (2013); de Graaff and van Apeldoorn (2018).
claims.an: Co-dependence plus competition parallels LAC states' hedging between both models.

claims.t: Without a theory of the 'normal' role of the state, claims of 'strong' state intervention fetishise particular institutions. For example, the CC literature overlooks 'hidden' US industrial policy, monetary policy and the military-industrial complex.
claims.q: the ‘hidden’ industrial policy in the United States
claims.an: Undercuts a liberal-market-versus-state-capitalist contrast in US–China competition narratives.

claims.t: Kurlantzick's quantitative threshold (state ownership stake or significant influence in more than one-third of a country's 500 largest companies by revenue) is an ad hoc, theoretically ungrounded indicator.
claims.q: We are not opposed to the attempt at quantification per se; rather, we are sceptical of the ad hoc construction of indicators

claims.t: The state never left, even in the most neoliberalised spaces and in so-called liberal market economies. Research must account for both its permanent role and its recently more visible role.
claims.q: the state has never left, even in the spaces of the world economy that have experienced the deepest rounds of neoliberalization and apparent state rollback
claims.e: van Apeldoorn et al. (2012) historical-materialist argument.

claims.t: The authors propose 'state–capital hybrids', concrete historically and geographically specific political forms mediating state–capital relations, as more useful than 'state capitalism'. Periodisation should rest on reconfigurations of political and economic power, not on forms or objectives.
claims.q: we suggest that the concept of state–capital hybrids, sometimes used in the literature, might be more useful than the category state capitalism

claims.t: Much of the literature relies on geographical imaginaries that pit an illiberal, opaque, corrupt and threatening Eastern capitalism against a pure liberal free-market Western capitalism. This 'othering', current in Western business and policy circles anxious about China and Russia, is politically dangerous and analytically misleading.
claims.q: much of the state capitalism literature still relies upon deeply problematic geographical imaginaries that tend to pit an illiberal, opaque, corrupt and threatening capitalism located in the East, against a pure liberal democratic free-market capitalism that allegedly predominates in the West.
claims.e: Conceptual critique; Miron (2015) as example ('[China] has state capitalism, not true capitalism').
claims.an: Useful for critically reading US strategic discourse on Chinese 'predatory' or state-led economics in LAC.

claims.t: Much state support for the internationalisation of Chinese SOEs comes from provincial states, often in partial autonomy from the central government. Methodological nationalism misses this multi-scalar dimension.
claims.q: much of the state support to the internationalization of Chinese SOEs is provided by provincial states, often in partial autonomy from the central government
claims.e: Gu et al. (2016), on Chinese development cooperation in Africa.
claims.an: Qualifies the 'centrally coordinated statecraft' version of M2.

claims.t: The renewal of state activism in Brazil under the Workers' Party was intimately connected to China's state-led capital accumulation and urbanisation and the resulting primary-commodity price boom (early 2000s to mid-2010s). Extraordinary commodity-export rents provided the material basis for that activism.
claims.q: the renewal of state activism in Brazil during the rule of the Workers’ Party was intimately connected to state-led capital accumulation and urbanization in China, and the boom in primary commodity prices that it generated from the early 2000s to the mid-2010s.
claims.e: Illustrative argument for uneven and combined development; no data given.
claims.an: Links Chinese demand-pull (M1) to LAC domestic political economy (M10) and the pink tide (M5).

claims.t: New state investment funds in Western economies (Ireland, France, Italy) are a reaction to growing state-controlled investment from the Middle East and China, showing that state capitalism develops through interstate competition.
claims.q: they are a reaction to the growing volumes of state-controlled investments from the Middle East and China in those economies.
claims.an: Analogy: US counter-statecraft (e.g. DFC) can be read as a reactive state–capital hybrid.

claims.t: The current state-capitalism literature neglects class configurations and surplus appropriation, monopoly capitalism, and the repressive and ideological functions of the state. It should engage with debates on mass surveillance, border militarisation and authoritarian neoliberalism.
claims.q: The literature should have something to contribute to debates about the rise of the mass surveillance state, the militarization of borders and authoritarian neoliberalism

claims.t: The U.S. model of capitalism as it developed in the 1990s and early 2000s was widely promoted as an ideal by business and policy elites, but the collapse of the U.S. financial system and the recession are likely to limit its attractiveness in both OECD and industrialising economies.
claims.q: The recent collapse of the U.S. financial system and the current recession are, however, likely to limit the attractiveness of this U.S. model in both OECD1 countries and industrializing economies.
claims.e: Interpretive essay drawing on comparative institutional literature.
claims.an: EXTRAPOLATION (not argued by Whitley): a decline in the legitimacy of the U.S. model after 2008 would weaken U.S. normative leverage in Latin America at the moment China's lending expanded (M13); Whitley does not discuss Latin America or China.

claims.t: A distinctive feature of the recent U.S. model was its reliance on the financial services industry as a key agent of economic growth, supported by the apparent success of the 'new' economy and deregulated finance.
claims.q: especially its reliance on the financial services
claims.an: Whitley does not use the terms 'financialisation' or 'shareholder value' anywhere in the article; this is his closest formulation of finance-led growth.

claims.t: There is no single U.S. model of business organisation and market structure across all industries and regions; the version promoted abroad was an idealised one.
claims.q: First, there is no single U.S. model of business
claims.e: Literature on sectoral and regional variety (Hollingsworth; Saxenian; Weiss).
claims.an: Cautions against treating 'the U.S. model' as monolithic when explaining U.S. foreign economic behaviour.

claims.t: Key institutional features of the neoliberal model urged on others (notably post-socialist Eastern Europe in the 1990s) did not apply to the U.S. economy as a whole; the U.S. state was much more proactive and promotional in some sectors than others.
claims.q: state was much more proactive and promotional
claims.an: Important caveat for the project: Whitley does NOT characterise the U.S. as having a uniformly weak state; he argues the exported model understated the U.S. state's role. Any claim that the U.S. 'lacks state coordination' must be qualified accordingly.

claims.t: The core institutions of the U.S./liberal market economy model concern corporate governance, competition policy and labour relations, and elevate market-based coordination above cooperation between companies and between firms and state agencies, with exit nearly always preferred to voice.
claims.q: and between firms and state agencies, with exit
claims.an: EXTRAPOLATION (not argued by Whitley): a coordination model built on arm's-length firm-state relations offers U.S. governments few institutional levers to steer private firms' overseas investments, consistent with reliance on private capital in foreign economic policy (M3). Whitley says nothing abou

claims.t: Postwar U.S. reformers in Germany and Japan prioritised antitrust legislation, separation of banks from large industrial companies, and anti-monopoly rules forbidding cartels, collective risk sharing and joint investment between firms, with firms seen as relying on the price mechanism in an arm's-length environment.
claims.q: antitrust legislation, the separation of the banks
claims.an: EXTRAPOLATION (not argued by Whitley): contrast with Chinese bundling of finance, SOE contractors and state banks (M2), which is precisely the kind of collective coordination the U.S. recipe prohibited.

claims.t: Japan's postwar bureaucratic-political coalition (MOF, MITI) organised recession cartels, restricted inward FDI and controlled foreign technology access, building a highly coordinated system that became an influential alternative to the U.S. model.

The rise of the East Asian NICs (South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore) reinforced doubts about the U.S. model's emphasis on free markets and a residual, passive state: the state played a major role in their success, family-controlled firms dominated, capital markets played a minor role, and competition policy rarely followed U.S. dictates.
claims.q: the state in these economies had played a major
claims.an: EXTRAPOLATION (not argued by Whitley): provides a comparative template for state-coordinated development models (incl. China's) that Latin American elites could find attractive after 2008 (M13).

claims.t: Liberal markets and a small state may have worked in the U.S. only for some industries in some periods; more coordinated, state-involved economies could be at least equally competitive in industries such as cars and consumer electronics.
claims.q: only for some industries in some historical periods

claims.t: The U.S. federal state has been extensively involved in supporting particular industries, especially those with military connections, and the vigour of antitrust enforcement has varied with political regimes and perceptions of national security.
claims.q: development of particular industries, especially
claims.an: Qualifies the 'weak U.S. state' stereotype: U.S. state activism is concentrated in defence/security-linked sectors. EXTRAPOLATION (not argued by Whitley): this may help explain why U.S. responses to China in LAC skew toward security framing rather than development finance (M12/M3).

claims.t: The newer Silicon Valley (SV) model features flexible project-based firms, fluid external labour markets with preserved managerial prerogatives over hiring and firing, equity-based incentives, informed venture capital and liquid capital markets for exit.
claims.e: Teece (2000); Casper (2007); Kenney & Florida (2000); Tylecote & Visintin (2008).

claims.t: Large, liquid capital markets are not sufficient for successful technology clusters: in the UK and other anglophone economies much venture capital and private equity activity has preferred short-term financial engineering to supporting risky new high-tech firms.
claims.q: more in short-term financial engineering
claims.an: Closest Whitley comes to a critique of short-termist, transaction-oriented private capital. EXTRAPOLATION (not argued by Whitley): private-capital-led U.S. engagement abroad would be prone to short-horizon, return-driven decisions, unlike patient state capital (M3, M9).

claims.t: The SV model depended on massive federal support for university research and training and large-scale military support and procurement; state funding and risk sharing for R&D are significant to U.S. economic success.
claims.q: on massive federal support for university
claims.an: Further evidence that Whitley sees a substantial, if sectorally selective, U.S. state role.

claims.t: Following the crisis, the expanded role of the financial services sector in the U.S. and UK since 1980s-1990s deregulation will decline and few policy makers will rely on financial innovation as the key to growth; the 'originate-and-distribute' model let lenders avoid responsibility and exit quickly from commitments while markets stayed liquid.
claims.q: responsibility for their decisions and exit quickly
claims.e: Interpretive assessment; MacKenzie (2005/2006) on financial economics.
claims.an: Whitley's characterisation of U.S. finance: low-commitment, transaction-based, exit-oriented. EXTRAPOLATION (not argued by Whitley): contrasts with long-tenor, commitment-based Chinese policy-bank lending in LAC (M2).

claims.t: The crisis reinforces doubts about 'ultraliberal' market economies in which ownership rights can be traded easily with few constraints on short-term economic opportunism; reliance on arm's-length coordination is becoming less attractive, especially in coordinated economies of continental Europe and East Asia, and rigid antitrust prohibitions on inter-firm cooperation are likely to weaken.
claims.q: ultraliberal market economies in which ownership

claims.t: There is no all-encompassing, highly coherent U.S. model that is more effective than other forms in all industries and markets; the success of particular U.S. models (e.g. SV) is sector-specific and dependent on particular supporting institutions.
claims.q: U.S. model of capitalism that is more effective

claims.t: Active crisis management by governments everywhere and the importance of state support for many U.S. companies render prohibitions on state steering of economic development unconvincing; adopting a U.S. model need not relegate the state to a passive bystander role.
claims.q: then, need by no means imply the relegation of
claims.an: Explicitly contradicts a reading of the U.S. model as inherently state-less.

claims.t: Whitley predicts that the attractiveness of fully-fledged market fundamentalism (as imposed on Eastern Europe in the early 1990s) will be greatly diminished, and that state steering, market regulation and support for particular firms and industries will be widely seen as legitimate, albeit in 'market friendly' ways — reinforcing tendencies in industrialising countries for the state to lead development, as in postwar East Asia.
claims.q: Most of these involve the state taking a more proactive role in economic development and regulation, albeit in "market friendly" ways.
claims.an: EXTRAPOLATION (not argued by Whitley): if correct, post-2008 legitimacy of state-led development would make Latin American governments more receptive to Chinese state-coordinated finance and less to U.S. market-fundamentalist prescriptions (supports M13 as an explanation for China's consolidation).

claims.t: The Cold War geopolitical environment in which the U.S. opened its markets to Japan and the NICs has changed considerably, so purely export-oriented industrialisation is no longer likely to deliver similar rates of rapid growth.
claims.q: industrialization is no longer likely to lead
claims.an: EXTRAPOLATION (not argued by Whitley): implies the U.S. no longer offers the market-access 'carrot' it once provided for allied development, a possible facet of the U.S. instrument gap (M3); not discussed by Whitley for Latin America.

claims.t: The editors argue that IMF adjustment programmes in 1980s Latin America and Troika programmes in Eurozone debtor countries were strongly similar and produced a 'lost decade', middle-class decline and rising inequality.
claims.q: The IMF adjustment programmes for Latin America and the Troika programmes for Europe's debt crisis countries bear indeed strong similarities and economic and social consequences leading to a lost decade
claims.e: Comparative framing of the Jean Monnet Network; no data in the introduction itself.
claims.an: Background for why IMF/Washington-style conditionality carries a negative legacy in LAC; relevant to M6 (attraction of non-conditional finance) only by analyst inference - the book does not discuss Chinese finance.

claims.t: The 1980s Latin American debt crisis was managed in the interests of creditor banks and creditor countries.
claims.q: which was managed in the interests of the creditor banks and countries
claims.e: Assertion drawing on Griffith-Jones' earlier work.
claims.an: Historical grievance about US/creditor-led crisis management; contextual for LAC distrust of Washington-centred finance.

claims.t: Latin American debtors' attempt to coordinate positions in the 1980s (Cartagena Group) had limited impact because of weak political commitment of debtor governments and divisive tactics by creditor governments.
claims.q: there was an attempt to coordinate different Latin American debtor positions (in the ad hoc Cartagena Group), but it had limited impact, due to insufficient political commitment by the Latin American debtor governments and effective divisive tactics by the creditor governments.
claims.an: Evidence of the historic limits of collective Latin American bargaining with Northern creditors - qualifies M4 (agency works bilaterally more than collectively).

claims.t: Due to rising political polarisation, existing Latin American regional organisations lost the capacity to intervene effectively in political crises.
claims.q: due to the increasing political polarisation in the last years, the existing regional organisations even lost the capacity to effectively intervene in the cases of (political) crisis to mediate a solution.
claims.e: Editorial assessment; developed in chapters 7 and 18.
claims.an: Fragmented regionalism means extra-regional partners deal with LAC country-by-country; relevant context for how China (and the US) engage bilaterally.

claims.t: After the lost decade and austerity, most key Latin American countries had a 'pink wave' of left-wing and/or populist governments followed by a 'blue wave of neoliberalism'; polarisation and instability increased in both regions.
claims.q: most of the key countries in Latin America experienced a "pink wave" of more left-wing and/or populist governments, followed by a "blue wave of neoliberalism"
claims.an: Political-cycle framing (M5). The book does not link these cycles to relations with China or the US.

claims.t: The pink wave created regional organisations and propelled Brazil, as a BRICS member, to act as a motor of South-South and sustainable development until about 2013.
claims.q: the rise at least of Brazil as one of the BRICS and motor of South... for a certain period, i.e. until about 2013.
claims.an: BRICS/South-South framing is part of the diplomatic context in which China-LAC ties grew; the book does not analyse China's role in BRICS.

claims.t: The crises in Venezuela and Brazil are partly linked to the 'resource curse' - over-dependence on oil and primary commodities, corruption, and economic decline when oil prices fell.
claims.q: In both cases, the economic and political crisis is partly related to the "resource curse", with an overdependence on petrol and other primary resources
claims.an: Supports the M10 reading that commodity-boom rents (which, externally, were heavily driven by Chinese demand - not stated here) created vulnerability when prices fell. The book does not name China in this passage.

claims.t: In Venezuela, economic mismanagement, a humanitarian crisis, political crisis and foreign-policy tensions with the USA together turned the government into a left-wing authoritarian regime.
claims.q: In the case of Venezuela, the mixture of the economic mismanagement and even humanitarian crisis, the political crisis and the foreign political tensions with the USA led to the conversion of the government into a left-wing authoritarian regime.
claims.e: Editorial synthesis; detailed analysis is in chapter 13 (outside this analyst's range).
claims.an: Lists US tensions as one contributing factor in Venezuela's authoritarian turn. This bears on M8: US pressure may have reinforced, not weakened, the regime. The authors do not say whether that pressure was effective.

claims.t: In Brazil, the economic slowdown was used to impeach the elected president and replace the left-wing agenda with a Washington Consensus programme; the leading left-wing candidate was then blocked from standing, opening the way for a far-right populist authoritarian government.
claims.q: the economic slowdown was used as a window of opportunity to impeach the elected president accusing her of creative accounting and reversing the left-wing government agenda into a Washington Consensus programme.
claims.an: Shows the editors treat the Washington Consensus as a partisan programme rather than a neutral technocratic model. That matters for M13: US-model legitimacy in LAC is politically contested.

claims.t: Closer EU-LAC cooperation could benefit both sides at a time of major trade tensions and help overcome the crisis of multilateralism.
claims.q: A more intensive cooperation of the two regions could be not only be mutually beneficial in times of major trade tensions but especially represent a valuable contribution to overcome the current crisis of multilateralism and global governance.
claims.an: This is the volume's normative project: the EU as a third partner for LAC. It is relevant to LAC diversification (M4). The book does not compare the EU with China or the US as partners.

claims.t: Since the 1970s Latin America (and Africa) suffered debt crises and commodity-price instability, while East Asia and especially China performed strongly.
claims.q: Latin America and - to a lesser extent - Africa were hit by debt crises in the early 1980s and late 1990s and by the instability of commodities prices, whereas the economies in (East) Asia have been performing strongly, in particular in China.
claims.e: Long-run macro comparison (WIFO, IMF, OECD data).
claims.an: One of very few China mentions in this range. It contrasts development trajectories: China's growth against LAC's crisis-prone, commodity-exposed path. The divergence is relevant background to M1 and M10 complementarity.

claims.t: Neoliberal policies against trade unions and the welfare state were first adopted in Chile after the 1973 military coup, then in the UK and USA.
claims.q: Neoliberal theories also legitimized policies against trade unions and the welfare state, first adopted in Chile after the military coup in 1973
claims.an: Origin story of the US/neoliberal model in LAC.

claims.t: In the 1970s the Latin American 'tiger economies' (Mexico, Argentina, Brazil) took on growing dollar debts to finance import surpluses, financed by recycled petrodollars, because a falling dollar made the debt look cheap.
claims.q: the "tiger economies" of that decade like Mexico, Argentina and Brazil took advantage of this valuation effect: they incurred more and more dollar debts to finance their import surplus
claims.e: Analysis of dollar exchange rate, world trade prices and real interest rates (Figs. 2.3-2.4; IMF, WIFO).

claims.t: US anti-inflation monetary policy and the 1980-85 dollar bull market drove the real interest rate on dollar debt from -6% to +18% (1979-81), triggering the 1982 debt crisis and a lost decade in Latin America.
claims.q: between 1979 and 1981, the real interest on an international dollar debt jumped from −6% to +18% (Fig. 2.4). One year later, the international debt crisis broke out
claims.e: Real interest rate series on dollar debt (Fig. 2.4).
claims.an: This places US monetary policy and dollar dominance at the origin of LAC's worst crisis. It is useful background for why LAC governments value financing that avoids dollar-cycle exposure and conditionality, though the book does not draw that link.

claims.t: Dollar appreciation after 1995 triggered the Asian crisis, then crises in Russia and Brazil; the roughly 60% depreciation of Brazil's real indirectly caused the collapse of Argentina's currency board in 2002.
claims.q: As an indirect consequence of the depreciation of the Brazilian real by roughly 60%, also the currency board of Argentina collapsed in 2002.

claims.t: Between 2002 and 2007 a falling dollar raised world trade (commodity) prices and made real interest on dollar debt negative again, easing emerging-market financial crises.
claims.q: Between 2002 and 2007, the dollar exchange rate again declined strongly
claims.an: Gives a financial/dollar-cycle explanation of the 2000s commodity boom, with financial speculation also cited (Fig. 2.5). It does not mention Chinese demand, which is a useful counterweight to purely China demand-pull (M1) accounts.

claims.t: Real-capitalist periods - including China since the early 1980s - are marked by influential theories that stress capitalism's crisis-proneness and legitimise a strong government and market regulation.
claims.q: During real-capitalist periods (as between ~1890 and 1914 and between ~1950 and the mid-1970s or in China since the early 1980s), those economic theories dominate or are at least influential which underline the crisis-prone nature of capitalism
claims.an: Classes China as a regulated, state-active 'real capitalism' model, in contrast with Western 'finance capitalism'. This is a conceptual tool for M13 (competing governance models).

claims.t: Following Arrighi, when Wall Street became dominant in the late 1970s the USA began financing China's expansion through joint ventures that also transferred technology.
claims.q: When the Wall Street became dominant in the late 1970s, the USA started to finance the expansion of the Chinese economy through joint ventures which also provide a continuous technology transfer
claims.an: Hegemonic-succession framing (systemic cycles of accumulation): finance-dominated hegemons fund their successors' real-economy growth. This is a theoretical lens for US-China rivalry, and the book does not apply it to LAC.

claims.t: Around 1990 the EU and the USA tacitly swapped policy concepts: the EU adopted restrictive, rules-based monetarism while the USA pursued 'trivial Keynesian' countercyclical policy, made easier by the dollar's reserve-currency privilege.
claims.q: an exchange of concepts took tacitly place around 1990. The EU took over the monetarist approach of regulating fiscal and monetary policy in a restrictive manner, whereas the USA adopted a "trivial Keynesian" approach.
claims.an: Suggests the US did not practise at home the austerity it promoted abroad. This is relevant to the credibility of the 'US/Washington model' in LAC, though the chapter does not discuss LAC directly here.

claims.t: Using a national currency, the US dollar, as the main international payment and reserve currency makes the international monetary system asymmetric. It automatically finances US deficits and spreads spillovers (liquidity cycles, financial risks) to the rest of the world.
claims.q: The use of a national currency - the US dollar - as the main vehicle of international payments and reserves makes the public good of the international monetary system (IMS) asymmetric, impeding its management for world interests
claims.an: Structural-power argument on dollar hegemony.

claims.t: Financial globalisation moves capital the wrong way for development: from poor to rich economies and from real to financial investment.
claims.q: capital movements flow in the wrong direction for sustainable economic development: from poor to rich economies and from real investments to financial ones
claims.e: Theoretical argument with reference to Artus (2019).

claims.t: US abuse of power - about one trillion dollars of extra debt a year under Trump, pressure on the Fed, and 'weaponisation' of the dollar - is speeding up consensus for reforming the international monetary system towards a multilateral currency.
claims.q: The recent evolution towards the abuse of power, both in US macroeconomic policies (one trillion dollars of additional debt per year under Trump's presidency with visible pressures upon the FED to depreciate the reserve currency) and in other vulgar 'weaponizations' of the dollar, is accelerating the conditions for a consensus for changing the IMS
claims.an: Directly relevant to M8. US financial coercion (dollar weaponisation) is presented as eroding US monetary legitimacy and pushing others towards alternatives. The chapter does not mention China or LAC here.

claims.t: The author proposes upgrading the IMF's SDR, a basket of US dollar, euro, pound, yen and renminbi, into a true multilateral reserve currency issued by the IMF acting as a multilateral central bank.
claims.q: transform this currency basket of the five main international currencies (the US dollar, euro, pound, yen and renminbi) into a genuine multilateral currency issued directly by the IMF
claims.an: The renminbi is mentioned only as an SDR component. There is no analysis of China's monetary role.

claims.t: The IMF was brought into the Troika for its 'know-how' and its reputation for Washington-Consensus-style adjustment programmes expected to push further neoliberal reforms. Germany switched to backing IMF involvement only after the first Greek bailout decisions had been taken.
claims.q: The IMF has been added to form the Troika, for its "know-how", already having the appropriate reputation about its Washington consensus style adjustment programmes, which would lead to more neoliberal reforms in the adjustment countries.
claims.e: Narrative and secondary sources (Thompson 2015; Rocholl and Stahmer 2016).
claims.an: Treats the 'Washington consensus style' as an exportable conditionality template, which links the European and LAC experiences of IMF conditionality.

claims.t: Following De Grauwe, entering a monetary union means losing control of the currency in which sovereign debt is issued, so member states are downgraded to the status of emerging economies vulnerable to market-forced default.
claims.q: In this sense, member countries of a monetary union are downgraded to the status of emerging economies.
claims.an: Policy-space concept: borrowing in a currency one does not control (as LAC with dollar debt) removes policy space.

claims.t: The way the euro crisis was managed (lack of solidarity, IMF-style adjustment) cost the EU credibility and international influence, and the European model of regional integration lost attractiveness worldwide.
claims.q: As a consequence, the European model of regional integration lost in attractiveness in various regions of the world.
claims.e: Assertion; trust data (57% to 31%) cited on p. 75.
claims.an: Relevant to LAC partner options: an EU weakened as a model and partner narrows the 'third way' between the US and China. This is analyst inference.

claims.t: At the global level the dominant debtor (the US) penalises creditors and changes the rules, whereas in EMU creditors dominate debtors. In both, the most powerful states become hegemons at the expense of multilateral equality.
claims.q: Interestingly, at global level, it is the debtor country, which penalizes the creditor countries and changes the rules, while at EMU level, it occurs the other way around.
claims.an: Hegemony framing relevant to US structural power.

claims.t: The Troika's mistakes - a one-size-fits-all approach and over-optimistic projections - repeated failings long documented in the literature on the IMF, causing social, political and institutional backlash.
claims.q: All these problems were not new; they have all been documented before in the literature on the IMF, which has also been criticized for the "one-size-fits-all" approach
claims.e: Literature review (Stiglitz 2002; Ostry et al. 2016; Atoyan and Conway 2011; Blanchard and Leigh 2013).
claims.an: Evidence that IMF conditionality kept a poor reputation into the 2010s. This is indirect context for M6 (appeal of non-conditional lenders), which the chapter does not discuss.

claims.t: When conditionality is seen as externally imposed, or as serving outside interests, opposition is high - especially when it imposes large losses. National 'ownership' (key to success, per the IMF itself) is then undermined.
claims.q: then opposition to the program conditionality is likely to be high, particularly when the proposed measures inflict economic losses on large parts of the population
claims.e: IMF (2006) guidelines; Gould (2003); Fernández and Rodrik (1991).
claims.an: General mechanism, shown here for Europe, behind sovereignty-based resistance to conditional finance. It supports M6 by analogy.

claims.t: Under the MoUs, governments of different ideologies applied the same policies - 'politics without policy' - which hollowed out domestic democracy and opened space for populist and Eurosceptic parties.
claims.q: It was as if it did not matter which government was in power; elections produced different governments, but not different policies.
claims.e: Schmidt (2015); Laffan (2014); parliamentary practice under MoUs.
claims.an: Mechanism linking external conditionality to populism. It parallels the introduction's claim about LAC after IMF austerity.

claims.t: A lobbying campaign by large banks (Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank and others) and their industry associations divided the 11 states backing the EU financial transaction tax. The tax was reduced to a narrow stamp duty on shares that will probably not be implemented.
claims.q: The "dirty" campaign of the financial lobby was successful
claims.e: Policy-process narrative; critique of Goldman Sachs (2013) estimates.
claims.an: Peripheral to the central question. It illustrates the political power of finance in Western policymaking (the 'finance capitalism' governance model).

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 135)
claims.t: Latin American regional institutions never prioritised harmonising macroeconomic policy or building crisis mechanisms, and the few multilateral initiatives created were not successful.
claims.q: Latin American regional institutions never prioritized the harmonization or the development of common macroeconomic policies or mechanisms to deal with financial crises, and the few multilateral initiatives created were not successful.
claims.e: Institutional mapping of Mercosur, UNASUR, ALBA, Pacific Alliance, CELAC, CAF and FLAR.
claims.an: With no regional liquidity or development-finance backstop, LAC states seek finance bilaterally from outside the region. This is consistent with (though not evidence of) demand for Chinese policy-bank lending and swap lines. Analyst inference.

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 137)
claims.t: When the 2008 liquidity crunch came, Mercosur members responded according to domestic priorities with no common policy. Brazil's unilateral 1999 devaluation had already 'left a shadow' on regional macro cooperation.
claims.q: When the international liquidity crunch came in 2008, Mercosur countries responded to the crisis according to their domestic priorities, and as a consequence, no common policies were set nor were any specific common interests discussed.

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 137)
claims.t: In 2008-09 all four Mercosur members ran effective countercyclical policies: liquidity expansion, tax exemptions, sector stimulus and credit expansion by state-owned financial institutions. Floating exchange rates helped absorb the shock, unlike in the rigid-peg 1990s.
claims.q: Countercyclical policies were effective in Mercosur countries, as all four member-states combined monetary and fiscal policies in order to avoid a heavier fall in consumption and investment
claims.an: Shows that LAC kept far more policy space in 2008 than in the 1980s or 1990s, without IMF programmes. Analyst note: buoyant commodity export revenues - not quantified or attributed to China here - helped make this possible.

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 138)
claims.t: UNASUR's Bank of the South, backed by Venezuela and Brazil as an alternative infrastructure financier to the Bretton Woods institutions and the IDB, was planned with USD 7 billion of capital. Unlike the BRICS New Development Bank, it was never capitalised and was suspended when UNASUR became paralysed.
claims.q: unlike the NDB, it was never capitalized, and the project was suspended with the paralysation of Unasur
claims.an: A failed home-grown alternative to US-dominated development finance (IDB, World Bank). Analyst inference: the gap left by an uncapitalised regional bank is one structural reason extra-regional state lenders (e.g. China Development Bank, China Eximbank) could gain ground. The book itself does not dis

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 138)
claims.t: ALBA promoted a non-capitalist model (Petrocaribe, the Sucre compensation currency). Sucre trade was dominated by Venezuela, mostly Venezuelan imports from Ecuador, and was undermined by corruption. ALBA built no mechanism for a common crisis response.
claims.q: Venezuela was a partner in 98% of Sucre trade, and the Venezuelan-Ecuador relationship alone accounted for 89% of Sucre trade
claims.an: Ideologically driven regional finance was shallow and oil-dependent (M5, M10).

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 138)
claims.t: The Pacific Alliance (Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru, 2011), a free-trade bloc formed in reaction to 21st-century socialism, made trade liberalisation and investment partnerships with Asia, 'especially China', its priorities.
claims.q: The Pacific Alliance was created in 2011 by Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru, and its priorities are to foster trade liberalization and establish investment partnerships with Asia, especially China.
claims.an: Important for the central question. The market-oriented, US-friendly bloc - set up as an ideological counter to ALBA - still made China a priority investment partner. This is evidence of cross-ideological pragmatism (it challenges ideology-only explanations under M5) and of hedging/diversification (

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 139)
claims.t: The Pacific Alliance's integrated stock market (MILA: Santiago, Colombia and Lima exchanges, joined by Mexico in 2014) had marginal results by 2015 and played no role in managing the 2008 crisis.
claims.q: this mechanism was not relevant in terms of managing the impact of the 2008 crisis.

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 139)
claims.t: CELAC has not prioritised macroeconomic issues and is mostly summit diplomacy, paralysed by polarisation over Venezuela (only 11 of 22 presidents at its last summit in 2017). Even so, it has been the region's platform for multilateral dialogue and cooperation with partners such as the EU and China.
claims.q: CELAC has been a platform for the region to dialogue and cooperate multilaterally with partners such as the EU and China.
claims.e: Caetano and Sanahuja (2019); Vadell (2018); summit attendance.
claims.an: Confirms CELAC as the interface for China-LAC multilateral engagement (the China-CELAC Forum is cited via Vadell 2018, p. 145). It shows China using region-to-region formats that exclude the US. Note that the authors describe CELAC as weak and divided.

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 140)
claims.t: CAF works mainly as a development bank rather than a regional relief fund. FLAR (1978) has a liquidity-fund mandate and could become a powerful Latin American regional financial arrangement if the largest economies joined.
claims.q: the characteristics of CAF's financing lines and projects indicate that it operates mainly as a development bank and less as a regional relief fund
claims.an: Brazil and Mexico are absent from FLAR, which weakens the regional safety net.

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 141)
claims.t: The 2006 joint issue of sovereign bonds by Argentina and Venezuela (Bonos del Sur) was a case of 'credibility borrowing' that eased Argentina's access to debt. It reflected Venezuela's oil-funded bid for regional leadership against Brazil's centre-left government.
claims.q: The joint issuance of sovereign bonds by Argentina and Venezuela in 2006 - the Bonos del Sur - is an interesting case of credibility borrowing between countries.
claims.an: Argentina, cut off from Western capital markets, turned to an oil-rich ideological ally for credit. The pattern foreshadows its later reliance on non-Western financing (external knowledge; not in this book).

claims.c: (Del Tedesco Lins and Ribeiro Hoffmann, 2021, p. 141)
claims.t: Latin American countries handled the 2008 crisis mainly at the domestic level because they lacked viable collective mechanisms.
claims.q: Latin American countries handled the impact of the 2008 crisis mainly at the domestic level as they lacked viable mechanisms to react collectively.

claims.t: Greek MoU conditionality had all the features of the 'traditional' IMF recipe - fiscal consolidation, liberalisation and labour-market internal devaluation - and failed to take Greece's political economy into account.
claims.q: The policy conditionality promoted through the MoUs had all the characteristics of the 'traditional' IMF recipe: fiscal consolidation, liberalization of the economy and, due to the inability to engage in external devaluation, labour market reforms aimed at internal devaluation.
claims.e: Case study of the three Greek programmes (2010, 2012, 2015) with Eurostat/Bank of Greece data.
claims.an: Comparative evidence on the costs of IMF-type conditionality.

claims.t: A key reason the Greek bailout failed was lack of ownership of the policies. Together with austerity, this let populist parties dominate politics. In 2018 three-quarters of Greeks did not trust the EU.
claims.q: One of the most important reasons for this failure has been the lack of ownership of the policies promoted.

claims.t: Despite a Troika bailout (about EUR 78bn) and austerity, Portugal avoided an explicitly populist revolt. The author attributes this to party-system make-up, consensual history, youth emigration and a left government that absorbed populist demands - adaptive capacity that cannot simply be replicated elsewhere.
claims.q: the government has managed to adopt some populist measures and tactics
claims.e: Case study; secondary literature and macro indicators.
claims.an: Peripheral. Shows that national institutions mediate how external conditionality turns into political outcomes.

claims.t: Italy received no external financial assistance in 2011; a technocratic government imposed austerity to calm markets. Only the ECB's 'whatever it takes' (July 2012) ended the crisis, showing it was an EMU-wide problem.
claims.q: The fact that only the intervention of a European power was able to solve the problem demonstrates how the 2011 Sovereign debt crisis was not only an issue of national public finances, but rather an EMU-wide problem.
claims.an: Contrast with LAC: a regional lender of last resort was decisive in Europe, and LAC has none (ch. 7).

claims.t: Unpopular austerity without a proper recovery created fertile ground for populism in Italy, leading to its first openly populist government.
claims.q: The lack of a proper economic recovery together with the unpopular austerity measures approved as a solution to stop the contagion of 2011 created a fertile ground for the spread of populism.

claims.t: In Argentina, Brazil and Mexico, domestic political concerns - not international actors or IMF pressure - were the main drivers of financial policy after 2008, even where this contradicted the IMF's stance on capital-flow management.
claims.q: this chapter argues that domestic concerns were the main drivers of financial policy making after the 2008 crisis even in countries with different institutional arrangements and macroeconomic trajectories such as Brazil, Mexico and Argentina.
claims.e: Comparative case study of exchange-rate and capital-control policy.
claims.an: Shows the largest LAC economies acting with autonomy from Washington-based institutions after 2008. This fits a broader picture of LAC agency (M4) that also shaped how they engaged extra-regional partners. China is not mentioned in the chapter.

claims.t: The Washington Consensus reforms in the three countries were combined with pegged exchange-rate regimes. These steps integrated them into the world economy but also triggered the crises of 1994 (Mexico), 1998-99 (Brazil) and 2001-02 (Argentina), whose severity matched each country's commitment to a hard peg.
claims.q: Most of the reforms were inspired by what was labeled the Washington Consensus, a set of liberalizing measures which, in the three cases here, were coupled with the adoption of pegged currency exchange regimes.
claims.e: Comparative narrative; Wiesner (2008); Kaminsky et al. (2009).
claims.an: Evidence of how the US-backed reform model became linked with crisis in the region, which bears on how legitimate the 'US model' is seen to be (M13).

claims.t: After Mexico's 1982 crisis Brazil's military government had to request IMF aid. A long series of failed economic plans under the IMF's agenda followed, generating 'a decade and a few years lost'.
claims.q: What followed was a struggle for macroeconomic stability amid a complete imbalance in external accounts and a long series of failed economic plans under the IMF's agenda.

claims.t: 1980s adjustment programmes did not rebalance external accounts, control inflation or restore growth. Governments did not strictly follow IMF policies, and Argentina and Brazil reached hyperinflation.
claims.q: Adjustment programs have not been effective in rebalancing external accounts and controlling inflation nor have they ensured output growth that would lift countries out of crisis with even the IMF policies not being strictly followed by governments.

claims.t: Argentina gained from the world boom to 2007, especially rising commodity prices. This gave it external-account room to set economic policy by domestic priorities despite being shut out of international financial markets since 2001.
claims.q: Argentina benefited from the world economy's prosperity period until 2007, particularly due to the rising price of commodities, which gave the country some comfort in the external accounts to set up the guidelines of economic policy in accordance with domestic policy priorities.
claims.an: Commodity-boom rents gave policy autonomy, the mechanism behind M1 and M10. External knowledge, not this book, links the boom largely to Chinese demand for soy etc.; record it as an inference.

claims.t: Holdout creditors litigating successfully in US courts have blocked Argentina from issuing debt abroad. As a result, since the mid-2000s Argentina has used 'creative' and interventionist funding schemes such as nationalising pension funds.
claims.q: a group of holdout creditors successfully litigating against Argentina in US courts has effectively posed an obstacle to the country's ability to issue debt abroad.
claims.an: Exclusion from US-jurisdiction capital markets created demand for alternative financing. Analyst inference: this context helps explain Argentina's later recourse to non-Western sources such as PBoC swap lines, which this book does not mention - verify externally.

claims.t: On the eve of 2008 Argentina ran twin surpluses, boosted by the commodities boom and a new 'macroeconomic populism' (Dornbusch and Edwards) in place since 2007.
claims.q: The economy was boosted by both the commodities boom and the new type of macroeconomic populism
claims.an: Commodity rents financing a populist macro regime (M10).

claims.t: Mexico was hit hard by the 2008 crisis because it is close to and dependent on the US economy (exports, remittances), mainly through currency depreciation. It recovered quickly thanks to inflation targeting, a floating rate and fiscal discipline.
claims.q: The proximity to the US economy, that had fueled Mexican exports, meant that the effects of the crisis were deeper, notably through currency depreciation.
claims.an: Contrasts Mexico's structural integration with the US against South America's commodity-export model. This qualifies any LAC-wide generalisation about China's expanding economic weight: Mexico's economic anchor remains the US.

claims.t: After 2011 Argentina, Brazil and Mexico managed capital accounts more closely. Brazil was a pioneer in using taxes to control capital flows, while Mexico was rewarded by rating agencies for its conservative approach.
claims.q: Brazil has been a pioneer in using taxes to control capital outflows. Mexico, on the contrary, has been rewarded by risk agencies for its conservative approach to economic policy.
claims.an: Evidence of policy-space use against IMF orthodoxy (the IMF later endorsed capital-flow management, per Gallagher and Tian).

claims.t: Argentina, Brazil and Mexico all took advantage of long and pronounced increases in commodity prices in the 2000s. Brazil and Mexico could attract capital and issue external bonds, while Argentina was increasingly isolated from international financial markets.
claims.q: Argentina, Brazil and Mexico took advantage of long and pronounced increases in commodity prices during the 2000s.
claims.an: Commodity super-cycle as an enabling condition. China not named.

claims.t: From 2007 Argentina intervened more heavily (manipulating inflation statistics, nationalising pension funds, YPF and Aerolíneas, conflicts with the central bank and the farm sector). This worsened market risk perception and drove capital outflows, offset by high commodity prices.
claims.q: These facts substantially deteriorated the risk perception of international markets and contributed, along with the crisis, to the severe capital outflows the country experienced since late 2007, whose adverse impacts on the balance of payments were offset by the benign effects of international commodity prices.
claims.an: Commodity export earnings cushioned the loss of Western investor confidence. This is relevant to M10 and to why commodity buyers mattered to governments in conflict with Western markets (analyst inference).

claims.t: When the global crisis hit, Mexico was highly dependent on the US economy and torn by drug-trafficking violence. In 2012 Peña Nieto brought back the PRI with a team of US-educated technocrats - a very different policy approach from Argentina's and Brazil's.
claims.q: When the global crisis erupted, Mexico was highly dependent on the US economy and torn by violence from confrontations related to drug trafficking.
claims.an: Shows US economic integration and the security/drug agenda shaping Mexico (M12), as well as elite socialisation in US economic orthodoxy.

claims.t: Across the three cases, domestic political choices outweighed international pressures in crisis management. Brazil's 2014 crisis, attributed to Rousseff's 'growth at any cost' policy, served as a pretext for a 'parliamentary coup', and discontent in disciplined Mexico produced a left-wing populist victory (López Obrador).
claims.q: domestic political choices prevailed over possible international pressures on crisis management and policy making.
claims.an: Supports reading LAC policy choices through domestic political economy rather than external alignment. This is a caution against ideology- or great-power-only explanations.

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 202)
claims.t: The 2008 global financial crisis triggered Brazil's political crisis, but domestic factors explain how deep it went and why Brazilian democracy is now fragile. These domestic factors set Brazil apart from other Latin American and European countries.
claims.q: the global financial crisis was a trigger of the crisis, but that domestic factors are key to understand the depth of the crisis, and the fragility of democracy at the present
claims.e: Interpretive political analysis drawing on Avritzer (2018/2019); narrative of 2013-2019 events.
claims.an: Framing claim for ch. 12. It treats external shocks as triggers and domestic politics as the amplifier. This is relevant when weighing ideology/political cycles (M5) against external economic drivers.

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 202)
claims.t: The authors say Brazil's current cycle of democratic instability resembles 1954 and 1964, when developmentalist and liberal models competed. The difference is that today, under neoliberal hegemony, the domestic alignments 'seem to reflect' the US-China contest for leadership rather than Cold War divisions.
claims.q: the current global context is of neoliberal hegemony, and the alignments seem to reflect the contest between the USA and China for leadership
claims.e: Assertion supported only by citations to Acharya (2018) and Ikenberry et al. (2018); the point is not developed further in the chapter.
claims.an: This is the passage the project flagged. It maps Brazil's domestic polarisation onto US-China great-power competition, but the chapter never shows which domestic coalition aligns with which power, or how. Treat it as a framing hypothesis, not a finding. Elsewhere in the volume (ch. 18, PDF 278) the

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 204)
claims.t: Brazil's economic deterioration before the 2016 impeachment came less from 'bad administration' than from global structural factors: the financial crisis, the fall in global demand for primary resources and the fall in the oil price.
claims.q: The deterioration of the economy resulted not necessarily by 'bad administration' but from global level structural factors such as financial crisis, the fall of global demand for primary resources and the fall of petrol price.
claims.an: This is consistent with the commodity-cycle exposure of LAC economies to external (largely Chinese) demand. The chapter does not name China as the demand source here; ch. 17 (PDF 263) and ch. 19 (PDF 298) do.

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 205)
claims.t: After the impeachment, Temer's government completely reorganised Brazilian foreign policy, moving from a South-South approach to alignment with the USA. Foreign policy had already become 'practically paralysed' after Rousseff's re-election.
claims.q: Foreign policy orientation was also completely reformulated under Temer, from a south–south approach to an alignment with the USA.
claims.e: Cites Vigevani and Cepaluni (2016), Saraiva (2014), De Oliveira et al. (2018), Mello (2018), Milani et al. (2017, 'graduation dilemma').
claims.an: This is evidence of a diplomatic re-alignment following a right turn. The chapter gives no data on whether Brazil-China trade or investment changed under Temer, so it cannot show whether diplomatic alignment translated into economic realignment. Ch. 18 (PDF 278) qualifies it: Temer's trade agenda al

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 205)
claims.t: In November 2016 the Temer government cut the state oil company's minimum 30% participation in oil exploitation and lifted its exclusive operating right in the deep-sea pre-salt fields. This was part of a broader neoliberal 'U-turn' that also included labour deregulation, social programme cuts and a 20-year constitutional spending cap.
claims.q: In November 2016, Temer's government succeeded to reduce the minimum quota of 30% of participation of the company in petrol exploitation and lift the exclusive exploitation right for the deep sea (pré-sal).
claims.an: This opened Brazilian pre-salt upstream to foreign operators. The chapter does not discuss which foreign firms benefited. Check externally whether Chinese NOCs (e.g. CNOOC, CNPC) increased their participation in pre-salt auctions after 2016. If so, it would be a case of a pro-US-aligned government l

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 208)
claims.t: Bolsonaro's government rests on three groups, the 'neoliberals' (Guedes: deregulation, privatisation, free trade), the 'military' and the 'ideological' (inspired by Olavo de Carvalho and the US alt-right). These groups share no coherent political project and advance contradictory, clientelist interests.
claims.q: These groups and their political agendas do not share a coherent political project, rather they advance mostly in clientelist fashion, specific interests which are often contradictory.
claims.an: This is relevant for testing M5. If the governing coalition is internally incoherent, pro-US ideological rhetoric (the 'ideological' wing) may coexist with pragmatic economic choices (the neoliberal/agribusiness interests) that keep China ties intact. The chapter itself does not draw this inference.

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 210)
claims.t: The authors identify the economic challenge as reversing the neoliberal development approach of the Bolsonaro government. That approach adds climate-change denial to a growth strategy based on extractivism and agribusiness, at the expense of sustainable development.
claims.q: the impact of the increase of a strategy of growth based on extractivism and agribusiness to the cost of a sustainable development approach
claims.an: Extractivism and agribusiness are the sectors most tied to Chinese demand (soy, iron ore), although the chapter does not say so. Analyst inference: a pro-US government that doubles down on agro-extractive growth may deepen structural dependence on the Chinese market (M10/M1).

claims.t: The involvement of external actors, namely Cuba, the United States, the Rio [Lima] Group, China and Russia, has turned Venezuela's crisis into a regional and global issue. The room for manoeuvre of regional institutions and of the international community is very limited.
claims.q: The involvement of external actors (Cuba, the United States, the Rio Group China and Russia) has made the Venezuelan situation a regional and global issue.
claims.an: This is the chapter's only mention of China. It does not analyse Chinese loans-for-oil, CDB financing or China's diplomatic support for Maduro. That is a notable omission for this project, so do not use the chapter as evidence on China's role in Venezuela. 'Rio Group' appears to be a slip (the Lima

claims.t: Venezuelan oil production fell by more than half, from 2.3 million b/d in January 2016 to 1.1 million b/d in January 2019. It then fell well below 1 million b/d after US sanctions on PDVSA were imposed and after nationwide blackouts, reaching about 717,000 b/d in November 2019.
claims.q: Production continues to collapse and is now well below the 1 million b/d mark following the implementation of U.S. sanctions on PDVSA, and more recently in the aftermath of widespread electrical blackouts
claims.e: Quotes CSIS (Verrastro and Stanley 2019); Table 13.1 from CEIC/OPEC.
claims.an: This is evidence that US coercive economic statecraft (M8) had large material effects on Venezuela's oil sector. Ch. 13 (PDF 217) says these effects did not translate into political change. It also has implications for Chinese loans-for-oil repayment, which the chapter does not discuss.

claims.t: The Maduro government's strategy was to pay its debt at almost any cost, including through new loans and bonds. Examples are Goldman Sachs's May 2017 purchase of US$2.8 bn in bonds at a 69% discount (US$865 m disbursed) and a US$2 bn loan from Russia's Rosneft collateralised with 49.9% of Citgo. Default nonetheless came in 2018.
claims.q: The Venezuelan government's political strategy has been to pay its debt commitments at almost any cost, even if that implies new loans or issuing new bonds.
claims.e: Cites Hausmann (2017), CEIC (2020), Reuters, elimpulso.com/Aristimuño Herrera & Asociados.
claims.an: The chapter names US (Goldman Sachs) and Russian (Rosneft) financiers as late-stage creditors but does not mention Chinese policy-bank lending. Ch. 19 (PDF 296) claims China 'owns most' of Venezuela's external debt, so the two chapters are inconsistent on this point.

claims.t: Every international initiative has utterly failed to move Venezuela's situation forward: UNASUR and Church mediation, sanctions on regime elites, suspension from Mercosur and President Trump's threat of military intervention. Maduro's position seems stronger, at least in the short term.
claims.q: Yet, what is striking is the utter failure of any and all of these initiatives to even minimally move the situation forward.
claims.e: Synthesis of the record 2014-2019; cites Sabatini (2017), New York Times (2016), Jacobs (2017), Latouche (2018a,b).
claims.an: This is evidence on the limits of US coercive instruments (sanctions, threats) in achieving political goals in LAC (M8 effectiveness). It is consistent with the premise that US pressure does not straightforwardly displace rival patrons. The authors do not, however, attribute Maduro's resilience to C

claims.t: The Trump administration escalated its rhetoric ('all options are on the table'), raising the risk of military intervention. Other external actors are also involved: about 20,000 Cubans, including troops and intelligence services, Russian military assistance, and alleged FARC, ELN and Hezbollah presence.
claims.q: The Trump administration has upped its rhetoric, declaring that "all options are on table", potentially increasing the risk of a military intervention (Parvaz 2019).
claims.an: It shows that US engagement with Venezuela was framed in security and coercive terms (M8, M12) rather than economic offers.

claims.t: The authors recommend that international actors focus on the external consequences of the crisis, such as refugees and planning for collapse, and support informal regional cooperation, rather than seek regime-level change. They say replacing UNASUR with PROSUR without regional consensus is counterproductive and that military intervention should be set aside.
claims.q: the attempt to replace UNASUR with PROSUR without the existence of regional consensus will be a counterproductive policy

claims.t: Economic explanations of right-wing populism (globalisation's 'left behind') are insufficient. Winners and losers of neoliberal globalisation form a coalition united by an anti-immigration platform and a shared sense of lost national identity, security and sovereignty, which psychoanalytic theory (Lacan, affect) helps explain.
claims.q: In fact, we can identify a coalition between "winners" and "losers" of neoliberal globalization, united on an anti-immigration platform and sharing a sense of loss of national identity, security, and sovereignty.
claims.e: Literature review; voting data (e.g. 39% of top-quarter UK earners voted Leave; 48% of top-third US earners voted Trump, Curtice 2016).
claims.an: A peripheral (European) chapter. Its conceptual relevance is that it treats 'loss of sovereignty' under neoliberal globalisation as a mobilising affect. That may help explain the rhetorical appeal of sovereignty and anti-elite discourses in LAC right turns, which do not necessarily translate into ec

claims.t: The EU's post-crisis economic governance reforms (ESM, Fiscal Compact, European Semester, Banking Union) saved the euro. They did not, however, address wage and fiscal imbalances, and they lacked democratic accountability. The reforms did not directly cause the rise of 'sovereignist' parties but acted as a catalyst for it.
claims.q: the economic crisis and the consequent EU institutional response, through the reforms of the European economic governance, did not directly cause the rise of sovereignist parties, but they acted as a catalyst of their success.
claims.e: Institutional analysis; Eurostat poverty data; Eurobarometer opinion data; EP seat table.
claims.an: Peripheral. It offers a governance-model lens: technocratic crisis management without accountability erodes legitimacy and fuels sovereignism. This is relevant to M13/M6 as an analogy for LAC's experience of IMF conditionality.

claims.t: During the Eurozone crisis, diffuse support for the EU (image, trust) fell sharply, especially in the periphery, and then largely recovered as economies recovered. Support for the euro proved resilient. The legitimacy loss was therefore 'potentially reversible', although a trust gap persisted in the periphery (55% mistrust in 2018).
claims.q: the loss of legitimacy proved potentially reversible when the problem which had caused it ceased to be so acute
claims.e: Eurobarometer surveys 70.1 (2008), 78.1 (2012), 86.2 (2016), 90.3 (2018); core vs periphery groups.
claims.an: Peripheral. Methodological note: it shows that elite/institutional legitimacy measured by opinion surveys tracks economic conditions closely. This is a caution when interpreting LAC public-opinion shifts toward the US or China (M11; compare D06).

claims.t: Eurosceptic parties entered government in Greece, Italy and (as supporters) Portugal, but produced no rupture with the EU or the euro. In 2015 SYRIZA backed down and accepted a new bailout rather than risk a Eurozone exit that would have been unpopular. In 2018 the Italian government cut its deficit when faced with an Excessive Deficit Procedure.
claims.q: After a 6-month standoff, the government changed course and accepted a new bailout rather than risk a disorderly Eurozone exit which would have been highly unpopular with the electorate.
claims.an: Analogy: anti-establishment governments facing high exit costs from existing economic structures tend to moderate in practice. This parallels the LAC observation that ideological turns rarely translate into economic decoupling (M5 cross-ideological pragmatism). The inference is the analyst's, not th

claims.t: In the first decade of the century, pink-tide governments and governments of other political orientations alike benefited greatly from the global natural-resource boom driven by China's growth. Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Mexico gained as oil exporters, Chile and Peru as copper exporters, and Brazil and Argentina as iron ore and soybean exporters.
claims.q: These left-of-center governments, as well as governments of other political orientations in Latin America during the first decade of this century, benefited greatly from the global natural resource boom caused by China's economic growth.
claims.an: This is the strongest direct China passage in this half of the book. It supports M1 (Chinese demand-pull) and, explicitly, cross-ideological benefit: right-leaning Colombia, Mexico, Chile and Peru gained too. That undercuts explanations based on ideological affinity alone (M5). Compare D11 (Ganchev)

claims.t: Although pink-tide leaders presented themselves as critics of neoliberalism and imperialism, they did not differ from their neoliberal counterparts in Peru and Colombia on mining, oil and industrial agriculture. Former Ecuadorian energy minister Alberto Acosta said Correa had 'replaced Uncle Sam with Uncle Chen', relying on China to sustain social programmes at the expense of real development.
claims.q: replaced Uncle Sam with Uncle Chen", relying on China "to sustain social programs and political position at the expense of real development
claims.e: Quotes Alberto Acosta via Zaitchik (2019, The Intercept).
claims.an: This is direct evidence for M10 (commodity rents financing governments) and for China replacing the US as the external economic anchor for some pink-tide governments. It also shows that extractivist convergence across ideologies made China useful to left and right alike. Compare D11 and D10 on subor

claims.t: Thanks to redistribution during the boom, about 70 million people were lifted out of poverty between 2002 and 2012 (ECLAC). The 2008 Global Financial Crisis reached Latin America only a few years later, through the collapse of natural-resource prices. Growth slowed and poverty gains eroded.
claims.q: The Global Financial Crisis of 2008 began to have impact on Latin America a few years later, through the collapse of natural resources' prices.
claims.an: This links the timing of the LAC crisis (c. 2012-2015) to the end of the commodity super-cycle. Ch. 18 (PDF 284) and ch. 19 (PDF 298) tie that end to China's slowdown.

claims.t: Frustration with eroding gains undermined the pink-tide governments. From 2015 neoliberal conservatives came to power: Macri (2015), Temer (2016), Piñera (2017) and Duque (2018). Bolsonaro's election in 2018 and Morales's ouster in 2019 signalled a move toward the far right, combining neoliberal economics with more authoritarian rule.
claims.q: This frustration and discontent eroded the support for pink-tide governments and, from 2015 onward, conservative politicians espousing a neoliberal ideology acceded to power once again in many Latin America countries
claims.an: This is the 'turn to the right' period in which US discourse increasingly targeted China. It is useful for testing whether right-wing governments reduced China ties: the chapter itself gives no economic data.

claims.t: The turn to the right is not homogeneous. Far-right, anti-democratic currents are strong only in a handful of countries, notably Brazil and Bolivia. AMLO's 2018 victory in Mexico, Macri's defeat by Alberto Fernández in 2019 and the 2019 protests against Piñera show a mixed picture. Brazil under Bolsonaro is an extremist outlier, not representative of regional right-wing populism.
claims.q: although we can discern a growing support for far-right, anti-democratic currents in Latin America, these currents seem stronger only in a handful of countries (Brazil and Bolivia, in particular)
claims.an: This qualifies any argument that a region-wide ideological right turn should produce a region-wide pivot to the US (M5).

claims.t: Opposition to Evo Morales included left-wing sectors and indigenous groups who opposed his extractivist development model. Since 2011, lowland indigenous groups had protested the construction of a highway through a national park and ancestral territory.
claims.q: it also included sectors identified with the Left who distanced themselves from Morales due to his disrespect for the popular vote and his extractivist development model
claims.an: This is domestic political-economy friction around extractivism (M10). The highway is not named in the text (presumably TIPNIS) and its financier/contractor is not identified. Do not attribute it to Chinese or other finance from this source.

claims.t: Chile, long lauded as a pro-market model, illustrates the limits of neoliberal inclusion. Despite growth, the 21% real income rise from 2000-2018 and poverty reduction under the centre-left, high inequality, privatised services and household debt triggered the 2019 mass protests.
claims.q: they also signaled widespread dissatisfaction with the high cost of living, growing indebtedness, privatization and inequality brought about the neoliberal economic model
claims.an: Relevant to M13: the legitimacy of the US-associated free-market model is contested even in its regional showcase.

claims.t: The authors argue that Bolsonaro and Economy Minister Guedes never proposed structural change. Their aim was to preserve and expand the free-market economy by attracting foreign capital in strategic sectors, deregulating labour and privatising strategic and non-strategic state-owned companies.
claims.q: they aim to preserve and expand the free market economy on the basis of attracting foreign capital in strategic sectors, deregulating labor relations, privatizing strategic and non-strategic state-owned companies
claims.an: Analyst inference: privatisation and openness to foreign capital in strategic sectors are origin-neutral. They create entry points that Chinese SOEs and investors could use (e.g. power, oil), whatever the government's pro-US ideology. The chapter does not discuss this. Verify externally (e.g. Chines

claims.t: In a footnote, the authors state that left and right in Latin America 'do not differ much' on the exploitation of natural resources. In 2019 Bolsonaro's government exacerbated climate scepticism and bore responsibility for Amazon fires.
claims.q: Notwithstanding we affirm that left and right do not differ much in relation to the exploitation of natural resources
claims.an: This is a clear statement of cross-ideological extractivist convergence, which helps explain why Chinese commodity demand remains attractive across political cycles (M1/M5).

claims.t: Brazilian extreme-right rule rests on 'politics of social antagonism' sustained by a class coalition of landowners, military, Evangelicals and upper classes. This coalition manipulates fear and exploits low trust in Congress and parties: per Latinobarómetro 2018, Brazil ranks 16th of 18 in confidence in Congress and last in confidence in parties.
claims.q: Bolsonaro was named by a coalition consisted of landowners, military, Evangelicals and upper economic classes as the one with answers to wide existential insecurities
claims.e: Access vs exercise of power framework (Mazzuca 2010); Latinobarómetro 2018; Nunes (2019).
claims.an: Landowners (agribusiness) are part of the coalition. The chapter does not note this, but their export interests are heavily China-oriented, a potential source of intra-coalition pragmatism (analyst inference; see D12).

claims.t: Temer's new foreign policy promised 'de-ideologisation', free trade and market opening. Trade liberalisation meant renewing ties with traditional partners (USA, Europe), focusing on 'new partners' in Asia, particularly China and India, and a commercial approach to Africa.
claims.q: Trade liberalization was a goal which meant a renewed relationship with traditional partners such as the USA and Europe; a focus on 'new partners' in Asia, particularly China and India
claims.an: This is direct evidence of cross-ideological pragmatism (M5) and hedging (M4). The centre-right, pro-US Temer government explicitly prioritised China as a commercial partner. It qualifies ch. 12's 'alignment with the USA' (PDF 204).

claims.t: Under Bolsonaro the trends were radicalised. Foreign Minister Ernesto Araújo equated 'globalism' with socialism and listed Brazil's preferred partners as Israel, the USA, LAC countries 'liberated' from the Foro de São Paulo, the 'new Italy', Hungary and Poland.
claims.q: among the partners he included Israel, USA, Latin-American countries 'which liberated themselves from the Foro de Sao Paulo', 'those who fight against tyranny in Venezuela', the 'new Italy', Hungary and Poland
claims.an: China is conspicuously absent from Araújo's list of partners. This is a test case for the gap between ideological diplomatic discourse and economic practice. Check externally whether Brazil-China trade and investment fell under Bolsonaro; see gaps_to_verify_externally.

claims.t: UNASUR's roots lie in Brazil's 1994 project for a South American Free Trade Area under the '4+1' strategy. The strategy was to negotiate the FTAA from group positions and avoid bilateral negotiations with the USA.
claims.q: that is, to engage with external markets from group positions and avoiding bilateral negotiations with the USA
claims.an: This is historical evidence of LAC collective hedging and bargaining vis-à-vis the US (M4), which predates China's rise in the region.

claims.t: In its early years UNASUR was considered successful. It helped resolve crises in Bolivia and Ecuador, and its South American Defence Council was seen as a space to counterbalance US military influence. The Bank of the South was conceived to mitigate IMF influence, and IIRSA was seen as necessary for infrastructure integration.
claims.q: The South American Council of Defence (SACD) was perceived as an original regional space able to counterbalance the US influence in military affairs
claims.an: This shows autonomy-seeking from US and IMF influence through regional institutions (M4/M6). Ch. 7 (covered in D26a) notes the Bank of the South was never capitalised.

claims.t: Maduro accepted UNASUR mediation while rejecting the OAS, which he saw as dominated by US interests. UNASUR's mediation failed, and the perception grew that it served the Venezuelan government. After 2015 right-wing governments, the 2017 deadlock over a Secretary General and the 2018 suspensions and withdrawals paralysed UNASUR.
claims.q: President Maduro initially accepted mediation by UNASUR, while rejecting the OAS, seen as dominated by US interests.
claims.e: Narrative; cites Closa & Palestini (2015), Riggirozzi & Grugel (2015).
claims.an: Perceived US domination of hemispheric institutions (OAS) reduces their usefulness as crisis managers for some governments (M6).

claims.t: Chávez announced ALBA in December 2001 as an alternative to the US FTAA proposal ('ALCA vs ALBA'). It expanded after 2006 under 21st-century socialism (Petrocaribe 2006, Sucre 2008, the 'Grandnationals'). It relied on Venezuela as paymaster under high oil prices, and most projects were never or only partly implemented.
claims.q: Initially ALBA was a Venezuelan unilateral initiative, announced by Chávez in the Summit of Association of Caribbean States held in Margarita Island, in December 2001, aiming at presenting an alternative to the US proposal of the FTAA
