claims.an: ALBA shows ideologically driven, rent-financed counter-hegemonic regionalism that collapsed with oil prices. This contrasts with China's more durable commodity-based links (inference).

claims.t: The 2008 global crisis initially did not affect ALBA because oil prices stayed high and Chinese and Indian oil demand remained stable. The situation changed only in 2013, when Chinese growth slowed and fracking became significant. The oil price fall to below US$30, which the text dates to 2014, then hit Venezuela and ALBA.
claims.q: The global crisis that started in 2008 initially did not affect the agenda of ALBA because oil prices remained relatively high, and the demand for oil by China and India continued stable for some years; only in 2013, when the Chinese economic growth slowed down and when fracking became an important source of oil production that situation changed.
claims.an: Chinese demand acted as a buffer after 2008 and its slowdown as a transmitter of the crisis (M1). This underlines LAC's structural exposure to China's growth cycle (M10).

claims.t: The Pacific Alliance (Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru) grew out of the 2007 Pacific Rim Arc initiative, which sought a common economic approach towards Asia. It was announced in the 2011 Lima Declaration and followed by the 2012 Framework Agreement and the 2014 Additional Protocol, which eliminated tariffs on nearly 95% of intra-regional imports. Its identity rests on neoliberalism and representative democracy.
claims.q: It can be seen as a follow-up from the Pacific Rim Arc initiative from 2007 that included countries from South and Central America and aimed at fostering a common economic approach towards Asia
claims.e: Cites Durán & Cracau (2016), Legler et al. (2018).
claims.an: This shows that the most pro-market and US-friendly LAC bloc was itself oriented toward Asia, i.e. China, from its origin: cross-ideological engagement with Asia (M5, M4). D26a records ch. 7's similar point.

claims.t: LAC regionalism is in crisis and redefinition. ALBA and UNASUR are in deep crisis, and PROSUR seeks a less political, more free-trade agenda. Bolsonaro's anti-globalist foreign policy, prioritising the USA 'as sole partner', raises doubts about Brazil's commitment to Mercosur, and Brazil under Bolsonaro will not exert regional leadership.
claims.q: the anti-globalist approach of Bolsonaro's government foreign policy and its prioritization of the USA and sole partner rise doubts about the Brazilian commitment to Mercosur
claims.an: Analyst: regional fragmentation reduces LAC's collective bargaining capacity vis-à-vis both the US and China. It may favour bilateral deals in which China's policy banks and SOEs are strong (M2/M4). This is an inference the authors do not make.

claims.t: The authors argue that LAC regionalism could be revived by advancing free trade, which would counterbalance protectionist trends including Trump's policies. This should not weaken social and productive dimensions, and countries must diversify and reduce dependence on commodity exports.
claims.q: We argue that the revitalization of Latin American regionalism could find a supportive pillar in the advancement of free trade, an agenda which could counterbalance protectionist trends, including the policies promoted by President Trump.
claims.an: This casts US protectionism under Trump as a negative for LAC trade, consistent with M3: restricted US market access pushes LAC toward other partners.

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 303)
claims.t: Chávez's and Maduro's anti-US and anti-Western foreign policy led Venezuela to reject the IMF and to increase cooperation with Russia and China. The authors describe China as 'a country which owns most of its external debt'.
claims.q: Instead, Venezuela increased cooperation with Russia and China, a country which owns most of its external debt.
claims.e: Editorial synthesis of ch. 13; no source given for the debt claim.
claims.an: This illustrates the M6/M5 pathway: governments in conflict with the US avoid IMF conditionality and turn to China and Russia. It is the volume's only explicit claim about Chinese finance. Treat the 'most of its external debt' quantification as unreliable and verify against Gallagher & Myers / Bosto

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 305)
claims.t: By 2010 most LAC countries were enjoying stability and growth driven, among other things, by external investment and Chinese demand for primary goods. The crisis was felt only from 2012-2013, when commodity and especially oil prices fell and fracking added pressure on prices.
claims.q: However, by 2010 most countries were enjoying stability and growth led by among others, external investments and Chinese demand for primary goods; the impact of the crisis began to be felt by 2012–2013.
claims.an: This supports M1: Chinese demand cushioned LAC from the 2008 crisis, unlike Europe. It also implies that LAC's dependence on China as a demand source became a transmission channel when Chinese growth slowed.

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 303)
claims.t: Brazil's countercyclical policies after 2008 initially succeeded. By 2011, however, US and European policies reduced capital flows to emerging economies and world demand for primary goods fell. Brazil used taxes to control capital outflows, but the political crisis followed from 2013.
claims.q: By 2011, however, the policy adopted in the USA and Europe reduced capital flows to emerging economies, and in addition, demand for primary goods decreased, as the world economy slowed down.

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 300)
claims.t: A key difference in crisis management is that the EU had regional institutions (the Eurogroup, later the ESM and Banking Union), whereas most LAC regional organisations developed no relevant collective mechanism. LAC countries dealt with the crisis individually, with limited collective support via CAF and FLAR and multilateral support from the IDB.
claims.q: most regional organizations in Latin America did not develop any relevant collective mechanism to deal with financial crisis
claims.an: The absence of regional financial backstops leaves LAC governments to seek external finance bilaterally, from the IMF, the US or China. That is relevant context for M2/M6 (analyst inference).

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 300)
claims.t: Former ECB President Draghi observed that the USA did not apply Washington Consensus-style austerity after the global financial crisis. It engaged in countercyclical fiscal policy, which brought a quicker recovery and return to price stability than in Europe. Meanwhile the EMU adopted Washington Consensus recipes and brought in the IMF, losing its attraction as a model.
claims.q: the USA did not apply the same kind of Washington Consensus austerity policies after the global financial crisis, but engaged into countercyclical fiscal policies which allowed a quicker recovery and return to price stability than Europe
claims.an: This is relevant to M13 (US model legitimacy): it highlights the perceived double standard between the austerity the US and IMF prescribed to LAC in the 1980s-90s and the US's own countercyclical response. That double standard feeds LAC scepticism of Washington-centred prescriptions. Compare D25 (Wh

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 300)
claims.t: The EMU's adoption of Washington Consensus recipes and its integration of the IMF into the Troika made the EU lose its attraction as a model of regional integration and of social policy.
claims.q: led to the loss of attraction of the EU as a model of regional integration and its social model
claims.an: This loss of Western model attraction (EU as well as US) is a possible permissive condition for LAC openness to alternative partners. The book does not draw this link explicitly.

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 299)
claims.t: The 2008 crisis supported the rise of emerging countries through the BRICS and the G20, which demanded proportional representation in the Bretton Woods institutions. EU international influence diminished correspondingly.
claims.q: The global financial crisis of 2008 supported the rise of the emerging countries with the creation of the BRICS and the G20, which demanded for reforms of the Bretton Woods institutions to represent them more proportionally.
claims.an: Systemic context for the rise of China and Brazil (both BRICS) as alternative poles. The chapter does not discuss China specifically.

claims.c: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 304)
claims.t: LAC regionalism has disintegrated. Several countries abandoned or formally renounced UNASUR's founding treaty and Brazil renounced CELAC. Former leaders of regionalism (Brazil, Venezuela) turned inward and adopted more nationalist foreign policies, and both show a trend toward militarisation of politics.
claims.q: the abandonment or formal renunciation of the founding treaties of organizations such as Unasur by several countries, and CELAC by Brazil
claims.an: CELAC is the platform for the China-CELAC Forum (D26a, ch. 7). Brazil's exit from CELAC under Bolsonaro is an ideological move against a multilateral channel that China uses. Its effect on bilateral Brazil-China economic ties is not assessed.

claims.t: Through first-mover advantages and network externalities, US tech corporations acquired global quasi-monopolies and became 'digital colonial masters' of the rest of the world, China partly excepted. Europe pays 'tributes' in money and data, remains technologically dependent, and should build its own public-interest European Software Consortium modelled on Airbus.
claims.q: In this way, US corporations became "digital colonial masters" of the rest of the world (except—in part—for China), and the latter has to pay "tributes" in the form of money and data and remains technologically dependent.
claims.e: Author argument; Airbus analogy; budget estimate EUR 15 bn/year (0.1% EU GDP).
claims.an: This is a conceptual tool on technological dependence and network-externality monopolies. It treats China as the partial exception that built its own digital ecosystem. It may be useful as an analogy for the LAC choice between US and Chinese digital infrastructure (e.g. telecoms), which the book doe

claims.t: Long-term real-economy investment predominates when short-term speculation is unprofitable. Examples are the industrial countries in the 1950s-60s and China since its early-1980s reforms.
claims.q: If short-term speculation is unprofitable, then long-term investment in the real economy predominates—as over the 1950s and 1960s in industrial countries or since the reforms in China in the early 1980s.
claims.an: The author presents China as a 'real-capitalist' regime in contrast to Western 'finance capitalism' (consistent with D26a's ch. 2 record). This is relevant to M13 discussions of the attractiveness of China's development model. Compare D24.

claims.t: The dollar's double role as US national currency and substitute world currency causes fluctuations in dollar-denominated commodity prices, the financial crises of dollar-indebted emerging economies and excessive US external debt. The author proposes target zones among the four major currencies (dollar, euro, renminbi, yen) as a step toward a global currency ('globo').
claims.q: The double role of the dollar as the national currency of the US and as a (substitute) world currency is a major cause of fluctuations in dollar-denominated commodity prices (including "oil price shocks"), of the financial crises of dollar-indebted emerging market economies and of the excessive external debt of the US
claims.an: The renminbi is treated as one of four major currencies. Dollar-system critiques underpin LAC interest in alternatives such as RMB swap lines (not discussed in the book).

claims.t: EFSI (the Juncker Plan) used a EUR 26 bn EU budget guarantee plus EUR 7.5 bn of EIB capital (EUR 33.5 bn) to target at least EUR 500 bn of investment in 2015-2020, an overall multiplier of 15x. By July 2018 EUR 70.4 bn had been approved and EUR 375.5 bn reportedly mobilised.
claims.q: The total amount of EUR 33.5 billion aims to leverage additional investment of at least EUR 500 billion between 2015 and 2020.
claims.e: EIB data, EIB (2019) multiplier methodology, interview material.
claims.an: This shows a Western model of de-risking and leveraging private capital with small public guarantees. It is analogous to the US DFC approach (M3: reliance on private capital) and contrasts with Chinese policy-bank direct lending (M2). The analogy is the analyst's.

claims.t: Leveraging private capital involves trade-offs. The more operations run through private intermediaries, the less strategic policy steer public institutions retain. Excessive financial-engineering risk transfers risk to the public sector while the private sector reaps the rewards. The EIB should take more 'economic' risk (projects, sectors, countries), not more financial-product risk.
claims.q: creates the danger that public entities (and ultimately the taxpayers) will bear the risks, while the private sector reaps all the rewards
claims.an: This is a conceptual tool for assessing Western 'mobilise private capital' development finance, which bears on M3: such finance yields less policy steer and slower, more indirect delivery than state-directed finance.

claims.t: After the financial crisis there was renewed support for public regional and national development banks, as the limits of purely private finance became evident. About a quarter of EFSI transactions went through national development banks.
claims.q: there had been renewed support for public regional and national development banks
claims.an: This is a broader legitimation of state-led development banking after 2008. It weakens the normative contrast between 'market' Western finance and Chinese policy-bank finance (M13). The inference is the analyst's.

claims.t: The euro area is the only monetary area without a genuine lender of last resort. Markets can therefore turn sovereign doubts into liquidity or even solvency crises, because national treasuries do not control the currency in which they borrow, as with Argentina's currency board with the dollar. The author proposes a European Debt Agency, blue/red bonds and an independent European Monitoring Board.
claims.q: because national treasuries cannot control, by definition, the currency and the exchange rate in which they issue their debt, like Argentina during its currency board with the dollar
claims.e: Author argument based on EMS/ERM experience.
claims.an: This draws the LAC-EU parallel of borrowing in a currency one cannot issue (dollar for LAC). It is relevant background to LAC vulnerability to US monetary conditions.

claims.t: Coordination among sovereign states never works for the 'general interest', only when governments perceive their own self-interest. Successful coordination requires mechanisms that make each state's self-interest in convergence visible.
claims.q: These lessons explain that coordination among sovereign states never works for the sake of "general interest" but only for the selfish interests of governments and their electorates.
claims.e: Lessons from four decades of EU policy coordination (Ghymers 1995, 2015).
claims.an: This is a rationalist principle that helps explain LAC governments' interest-driven, rather than values-driven, choices between partners (M4). The author applies it to EU-LAC cooperation in ch. 24.

claims.t: Post-crisis EMU reforms focused on risk avoidance and surveillance (fiscal rules, the European Semester, the MIP, the Banking Union's supervision pillar) largely succeeded. Risk-sharing reforms (EDIS, a euro-area budget/fiscal capacity, Eurobonds, FTT) met major resistance, especially from creditor states. The intergovernmental ESM and Eurogroup remain democratically unaccountable.
claims.q: the reforms with a focus on "risk-avoidance" and stronger "surveillance" and "monitoring" had more success
claims.e: Review of EU reform proposals (Commission, EP resolutions, Four/Five Presidents' reports, Meseberg Declaration).
claims.an: Peripheral (EU institutional design).

claims.t: Quoting Draghi, the US ran a 3.6% average deficit in 2009-2018 while the euro area ran a 0.5% surplus. The US combined a capital markets union with countercyclical fiscal policy, and recovered sooner.
claims.q: The US had a deficit of 3.6% on average from 2009 to 2018, while the euro area had a surplus of 0.5%.
claims.an: Same double-standard theme as C542 (M13).

claims.t: The author proposes a 'costless' formula for EU-LAC cooperation: bottom-up networks of civil servants, experts and SMEs on the REDIMA model, Bi-regional Minister Councils, and mutual monitoring of macroeconomic, social, environmental and productivity policies. He frames it as an 'EU-LAC Monnet Plan' to give substance to the 1999 Rio Strategic Alliance.
claims.q: the purpose of this chapter is to propose a costless formula of bi-regional cooperation between the EU and the Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) region
claims.e: Proposal based on REDIMA/ECLAC (Ghymers 2005) and African monetary union experiences.
claims.an: Analyst: the proposal is explicitly 'costless' and has no financing component. It contrasts sharply with China's bundled finance-plus-construction offer (M2), and it parallels the Western 'rhetoric without commensurate finance' problem in M3, here for the EU rather than the US.

claims.t: The EU-LAC 'Strategic Alliance' declared in Rio in 1999 has had 'too timid content and few realizations in two decades'.
claims.q: which was declared in 1999 in Rio by the EU and the LAC countries but with a too timid content and few realizations in two decades
claims.an: This is an insider (EU-affiliated) admission that a Western partnership with LAC under-delivered for two decades. It supports the broader point that Western strategic declarations toward LAC have not been matched by substantive programmes, which leaves room for China (M3/M15 analogue).

claims.t: LAC's long-run total factor productivity growth was negative (-0.11% a year, 1960-2014); among regions only Sub-Saharan Africa did worse (-0.5%). IDB estimates that with Emerging Asia's investment rate and efficiency, LAC GDP in 2017 would have been six times higher.
claims.q: the TFP growth for the CELAC economies is even worst since it is negative (−0.11% per year), and only the very poor region of Sub-Saharan Africa registers a worse performance (−0.5%)
claims.an: This is structural context for M10: commodity-led growth without productivity gains.

claims.t: Latin American economies are more integrated with external actors such as China than with each other, but with weaker transmission to national economies. Only 9% of the foreign value added in LAC exports is sourced intra-regionally, against 50% in the EU and 40% in Asia. LAC is also the least open region and the least integrated in global value chains (Chile 52%, Brazil 35%, Argentina 31% GVC participation).
claims.q: Latin American economies are more integrated with external actors (e.g. China) than intra-regionally but with less transmission to the national economies.
claims.e: Cadestin et al. (2016), OECD (2019), IMF (2017), Morgan (2017).
claims.an: This supports the premise that LAC's external integration with China is deep. It also qualifies it on development quality: China links are enclave-like with weak domestic spillovers (M10 subordinated integration; compare D10, D09). Chile's high GVC participation is driven by 'forward' copper exports

claims.t: The author argues that the EU and LAC share values and socio-economic objectives more than any other pair of regions. That, combined with complementary productivity gaps, makes LAC the best candidate for an EU strategic alliance built on SME integration into joint GVCs, modelled on Germany/Austria's integration of Central and Eastern Europe.
claims.q: The EU and the LAC share the same values and socio-economic objectives more than with any other regions, making the LAC area the best candidate for a successful alliance with the EU.
claims.an: This is a values-based pitch for a 'third' partner. Analyst: it presumes shared values drive partnership, while the corpus evidence (e.g. C518, C528) suggests LAC choices are largely interest- and demand-driven.

claims.t: In Latin America's financial crises the regional factor played virtually no role. Creditors always came from outside the region, 'as did and still does the big power with heavy political clout in the Western hemisphere'.
claims.q: And in Latin America's financial crises, the creditors always came from outside the region as did and still does the big power with heavy political clout in the Western hemisphere.
claims.an: The epilogue implicitly acknowledges US hemispheric dominance of LAC crisis finance. Combined with the lack of regional backstops (C541), this frames why alternative external creditors (e.g. China) could gain traction. The inference is the analyst's.

claims.t: Argentina's recurring crises and Greece in the early 2010s show that countries on the verge of bankruptcy can afford only 'small portions of sovereignty and democracy', unless they are too big to fail. The IMF's recipe has hardly changed. Populism caused by debt crises can be left or right but is always associated with policy failures.
claims.q: Both countries discovered in their own painful way that on the verge of bankruptcy they could afford only small portions of sovereignty and democracy.
claims.an: This frames the sovereignty cost of IMF conditionality. It is relevant to M6: why non-conditional (e.g. Chinese) finance can appeal to indebted LAC governments. The book does not make this link.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 9)
claims.t: China pursues a three-fold strategy in Latin America: securing commodities (most important), opening markets for manufactures, and ensuring adherence to the one-China principle.
claims.q: first, and most importantly, to secure the provision of oil, minerals and agricultural products; second, to create access to new markets for the country's growing export volume of manufactured products; and third to make sure that Latin American governments adhere to the 'one China principle' in their foreign relations.
claims.e: Authors' synthesis of the literature and the Ecuador case.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 2)
claims.t: China's influence in Latin America has increased significantly but remains overshadowed by the US.
claims.q: while China's influence in Latin America has undoubtedly increased significantly during the last half-decade, its role is still overshadowed by the US.
claims.e: Overall argument; US share of FDI and trade.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 2)
claims.t: China–Latin America trade rose from US$13bn in 2000 to US$180bn in 2010 (+50% on 2009), exceeding Hu Jintao's US$100bn target for 2010 by 2007.
claims.q: China's trade with the region totalled 180 billion USD in 2010, up 50 percent from 2009
claims.an: The rapid rebound after 2009 is consistent with D06's crisis-cushion argument.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 2)
claims.t: The neorealist view holds that China pursues 'containment through surrogates' and soft-balancing, taking advantage of a power vacuum created by declining US and Russian interest in Latin America.
claims.q: China, so the argument goes, is taking advantage of a power vacuum in the region that was created by the United States' and Russia's declining interest in Latin America

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 2)
claims.t: Leftist governments produced a pragmatic convergence with China around a larger state role in the economy.
claims.q: As a result of many leftist governments in Latin America, an interesting pragmatic convergence with China has come about
claims.an: The authors later limit this to economic pragmatism, not model adoption.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 4)
claims.t: Isolating Taiwan is perhaps the PRC's highest-ranking political objective in Latin America, where 11 of Taiwan's 23 diplomatic allies were located. Costa Rica switched recognition to the PRC in 2007.
claims.q: The diplomatic isolation of Taiwan has been perhaps the highest-ranking key political objective for the PRC in Latin America

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 4)
claims.t: China and Argentina engage in quid pro quo multilateral diplomacy: Argentina abstains on US-sponsored resolutions on China's human rights, China supports Argentina on the Malvinas, and in 2005 they jointly opposed US/EU farm subsidies at the WTO.
claims.q: Argentina has abstained from voting on the US-sponsored resolutions to investigate China's human rights situation, while the PRC has continuously supported Argentina's position on the Islas Malvinas (Falkland Islands)
claims.an: Conflicts with Piccone (2016) as cited in D06; check UN voting records.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 5)
claims.t: In 2010 China overtook the US as Brazil's largest trading partner, with trade above US$56bn.
claims.q: In 2010, China overtook the US as Brazil's biggest trade partner with a volume of more than 56 billion USD.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 5)
claims.t: Chinese FDI reached ~US$15bn in LAC in 2010 (9% of the region's FDI), more than 90% in natural-resource extraction, making China the third-largest investor after the US and the Netherlands. Chinese FDI had barely registered before 2009.
claims.q: More than 90 per cent has been invested in natural resource extraction.
claims.an: The 2010 surge is largely Brazilian and Argentine oil and mining M&A, a step change after the 2008–09 crisis.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 10)
claims.t: Official PRC FDI figures are inflated by tax-haven routing: US$22bn cumulative by end-2006 falls to ~US$1.9bn excluding tax havens.
claims.q: according to PRC official data, Latin Amerika had received 22 billion USD in cumulative PRC investment by the end of 2006. When the tax havens were excluded, only approximately 1.9 billion USD remained
claims.an: Data traceability point, consistent with D06 note 2.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 6)
claims.t: Obama's March 2011 Latin America visit was widely interpreted as an attempt to reassert US economic leadership in response to China's growing presence.
claims.q: has widely been interpreted as an attempt to reassert economic leadership in the region that Washington has traditionally dominated.
claims.e: Authors' reading of commentary; no specific source.
claims.an: This is early US rhetorical reassertion; per C19 the authors see it as not changing US low prioritisation.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 6)
claims.t: Chinese long-term supply deals lock in commodities on favourable terms; for example, a 2005 US$2bn joint venture guarantees China 836,250 t of Chilean copper over 15 years at US$2.07/lb when copper traded above US$4/lb in 2011. This 'primatisation' risks a centre–periphery pattern.
claims.q: Considering that copper was trading above four USD a pound in 2011, China is getting copper at far below market prices
claims.e: James (2011, LA Times); Jenkins & Dussel Peters (2009).
claims.an: This is commonly known as the Codelco–Minmetals deal, but the text does not name the parties; verify externally.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 7)
claims.t: Chinese retail shops have proliferated across Ecuador, many operating informally. Local businesses suspect Chinese state subsidies, but there is no hard evidence.
claims.q: According to government estimates, a majority of Chinese businesses do not operate legally in the country.
claims.e: Government estimates; author interview with the Cuenca Chamber of Commerce (Aug 2007).
claims.an: Bottom-up Chinese commercial presence and local resentment.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 7)
claims.t: China–Ecuador trade grew 5.5 times, from US$436m in 2004 to US$2.4bn in 2010, mainly through rising Chinese exports to Ecuador.
claims.q: Between 2004 and 2010 China's total trade with Ecuador grew 5.5 times from 436 million USD to 2.4 billion USD in 2010 - mainly due to rapidly increasing Chinese exports to the Andean country
claims.e: Xinhua Economic News Service (13 Aug 2008); Chinese Ministry of Commerce.
claims.an: Ecuador runs a deficit with China, consistent with D07 (Ecuador −US$615m in 2005).

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 7)
claims.t: Access to Ecuadorian oil is China's primary interest in Ecuador, ahead of trade. Ecuador has 6.03bn barrels of proven reserves, and Chinese-owned Andes Petroleum produces 12% of output.
claims.q: Growing trade, however, is only secondary to China's quest for access to Ecuadorian oil.
claims.an: The text does not discuss oil-backed loans or presales.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 8)
claims.t: Chinese state firms acquired a sizeable stake in Ecuador's oil sector: a 2005 joint venture bought EnCana's assets for US$1.42bn, and Andes Petroleum produces 62,000 bpd.
claims.q: Andes Petroleum produces 62,000 barrels per day, equal to 12 percent of Ecuador's total, state and private, crude oil output
claims.an: M&A of Western-owned assets: China consolidates by buying out Western firms.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 8)
claims.t: Chinese firms plan a US$3bn investment in Ecuador's Corriente Copper Belt, with production expected from 2013, but poor transport infrastructure is a bottleneck.
claims.q: improvements to Ecuador's transport infrastructure are crucial for Chinese investments and generally FDI to take full effect.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 8)
claims.t: Chinese investment in Ecuador has been accompanied by modest development aid and soft-power measures (2006 loans, 2009 agreements, Confucius Institute 2010, tourism status 2006), and Ecuador has reaffirmed its one-China policy in return.
claims.q: In line with the global trend in China's foreign economic relations, Chinese investment in Ecuador has been accompanied by development aid.
claims.an: The sums cited are tiny (US$ millions), which contrasts with the later multi-billion policy-bank lending not covered here.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 8)
claims.t: China has not exploited closer ties with left-wing regimes (Venezuela, Bolivia, Ecuador) to diminish US power and 'tacitly acquiesces to the Monroe Doctrine'. It rejected Chávez's advances despite Venezuela sending ~20% of its oil exports to China and over US$32bn in announced loans.
claims.q: But so far China has not been interested in fully exploiting the potential that having closer relations with the socialist, left-wing regimes – particularly that of Venezuela but also Bolivia and Ecuador
claims.an: This is evidence against a purely ideology-driven explanation on China's side: Beijing pursues pragmatic economic ties and avoids provoking Washington, which may itself help explain why expansion continued without triggering strong US counteraction.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 9)
claims.t: The Chinese presence in Latin America is not a high priority for Washington and lacks sufficient strategic and political importance for it, though US perception may change.
claims.q: the Chinese presence in Latin America is not a high priority for Washington; China's relations with the region have remained a minor issue because they lack sufficient strategic and political importance for the United States.
claims.an: Directly relevant: US inattention as an enabling condition before the later rise of US strategic discourse.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 9)
claims.t: Some Latin American governments see partnership with Beijing as a means to soft-balance or hedge against traditional US hegemony.
claims.q: there can be little doubt that some governments perceive a partnership with Beijing as a welcome means of soft-balancing or hedging against traditional US hegemony in the region.
claims.an: This is the 'China card' argument.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 9)
claims.t: Latin American governments embrace China as part of multidirectional diplomacy aimed at moderating, not substituting, US hegemony, and behave as rational opportunity maximisers, especially in economic hardship such as 2008–09.
claims.q: Their main interest is moderating US hegemony, not substituting it.
claims.an: Explains continued engagement with China regardless of US discourse: diversification is a rational default, not an alignment choice.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 9)
claims.t: Latin American governments may rightly complain of a frequent lack of serious US attention and of narrowly defined US security interests.
claims.q: Latin American governments may rightly complain about a frequent lack of serious attention on the part of the United States and the latter's rather narrowly defined national security interests
claims.an: The US security focus crowds out economic engagement.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 10)
claims.t: US trade and investment in Latin America are much larger than China's and qualitatively different, as a provider of high-tech and knowledge-based goods and services, so China cannot supersede the US.
claims.q: US trade and investment in Latin America is not only much larger than that of China, but Washington's economic engagement has so far also been qualitatively different from that of China – as a provider of high tech and knowledge-based goods and services.
claims.e: Authors' conclusion; ECLAC FDI shares (US 17% vs China 9% of 2010 FDI).
claims.an: Counter-evidence: the US remained the dominant economic partner overall as of 2011.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 10)
claims.t: Open embrace of the Beijing Consensus is unlikely, since convergence is only pragmatic economic interest and Latin Americans reject authoritarianism.
claims.q: China is not attractive a model for governance due to the strong rejection of even the slightest hint at authoritarianism across most parts of Latin America.
claims.an: Consistent with D06's cited 19.6% approval of China's development model.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 3)
claims.t: During the early Cold War, China's interest in Latin America was a distant third priority, driven mainly by its anti-US stance. After 1971–72 relations became pragmatic and issue-oriented, and by the end of the 1970s China had diplomatic relations with most major Latin American states.
claims.q: the motivation of the Chinese leadership to include Latin America in its foreign policy, albeit in a distant third position behind Asia and Africa, was mainly linked to Beijing's anti-US stance
claims.an: Historical contrast: the ideological phase gave way to pragmatism.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 5)
claims.t: Japan's share of Latin America's trade fell from 11.4% (1990) to 6.5% (2005) while other Asian countries rose from 7.6% to 22.5%.
claims.q: Japan accounted for 11.4 percent of Latin America's total trade in 1990. By 2005 this statistic was reduced to 6.5 percent, whereas other Asian countries showed a rapid increase from 7.6 percent to 22.5 percent
claims.an: Japan's decline is a comparative case of an Asian partner losing position.

claims.c: (Salinas de Dosch and Dosch, n.d., p. 5)
claims.t: China has signed FTAs with Chile (in force 2006), Peru (in force 2010) and Costa Rica (signed 2011).
claims.q: So far, China has signed three FTAs in Latin America: with Chile (in force since 2006), Peru (in force since 2010) and Costa Rica (signed in 2011).
claims.an: FTA partners include centre-right/market-oriented governments (Chile, Peru, Costa Rica), which shows cross-ideological pragmatism (M5).

claims.t: China–Latin America trade grew from US$13bn in 2000 to US$180bn in 2010, up 50% from 2009; Hu's US$100bn target for 2010 was exceeded by 2007.
claims.q: China's trade with the region reached 180 billion USD in 2010, evincing not only an increase of 50 per cent from 2009 but also a pattern of sharp growth since 2000, when the China–Latin America trade volume stood at just 13 billion USD.
claims.an: The Xinhua (2008) reference in the bibliography is titled 'China's Trade with Ecuador in May 2008', an odd source for the region-wide target claim.

claims.t: The relationship has been driven mainly by a mutual desire to accelerate economic exchange.
claims.q: this budding relationship has been driven mainly by a mutual desire to accelerate economic exchange
claims.e: Authors' reading of the issue's articles.

claims.t: Chinese SOEs such as PetroChina and Sinopec have often succeeded in acquiring shares in Latin American oil and mineral exploration companies.
claims.q: the often successful attempts of Chinese state-owned corporations (such as PetroChina and Sinopec) to acquire shares in Latin American oil and mineral commodities exploration companies

claims.t: Strategic partnerships, military training and CCP party ties seemingly support a neorealist view of China balancing US dominance. Li (2008) sees China exploiting a power vacuum left by declining US and Russian interest.
claims.q: These examples of the intensifying Sino-Latin American links seemingly support a neorealist perspective
claims.an: Li 2008 is cited at p. 195 of the chapter; the power-vacuum claim is cited, not demonstrated.

claims.t: Chinese FDI reached about US$15bn in 2010 (9% of regional FDI), more than 90% in natural-resource extraction, mainly in Brazil, Argentina and Peru. China is the third-largest investor and is narrowing the gap with the US.
claims.q: More than 90 per cent has been invested in natural resource extraction. The main recipient countries were Brazil, Argentina and Peru.
claims.an: Inflow (flow) data. The country amounts for Brazil, Argentina and Peru are not given.

claims.t: Official PRC investment data overstate Chinese FDI in Latin America because of tax-haven routing (US$22bn cumulative by 2006 vs about US$1.9bn excluding havens).
claims.q: When the tax havens were excluded, only approximately 1.9 billion USD remained
claims.an: An important caveat on data quality for any measure of Chinese FDI stock.

claims.t: The US remains the largest investor (17% of US$113bn in 2010), but the gap with China is gradually narrowing; Chinese FDI had barely registered until 2009.
claims.q: Until 2009, Chinese FDI had barely registered.
claims.an: Shows US investment still ahead in 2010; Chinese expansion is recent.

claims.t: Agreements signed on Xi Jinping's June 2011 tour strengthened China's access to Chilean copper and Uruguayan soy and cemented its role in Cuban oil, including Gulf of Mexico fields.
claims.q: not only strengthen China's access to Chilean copper and Uruguayan soy but also cemented Beijing's role in the development of Cuban oil

claims.t: Obama's March 2011 tour, his first to the region in almost two years, was widely read as an attempt to reassert US economic leadership. The superiority of the US market-reform model can no longer be taken for granted.
claims.q: Yet, the success story and any superiority of the US-backed model of market reform can no longer be taken for granted.
claims.an: An example of US discourse and visibility without new instruments described.

claims.t: Under many leftist governments, a pragmatic convergence with China has emerged around a larger state role in the economy (Fernández Jilberto and Hogenboom 2010).
claims.q: China and Latin America have both been moving in the direction of a development model in which there is reconciliation of state and market

claims.t: In the early 1960s China's interest in Latin America was a distant third priority and mainly reflected its anti-US stance. Its flirtation with communist movements had very limited impact, and after the Sino-Soviet split it shifted to established governments.
claims.q: albeit in a distant third position behind Asia and Africa, was mainly linked to Beijing's anti-US stance
claims.an: Historical background.

claims.t: After the Kissinger and Nixon visits (1971–72), relations became pragmatic, issues-oriented and free of ideology. By the end of the 1970s China had relations with most major states, and 1970s–80s ties rested on political quid pro quo (UN entry votes vs support for 200-mile sea claims).
claims.q: paved the way for pragmatic and issues-oriented relations between Beijing and Latin American capitals, free of any ideological ballast
claims.an: Supports the cross-ideological pragmatism reading.

claims.t: Isolating Taiwan has been perhaps the PRC's highest-ranking political objective in Latin America. Of Taiwan's 23 allies, 11 were in Latin America, and Costa Rica's 2007 switch was a serious setback for Taipei.
claims.q: The diplomatic isolation of Taiwan has been perhaps the highest-ranking key political objective for the PRC in Latin America

claims.t: Argentina and China practise UN quid pro quo: Argentina abstains on US-sponsored China human-rights resolutions, and the PRC supports Argentina on the Malvinas. In 2005 they took a common stance against US and EU agricultural subsidies at the WTO.
claims.q: Argentina has abstained from voting on the US-sponsored resolutions to investigate China's human rights situation
claims.an: The text cites 'Olivia 2010'; the reference list has 'Oliva, Carla V. (2010)'.

claims.t: Brazil and China built a strategic partnership in science and technology aimed at breaking developed nations' monopoly. In 2010 China overtook the US as Brazil's largest trade partner (more than US$56bn).
claims.q: In 2010, China overtook the US as Brazil's biggest trade partner with a volume of more than 56 billion USD.
claims.an: A case where China displaced the US as the top trade partner.

claims.t: Historically, geostrategic and ideological concerns preceded economic interests. China–Latin America trade and investment were insignificant until well into the 1990s, and Japan led East Asian economic engagement.
claims.q: there can be little doubt that general foreign policy and geostrategic concerns, along with ideological considerations, preceded economic interests
claims.e: Literature; Japan trade share 11.4% (1990) to 6.5% (2005) vs other Asia 7.6% to 22.5% (Rose 2010).

claims.t: China's early 21st-century charm offensive, peaking first with Hu's 2004 tour, captured attention. Paz notes that Lula, Kirchner and Chávez spent more time in Beijing than in Washington.
claims.q: have spent more time in Beijing than in Washington
claims.an: A contrast in high-level attention favouring China.

claims.t: China has three FTAs in Latin America: Chile (in force 2006), Peru (in force 2010) and Costa Rica (signed 2011).
claims.q: So far, China has signed three FTAs in Latin America: with Chile (in force since 2006), Peru (in force since 2010) and Costa Rica (signed in 2011).
claims.an: Note: FTA partners include Chile, a US FTA partner, which illustrates hedging rather than ideology.

claims.t: The OECD and other international organisations hold that, except for Mexico, Latin American exports are not significantly affected by Chinese competition because the traded goods are dissimilar. Regional business organisations see a serious threat.
claims.q: with the exception of Mexico, Latin American exports are not significantly affected by Chinese competition due to the dissimilarity of the traded goods
claims.e: Jenkins and Dussel Peters 2009 summarising OECD and other views.
claims.an: The core complementarity claim: structural dissimilarity of goods.

claims.t: Chinese firms have secured long-term commodity supplies: a decade of oil from Venezuela and Brazil; wheat, soybeans, natural gas and iron ore from Argentina; and Chilean copper under a 2005 US$2bn JV at a fixed US$2.07/lb, far below 2011 prices.
claims.q: Under the terms of a 2 billion USD joint venture, agreed upon in 2005, China is guaranteed 836,250 metric tonnes of Chilean copper over 15 years, at rates fixed to the (then) market price of 2.07 USD per pound.
claims.an: The doc does not name the JV partners; verify externally.

claims.t: This primatisation of exports to China risks a return to the centre–periphery trade pattern.
claims.q: spells the danger of a possible return of the centre–periphery trade pattern

claims.t: China's economic interests are driven by the need for a steady, increasing flow of commodities and raw materials. Its political and geostrategic motives are harder to assess.
claims.q: the interests are mainly driven by the need for a steady, and increasing, flow of commodities and raw materials to keep China's economy growing

claims.t: Mols distinguishes strategic partners (Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Venezuela), cooperative partners (Chile, Peru, Cuba) and friendly-cooperative partners (Central America and the Caribbean).
claims.q: strategic partners (Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Venezuela), cooperative partners (Chile, Peru and Cuba) and friendly-cooperative partners (Central America and the Caribbean)

claims.t: China has not exploited closer ties with left-wing regimes to diminish US power and tacitly accepts the Monroe Doctrine. It was reluctant to join Venezuela's anti-American rhetoric despite announcing more than US$32bn in loans and taking about 20% of Venezuelan oil exports.
claims.q: the PRC has been reluctant to hop onto the Venezuelan bandwagon of anti-American rhetoric
claims.an: Challenges ideology-driven explanations on the Chinese side, while China still financed the most anti-US government heavily.

claims.t: China's presence in Latin America is not a high priority for Washington and has remained a minor issue lacking strategic importance. The perception may change, and the US is watching whether China disrupts existing patterns of bi- and multilateralism.
claims.q: the Chinese presence in Latin America is not a high priority for Washington; China’s relations with the region have remained a minor issue because they lack sufficient strategic and political importance
claims.an: Contemporaneous evidence of US inattention circa 2011, before the later securitised discourse.

claims.t: China is not yet a firmly established power in Latin America; its rise there is recent.
claims.q: For the time being, however, China is not a firmly established power in Latin America, and Beijing's rise on the continent is a relatively recent phenomenon.

claims.t: Left-wing governments perceive partnership with Beijing as soft-balancing or hedging against US hegemony. Yet all Latin American governments diversify, aiming to moderate US hegemony, not substitute it. As rational opportunity maximisers, especially after 2008–09, they welcome every trade and investment opportunity.
claims.q: All Latin American governments have diversified their foreign relations. Their main interest is moderating US hegemony, not substituting it.
claims.an: The central explanation: demand-side opportunity maximisation rather than ideological realignment; the 2008–09 crisis increased receptiveness.

claims.t: Latin American governments have little economic reason to replace dependency on the US with dependency on China.
claims.q: why should they be interested in replacing a decades-long dependency on the United States by a new dependency on China?

claims.t: China is building a multilateral regional presence: founding member of FEALAC, OAS permanent observer, ties with the Rio Group, the Andean Community and CARICOM. It joined the IDB in 2008, committing US$350m.
claims.q: In 2008, China joined the Inter-American Development Bank and committed 350 million USD to public and private sector projects.

claims.t: PRC aid and related investment projects in the hemisphere (2002–2007, US$26.7bn) were mostly in natural resources and strongly commercial, less infrastructure-oriented than in Africa and Southeast Asia.
claims.q: The emphasis on natural resources implies a strongly commercial nature to China's aid in Latin America, less oriented toward infrastructure development than China's foreign assistance to Africa and Southeast Asia

claims.t: There is no agreed or replicable China model: Wen Jiabao repudiated it, and China's scale and its prior state socialism cannot be replicated. Still, China's stable government and independent voice towards the US are appealing.
claims.q: These conditions cannot be replicated, even in Latin America
claims.e: Naughton 2010; China Daily 2011; Chen and Goodman 2012.
claims.an: This weakens governance-model emulation as an explanation; China's appeal is economic and symbolic rather than emulation.

claims.t: Mexico, though all but in a trade war with China for a decade, keeps a very close political relationship with it in the UN.
claims.q: All but in a trade war with the PRC for much of the last decade, the two countries' political relationship is nonetheless very close in international forums such as the United Nations
claims.an: Political closeness without economic complementarity.

claims.t: Brazil (Jenkins): engagement with China has so far been positive and improved the trade balance, but it has restructured the economy; iron ore and soy producers benefit, with evidence of de-industrialisation.
claims.q: Iron ore and soybean producers have benefitted greatly, but there is otherwise evidence of de-industrialisation.
claims.e: Summary of Jenkins' article in the issue.

claims.t: Mexico (Hernández): unlike Brazil and most Latin American countries, Mexico has no complementarity with China. It fears a 'China threat' and trade war, heightened by WTO rules and the end of a ten-year moratorium. It cannot win this battle and needs domestic policy change.
claims.q: Unlike with Brazil, or indeed most other Latin American countries, there is no complementarity between the PRC and Mexico
claims.an: Mexico is an important limiting case: China's economic relationship rests on complementarity and does not expand the same way where economies compete.

claims.t: Peru (Gonzalez-Vicente): China is a location for transnational production rather than a self-contained economy. The poor in both countries lose from globalisation, and bilateral dependency is too simple a frame even though China buys Peruvian primary products, invests in mining and sells manufactures.
claims.q: He argues that dependency in terms of bilateral relations is too simple a conclusion, even when, as in this case, the PRC buys primary products from Peru, invests in mining there, and sells manufactures into the local market.

claims.t: Chile (Gachúz): a major recipient of Chinese investment, especially in copper mining. It gained greatly from its FTA with China but needs value-added and services exports and policy and attitude change.
claims.q: if it is to continue growing it needs to develop exports in value-added products and in services

claims.t: Cuba (Hearn): China, often criticised for not following international economic norms elsewhere in Latin America, is encouraging Cuba to liberalise. It draws legitimacy from shared communist history while retaining state power over its internationally active enterprises.
claims.q: is in fact encouraging Cuba to liberalise its economic structures

claims.t: China's relations with Latin America are steadily moving beyond economics into social, political and cultural interactions.
claims.q: China's relations have steadily been moving beyond economics to involve social, political and cultural interactions.
claims.e: Hearn and León-Manríquez 2011; the issue's articles.

claims.t: Over the last decade Chinese investment in LAC grew substantially and diversified away from natural resources toward other industries.
claims.q: Over the last decade China’s investment in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) has increased substantially in volume and become more diversified from natural resources to other industries.
claims.e: M&A data, MOFCOM FDI data (abstract and Section II).

claims.t: LAC's export share to China rose from 1.3% (2000) to 14.5% (2020). LAC's share of China's outward investment stock rose from 12% (2014) to a peak of 21.4% (2017).
claims.q: the percentage of LAC’s exports to China of its total exports increased from 1.3 percent in 2000 to 14.5 percent in 2020. The stock of Chinese investment in LAC as a share of China’s total overseas investment stock, after remaining stable for most of the early 2000s, increased from 12 percent in 2014 to a peak of 21.4 percent in 2017.
claims.e: Aggregate trade and FDI stock statistics (no specific source given in the passage; the latter likely MOFCOM).
claims.an: The 21.4% LAC share of China's OFDI stock is largely driven by OFCs; compare the 4% Asia share of LAC FDI stock excluding OFCs (p. 8).

claims.t: Chinese investment in electricity generation and distribution in LAC continued despite intensifying US–China trade frictions. Examples are State Grid's US$3bn purchase of Chilquinta (Chile, October 2019) and China Yangtze Power's US$3.6bn purchase of Luz del Sur (Peru, December 2019), both previously owned by US firm Sempra Energy.
claims.q: Not even the intensification of the U.S.-China trade frictions could dampen China’s investment spree in this area.
claims.e: Two named transactions; 'more than a dozen acquisition deals' with average size over US$1bn.
claims.an: This bears directly on the central question: US–China friction did not stop strategic utility acquisitions from a US seller. The paper does not discuss any US attempt to block these deals.

claims.t: Push factors include China's capital-account liberalisation and the BRI, three China–LAC regional funds set up since 2015 (CLAI US$30bn, CLAC US$10bn, a US$20bn infrastructure special loan programme), and the global financial cycle. Commercial viability and pull factors also matter.
claims.q: In LAC alone, China has set up three regional funds since 2015 to back up its investment in LAC: the China-LAC Industrial Cooperation Investment Fund (CLAI Fund) with a size of US$30 billion; the China-LAC Cooperation Fund (CLAC Fund) of US$10 billion; and the Special Loan Program for China-Latin America Infrastructure of US$20 billion
claims.e: Literature (Calvo et al. 1993; Bruno and Shin 2015); Myers and Ray (2021) for the fund sizes.

claims.t: The authors argue that excess-capacity reduction under the 2015 Supply-Side Structural Reforms makes overseas investment a natural choice for Chinese corporations, especially SOEs with asset-expansion and national-strategy mandates.
claims.q: a shift toward overseas markets for investment opportunities becomes a natural choice for Chinese corporations, especially the large state-owned enterprises (SOE) that often have the mandates of keeping asset expansion and supporting national development strategies such as capacity reduction and the BRI.
claims.e: Argument supported by the electricity example and Table A.5 regressions.

claims.t: Electricity example: China's electricity output rose from 4.2 to 7.2 thousand TWh (2010–2018) while the US stayed at 4.2. By 2018 the top five Chinese state-owned electricity companies had completed US$18bn of overseas acquisitions, three times their domestic acquisitions. LAC per-capita electricity consumption is 50% of China's and 25% of the OECD's.
claims.q: electricity companies had completed overseas acquisitions for US$18 billion, three times the value of their domestic acquisitions.
claims.e: China Electricity Council; Li et al. (2020); Figure 1.

claims.t: Investment gaps constrain LAC's electricity sector, and Chinese investment through acquisitions or joint ventures can help fill them.
claims.q: Investment gaps are believed to be a main constraint to faster development in the sector (Ruiz Nunez and Wei 2015; Castellani et al. 2019). Chinese investment, whether through acquisitions or joint ventures, can indeed help fill these gaps.
claims.e: Ruiz Nunez and Wei (2015); Castellani et al. (2019).

claims.t: Only a small share of Chinese FDI goes to LAC: US$6.4bn in 2019 (5% of total), of which US$4.3bn was registered to Caribbean OFCs that are mostly not the final destination.
claims.q: In 2019, LAC attracted US$6.4 billion FDI from China, accounting for 5 percent of China’s total outward FDI (Figure 2, left panel). Out of this total, US$4.3 billion were registered as outflows to offshore financial centers (OFCs) in the Caribbean
claims.an: This qualifies the scale of Chinese FDI in LAC. Flows in 2019 were modest and mostly routed through OFCs.

claims.t: Including OFCs, Asia (particularly China) accounts for almost a third of LAC's inward FDI stock, ahead of Europe (30%) and the US (20%). Excluding OFCs, Asia's share is only 4%.
claims.q: When excluding OFCs, however, the share of Asia in LAC’s inward FDI stock accounts for just 4 percent, indicating that a large portion of Asian investment to the region is channeled through OFCs.
claims.an: This is important for the central question: measured by FDI stock net of OFCs, China/Asia remains small next to Europe and the US.

claims.t: Brazil is the main destination of Chinese investment in both MOFCOM and M&A data. Chinese M&A in Brazil nearly doubled from US$12.5bn (2011–14) to US$23bn (2015–18), about 5% of 2018 GDP. MOFCOM also shows Venezuela, Argentina, Ecuador and Peru as important destinations, which the M&A data do not reflect.
claims.q: Chinese M&A in Brazil almost doubled from US$12.5 billion in 2011-14 to US$23 billion in 2015-18, or about 5 percent of Brazil’s GDP in 2018.
claims.e: MOFCOM FDI stock; Thomson Reuters M&A; Figure 5.

claims.t: From 2001 to 2018, Chinese M&A in LAC was concentrated in basic materials and energy, driven by China's commodity demand and its strategy to secure natural resources.
claims.q: during 2001-18, Chinese investment in LAC had a high concentration in the basic material and energy sector (Table 1). Not surprisingly, this was driven by China’s growing demand for commodities, a major exports of LAC, and its strategy to shore up natural resources

claims.t: Since 2013 the surge in Chinese overseas M&A spread across sectors globally, but in LAC it was concentrated in utilities.
claims.q: The surge of Chinese overseas M&A since 2013, however, was almost evenly distributed among consumer goods, financial services, industrial goods, telecommunication services and utilities. In LAC, the surge mostly took place in the utility sector

claims.t: Sectoral complementarity measured by RCA (2015–18): LAC has high RCA in basic materials and energy, and China has high RCA in utilities, consumer goods and telecom.
claims.q: LAC has relatively high RCA in basic materials and energy while China has high RCA in utilities, consumer goods and
claims.e: Table 2; WITS and IMF trade-in-services data; Balassa RCA.
claims.se: basic materials; energy; utilities; consumer; telecom

claims.t: Econometric finding: before 2015 China was more likely to invest where it had low RCA and the destination had high RCA. In 2015–18 this reversed, toward sectors where China has high RCA and the destination low RCA. The shift is most pronounced in LAC, and advanced-economy M&A shows no such shift.
claims.q: Chinese M&A can be associated with sectoral complementarity between China and the destination countries, but this complementarity seems to have shifted at the sectoral level as China tilts towards areas where it has a comparative advantage in the global markets. This shift is even more pronounced when we consider Chinese M&A in LAC

claims.t: LAC experienced the most drastic change in Chinese investment behaviour before and after 2015 of any region, followed by MENA and North America.
claims.q: it is LAC that has witnessed the most drastic transformation of Chinese investment before and after 2015

claims.t: Pull factors: Chinese firms invest more in countries with faster growth, lower inflation, an appreciating REER and better rule of law. Prior exports to China increase Chinese M&A (trade leads investment), while large imports from China reduce it.
claims.q: Countries with stronger institutions tend to receive more Chinese M&A than those with weaker institutions, at least along some dimensions of the insitutional environment.
claims.e: Control coefficients in Tables A.1–A.2, 'in line with IMF (2017)'.
claims.an: This challenges the view that Chinese capital prefers weak-governance states, at least for M&A.

claims.t: Trade precedes investment: a destination's exports to China open the door to later Chinese M&A, as in the Japan and South Korea cycle of 1970–90.
claims.q: The fact that the destination country was already exporting to China contributes positively to Chinese M&A towards that country. This is consistent with the idea that trade is followed closely by FDI
claims.e: Positive Ln(export to China) coefficient (e.g. 0.093***, Table A.1); Khan et al. (2012).

claims.t: Since 2015, higher-value Chinese M&A in LAC has occurred in sectors where either China or LAC has high RCA, which the authors attribute to large deals in commodities and utilities.
claims.q: These results are perhaps driven by the large size of the Chinese M&A in LAC’s commodity sector (where LAC has high RCA and China has low RCA) and utility sector (where LAC has low RCA and China has high RCA).

claims.t: After 2015, Chinese overseas M&A resembles advanced-economy M&A, both in LAC and elsewhere.
claims.q: Overall, as shown in Figure 10, Chinese overseas M&A resembles more the behavior of the advanced economies after 2015, both in LAC and in the rest of the destination countries.
claims.an: This normalises Chinese behaviour: post-2015 investment looks commercially conventional, which qualifies purely geopolitical explanations.

claims.t: The shift is associated with China's rebalancing and excess capacity, not with changes in China's RCA. Years of overinvestment built up excess capacity in sectors where China is internationally competitive, and falling capacity utilisation pushed firms, including SOEs with growth targets, abroad.
claims.q: years of overinvestment has led to buildup of excess capacity in certain sectors of the Chinese economy, much of which happens to be in sectors where China also demonstrates international competitiveness
claims.e: Figure 11; Table A.5 (FAI proxy and PPI robustness).
claims.an: This is an emergent push explanation that fits neither M1 nor M2 cleanly.

claims.t: The effect of excess capacity (cumulative investment) on overseas M&A is even larger for Chinese investment in LAC.
claims.q: The effect is even larger for China’s investment

claims.t: Chinese investment in LAC has historically been concentrated in commodities (metals and minerals) with environmental costs, but China and LAC have taken steps to limit them. CDB and China Exim apply safeguards and ex-post EIAs, and Chinese electric power investment in LAC is mostly hydropower and wind.
claims.q: Li et al (2020) find that most of Chinese electric power investments in LAC is in the renewable energy sectors of hydropower and wind.
claims.e: Ray and Gallagher (2016); Küblböck et al. (2019); Li et al. (2020).

claims.t: Policy recommendation: LAC should exploit complementarity in sectors where China has comparative advantage and LAC does not (utilities, consumer goods, telecom), steer Chinese investment to its investment gaps, and maintain macro stability and strong institutions as pull factors.
claims.q: LAC stands to benefit by directing Chinese investment to address LAC’s own investment gaps.
claims.e: Table 2 RCA and the FDI-spillover literature.

claims.t: China might be supporting counter-cyclical FDI in LAC as US and European investment declines: China's outward FDI rose 3.3% in 2020 while global FDI fell 42%.
claims.q: China might be supporting counter-cyclical FDI in LAC countries, seizing opportunities for market share as U.S. and European investment in the region declines, contributing to consolidating a trend which started about a decade ago.
claims.e: UNCTAD Investment Trends Monitor (January 2021); Xinhua and gov.cn.

claims.t: Headwinds: high corporate debt, LAC sovereign and corporate debt vulnerabilities, China's slowing growth that has made policy banks more selective (some struggling with risky LAC portfolios, including potential losses in Venezuela), and GVC reorganisation could reduce Chinese FDI to LAC.
claims.q: Chinese FDI could also slow down because of China’s slowing economic growth that has already forced its policy banks to be more selection on overseas projects, especially as some continue to struggle with some risky portfolios in Latin America, including potential losses in Venezuela.
claims.e: Çelik et al. (2020); Borga et al. (2020); qualitative reasoning.

claims.t: LAC could benefit from MNEs moving production out of China, but no LAC country appears in the Economic Prosperity Network of trusted partners proposed by the US (Australia, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Vietnam).
claims.q: LAC countries could take advantage of this process, but so far, no LAC country appears in the Economic Prosperity Network proposed by the
claims.e: Authors' observation on the US initiative.
claims.an: This is evidence of a US instrument gap: the US supply-chain alliance offered LAC no role. The passage spans pp. 23–24.

claims.t: ECLAC frames the diversification of the region's export basket to China as the main challenge in bilateral trade.
claims.q: notes that the diversification of the region’s
claims.an: Sets the frame for the document: deepening, not questioning, the relationship; diversification is the policy goal.

claims.t: In 2016 China became the world's second largest foreign investor while FDI flows to LAC fell for the second year running; ECLAC argues a major realignment is possible if both sides develop strategies that expand and diversify the sectors receiving Chinese investment.
claims.q: second largest foreign investor, FDI flows to Latin America and the Caribbean fell for the second year running
claims.an: Proposal layer: ECLAC's call for sector diversification of Chinese FDI is not evidence of an existing shift.

claims.t: The US 'America First' trade policy (2017) is protectionist, shifts from multilateralism to bilateralism, withdrew the US from TPP and TISA, criticises the WTO, renegotiates NAFTA and intimates renegotiation of FTAs with Chile, Colombia, Panama, Peru, Central America and the Dominican Republic.
claims.q: the United States from the Trans-Pacific Partnership
claims.an: Analyst: ECLAC presents US protectionism as a source of uncertainty in global trade governance, the context in which the CELAC-China forum meets; it implies a narrowing of US market-access offers to LAC (M3), though the document does not draw that link explicitly.

claims.t: China is a main engine of global growth: over 15% of global GDP in 2016, 22.5% of global industrial GDP and 30% of global agricultural value; it accounted for more than 40% of global GDP expansion in 2016.
claims.q: largest industrial GDP, insofar as it represents 22.5% of
claims.e: World Bank WDI-based ECLAC figures (Figure I.5).

claims.t: China is shortening its value chains: the share of parts and components in its non-oil imports fell from 57% to 48% since 2000, as it substitutes domestic output for imported high-tech parts, driven by Made in China 2025 (launched 2015), which targets 40% domestic content of components and materials by 2020 and 70% by 2025.
claims.q: Today China produces many inputs that it previously had
claims.e: COMTRADE data (Figure I.7) and description of Made in China 2025.
claims.an: Analyst: implies China's import demand is tilting further toward raw materials rather than intermediate manufactures, which reinforces the inter-industry pattern documented in chapter III.

claims.t: China's total indebtedness reached nearly 250% of GDP in 2016 (165% before the global financial crisis), concentrated in state-owned enterprises; rising defaults could trigger bank deleveraging and interest-rate hikes.
claims.q: economy reached nearly 250% of GDP in 2016, compared
claims.an: A downside risk to the continuity of Chinese finance and demand.

claims.t: The Belt and Road Initiative (announced 2013) could total a trillion dollars of funding; China announced US$14.5 billion more for the Silk Road Fund, 60 billion yuan (US$8.7 billion) of development aid, US$300 million for emergency food and US$145 million in South-South cooperation subsidies.
claims.q: for the Belt and Road Initiative could amount to a
claims.an: BRI is described here as Asia-Europe-Africa; the LAC extension is not discussed in pp. 1-52.

claims.t: Since 2008 China's central bank has signed at least 30 currency swap agreements totalling more than US$474 billion, including with Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Suriname, used to promote bilateral trade and strengthen reserves.
claims.q: 2008, China’s central bank has signed at least 30 currency

claims.t: Estimated Chinese loan commitments to LAC governments in 2005-2016 total more than US$141 billion, almost all from the China Development Bank and China Exim Bank; CDB participated in 80% of loans; 93% went to Venezuela (44%), Brazil (26%), Ecuador (12%) and Argentina (11%).
claims.q: the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (44%), Brazil (26%),
claims.e: Estimates from Gallagher and Cipoletta (2017, unpublished), Figure I.14. ECLAC notes official data are not detailed enough for case-by-case breakdown.
claims.an: Strong concentration in four countries, three of them with left/populist governments at the time (VEN, ECU, ARG) plus Brazil; analyst note only, the document does not discuss ideology.

claims.t: Chinese loan commitments to LAC (2005-2016) exceed the sovereign credits granted by the IDB (US$117.8 billion), the World Bank (US$85.5 billion) and CAF (US$55.1 billion) over the same period.
claims.q: This exceeds the amount of funding that Latin America and the Caribbean received from institutions such as the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), the World Bank and the Development Bank of Latin America (CAF)
claims.an: Supports a finance-scale explanation; US bilateral instruments are not compared.

claims.t: The main recipients of Chinese finance have significant hydrocarbon deposits, and some loan agreements include a counterpart commitment to supply petroleum products.
claims.q: funding have significant hydrocarbon deposits, and so the

claims.t: More than half of Chinese lending to LAC goes to infrastructure (52%), almost a third to hydrocarbons and power (31%), 8% to mining, 7% other, 1% budgetary support and 1% trade finance (2005-2016).
claims.q: Chinese banks funnel more than half their total lending

claims.t: Loan-for-oil deals account for around 50% of total Chinese funding; these channelled over US$74 billion in four years, mainly to Venezuela (six loans since 2008, US$44 billion), Brazil (2009, US$10 billion) and Ecuador (four loans since 2009, US$5 billion). The mechanism secures repayment through oil shipments and lowers risk premiums in riskier markets.
claims.q: Such instruments have been used to channel over
claims.an: Core evidence of state-coordinated, commodity-backed finance.

claims.t: Interest rates on Chinese loans could be slightly higher than market options for many LAC countries, but not always, especially for countries with restricted access to international capital (several of China's leading borrowers); the lowest rates (2%) were Exim loans to Bolivia and Jamaica in 2010, booked as ODA.
claims.q: The interest rates on Chinese loans could be slightly higher than other market options for many of the region’s countries
claims.an: Qualifies a 'cheap Chinese money' narrative: the attraction lies in access for credit-constrained borrowers rather than in price.

claims.t: ECLAC attributes the growth of Chinese finance since 2005 to a Chinese economic and political strategy: diversifying foreign exchange reserves, promoting the renminbi, directing Chinese firms to invest in natural resources, a geopolitical strategy and consolidating allegiances.
claims.q: a strategy for consolidating allegiances.
claims.an: Notable that a UN body names geopolitical and allegiance motives explicitly.

claims.t: China has currency swap agreements with four LAC central banks (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Suriname) totalling close to US$49 billion since 2009, meant to facilitate trade and investment in yuan and used as relief against weakening reserves (e.g. Argentina in 2015).
claims.q: in Latin America since 2009 are the currency swap agreements
claims.e: Section I.D.3 and Map I.2 (Arner and Soares 2016).

claims.t: At the First China-CELAC Ministerial Meeting (2015) China announced it would raise trade with LAC to US$500 billion and invest US$250 billion (mostly infrastructure) over the next decade; the 2018 meeting is expected to extend cooperation into industry, infrastructure and sustainable development.
claims.q: US$ 500 billion and would make investments in the region
claims.an: Announced pledges, not realised flows; check against later data.

claims.t: China has had more success than LAC in reducing poverty: extreme poverty in Latin America is three times China's, and China cut its poverty rate by 45 percentage points vs 12.4 points in Latin America between the comparison periods (c. 2002 to 2013-2014).
claims.q: points, Latin America reduced it by 12.4 percentage points
claims.e: ECLAC household-survey tabulations and World Bank data (Figures II.1-II.2).
claims.an: Contextual: a 'development model' comparison that underpins ECLAC's interest in learning from China.

claims.t: Human-capital gaps: China's secondary gross enrolment jumped from 61.0% to 94.3% (2000-2015) vs 85.2% to 92.9% in LAC; only 10 Latin American universities are in the ARWU top 500 versus 45 in China (50 with Hong Kong), and only Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Mexico appear; 34% of LAC students (9 countries) scored below PISA level 1 in mathematics.
claims.q: 10 Latin American universities are among the 500 best in
claims.e: UNESCO, ARWU and OECD PISA 2015 data (Figures II.4-II.5).
claims.an: Relevant to the capability gap behind the commodity-for-manufactures exchange.

claims.t: LAC-China goods trade was projected to grow 16% in 2017 to US$266 billion, close to the 2013 record of US$268 billion, after three years of contraction (cumulative -14%); LAC exports to China were projected to grow 25% in 2017 mainly on higher commodity prices, after falling 25% between 2013 and 2016 (vs an 11% fall in imports).
claims.q: of the trade in goods between the region and China is to
claims.e: ECLAC projections on COMTRADE data (Figure III.1).
claims.an: Shows that the relationship's value is price-driven (commodity cycle) rather than a structural deepening.

claims.t: In 2017 China was projected to take 10% of LAC goods exports and supply 18% of imports; China has been LAC's second largest source of imports since 2010 and is close to displacing the EU as second largest buyer. LAC's weight in China's trade peaked in 2011 (6.5% of exports, 7.5% of imports) and fell to 5.4% and 6.4% in 2016.
claims.q: 10% of the region’s total goods exports and accounted
claims.an: Asymmetry: China matters more to LAC than LAC to China, and LAC's weight in Chinese trade fell after 2011, qualifying a story of continuous expansion.

claims.t: LAC's trade with China runs a deficit (about US$67 billion in 2017). South America's balance is near equilibrium (surplus in commodities and resource-based manufactures offsets the deficit in other manufactures), while the Caribbean, Central America and Mexico's deficit rose from US$3.0 billion in 2000 to US$78.0 billion in 2016, almost all in industrial goods.
claims.q: the Caribbean, Central America and Mexico report an
claims.an: Sub-regional split: complementarity for South America, manufacturing competition for Mexico/Central America.

claims.t: Only Venezuela, Brazil and Chile traditionally ran trade surpluses with China, from a small number of commodities; Peru joined them in 2016. Mexico alone accounts for two-thirds of the total trade deficit of deficit countries: only 1.4% of its 2016 exports went to China, while 18% of its imports came from there.
claims.q: Traditionally, only three countries in the region have run
claims.e: COMTRADE (Figure III.3: 2016 balances, e.g. Brazil +11,770, Mexico -64,109 US$ million).

claims.t: LAC's export basket to China is much less sophisticated than its exports to the rest of the world: in 2016 commodities were 72% of exports to China (27% to the rest of the world) and low-, medium- and high-tech manufactures only 8% (57%); conversely manufactures were 91% of imports from China (68% from the rest of the world). Trade remains clearly inter-industry: raw materials for manufactures.
claims.q: inter-industry: raw materials for manufactures.
claims.an: Core evidence of structural complementarity with dependency-type risks.

claims.t: Five commodity products account for 70% of LAC exports to China (2016): soybeans 21.8%, copper ore and concentrates 15.6%, iron ore 12.8%, refined copper 10.5% and oil 8.8%; the top 20 (84.8%) are almost all mining, hydrocarbons, agricultural and forestry products, the only industrial items (gearboxes, vehicles) representing 1%. In most LAC countries the number of products exported to the region's own market exceeds those exported to China by more than ten times.
claims.q: Just five products, all of them commodities, account for
claims.an: Copper products combined (ore 15.6 + refined 10.5 + unrefined 1.4 + scrap 0.7) = 28.2% of LAC exports to China in 2016 (analyst sum of Table III.1).

claims.t: Agriculture is presented as a promising option for diversifying exports to China: LAC's agricultural surplus with China was almost US$23 billion in 2016; agriculture's share in LAC exports to China rose from 20% (2010) to 30% (2016); China's share of LAC agricultural exports rose from under 3% (2000) to 13% (2016); LAC's share of China's agricultural imports rose from 16% to 26%, almost equal to Canada and the US combined.
claims.q: Agriculture is a promising option for diversifying the region’s exports to China
claims.an: LAC gaining agricultural market share in China relative to the US and Canada is relevant to US-China competition (analyst).

claims.t: LAC agricultural exports to China are highly concentrated: soybeans were 72% of the value in 2016; processed products (except wine) have a minimal share; Brazil alone contributes 70% and Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Uruguay together 97%.
claims.q: contributes 70% of the value of the sector’s shipments to

claims.t: In seven LAC countries with data (Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Mexico, Uruguay), the number of firms exporting to China per 100,000 inhabitants rose over the past decade for both SMEs and large firms, but the average number of products exported per firm varies and has fallen in several cases.
claims.q: In the seven countries of the region where such information
claims.an: Country-level values in the figures could not be reliably assigned from the text extraction.

claims.t: Global FDI was US$1.7 trillion in 2016 (-2%); developed economies regained 59% of the total while developing economies' share fell from 53% (2014) to 37%; average FDI inflows to Latin America fell 7.8%.
claims.q: and in Asia (15%), while average inflows dropped by
claims.e: UNCTAD WIR 2017 and official figures (Figure IV.1).
