claims.t: Chinese companies' cross-border acquisitions rose 80% in 2016 to a record US$92.221 billion net, while acquisitions originating in the United States fell 39%; 91% of global M&A value targeted developed economies.
claims.q: a result of Chinese companies’ acquisitions: up 80% in 2016

claims.t: By 2016 China was the world's second largest investor: its share of global FDI outflows rose from 1.3% a decade earlier to 12.6% (US 20.6%); outward investment hit a record US$183.1 billion, exceeding inflows for the first time, making China a net investor. The 'Go Global' strategy integrates China into sophisticated sectors, particularly via M&A tied to fourth-industrial-revolution technologies.
claims.q: largest investor after the United States (20.6%).

claims.t: The fastest growth in Chinese outward FDI went to developed economies. In 2016, 51% of Chinese FDI went to Europe and North America. Chinese investment in the United States and Europe rose by 130%, from US$41 billion in 2015 to US$94 billion in 2016.
claims.q: In 2016, 51% of FDI from China went to Europe and North America.
claims.e: Figure IV.5 (FDI outflows by destination group, 2005-2016), based on China Global Investment Tracker (AEI/Heritage Foundation).
claims.an: This puts LAC in context: in 2016 it was a minor destination for Chinese outward FDI compared with developed economies. Chinese expansion in LAC is therefore not the main thrust of Chinese OFDI.

claims.t: Chinese M&A in Europe and the US was mainly in high-tech activities and capital goods, which shows a search for strategic assets. M&A gives quick access to knowledge, technological capacity, brands, clients and markets.
claims.q: Most mergers ... and acquisitions in Europe and the United States were in ... high-tech activities and capital goods, indicating that Chinese ... companies are looking for high-quality strategic assets.
claims.e: Figure IV.6 sector breakdown of Chinese cross-border M&A, 2015-2016 (Bloomberg).

claims.t: US and EU antitrust authorities blocked ChemChina's US$44 billion acquisition of Syngenta in 2016. Without this, Chinese investment in the US and Europe in 2016 would have been even higher. The deal was later approved in June 2017.
claims.q: The total value would have been even higher if antitrust ... authorities in the United States and the European Union had not blocked the acquisition of Syngenta, a Swiss ... agrochemical and seed company, by ChemChina, in ... 2016.
claims.e: Narrative statement next to Figure IV.5.
claims.an: This is antitrust review, not national-security screening, and the block was temporary (approved June 2017). It is weak evidence of Western regulatory friction only. It involves no LAC country.

claims.t: Chinese M&A in LAC was a small share of the total and was concentrated in a few sectors. LAC received barely 4% of Chinese M&A value in 2015-2016, and 88% of it went to energy and mining. ECLAC reads this as a strategy to exploit natural resources and supply the energy market.
claims.q: The vast majority of ... acquisitions (88%) were in the energy and mining sectors, ... indicating that Chinese companies’ strategy in the region is ... to exploit natural resources and supply the energy market.
claims.e: Figure IV.6 (Bloomberg): LAC panel shows electrical power 65%, mining 23%.
claims.an: This supports resource-seeking and energy-market-seeking motives. The small share (4%) qualifies any idea that LAC is central to Chinese M&A.

claims.t: Total FDI inflows to LAC fell 7% in 2016, the second consecutive decline. FDI still equalled 3.6% of GDP, against a 2.5% global average. Brazil (47%), Mexico (19%) and Colombia (8%) were the main recipients.
claims.q: In 2016, investment in Latin America and the Caribbean fell for ... the second year in a row, reaching levels similar to those seen ... six years ago.
claims.e: Figure IV.7; ECLAC official figures and estimates as of 15 June 2017.
claims.an: This refers to total FDI from all origins, not Chinese FDI.

claims.t: Between 2005 and 2017 the sectoral composition of announced investment in LAC shifted away from fossil fuels towards renewables. Fossil fuels fell from 30% of announced value in 2006 to 10% in 2017. Renewables rose from 1% in 2005 to 18% in 2016 (US$13 billion). ECLAC presents non-conventional energy as an opportunity for Chinese investment.
claims.q: The value of investment announced in the fossil fuel sector ... fell from 30% of the region’s total in 2006 to 10% in 2017.
claims.e: Figure IV.8 (Financial Times fDi Markets announcements, all origins).

claims.t: China has major weight in alternative energy globally, yet Chinese companies made only 2% of announced renewable-energy investment in LAC between 2005 and October 2017. The European Union (63%) and North America (22%) dominated. Renewables did grow within China's own announcements, from nothing before 2010 to 5% of China's total announced in 2011-2016.
claims.q: Despite China’s considerable clout in alternative energy ... production globally, investment announced by Chinese ... companies only accounted for 2% of the total in the sector ... in Latin America and the Caribbean between 2005 and ... October 2017.
claims.e: Figure IV.9 (fDi Markets announcements by origin).
claims.an: Up to 2017, Western investors, not Chinese ones, led LAC renewable greenfield announcements. Compare with later claims of Chinese dominance in LAC energy transition (e.g. D15).

claims.t: Chinese FDI in LAC rose markedly over 2005-2016, to close to US$90 billion, about 5% of LAC FDI inflows. For 2017 ECLAC estimated more than US$25 billion (around 15% of inflows), driven by acquisitions of Brazilian electricity companies.
claims.q: Close to US$ 90 billion have entered the region from China ... between 2005 and 2016, representing approximately 5% of ... FDI inflows to Latin America and the Caribbean.
claims.e: Figure IV.10; ECLAC estimates combining M&A and announced projects (FT fDi Markets, Bloomberg).
claims.an: The 2017 jump is driven by state-owned acquirers (State Grid, SPIC, CTG; Table IV.1), which is consistent with M2. The document itself does not frame this as state coordination.

claims.t: Chinese FDI in LAC is highly concentrated by country. Brazil received 55% (2005 to 2017 estimates), Peru 17% and Argentina 9%, so the top three received 81%.
claims.q: Brazil has received 55% of investments made by Chinese ... companies in the region since 2005, including 2017 estimates, ... followed by Peru, with 17%, and Argentina, 9%.
claims.e: Figure IV.11: estimated FDI inflows from China by destination (21 countries), 2005-October 2017.
claims.an: Consolidation is uneven: Chinese FDI is not region-wide. Most of the 21 countries received under US$2 billion over 12 years.

claims.t: Since 2010 Chinese FDI in LAC has diversified across sectors. Mining received 27% of announced value for 2004-October 2017. Metals and fossil fuels fell from 42% and 18% of announcements (2004-2010) to 20% and 6% (2011-2017). Telecommunications, real estate, food and renewables gained.
claims.q: This ... change was offset by higher investments in sectors such ... as telecommunications, real estate, food or renewable energy, indicating that Chinese companies are interested in entering new sectors in the region.
claims.e: Figure IV.12A: announcements by Chinese companies by sector, 2004-2010 vs 2011-2017 (FT fDi Markets).
claims.se: mining; metals; oil-gas; telecommunications; real estate; food; renewable energy
claims.an: This supports consolidation through diversification beyond commodities after the boom. It qualifies a pure demand-pull/commodity explanation for the post-2011 period.

claims.t: Energy is the main target of Chinese M&A in LAC: 49% of the total amount, plus 12% to renewables, 9% to mining and 33% to utilities. The large 2017 increase came from the sale of major Brazilian energy companies worth over US$17 billion.
claims.q: the considerable growth in ... Chinese investments in 2017 was due to the sale of major ... Brazilian energy companies, the value of which exceeded ... US $ 17 billion.

claims.t: Besides FDI, China and LAC are linked through construction contracts. These are often awarded by the State and funded by Chinese banks. In 2011-2016 they were worth nearly US$40 billion, 40% more than new projects plus M&A (US$28 billion), and were concentrated in energy (66%; large hydro 40%) and transport (16%).
claims.q: In many cases, these construction contracts are awarded by the State and receive funding from Chinese banks.
claims.e: Figure IV.13 (China Global Investment Tracker; fDi Markets; Bloomberg).
claims.an: This is direct evidence for M2 bundling (state contracts + Chinese bank finance + Chinese contractors). FDI figures alone understate the Chinese economic footprint.

claims.t: LAC renewable capacity grew fast in recent years. Solar entered the South American matrix only in the last three years, wind expanded in Brazil and Uruguay, and hydro rose sharply after 2014. In Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, solar and wind grew in 2015 and slowed in 2016.
claims.q: In South America, solar energy has been incorporated into ... the renewable energy matrix only in the last three years.

claims.t: Investment in renewable energy in LAC excluding Brazil peaked in 2014 at US$14 billion. It fell by almost 50% in 2016, mainly because of the drop in oil prices since 2013. Brazil peaked in 2008 at US$11.5 billion (bioethanol, PROINFA) and has held at about US$7 billion a year.
claims.q: One of the main reasons for this was the substantial drop in oil prices since 2013.

claims.t: LAC has unparalleled solar and wind resources, and its hydro resources can act as 'natural storage' for intermittent sources. Exploiting them needs investment in electrical interconnections within and among countries.
claims.q: The region has unparalleled solar and wind energy resources.
claims.e: Map V.1 (IDB/Paredes 2017 wind and solar potential).
claims.an: This is an endowment claim relevant to the FE module.

claims.t: South American generation plans now favour medium-sized plants, and the region seriously lacks interconnections. ECLAC sees this as an opportunity for cooperation between China's technological and financial capacities and the region's strategic plans.
claims.q: there is ... a serious lack of interconnections, potentially providing an ... opportunity for cooperation between China’s technological ... and financial capacities and the strategic plans of the ... region’s countries.
claims.e: Map V.2 (ECLAC unpublished 2017 study on energy networks); mention of IDB-backed SINEA.
claims.an: Proposal layer.

claims.t: Infrastructure provision and quality in LAC lag behind. Infrastructure quality causes the widest gap in logistics performance (LPI 2016: LAC infrastructure 2.46 vs Germany 4.44). Infrastructure investment fell from 3.6% of GDP in 1980-1989 to 2.2% in 1990-2015, and per capita investment is below China's.
claims.q: Weak public and private infrastructure investment is one ... of the reasons why the provision and quality of these ... services are severely limited in Latin America.
claims.e: Figures V.4-V.7 (World Bank LPI; IDB-CAF-ECLAC infrastructure investment data).
claims.an: Structural infrastructure gap = demand for Chinese engineering/finance (FE: endowment asymmetry).

claims.t: China is an important potential partner for LAC infrastructure because of its domestic experience in large transport and energy projects and the financing it can offer. Chinese involvement in LAC has mostly been turnkey projects.
claims.q: China ... is an important potential partner for the region, owing to ... the competencies and experience developed in executing ... and managing projects in China itself and to the financing ... opportunities for infrastructure projects.
claims.e: Section heading and text, Figure V.8 (National Bureau of Statistics of China).

claims.t: China's turnover from executed construction contracts in LAC rose from US$168 million in 2000 (2% of China's total) to US$16.4 billion in 2015 (10.6%). This made LAC the third destination region after Asia (44.8%) and Africa (35.6%). The largest turnkey contracts by value were in Venezuela (38.3%), Brazil (15.4%), Ecuador (12.9%), Mexico (6.6%) and Argentina (5.3%).
claims.q: The countries of the region ... which have signed the largest turnkey contracts with ... Chinese companies in terms of value are the Bolivarian ... Republic of Venezuela (38.3%), Brazil (15.4%), Ecuador ... (12.9%), Mexico (6.6%) and Argentina (5.3%).
claims.e: Figure V.8, NBS China data on executed (completed-work) contracts.
claims.an: Venezuela and Ecuador lead, alongside non-left Mexico. Cross-ideological, but weighted to countries that also receive Chinese policy-bank loans (see the bank-finance claims on PDF p. 70).

claims.t: Chinese firms have shown little appetite for infrastructure PPPs, which require more commitment and carry long-term risk. Chinese PPP investment of US$7.663 billion in 2000-2016 was only 1.3% of all PPP investment in LAC (US$592 billion). It went to Brazil (60.7%, 99% energy), Colombia (14.8%), Jamaica (13.7%) and Mexico (4.0%).
claims.q: To date, Chinese companies have shown little appetite for ... public-private investment projects in Latin America and ... the Caribbean, which require greater commitment and ... present long-term risks.
claims.an: Chinese firms prefer contractor/turnkey roles to long-term equity risk. This is a limit on Chinese infrastructure consolidation.

claims.t: Since 2010, Chinese public bank financing to LAC (China Development Bank, China Eximbank) has been larger than the loans of each of the IDB, the World Bank and CAF. It grew from US$30 million in 2005 to a peak of US$35.7 billion in 2010 and averaged US$14.1 billion a year in 2011-2016. 93% went to the infrastructure sector broadly defined, including oil and coal extraction (31.0%).
claims.q: With regard to Chinese ... public banks, the amount of financing provided to Latin ... America and the Caribbean since 2010 has exceeded the ... individual loans from the Inter-American Development Bank ... (IDB), the World Bank and the Development Bank of Latin ... America (CAF).
claims.e: Figure V.10 (Inter-American Dialogue China-Latin America Finance Database and sector news).
claims.se: development finance; infrastructure; oil-gas; transport; electricity
claims.an: The comparison is with multilateral lenders, not US agencies. It indirectly bears on M3.

claims.t: Chinese bank funding has been concentrated in countries with the greatest difficulty accessing external credit or rich in natural resources: Venezuela 44.0%, Brazil 26.0%, Ecuador 12.3%, Argentina 10.8%. About 15% took the form of commodity-backed loans (e.g. oil), which offset default risk.
claims.q: Funding has been concentrated in the countries of the region ... that have had the greatest difficulty accessing external ... credit or that are rich in natural resources
claims.an: Credit-constrained borrowers (Venezuela, Ecuador, Argentina) + resource collateral. Consistent with gap-filling and loans-for-oil explanations (D01).

claims.t: The countries receiving Chinese bank financing tend to be the sites of turnkey projects. ECLAC says there is a 'certain correlation' between the two, which suggests that finance and construction are bundled.
claims.q: There is also a certain correlation between the countries ... receiving this bank financing and those that are the sites ... of turnkey projects.
claims.e: Comparison of Figure V.10 and turnkey shares (p. 67); no statistical test reported.

claims.t: Three China-LAC regional funds were set up in 2014-2015 and are beginning operations. Two are administered by CDB: the US$20 billion China-LAC Industrial Cooperation Investment Fund and the US$10 billion Special Loan Program for China-LAC Infrastructure. Eximbank administers the US$10-15 billion China-LAC Cooperation Fund.
claims.q: three regional investment funds were established ... between 2014 and 2015, which are beginning operations

claims.t: Emission trends of LAC and China diverge. LAC emits about 4 GtCO2-eq a year (growth 0.7% a year since 1990) and China 11.6 GtCO2-eq (6% a year). China's share of global emissions rose from 8% in 1990 to 24%, while LAC's fell from 10% to about 8%.
claims.q: Latin America emits around 4 GtCO2-eq per year, while ... China emits 11.6 GtCO2-eq.

claims.t: LAC's electricity matrix is relatively clean: 57% of electricity comes from non-fossil sources, mainly hydro. Fossil fuels make up 74% of energy production in LAC and 88% in China. China, a leading producer of renewable energy technologies, saw its non-hydro renewable share rise to 4% by 2014.
claims.q: 57% of electricity is ... currently generated from non-fossil fuel sources.

claims.t: Forest endowments contrast. LAC has 927 million hectares of forest (about a quarter of the world) but lost about 97 million hectares in 1990-2015. China gained 51 million hectares. Agriculture is cited as the leading global cause of deforestation.
claims.q: Around 97 million hectares were ... lost in the region between 1990 and 2015
claims.e: Table V.1 and Figure V.19 (World Bank WDI).
claims.an: The document does NOT link LAC deforestation to Chinese demand in this section.

claims.t: LAC invests far less in R&D than China. LAC spends 0.7% of GDP and China 2.2%, and Brazil (1.28%) is the only LAC country between 1% and 2%. China raised its share of global R&D from 4.7% in 2000 to 24% in 2015, while LAC moved only from 3.2% to 3.5%.
claims.q: While the region accounted for 3.2% ... of global R&D investment in 2000, in 2015 that figure had risen only to 3.5%.
claims.an: This is a technology-endowment asymmetry (FE).

claims.t: Latin America failed to use the commodity price boom to build a science, technology and innovation strategy as a driver of growth. Its R&D progress was therefore weak compared with China.
claims.q: Latin America failed to capitalize on the boom in ... commodity prices to develop a strategy focusing on science, technology and innovation as the key driver of growth and ... development.
claims.e: Interpretive statement supported by the R&D share data (Figure VI.3).
claims.an: A dependency-type mechanism: commodity rents (largely from Chinese demand, per Part A) were not converted into capabilities, which reproduces inter-industry complementarity.

claims.t: LAC innovation policy has been held back by low spending, little private-sector involvement and the subordination of R&D to macroeconomic policy. Other factors are institutional weakness and poor coordination with structural-change strategy. This contrasts with China, Finland and Korea, which closed productivity gaps quickly.
claims.q: This is in stark contrast to the policies implemented in ... countries like China, Finland and the Republic of Korea, ... which have been able to close the productivity gaps with ... developed countries relatively quickly.
claims.an: This is a governance-model comparison favourable to Chinese industrial policy.

claims.t: The complexity of China's economy rose sharply in 1995-2014, while it stagnated in Mexico and declined in Argentina, Brazil and the region as a whole. Argentina and Brazil are experiencing premature deindustrialization and have specialised further in commodities and natural-resource-based manufactures.
claims.q: Argentina and Brazil are experiencing premature ... deindustrialization, having stepped up their specialization in commodities, natural resource-based manufactures and ... low-productivity services.
claims.e: Figure VI.5 (Hidalgo-Hausmann economic complexity index, Observatory of Economic Complexity, 1990-2016).
claims.an: The document does not causally attribute deindustrialisation to China in this section. Linking it to Chinese competition is an inference for other docs to test.

claims.t: Mexico is an exception: its production structure is more diversified thanks to automotive manufacturing. The auto industry provides 18% of manufacturing output, a US$52 billion yearly trade surplus, an FDI stock of over US$51.2 billion and 900,000 direct jobs. This gives Mexico the highest complexity index in LAC.
claims.q: Mexico has thus become the world’s ... seventh largest supplier and the fourth largest exporter ... of vehicles, which accounts for the country having the ... highest economic complexity index in Latin America.
claims.an: Mexico's endowment profile differs from South America's and is less complementary to China (FE).

claims.t: China is close to the Industry 4.0 technology frontier. 57% of companies surveyed in China say the country is ready for early adoption, and China is among the top four holders of IoT patents (2010-2012). The major LAC countries have not attained minimum standards in five enabling technologies.
claims.q: The major Latin American countries have not attained ... minimum standards in the five enabling technologies of ... industry 4.0, which are: broadband, data centres, cloud ... computing, big data and the Internet of things.
claims.e: Figures VI.8-VI.9 (Infosys survey; USPTO/EPO patents); text.
claims.an: Digital capability asymmetry (FE).

claims.t: Manufacturing is the backbone of the Chinese economy. China increased its share of global manufacturing eightfold from 2000 to 2014, to close to 25% of global manufacturing value added, at the expense of the US, Japan, Italy, France and the UK.
claims.q: From 2000 to 2014, China increased its share of global ... manufacturing eightfold

claims.t: China is the largest market for industrial robots, with about 87,000 sold in 2016. Its robot density rose from 25 to 68 per 10,000 manufacturing employees in 2013-2016. In LAC, Mexico (20) and Brazil (10) have the highest robot densities, against a world average of 74.
claims.q: In Latin America, Mexico has the highest robot density, ... with only 20 units per 10,000 manufacturing workers, ... followed by Brazil, with 10 units; the world average ... stands at 74 units per 10,000 workers.

claims.t: LAC-China trade recovered its dynamism in 2017; it had grown 22-fold in 2000-2013. Its shortcomings persist: most LAC countries run deficits with China, and the exchange is purely inter-industry (raw natural resources for manufactures). The export basket is highly concentrated and has contributed little to diversification.
claims.q: it is a purely inter-industry exchange, in which ... the region almost exclusively exports natural resources ... (especially in their raw form) and imports a wide range ... of manufactured goods.
claims.e: Concluding synthesis of chapter III (Part A) data.
claims.an: Trade expansion and consolidation alongside persistent asymmetry. This supports the premise's 'expanding' claim and the dependency reading.

claims.t: The inter-industry nature of LAC-China trade mainly results from complementary factor endowments, especially for South American raw-material exporters. Geographic distance (which limits intermediate-goods exchange), LAC's limited technological capacities, and linguistic, cultural, legal and regulatory barriers in the Chinese market add to it.
claims.q: Its inter-industry ... nature is mainly the result of the complementarity between ... their respective existing endowments of productive factors, ... particularly in the case of the South American economies that export ... raw materials.
claims.an: Key FE statement. ECLAC explicitly invokes factor-endowment complementarity, differentiated by subregion (South America).

claims.t: The food sector is a diversification opportunity. China is a net food importer and LAC a net exporter, and LAC's vast natural and water resources give it a comparative advantage as a supplier of safe, high-quality food. Meeting Chinese consumer and SPS/labelling requirements is the condition.
claims.q: A notable example is the food ... sector, in which China is a net importer and the region a ... net exporter.
claims.an: Proposal plus an endowment interpretation.

claims.t: ECLAC says the Belt and Road Initiative could benefit the region by boosting trade between Asia, Europe and Africa and demand for LAC products. Maritime, air and digital routes could bridge the distance.
claims.q: The One Belt and One Road Initiative could ... benefit the region by boosting trade between Asia, Europe ... and Africa and demand for products from Latin America ... and the Caribbean.

claims.t: The first China-CELAC Cooperation Plan 2015-2019 targeted US$500 billion in trade by 2025. ECLAC argues that quantitative targets alone will not fix structural shortcomings, and that the second Plan should include quantifiable export-diversification targets and a timetable of actions (thematic awareness meetings, digital platforms for SMEs, China's inland provinces).
claims.q: the ... second China-CELAC Cooperation Plan should incorporate ... quantifiable targets for the diversification of regional ... exports to China.
claims.an: Proposal.

claims.t: Chinese FDI in LAC has been concentrated in natural-resource-intensive sectors (mining, oil and gas). Over the last five years it has increasingly targeted telecommunications, the automotive industry and non-conventional energy, sectors ECLAC sees as crucial for LAC development.
claims.q: over the last five ... years, Chinese investments have increasingly targeted ... telecommunications, the automotive industry
claims.se: mining; oil-gas; telecommunications; automotive; renewable energy

claims.t: The positive effects of FDI are not automatic. In most cases, results on technology transfer, R&D and good-quality jobs have fallen short of expectations. LAC must therefore rethink FDI-attraction strategies, and Chinese investment should be channelled into more technologically advanced activities linked to SMEs.
claims.q: The results in ... terms of transferring technology, promoting research and ... development and creating good-quality jobs have, in most ... cases, fallen short of expectations.
claims.e: Concluding remarks; no Chinese-specific evaluation data given.

claims.t: The first Plan set a target of a reciprocal FDI stock of at least US$250 billion by 2025, but ECLAC notes it is hard to quantify Chinese FDI in the region. It proposes that the second Plan include diversification targets for Chinese FDI by sector and by destination country, since FDI is heavily concentrated in a few South American countries.
claims.q: The number of countries that receive Chinese ... FDI, which is currently heavily concentrated in a few ... South American countries, should also be expanded.
claims.an: Proposal.

claims.t: China has the capacities (engineering services and financing) to undertake infrastructure projects in LAC. Public-private partnerships with an interregional approach, a better regulatory framework and better governance would be needed, with mutual benefits under a broad definition of sustainability.
claims.q: China has the necessary capacities to undertake infrastructure ... projects in the region, both with regard to providing ... engineering services and financing.
claims.an: Proposal layer.

claims.t: ECLAC sees clear cooperation opportunities with China in electric transport, renewable energy and carbon pricing. These would come through exchange of experiences, technical capacity building and specific investment projects under the Paris Agreement framework.
claims.q: there are ... clear opportunities for cooperation in the areas of electric ... transport, renewable energy and carbon pricing.
claims.an: Proposal.

claims.t: For STI, ECLAC proposes that the second China-CELAC Plan include collaboration on national innovation systems, R&D on operation and IT convergence, and pilot Industry 4.0 R&D (robotics, IoT, big data, cloud, AI) in areas of common interest such as natural resources and advanced manufacturing. Joint university research and researcher exchange are also proposed.
claims.q: pilot R&D initiatives in the new Industry 4.0 technologies, ... such as advanced robotics, the Internet of things, ... big data analytics, cloud computing and artificial ... intelligence.
claims.an: Proposal.

claims.t: ECLAC proposes cooperation on shared social challenges under the SDGs: poverty, inequality, social protection, education, food security and ICT for social policy. This would include shared socioeconomic analysis and databases.
claims.q: Latin America and the Caribbean and China face a number ... of shared social challenges with regard to achieving the ... Sustainable Development Goals.
claims.an: Proposal; low relevance.

claims.t: Chinese ODI accounted for 7.57% of total FDI in LAC in 2019, and for 1.21% of gross fixed capital formation and 0.24% of GDP.
claims.q: accounted for 7.57% of total FDI in LAC
claims.e: Author's statistics; the source is not stated in the sentence.
claims.an: A modest macro footprint relative to the political attention China receives.

claims.t: China's 'Go Global' strategy to secure food and resource supply in LAC was carried out almost exclusively through public (state) ODI.
claims.q: nearly exclusively
claims.e: Citations: Urdinez et al. 2016; Dussel Peters 2012.

claims.t: Under the Belt and Road Initiative, China and LAC built a '1+3+6' framework (China–LAC Cooperation Plan 2015–2019) for trade, investment and financial cooperation in six fields: energy and resources, infrastructure, agriculture, manufacturing, scientific innovation and IT.
claims.q: Under the ‘Belt and Road’ initiative China and LAC,
claims.an: Framework of state-level coordination; the model does not test its effect.

claims.t: Since 2005 China Development Bank and China Eximbank have provided more than US$138bn in loan commitments to LAC countries and state-owned firms; Chinese commercial banks have also made dozens of loans since 2012.
claims.q: Bank have provided more than $138 billion in loan commitments to LAC
claims.an: Loans are outside the CGE shock; only FDI is modelled.

claims.t: Chinese SOEs investing in extractive subsidiaries in LAC have sought weak host institutions, whereas those investing in trading subsidiaries have sought strong rule of law.
claims.q: Chinese SOEs investing in extractive

claims.t: A fall in China's GDP growth and in its imports of crude oil and minerals would depress LAC commodity prices and growth, possibly causing regional recessions; resource-export sectors are capital-intensive and generate few jobs.
claims.q: A decrease in China’s GDP growth rate
claims.e: Literature (Gruss 2014; IDB 2016; Kireyev & Leonidov 2016; Ray et al. 2017).

claims.t: About 90% of Chinese ODI to LAC flows into the Cayman Islands and the (British) Virgin Islands and is later reinvested elsewhere in LAC; these two jurisdictions held 97.6% of China's US$693.74bn ODI stock in LAC in 2021, so NBSC data do not reflect the real scale or destination of investment.
claims.q: 90% of Chinese ODI in LAC
claims.an: Methodological point central to measuring China's footprint: official figures overstate tax havens and understate real host countries.

claims.t: China's ODI flows peaked at over US$196bn in 2016 and rose to US$153.7bn in 2020 against the global trend; LAC became the second-largest destination in 2020, and Chinese ODI in LAC nearly tripled in 2020 after halving in 2019.
claims.q: the second largest destination of Chinese ODI
claims.an: Contradicts the image of retreat from LAC during COVID, but the figures are dominated by Cayman/BVI.

claims.t: Chinese firm-level ODI stock (to 2019) is concentrated in Mining in nearly every host (Ecuador 98.9%, Colombia 93.71%, Bolivia 87.13%, Peru 66.78%, Venezuela 52.29%, Chile 46.19%, Argentina 42.40%, Brazil 40.58%), with Electricity-Gas-Water the second most popular sector.
claims.q: In general Mining is the most heavily invested sector invested by
claims.e: RED ALC–China and China Global Investment Tracker, mapped to GTAP sectors (Fig. 2).
claims.an: 'Mining' in GTAP includes coal, crude oil, gas and minerals nec, so oil and lithium/copper cannot be separated.

claims.t: Mexico differs from other LAC hosts: 48.23% of Chinese ODI stock is in manufactures (especially Electronics and Machinery), with Mining 21.14%, EGW 14.36%, trade 8.04% and communications 6.07%.
claims.q: Mexico as a destination of Chinese MNEs differs from other LAC
claims.an: Manufacturing-oriented Chinese FDI in Mexico is linked by the author to global production networks and NAFTA embeddedness.

claims.t: China's exports to LAC are dominated by Electronics (57.82% of Chinese exports to Mexico), Machinery, Textiles, Chemicals, Mineral products and Motors; LAC exports to China are concentrated in Mining, Mineral products, Agriculture and Food processing, with export variety 'relatively single' everywhere except Mexico and Panama.
claims.q: except for Mexico and Panama, other LAC countries’

claims.t: China's and LAC's GDP structures, export tendencies and import dependencies are complementary: LAC relies on manufacture imports, while China relies on Mining (36.33% of domestic consumption) and Agricultural imports.
claims.q: China and LAC economies are complementary
claims.an: This is the paper's operationalisation of complementarity.

claims.t: GTAPinGAMS is a static Arrow–Debreu general-equilibrium model assuming perfect competition and full employment; the Chinese ODI shock enters as a sector-specific increase in host capital stock.
claims.q: with assumptions of perfect competition and full employ
claims.an: Full employment means that new capital raises wages and output by assumption; there is no unemployment absorption channel.

claims.t: [model_result] Chinese investment raises GDP in all regions: Chile 7.68–9.12%, Argentina and Peru about 6–8%, Ecuador about 5%, Brazil 3.67%, Venezuela, Bolivia, Mexico, Colombia and Panama about 2%, and the rest of LAC within 0.77%.
claims.q: Chile is the biggest benefactor with GDP growth between 7.68% and
claims.e: CGE simulation, Table 6, three consumption functions.
claims.an: Large magnitudes, e.g. Chile +7.68–9.12% GDP from FDI stock alone, are best read as upper-bound comparative statics.

claims.t: [model_result] China's GDP rises 0.34% (CDE) to 1.35% (LES) and US GDP 0.12% (CDE) to 0.98% (LES); the rest of world changes by -0.01% under CDE and gains under CD and LES.
claims.q: The U.S. also
claims.an: Positive-sum result for the US runs against zero-sum competition narratives.

claims.t: [model_result] Consumption is the main driver of GDP growth in nearly all regions; in Peru, Chile, Argentina, Ecuador and Brazil government expenditure and investment also rise, and there is no crowding-out of local investment.
claims.q: There are no crowd out effects on local investment by

The largest increases in trade value are in Brazil and Mexico, and the largest percentage increases in Chile, Venezuela, Ecuador and Bolivia.
claims.q: all of the host economies improve current account balances because for

claims.t: [model_result] Wages rise in nearly all LAC hosts except Panama (e.g. 4.3–9.5% under CD in Chile, Argentina, Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador and Brazil); returns to land and natural resources roughly double in Chile, rise more than 80% in Argentina and Peru and nearly 60% in Brazil and Ecuador; capital rental rates fall where ODI-led capital is abundant.
claims.q: The return on land and natural resource and capital has doubled in
claims.e: Table 9; explained by factor complementarity in production.
claims.an: Large rent increases for resource owners create domestic constituencies for Chinese investment (analyst inference).

claims.t: [model_result] Mining output expands by about 21.5% to 49.8% (especially Peru, Chile, Argentina and Brazil) and Electricity-Gas-Water by 25.1% to 74.3% (Peru, Chile, Argentina, Panama); Petroleum output rises in all hosts except Colombia; Argentina's Machinery (+85.9%) and Dwelling (+29.5%) and Panama's transport (+60.1%) also expand.

claims.q: Crowd-out effect takes place in Chile,
claims.an: This is the core of the 'double-edged' finding (Dutch-disease-type reallocation).

claims.t: [model_result] LAC mining exports to China change most (especially Brazil, Chile, Peru), while LAC agricultural exports to China fall slightly; LAC and China become 'closely bundled' in mining, so Chinese fluctuations will hit LAC export revenues.
claims.q: Mining exports from LAC to China change most,

claims.t: [model_result] Chinese exports of Electronics, Textiles, Machinery, Chemicals and business services to LAC rise (e.g. electronics +US$943m to Brazil and +US$563m to Peru; business/trade services +US$461m to Brazil and +US$108m to Chile), except electronics to Venezuela (-US$1,398.39m), where Chinese investment replaces exports.
claims.q: reduce largely by 1398.39 million dollars.

claims.t: Relatively developed LAC economies with fuller industrial systems (Brazil, Mexico) benefit more and face less manufacturing squeeze; Mexico (Electronics/Machinery) and Panama (transport, recreation, trade services) keep specialising in their advantages.
claims.q: Relatively economically developed economies in

claims.q: foreign exchange earnings that limits government’s capacity of counter

claims.t: Chinese investment in electricity, gas, water and transport infrastructure has improved quality of life; EGW supply in Peru, Chile, Argentina and Panama rises 25.1–74.3%, and large hydropower stations relieve local power-supply pressure.
claims.q: The construction of large hydropower stations in
claims.e: Simulation results plus a general assertion about hydropower.

claims.t: Policy: LAC should absorb technology and management skills from Chinese MNEs (PPPs), build a regional alliance to coordinate 'gradient transfer' of sectors, use infant-industry tariffs as a short-term measure, and adopt industry-oriented FDI policy.

claims.an: These are proposals, not evidence.

timeline.src: Inter-American Dialogue: Xi's Latin America Tour — https://thedialogue.org/blogs/2014/07/xis-latin-america-tour

timeline.ev: During Xi's state visit to Brazil after the BRICS summit in Fortaleza, deals include Chinese purchases of 60 Embraer E190s (US$3.2bn), a rail cooperation agreement and a US$5bn China Exim credit for Vale's ships.
timeline.sg: Bilateral deals that accompanied the China–LAC leaders' meeting in Brasília.
timeline.src: Space Daily/Solar Daily (AFP): China leader signs Brazil deals on Latin America trip (AFP) — https://www.solardaily.com/reports/China_leader_signs_Brazil_deals_on_Latin_America_trip_999.html

timeline.ev: Xi Jinping and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner establish a comprehensive strategic partnership in Buenos Aires and sign agreements including two Santa Cruz hydro dams, Belgrano Cargas rail upgrades and an US$11bn currency swap.
timeline.sg: Locked in Chinese financing for Argentina's flagship infrastructure while Buenos Aires was shut out of capital markets.
timeline.src: Letra P: Junto a Boudou y Domínguez, el presidente chino destacó acuerdos — https://www.letrap.com.ar/nota/2014-7-19-junto-a-boudou-y-dominguez-el-presidente-chino-destaco-acuerdos

timeline.ev: Xi Jinping arrives in Caracas for a state visit at which China and Venezuela raise ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership.
timeline.sg: Confirmed Beijing's backing for Maduro; China–Venezuela financing mechanisms were then put at more than US$50bn.
timeline.src: China Daily: Xi's visit lifts Venezuelan ties — https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/world/2014xibricssummit/2014-07/21/content_17872188.htm

timeline.ev: Xi Jinping holds talks with Raúl Castro in Havana; the two sides sign 29 cooperation agreements, including a credit line for a multipurpose terminal at the port of Santiago de Cuba.
timeline.sg: Reaffirmed party-to-party solidarity and economic support for Cuba's reforms, months before the US–Cuba thaw.
timeline.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the PRC: Xi Jinping Holds Talks with President Raúl Castro of Cuba — https://www.mfa.gov.cn/eng/wjb/zzjg_663340/ldmzs_664952/xwlb_664954/202406/t20240606_11401699.html

timeline.ev: Glencore closes the US$7bn sale of Peru's Las Bambas copper project to an MMG-led consortium.
timeline.sg: Biggest Chinese mining acquisition in Latin America, making China a major copper producer in Peru.
timeline.src: NS Energy: Glencore closes $7bn Las Bambas mine sale in Peru — https://www.nsenergybusiness.com/news/newsglencore-closes-7bn-las-bambas-mine-sale-in-peru-040814-4334159/

timeline.ev: Evo Morales (MAS) wins a third term as Bolivia's president with 61.36% against Samuel Doria Medina (24.23%).
timeline.sg: Extended MAS rule; a 2013 court ruling had let Morales run on the grounds that his first term predated the 2009 constitution.
timeline.src: IFES ElectionGuide: IFES ElectionGuide: Bolivian Presidency 2014 — https://www.electionguide.org/elections/id/2447/

timeline.ev: Dilma Rousseff (PT) is narrowly re-elected in Brazil's runoff with 51.64% against Aécio Neves (PSDB, 48.36%).
timeline.sg: The narrow, polarised result preceded the recession and her 2016 impeachment.
timeline.src: IFES ElectionGuide: IFES ElectionGuide: Brazilian Presidency 2014 Round 2 — https://www.electionguide.org/elections/id/2810/

timeline.ev: Argentina's central bank makes its first drawing on the July 2014 PBoC swap line (up to 70bn yuan / US$11bn), requesting the equivalent of US$814m.
timeline.sg: The first time Argentina used Chinese liquidity to prop up its reserves.
timeline.src: Central Banking: Central Bank of Argentina borrows $814m through China swap line — https://www.centralbanking.com/central-banking/news/2378954/argentina-central-bank-borrows-usd814m-through-china-swap-line

timeline.ev: First tripartite memorandum among Peru, Brazil and China on the transcontinental (bi-oceanic) railway, estimated at $10bn and six years of construction (country names and amount partly truncated).
timeline.src: (Urdinez et al., 2016, p. 25)

timeline.ev: Tabaré Vázquez (Frente Amplio) wins Uruguay's presidential runoff with 56.63% against Luis Lacalle Pou (National Party, 43.37%).
timeline.sg: A third consecutive Frente Amplio term.
timeline.src: IFES ElectionGuide: IFES ElectionGuide: Uruguayan Presidency 2014 Round 2 — https://www.electionguide.org/elections/id/2329/

timeline.ev: Obama and Raúl Castro announce moves to restore US–Cuba diplomatic relations.
timeline.sg: Removed a long-standing regional grievance against Washington.
timeline.src: Times of Israel (AP): US reestablishing diplomatic relations with Cuba — https://www.timesofisrael.com/us-reestablishes-relations-with-cuba/

timeline.ev: Political unrest in US–Panama relations over US asylum for ex-president Martinelli and the Panama Papers
timeline.src: (Zelicovich and Yamin, 2024, p. 63)

timeline.ev: China's policy banks become the largest annual public creditors to Latin American governments.
timeline.src: (Feng and Zeng, 2022, p. 191)

timeline.ev: Clear drop in foreign financial inflows to Brazil following end of commodity boom
timeline.src: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 484)

timeline.ev: Cambiemos (Juntos por el Cambio) brings Mauricio Macri to the presidency.
timeline.src: (Bonnet, 2024, PDF p. 8)

timeline.ev: China deploys warships to evacuate nationals from Yemen, describing it as consented humanitarian relief.
timeline.src: (Seppänen and Smith, 2025, p. 398)

timeline.ev: EFSI (Juncker Plan) launched with EUR 33.5 bn to leverage EUR 500 bn by 2020.
timeline.src: (Griffith-Jones, 2021, p. 325)

timeline.ev: SYRIZA-led Greek government accepts a third bailout after a six-month standoff.
timeline.src: (Verney and Katsikas, 2021, p. 262)

timeline.ev: China launches Supply-Side Structural Reforms, with capacity reduction as a key element ('new normal').
timeline.src: (Ding et al., 2021, p. 5)

timeline.ev: China sets up regional funds for LAC from 2015: the CLAI Fund (US$30bn), the CLAC Fund (US$10bn) and the Special Loan Program for China–Latin America Infrastructure (US$20bn).
timeline.src: (Ding et al., 2021, p. 5)

timeline.ev: China launches Made in China 2025.
First Ministerial Meeting of the China-CELAC Forum: China announces US$500 billion trade target and US$250 billion investment over a decade.
Chinese swap used as relief for weakening foreign-exchange reserves in Argentina.
First China-CELAC Cooperation Plan 2015-2019 sets targets of US$500 bn trade and a reciprocal FDI stock of at least US$250 bn by 2025 (adoption date not stated in this part).
China launches Made in China 2025 and Internet Plus programmes.
China–LAC Cooperation Plan (2015–2019) and the '1+3+6' framework for trade, investment and financial cooperation in six fields.
MOFCOM announces that ODI will be counted by final destination rather than first territory entered (not applied in subsequent bulletins).

China announces three new region-wide funds totalling US$35bn: the US$10bn China–LAC Industrial Cooperation Investment Fund (CLAI), a US$20bn Special Loan Program for infrastructure and US$5bn for the China–LAC Cooperation Fund.
timeline.sg: Shifted part of China's LAC finance from bilateral loans toward fund-based and equity instruments.
timeline.src: Boston University Global Development Policy Center: China-Latin America Economic Bulletin 2016 — https://www.bu.edu/pardeeschool/files/2016/04/China-LAC.Bulletin_2016.pdf

timeline.ev: Chinese policy-bank lending to LAC reaches about US$29bn, the second-highest year on record, with Brazil, Ecuador and Venezuela taking 95% of it.
timeline.sg: A final lending surge before Chinese sovereign loans to the region fell sharply.
timeline.src: Inter-American Dialogue: China–Latin America Finance (loans report) — https://thedialogue.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Dialogue-LoansReport-v4-lowres.pdf

timeline.ev: Peace Ark's Mission Harmony-2015 includes stops in Barbados, Grenada, Mexico and Peru.
timeline.sg: Second PLA Navy hospital-ship deployment to Latin America and the Caribbean.
timeline.src: Wikipedia: Chinese hospital ship Daishan Dao — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_hospital_ship_Daishan_Dao

timeline.ev: Xi Jinping and Rafael Correa agree in Beijing to establish a China–Ecuador strategic partnership.
timeline.sg: Made Ecuador, then China's second-largest LAC borrower, a formal strategic partner on the eve of the first China–CELAC ministerial.
timeline.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the PRC: Xi Jinping Holds Talks with President Rafael Correa of Ecuador — https://www.mfa.gov.cn/eng/wjb/zzjg_663340/ldmzs_664952/xwlb_664954/202406/t20240606_11401907.html

timeline.ev: First Ministerial Meeting of the China–CELAC Forum opens in Beijing, adopting a 2015–2019 Cooperation Plan.
timeline.sg: Institutionalises China's multilateral channel to LAC without the US.
timeline.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the PRC: Xi Jinping speech at the opening of the First Ministerial Meeting of the China-CELAC Forum — https://www.mfa.gov.cn/eng/xw/zyjh/202405/t20240530_11340816.html

timeline.ev: Xi Jinping and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner issue a joint statement deepening the comprehensive strategic partnership during her state visit to Beijing, with Xi singling out nuclear power for 'special attention'.
timeline.sg: Set up the nuclear and infrastructure package that Macri and later Milei would revisit.
timeline.src: People's Daily Online: Xi, Argentine president pledge to deepen ties — https://en.people.cn/n/2015/0205/c90883-8846097.html

timeline.ev: Obama signs Executive Order 13692, declaring a national emergency over the 'unusual and extraordinary threat' posed by the situation in Venezuela and sanctioning seven officials.
timeline.sg: Started the US sanctions architecture on Venezuela, whose main creditor and oil buyer was China.
timeline.src: NPR (via MPR News): Obama imposes sanctions on Venezuela, invoking emergency powers — https://mprnews.org/story/2015/03/09/npr-sanctions-venezuela

timeline.ev: Obama and Raúl Castro hold a historic meeting at the Seventh Summit of the Americas in Panama.
timeline.sg: High point of US multilateral re-engagement in the hemisphere.
timeline.src: NPR: Obama, Castro Sit For Historic Meeting At Americas Summit — https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2015/04/11/398950752/historic-meeting-expected-between-obama-castro-at-americas-summit

timeline.ev: Premier Li Keqiang tours Brazil, Colombia, Peru and Chile; in Brazil he signs 35 agreements that Dilma Rousseff says carry about US$53bn in promised investment, and in Lima announces a feasibility study for a transcontinental railway.
timeline.sg: The high-water mark of Chinese investment pledges in South America, many of which (like the railway) never materialised.
timeline.src: Americas Society/Council of the Americas: Li's Trip a Watershed in China–Latin America Ties — https://as-coa.org/articles/lis-trip-watershed-china-latin-america-ties

timeline.ev: The rescission of Cuba's designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism takes effect.
timeline.sg: Part of the Cuba thaw that briefly reduced a long-standing irritant in US relations with Latin America and the Caribbean.
timeline.src: Greenberg Traurig: Cuba removed from U.S. state sponsors of terrorism list — https://gtlaw.com/de/insights/2015/6/cuba-removed-from-us-state-sponsors-of-terrorism-list

timeline.ev: LAC-China Infrastructure Fund (with IDB) enters into force.
timeline.src: (Urdinez et al., 2016, p. 25)

timeline.ev: The United States and Cuba formally restore diplomatic relations and reopen embassies in Washington and Havana.
timeline.sg: Removed the Cuba grievance from US–LAC relations that China and regional bodies had used to frame US isolation.
timeline.src: Latin America Working Group: Press release: US and Cuba to open embassies in Havana and Washington — https://www.lawg.org/press-release-us-and-cuba-to-open-embassies-in-havana-and-washington-2/

timeline.ev: Secretary of State John Kerry presides over the flag-raising at the reopened US Embassy in Havana.
timeline.sg: Showed the peak of the Obama-era opening, later rolled back under Trump.
timeline.src: The Jakarta Post (AFP): Flag raised over US embassy in Cuba — https://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2015/08/14/flag-raised-over-us-embassy-cuba

timeline.ev: Guatemalan President Otto Pérez Molina resigns a day after Congress stripped his immunity (132–0) over the La Línea customs-fraud scheme; Vice-President Alejandro Maldonado completes his term.
timeline.sg: A landmark anti-corruption case built with UN-backed prosecutors.
timeline.src: Wikipedia: Otto Pérez Molina — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_P%C3%A9rez_Molina

timeline.ev: House hearing 'China's advances in Latin America and the Caribbean'
timeline.src: (Leiva Van de Maele, 2026, p. 915)

timeline.ev: Protests against changes to the Las Bambas project leave four dead (per MMG), and Peru declares a state of emergency in Apurímac.
timeline.sg: Began a long series of community conflicts at the Chinese-owned mine.
timeline.src: Mining.com: Mining protests turn deadly in Peru — https://www.mining.com/?p=835032

timeline.ev: Jimmy Morales (FCN) wins Guatemala's presidential runoff with 67.40% against Sandra Torres (UNE, 32.60%).
timeline.sg: Victory for a political outsider after the 2015 corruption crisis.
timeline.src: IFES ElectionGuide: IFES ElectionGuide: Guatemalan Presidency 2015 Round 2 — https://www.electionguide.org/elections/id/2876/

timeline.ev: China Three Gorges wins the concessions for Brazil's Jupiá and Ilha Solteira hydropower plants, agreeing to pay R$13.8bn (about US$3.7bn).
timeline.sg: Made CTG one of Brazil's largest private power generators.
timeline.src: IPP Journal: Enel Green Power, China Three Gorges and Cemig win hydropower projects in Brazil — https://ippjournal.com/news/enel-green-power-china-three-gorges-and-cemig-win-hydropower-projects-in-brazil

timeline.ev: Mauricio Macri wins Argentina's runoff against Daniel Scioli (51.3%).
timeline.sg: Start of the centre-right turn; Macri re-engaged Washington while keeping China ties (swap, nuclear talks).
timeline.src: Philippine Daily Inquirer (AFP): Argentine President-elect Macri wins with 51.3%—officials — https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/743798/argentine-president-elect-macri-won-with-51-3-officials

timeline.ev: Congress (President Eduardo Cunha) accepts the impeachment case against Rousseff.
timeline.src: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 204)

timeline.ev: Obama signs the FY2016 Consolidated Appropriations Act (P.L. 114-113), providing up to US$750m for Central America to support the Northern Triangle's Alliance for Prosperity plan.
timeline.sg: The largest US aid package for the Northern Triangle in years, the benchmark against which later Chinese offers to El Salvador and Honduras were compared.
timeline.src: Congressional Research Service (via EveryCRSReport): President Obama's $1 Billion Foreign Aid Request for Central America (CRS IN10237) — https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/20160105_IN10237_b24e26dbf9277ad8c2be9bece04573c21b2a18f4.html

timeline.ev: Argentina–China nuclear plants agreement (three plants, $15bn) concluded during the 2016 Nuclear Security Summit in Washington (per note 4). Note text truncated ('2016 Nuclear Sec...'); 'Security Summit' is the analyst's reading.
timeline.src: (Urdinez et al., 2016, p. 25)

timeline.ev: Coca-Codo Sinclair hydroelectric dam completed. It later suffers degrading materials and environmental damage.
timeline.src: (Albright, 2025, p. 79)

timeline.ev: Xi Jinping state visit to Ecuador.
timeline.src: (Albright, 2025, p. 79)

timeline.ev: Latin America invited to join BRI at China-CELAC meeting
timeline.src: (Stallings, 2025, p. 331)

timeline.ev: Impeachment of Dilma Rousseff; PT leaves office
timeline.src: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 488)

timeline.ev: Peruvian election between Kuczynski and Keiko Fujimori; Kuczynski wins
timeline.src: (Bibi, Cerpa Vielma and Perfeito da Silva, 2026, p. 490)

timeline.ev: Impeachment and removal of Dilma Rousseff; Temer interim government.
timeline.src: (Bonnet, 2024, PDF p. 3)

timeline.ev: Chile begins renegotiating lithium contracts with Albemarle and SQM, redistributing benefits to local government and communities.
timeline.src: (Sanchez-Lopez, 2023, p. 36)

timeline.ev: Climax of large-scale state financing model: energy >80% of Chinese infrastructure finance; average policy-bank project >800 MW.
Purchase of majority shares of Tenke Fungurume (2016–2017) by Chinese interests; Chinese-controlled output exceeds half of DRC and world chemical-refinery feedstock.
Cobalt traceability initiatives emerge after 2016, driven by concerns about human rights abuses in the DRC.
timeline.src: (IEA and OECD, 2025, p. 63)

timeline.ev: US and EU antitrust authorities block ChemChina's US$44 billion acquisition of Syngenta (Swiss agrochemical/seed company).
China Molybdenum Co. acquires Anglo American's niobium and phosphates assets in Brazil (US$1,500 million).
China Three Gorges Corporation acquires Duke Energy International, Brazil Ltda. (US$1,200 million).
Hainan Airlines acquires 23.7% of Azul S.A. (US$450 million).
China's Policy Paper on Latin America and the Caribbean (Xinhua 2016), cited as the source of the six cooperation fields.
China's ODI flows peak at over US$196bn.
China grants Venezuela its first restructuring of oil-backed loans, a principal moratorium, after oil prices fell to about US$30.
timeline.sg: Start of distress in China's largest LAC loan book.
timeline.src: AidData: How China's oil-backed lending in Venezuela fell into distress—and what might come next — https://www.aiddata.org/blog/how-chinas-oil-backed-lending-in-venezuela-fell-into-distress

timeline.ev: At the White House, Obama and Juan Manuel Santos mark 15 years of Plan Colombia (nearly US$10bn since FY2000) and announce 'Peace Colombia', a US$450m support package for the peace process.
timeline.sg: Renewed the closest US partnership in South America as China expanded its trade with Colombia.
timeline.src: Congressional Research Service (via EveryCRSReport): U.S. Assistance to Colombia: Peace Colombia (CRS Insight IN10454) — https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/20160303_IN10454_28b6bea5bb8180d52d943a51680aee21fb5524fc.html

timeline.ev: Bolivian voters reject (51.30% No) a constitutional amendment that would have let Morales seek another term; a Constitutional Court ruling in November 2017 removes term limits anyway.
timeline.sg: Overriding the referendum result fuelled the legitimacy crisis around the 2019 election.
timeline.src: Wikipedia: 2016 Bolivian constitutional referendum — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Bolivian_constitutional_referendum

timeline.ev: Obama arrives in Havana for a three-day visit, the first by a sitting US president to Cuba since 1928.
timeline.sg: The symbolic peak of an effort to end the 'Cold War in Latin America' and rebuild US standing in the region.
timeline.src: KGOU / NPR: Cuba, Argentina ready for softer U.S. relations after historic Obama visits — https://www.kgou.org/world/2016-03-25/cuba-argentina-ready-for-softer-u-s-relations-after-historic-obama-visits

timeline.ev: Obama visits Argentina (23–24 March) and meets newly elected President Mauricio Macri, ending years of strained ties under Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.
timeline.sg: A US effort to win back Argentina, which under Kirchner had deepened financial and space cooperation with China.
timeline.src: KGOU / NPR: Cuba, Argentina ready for softer U.S. relations after historic Obama visits — https://www.kgou.org/world/2016-03-25/cuba-argentina-ready-for-softer-u-s-relations-after-historic-obama-visits

timeline.ev: Coca Codo Sinclair (1,500 MW) begins supplying the national grid (generation counted from April 2016).
Trump campaign rally in Indiana: China accused of 'rap[ing]' the US; anti-China national mood mobilised in the 2016 campaign
timeline.src: (Leiva Van de Maele, 2026, p. 920)

timeline.ev: Pedro Pablo Kuczynski narrowly wins Peru's runoff against Keiko Fujimori (Fujimori concedes 10 June).
timeline.sg: Market-oriented government; PPK made his first state visit as president to China.
timeline.src: Al Jazeera: Peru election: Keiko Fujimori concedes defeat — https://www.aljazeera.com/amp/news/2016/6/11/peru-election-keiko-fujimori-concedes-defeat

timeline.ev: UNCLOS Annex VII tribunal rules against China in South China Sea arbitration; Wang Yi calls it 'bad-faith dramatization' but not interference.

timeline.ev: Senate convicts Rousseff in the impeachment trial (61 votes to 20); Temer becomes president.
timeline.src: (Ribeiro Hoffmann and De Souza Guilherme, 2021, p. 204)

timeline.ev: Brazil's Senate removes Dilma Rousseff; Michel Temer sworn in as president.
timeline.sg: Ends 13 years of PT rule; Temer pursued privatisations that drew major Chinese investment in Brazilian energy.
timeline.src: Al Jazeera: Brazil's Senate strips Dilma Rousseff of presidency — https://www.aljazeera.com/amp/news/2016/8/31/brazils-senate-strips-dilma-rousseff-of-presidency

timeline.ev: Argentine Foreign Minister Susana Malcorra and Wang Yi sign an additional protocol in Hangzhou stating that the Neuquén deep-space station is for exclusively peaceful use.
timeline.sg: The Macri government's attempt to answer domestic and US concerns about military use of the station.
timeline.src: Cancillería Argentina: Argentina y China reafirman el uso pacífico de la estación espacial de Neuquén — https://cancilleria.gob.ar/es/actualidad/comunicados/argentina-y-china-reafirman-el-uso-pacifico-de-la-estacion-espacial-de

timeline.ev: Temer tells investors in New York the impeachment happened because Rousseff refused the neoliberal programme (per Carta Capital).

timeline.ev: IMF includes the renminbi in the SDR basket.
Colombian voters narrowly reject the peace agreement with the FARC, 50.22% No to 49.78% Yes.
timeline.sg: Forced renegotiation of the US-backed peace deal and polarised Colombian politics.
timeline.src: Wikipedia: 2016 Colombian peace agreement referendum — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Colombian_peace_agreement_referendum

timeline.ev: Temer government cuts the state oil company's minimum 30% participation and ends its exclusive operating right in the pre-salt.

Paris Agreement enters into force; by the time of writing ratified by China and 30 LAC countries.

timeline.sg: Further consolidation of Ortega's rule.
timeline.src: IFES ElectionGuide: IFES ElectionGuide: Nicaraguan Presidency 2016 — https://www.electionguide.org/elections/id/2665/

timeline.ev: Donald J. Trump (R) and Michael R. Pence win the US presidential election with 304 electoral votes to 227 for Hillary Clinton (D).
timeline.sg: Change of US administration; Leiva Van de Maele (2026) dates the shift in US policy toward China in Latin America to the administration that took office after the 2016 election.

timeline.ev: On the first state visit by a Chinese president to Ecuador, Xi Jinping and Rafael Correa raise ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership and pledge Chinese help with post-earthquake reconstruction.
timeline.sg: Elevated Ecuador to China's top partnership tier in the region.
timeline.src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the PRC: Xi Jinping Holds Talks with President Rafael Correa of Ecuador — https://www.mfa.gov.cn/eng/wjb/zzjg_663340/ldmzs_664952/xwlb_664954/202406/t20240606_11402711.html
