props.proposition: Chinese demand for primary commodities is the base layer of China's economic presence in Latin America: it drove the 2003–2013 export boom and remains largely insensitive to host-government ideology and to US political influence.
props.scope_countries: South America (BRA, ARG, CHL, PER, URY, BOL, ECU, VEN)
props.note: Strongest and most convergent finding in the corpus. Urdinez et al. (2016) provide the sharpest test: commodity exports to China and Chinese private-firm FDI do not respond to US influence. Albright (2025) qualifies it for lending: trade with China does not predict which lender a borrower chooses.

props.proposition: The Chinese export-complementarity effect is geographically bifurcated: South America complements China, while Mexico and Central America compete with it and remain locked into US value chains (NAFTA/CAFTA-DR/USMCA).
props.scope_countries: MEX; Central America vs South America
props.note: D08-C31 (Chinese FDI stock in Mexico >US$28bn in 2004) is coded as contradicting but is very probably erroneous (see X_corrections).

props.proposition: Between c.2007 and 2015 China's state-coordinated finance (CDB and China Exim) became the largest annual official lender to Latin American governments, with very large, infrastructure- and energy-oriented loans bundled with Chinese contractors and goods.
props.scope_countries: VEN, BRA, ECU, ARG (≈90% of volume)
props.note: Over 2008–2019 as a whole the World Bank still lent more than China (D03-C01). 'Largest' refers to annual flows in peak years and to loan size, not cumulative totals.

props.proposition: Chinese policy-bank lending was concentrated in high-risk, market-excluded borrowers (Venezuela, Ecuador, Argentina): China acted as a lender of last resort where Western private and multilateral capital would not go — a 'rupture-gap' effect.
props.note: Emergent explanation not in the original M-list: ruptures with the US/IFIs (default, expulsion of the World Bank, nationalisations) open financing gaps that risk-tolerant state capital fills. D01-C14 notes Chinese and IFI loans hardly overlap, which is consistent with gap-filling but cuts against direct competition.

props.proposition: Chinese loans are not 'cheap' or unconditional: they carry commercial rates, shorter maturities, procurement ties and (often) oil collateral, but no macroeconomic or governance conditionality; borrowers value speed, scale and the finance-plus-builder package.
props.note: Alami and Dixon (2020), citing Kaplan (2016), characterise Chinese lending as 'patient capital' with longer horizons, in tension with Gallagher and Irwin's maturity data (10.7 vs 18.0 years).

props.proposition: Ideology shapes the form and visibility of ties with China (sovereign borrowing, symbolic alignment, public opinion) more than their volume: leftist governments were more likely to borrow from China, but trade and much investment persisted under right-of-centre governments.
props.scope_countries: LAC; esp. ECU, BOL, BRA, ARG
props.note: Ganchev (2020) states non-leftist governments would have been unlikely to engage China beyond trade (D11-C25), yet his own data show Chinese FDI in Ecuador and Bolivia's China debt share persisting after the Pink Tide (D11-C27).

props.proposition: Latin American governments hedge and compartmentalise: they accept Chinese economic opportunities while keeping security alignment with Washington; the US 'hegemonic ceiling' in security coexists with Chinese economic weight.
props.scope_countries: LAC (14-country index); PAN, URY, BRA, CHL, PER as true hedgers
props.note: Sims and Lee's index covers goods trade and major arms imports only (not loans/FDI) and has acknowledged measurement problems.

props.proposition: Borrowing from China was often motivated by distancing from the US and diversification of financial dependence, not by attraction to China or its model.
props.note: Interview evidence is concentrated on Ecuador (Albright 2025).

props.proposition: The US response to China in Latin America was belated: China was recognised as a problem from c.2005, but no significant countermeasures were adopted until 2017, because the political stream (national mood, elite consensus) did not align earlier.
props.note: Sims and Lee (2025) caution that declining US engagement alone cannot explain hedging, which persisted across administrations.

props.proposition: Since 2017 US counter-statecraft has relied mainly on 'carrots' that were frequently promises without commensurate disbursements (Growth in the Americas/America Crece, B3W, APEP), plus warnings; coercive 'sticks' were rare until 2025.
props.note: Leiva Van de Maele (2026) argues the shift was 'not only rhetorical' (D20-C07) but documents few financed instruments; the 2025 US$20bn Argentina swap and DFC's Ecuador debt-for-nature guarantee show that state finance is available when Washington chooses to deploy it.

props.proposition: US pressure has been effective at denial in specific strategic nodes (telecom backbone, ports, canal-adjacent projects, EV plants in the USMCA space) but has not reversed trade or commodity flows.
props.note: Panama: PCCP port, northern railway and Amador embassy dropped (D04), BRI exit 2025 and annulment of the CK Hutchison concession 2026 (external). Chile: 2019 submarine cable (D20). Mexico: BYD plant stalled (external; attributed in reporting to Beijing's approval, not US action — causal attribution uncertain).

props.proposition: US engagement priorities in Latin America have been securitised (counter-narcotics, migration, organised crime), and since 2025 increasingly militarised, which offers Latin American governments few economic alternatives to Chinese trade and capital.
props.note: Felbab-Brown (2026) is a policy statement; securitisation is well documented for the US agenda but its causal effect on LAC economic choices is inferred.

props.proposition: China's economic instruments shifted after c.2015–2019: sovereign policy-bank lending collapsed, replaced by SOE acquisitions of strategic utilities, private-firm investment in renewables/EVs/lithium, and trade — consolidation through ownership rather than expansion through credit.
props.note: This is the key qualification of the central premise: China is not expanding on every instrument — sovereign lending fell to near zero in 2020 — but it consolidated in strategic assets. Gao (2026, p. 167) attributes the 'small is beautiful' turn to BRI sustainability demands and the risk of sovereign over-indebtedness in recipients; the M&A shift (2015–2021) is a distinct trend (p. 169).

props.proposition: China's dominance of mineral processing and battery manufacturing structurally binds Lithium Triangle and copper producers to Chinese value chains, regardless of the producer's political alignment.
props.note: Chile is the main counter-case: low lithium export dependence on China (15% in 2018), US firm Albemarle as incumbent, and a 2023–2026 Codelco–SQM state-led arrangement that sidelined Tianqi.

props.proposition: Western responses in critical minerals have been primarily regulatory and denial-oriented (IRA FEOC rules, traceability, investment screening, minerals frameworks) rather than offering processing capacity or market substitution in Latin America.
props.note: Evidence for post-2025 US minerals agreements comes from external verification; their implementation is too recent to assess.

props.proposition: China's normative offer — non-intervention, sovereignty, 'no political strings' — resonates with a Latin American legal tradition forged against US intervention, but carries its own conditions (Taiwan, UN votes) and is applied selectively.
props.note: Most of this evidence is not LAC-specific (D21–D23); its application to LAC is the author's inference.

props.proposition: Taiwan recognition is the main explicitly political condition attached to Chinese engagement; diplomatic switches (Costa Rica 2007 to Honduras 2023) were followed by intensified economic ties, but switches did not automatically produce political realignment away from the US.
props.scope_countries: CRI, PAN, DOM, SLV, NIC, HND; PRY (counter-case)
props.note: Costa Rica is the puzzle case: switched in 2007 but remains strongly US-aligned (Sims and Lee 2025).

props.proposition: Chinese state-backed investment is more tolerant of political and geopolitical risk than US private investment, so heightened geopolitical risk deters US but not Chinese FDI.
props.scope_countries: ARG, BRA, CHL, COL, MEX, PER, VEN
props.note: Single econometric study with serious reported data problems (N inconsistency, implausible SEs). Domínguez et al. (2006) show Chinese caution in Venezuela before 2006 ('too much risk for little return').

props.proposition: The commodity boom financed the Pink Tide and its end contributed to the right turn; political cycles therefore follow the external economic cycle as much as they shape alignment with China or the US.
props.scope_countries: BRA, CHL, PER, ARG, ECU, VEN
props.note: Bibi et al. (2026) explicitly disclaim causality; association only.

props.proposition: Deepening commodity ties with China reproduce dependency: re-primarisation, trade deficits in manufactures and environmental/social costs; the benefits are real but unevenly distributed.
props.note: Record LAC trade deficit with China of US$95.8bn in 2024 (external).

props.proposition: Public opinion of China in Latin America has been broadly favourable and stable, driven more by trade surpluses and presidential ideology than by Chinese soft-power instruments; China's development model has limited appeal.
props.note: Data end in 2016.

props.proposition: China's restraint toward the US in the hemisphere (avoiding military alignment, acquiescing to US primacy, caution with Venezuela pre-2006) lowered the salience of its economic expansion in Washington and so contributed to the belated US response.
props.note: Inference linking two literatures; D20 shows military commanders flagged China from 2005 nonetheless.

props.proposition: Latin American agency is constrained by state capacity and macro-fragility: strong bureaucracies (Brazil, Chile) bargain and diversify; fragile states turn to whichever patron offers the fastest relief.
props.scope_countries: BRA, CHL vs ARG, BOL, ECU, VEN
props.note: Bolivia's lithium contracts with CBC/CATL and Uranium One stalled in the legislature (external), and Argentina's 2025 reliance on a US Treasury swap illustrate the 'fastest relief' logic in both directions.

props.proposition: Announced Chinese commitments systematically exceed realised outcomes; pledges (2004 US$100bn, 2014 US$250bn, 2025 RMB66bn credit line) are poor indicators of material presence.
props.note: The same announced-vs-realised gap applies to US initiatives (America Crece, B3W, APEP) — the rhetoric–outcome gap is not unique to Washington. The 2004 'US$100bn' figure is itself recorded inconsistently in the corpus: an investment pledge to 2014 (D08-C11) vs a trade target for 2010 (D27-C03) — see contradiction C02.

props.proposition: Chinese economic presence brings governance and illicit-economy externalities (precursor chemicals, underground banking, illegal mining finance, IUU fishing, surveillance technology) that the US increasingly uses to frame China as a security problem.
props.scope_countries: MEX, PER, BOL, ECU, ARG, Amazon basin
props.note: Barreto Rodrigues and Franchi (2026) document Amazonian criminal convergence without attributing it to the Chinese state; China-linked actors appear only as criminal groups.

props.proposition: Western (US and EU) alternatives to Chinese finance in Latin America have historically under-delivered relative to announcements, and the absence of a regional financial backstop left space for external state lenders.

US influence indicators in Latin America declined during the 2000s and 2010s, and China's state-linked actors (but not private firms or commodity trade) moved into the space left by declining US influence.
props.note: Direct disagreement in the corpus: Urdinez et al. read China's state-linked finance as contestation of US hegemony; Gallagher and Irwin read the same lending as primarily commercial. Alami and Dixon (2020) further question the coordination of Chinese state capital (provincial autonomy, weakly regulated SOEs).

props.proposition: Socio-environmental contestation and public scepticism of Chinese projects have reshaped the FORM of Chinese engagement (smaller projects, renewables, acquisitions) and weakened China's image where FDI is visible, but have rarely reversed economic ties at the national level.
props.note: Surfaced by auditing the NotebookLM synthesis (N24). Bolivia's 2019 cancellation of the German ACISA lithium JV after Potosí protests (D14-C18) shows local contestation can block projects regardless of investor nationality. Corpus evidence on labour-union mobilisation is thin.

props.proposition: China–Latin America complementarity is rooted in differences in factor endowments and productive capabilities: South American natural-resource and land endowments versus China's manufacturing capacity, capital and technology. But it is uneven across countries and asymmetric in value capture: it concentrates host activity in extraction and energy, with limited domestic processing and technological spill-overs, and its benefits are conditional rather than automatic.
props.scope_countries: South America (BRA, ARG, CHL, PER, BOL, ECU, COL, VEN); Mexico as counter-case
props.note: Added with the factor-endowment module (D28–D31). Each source measures complementarity differently: qualitative (Dosch and Goodman), Balassa revealed comparative advantage (Ding et al.), GTAP economic structure (Zhou) and trade composition (ECLAC). None reports mineral reserves or processing capacity by country, so the processing and battery stages rest on the core corpus (Gao; Sanchez-Lopez; Gulley; IEA and OECD). Zhou's gains are CGE simulations under full employment and perfect competition. Ding et al. find that after 2015 China invested where China, not the host, had comparative advantage (utilities).

mechs.prediction: China's economic presence should track commodity endowments and Chinese import demand, not host ideology or US influence; expansion should be strongest where economies complement China (South America) and weakest where they compete (Mexico, Central America).
mechs.cases: Brazil (soy, iron ore), Chile and Peru (copper), Argentina (soy), Uruguay (agri-food), Lithium Triangle
mechs.counterexamples: Mexico and Central America: competition rather than complementarity (D07-C07, D08-C30, D09-C09); trade does not predict lender choice (D03-C16)
mechs.scope_conditions: Strong for trade and resource FDI; weak for sovereign finance and political alignment.
mechs.assessment: Strongly supported. The most robust explanation for the persistence of China's trade footprint across ideological cycles; cannot by itself explain sovereign lending patterns or Taiwan-related variation. The factor-endowment sources (D28–D31) confirm the endowment basis but qualify its form: after 2015 Chinese M&A followed China's own comparative advantage (utilities) rather than the host's (Ding et al., 2021), and modelled gains come with crowding-out of other sectors in small resource-based economies (Zhou, 2023).
mechs.gaps: Corpus trade data mostly end before 2016; post-2020 volumes rely on external verification (US$518bn in 2024; ~US$565bn in 2025).

mechs.prediction: Chinese state-linked actors (policy banks, SOEs) should behave differently from private firms: larger, riskier, bundled finance-and-construction packages, concentrated where political/strategic payoffs are higher.
mechs.cases: Venezuela and Ecuador loans-for-oil; Argentina rail and dams; Chile/Peru utility acquisitions (State Grid, CTG, China Southern Power Grid); Chancay port
mechs.counterexamples: Commercial terms and profit-seeking (Gallagher and Irwin 2015); provincial and firm-level autonomy fragments 'China Inc.' (Alami and Dixon 2020); collapse of policy-bank lending after 2015 shows that the state instrument is not unconditionally sustained.
mechs.scope_conditions: Strongest for 2007–2015 sovereign lending and post-2015 strategic acquisitions; weak for private-firm FDI and commodity trade.
mechs.assessment: Supported, with an important debate over motive (contestation vs commercial). The corpus converges on the capability asymmetry (scale, speed, bundling, risk tolerance) even where it disagrees on intent.
mechs.gaps: Disbursement data for most loans are not in the corpus; external data show cumulative CDB+Exim commitments >US$120bn (2005–2023).

mechs.prediction: US rhetoric should outpace US-financed offers; US official initiatives should be smaller, slower and more dependent on private capital than Chinese offers; borrowers should cite lack of Western capacity.
mechs.cases: America Crece (promise without financing data), B3W tour (2021), APEP (2022–23), Panama aid falling 2017–20
mechs.counterexamples: US$20bn Treasury swap with Argentina (2025) and DFC reauthorisation to US$205bn (2025) show that the US can deploy state finance when politically prioritised; Leiva Van de Maele (2026) argues instruments were always available.
mechs.scope_conditions: The 'gap' is less a structural incapacity than a selective deployment: US state finance is concentrated on politically aligned governments and security goals.
mechs.assessment: Supported for 2001–2024 as a description of outcomes; reframed by the evidence as a political-economy choice (reliance on private capital and Congressional/budget constraints) rather than an absolute lack of tools.
mechs.gaps: No systematic disbursement data on DFC/EXIM/APEP in LAC in the corpus; external DFC data report only aggregate Western Hemisphere exposure (US$11.8bn incl. North America).

mechs.explanation: Latin American agency, hedging and diversification
mechs.prediction: Governments should use China to diversify finance and markets while preserving US security ties; patterns should vary with domestic capacity, not just with great-power pressure.
mechs.cases: Brazil (soft balancing, Porto do Açu with US exercises), Chile (trading state; lithium and F-16s), Panama, Uruguay, Ecuador (diversifying finance after 2013)
mechs.counterexamples: Mexico and Central America locked into US alignment (hegemonic ceiling); Venezuela and Cuba pushed into dependence on China by sanctions.
mechs.scope_conditions: Hedging requires bureaucratic capacity and macro-stability; fragile states turn to whichever patron offers fastest relief.
mechs.assessment: Strongly supported. Central to explaining why US discourse does not translate into realignment: Latin American states compartmentalise economic and security relations.
mechs.gaps: Hedging measures (Sims and Lee) exclude finance and FDI.

mechs.prediction: Left governments should deepen ties with China and right governments should reverse them.
mechs.cases: Ecuador under Correa vs Lasso/Noboa (FTA with China signed 2023 under Lasso); Brazil under Bolsonaro (trade continued); Argentina under Macri and Milei (swap retained but its use reduced; US swap 2025)
mechs.counterexamples: Cross-ideological continuity of China ties (Pinochet to Concertación; PT to armed forces); China's caution with Chávez; Pacific Alliance's Asia orientation.
mechs.scope_conditions: Ideology predicts sovereign borrowing choices and rhetoric/public opinion, not commodity trade volumes.
mechs.assessment: Partially supported. Ideology is a modifier of form, not the driver of volume.
mechs.gaps: Effect of the 2023–2026 right turn (Milei, Noboa, Paz, Kast, Asfura, Fujimori, de la Espriella) on Chinese economic presence is too recent to measure.

mechs.prediction: Borrowers should prefer Chinese finance because it lacks policy conditionality, and Chinese discourse on non-intervention should resonate with Latin American sovereignty traditions.
mechs.cases: Ecuador's preference for 'commercial' over 'policy' conditionality; Montevideo/OAS non-intervention tradition
mechs.counterexamples: Chinese strings: Taiwan, UN votes, procurement ties, oil collateral; selective use of economic pressure (Argentina anti-dumping retaliation, Norway salmon).
mechs.scope_conditions: Matters for sovereign finance under governments hostile to IMF/US conditionality.
mechs.assessment: Supported as a reason for borrower preference; the 'no strings' claim is overstated.

mechs.prediction: China's processing dominance should bind producers to Chinese buyers and attract Chinese upstream investment irrespective of political alignment; Western responses should be regulatory/denial-oriented.
mechs.cases: Tianqi–SQM (2018), Ganfeng (Cauchari-Olaroz, Mariana), Zijin (Tres Quebradas), CBC/CATL in Bolivia, Codelco–SQM (Chile, 2023–26)
mechs.counterexamples: Chile's low China dependence for lithium exports and state-led Codelco–SQM arrangement; Bolivia's failure to implement Chinese contracts; US frameworks with Argentina, Ecuador, Paraguay and Peru (Feb 2026).
mechs.scope_conditions: Strong where provincial/decentralised governance lets firms negotiate directly (Argentina); weaker where a strong state firm or US incumbent exists (Chile).
mechs.assessment: Strongly supported for structural market position; whether ownership translates into durable control is uncertain.
mechs.gaps: Corpus lacks post-2023 lithium data; external data confirm 2025 production start at Mariana and Tres Quebradas.

mechs.prediction: US pressure should block Chinese projects where the US has leverage (security dependence, market access, proximity) and fail where targets have outside options.
mechs.cases: Chile submarine cable (2019), Panama (projects dropped 2019–21; BRI exit 2025; ports 2025–26), Mexico (USMCA constraints; Mexican tariffs on Chinese imports 2025)
mechs.counterexamples: Venezuela sanctions pushed oil toward China until 2026; Panama's trade with China kept growing after 2019; El Salvador/DR aid cuts reversed.
mechs.scope_conditions: Effective at denial in discrete strategic nodes under high US leverage; ineffective at reversing diffuse market flows.
mechs.assessment: Supported with scope conditions: denial without substitution.
mechs.gaps: Effects of the 2025–2026 coercive turn (tariffs, Venezuela operation, Shield of the Americas) on Chinese economic presence are not yet observable.

mechs.prediction: State-backed Chinese investors should be less deterred by risk than US private investors.
mechs.counterexamples: Chinese reluctance in Venezuela pre-2006; Chinese losses in Venezuela led to lending halt after 2016.
mechs.assessment: Weakly supported (single study with data problems).

mechs.prediction: Commodity integration with China should deepen re-primarisation and constrain policy space; cycles of boom and bust should shape domestic politics.
mechs.cases: Brazil reprimarisation (raw materials ~55% of exports), Peru copper >60%
mechs.counterexamples: Growth and poverty reduction during the China boom (Stallings).
mechs.scope_conditions: Explains the costs and political feedback of China ties, not their persistence per se.
mechs.assessment: Supported as context and as a feedback mechanism; it explains why ties persist despite costs (lack of alternative markets).

mechs.prediction: Favourable publics should sustain ties; China's model should attract.
mechs.counterexamples: Limited appeal of China's development model (19.6% approval).
mechs.assessment: Weak as an explanation of persistence; opinion follows material gains and presidential ideology.

mechs.prediction: A securitised US agenda should crowd out economic offers and frame China as a security problem.
mechs.cases: Northern Triangle focus (Panama budget cut); Shield of the Americas (2026); fentanyl precursors
mechs.counterexamples: US–China AML cooperation 2024 shows security can be a cooperative domain.
mechs.assessment: Supported as a description of US priorities; causal effect on LAC economic choices inferred.

mechs.explanation: Financial crises, policy space and models of capitalism
mechs.prediction: Post-crisis legitimacy loss of Washington-Consensus policies and the 2008 crisis should raise demand for alternative finance and state-led models.
mechs.cases: Ecuador after 2008 default; Argentina after holdout litigation
mechs.counterexamples: Domestic politics, not external models, drove crisis management (Del Tedesco Lins 2021).
mechs.assessment: Contextually supported; 'state capitalism vs liberal capitalism' is analytically loose (Alami and Dixon) but captures the instrument asymmetry.

mechs.prediction: Chinese state finance and SOE FDI should avoid Taiwan allies; switches should be rewarded.
mechs.cases: Panama 2017, Dominican Republic and El Salvador 2018, Nicaragua 2021, Honduras 2023; Paraguay as holdout
mechs.counterexamples: Trade growth did not shift UN voting; Costa Rica remains US-aligned.
mechs.assessment: Supported for China's allocation of state-linked capital; weak as a predictor of broader realignment.
mechs.gaps: Delivered vs promised rewards after switches not measured in the corpus.

mechs.prediction: US responses should lag Chinese advances until domestic political conditions align.
mechs.cases: 2001–2016 'relaxed' response; 2017 inflection; 2025 National Security Strategy reasserting the Monroe Doctrine
mechs.counterexamples: Hedging persisted across administrations with different engagement levels.
mechs.scope_conditions: Explains timing of the US response, not the persistence of Chinese ties after 2017.
mechs.assessment: Strongly supported for 2001–2017; insufficient for 2017–2026, when attention was high but Chinese trade kept growing.

mechs.prediction: Ruptures between LAC governments and the US/IFIs/markets create financing gaps filled by risk-tolerant state capital; ties outlast the governments that created them.
mechs.cases: Ecuador after 2008 default; Venezuela; Argentina after holdout litigation; Bolivia
mechs.counterexamples: Ecuador kept borrowing from China after regaining market access (persistence), but China's share fell from >80% to 53%.
mechs.assessment: Supported; emerges from D01, D09, D11 and D03.

mechs.prediction: Where the US has security or market leverage it can deny China specific strategic assets, but without offering markets or capital of comparable scale it cannot displace China's trade-and-ownership footprint.
mechs.cases: Panama, Chile, Mexico vs Brazil, Peru, Argentina
mechs.counterexamples: Argentina 2025: US financial rescue produced partial substitution (reduced use of PBoC swap).
mechs.assessment: The paper's integrating argument; consistent with the bulk of the evidence but built by synthesis rather than tested in any single source.
mechs.gaps: Requires systematic project-level data on US denial episodes and on post-2025 outcomes.

contra.topic: Motive of Chinese state finance: commercial vs geopolitical contestation
contra.position_a: Primarily commercial / neo-developmental: commercial rates, risk reduction, national champions' market share.
contra.position_b: Contestation of US hegemony: state-linked finance and SOE FDI fall where US influence is high and avoid Taiwan allies.
contra.analyst_reading: The positions concern different questions: motive (D01) vs allocation pattern (D02). Both are compatible with an accommodation reading (D02 itself offers it). The paper treats motive as indeterminate and focuses on observable capability asymmetries.

contra.position_a: Investment pledge to 2014 (US$100bn), already falling short by 2006.
contra.status: contested in sources; external reporting mixed (X-K002)
contra.analyst_reading: The ambiguity itself illustrates how announcements are recoded over time; the paper does not use the figure as evidence of realised investment.

contra.position_a: Shorter maturities (10.7 vs 18.0 years) and commercial rates.
contra.position_b: 'Patient capital' with longer horizons giving fiscal space (Kaplan, cited second-hand).
contra.analyst_reading: 'Patience' may refer to tolerance of risk and political cycles rather than contractual maturity.

contra.position_a: Leftist governments far more likely to borrow from China; non-leftist governments unlikely to engage beyond trade.
contra.position_b: Cross-ideological, multi-partisan support; ties persisted after the Pink Tide.
contra.analyst_reading: Ideology predicts sovereign borrowing and public opinion; it does not predict commodity trade or, after 2015, much of FDI.

contra.topic: Does trade with China drive financing choices?
contra.position_a: Earlier literature (as summarised by Albright 2025) found that trade ties predict Chinese lending.
contra.position_b: Trade does not predict lender choice.
contra.analyst_reading: Supports separating the market layer from the state-finance layer.

contra.position_a: US carrots were mostly promises; aid to Panama fell; FY2019 LAC request cut 34%.
contra.position_b: Instruments were 'readily available'; the obstacle was politics; the 2017 shift was not only rhetorical.
contra.analyst_reading: Availability of tools ≠ deployment at scale. The paper frames the gap as a political-economy choice (selective deployment), consistent with the 2025 Argentina swap.

contra.position_a: Clear trade-off between alignment with the US and Chinese economic attention.
contra.position_b: Aligned countries that move economically closer to China receive MORE US aid; hedging pays.
contra.analyst_reading: The trade-off concerns Chinese state finance; the payoff concerns US aid responses — both can hold.

contra.topic: Effect of BRI membership on FDI
contra.position_b: BRI lowers total FDI; Brazil (non-member) is largest recipient of Chinese FDI.
contra.status: within one study with data problems
contra.analyst_reading: BRI membership is a weak indicator of material presence.

contra.topic: China's share of Venezuela's external debt
contra.position_a: China 'owns most' of Venezuela's external debt.
contra.position_b: External estimates: US$10–20bn owed to China vs ≈US$240bn total (2026).
Widespread negative online discourse; low approval of China's model (19.6%); FDI erodes image.
contra.analyst_reading: Generalised favourability coexists with project-level and model-level scepticism.

contra.topic: Durability of Chinese control in minerals and energy
contra.position_a: A 'silent monopoly' / structural domination embedded in technical and institutional fabric.
contra.position_b: Ownership will not necessarily secure future dominance; US–China rivalry creates uncertainty; host states pursue domestic processing.
contra.status: unresolved; post-2023 evidence (Codelco–SQM; Bolivia stalls) favours B in Chile and Bolivia, A in Argentina and Peru

contra.position_a: US pressure succeeded (Chile cable; Panama projects dropped).
contra.position_b: Pressure counter-productive or ineffective where targets have outside options; sanctions failed in Venezuela.
contra.analyst_reading: Denial works at discrete nodes under high leverage; it does not reverse diffuse flows.

countries.name: Argentina
countries.politics: Kirchner (2003) → Fernández de Kirchner (2007, 2011) → Macri (2015) → Fernández (2019) → Milei (2023)
countries.china: Soy-and-commodity complementarity; PBoC swap since 2009; CDB/China Exim finance for rail and dams while excluded from markets by holdout litigation; Lithium Triangle hub (≈one-third of Chinese lithium investment 2017–2020); Neuquén space station. BRI MoU signed 2022.
countries.us: Holdout litigation in US courts kept Argentina from markets; under Milei the US Treasury extended a US$20bn swap (Oct 2025), of which US$2.5bn was drawn and repaid; critical-minerals framework (Feb 2026).
countries.assessment: Chinese projects survived four changes of government (Santa Cruz dams reactivated 2026; lithium projects producing from 2025), but the 2025 US rescue shows partial substitution when Washington deploys state finance: the activated PBoC swap tranche fell from ≈US$5bn (2023) to ≈US$1bn (end-2025).

countries.name: Bolivia
countries.politics: Morales (2005/06) → Áñez (2019 interim) → Arce (2020) → Paz (2025)
countries.china: Tin and minerals trade; China's share of Bolivian external debt rose to ≈9% by 2014 while World Bank share fell from >34% to 8.7%; Chinese construction services at Uyuni; lithium contracts with TBEA (2019) and CATL-led CBC (2023) never implemented.
countries.us: Rupture under Morales: coca disputes, alleged US plotting and the Snowden-related forced landing of his plane (D11-C14).
countries.assessment: Ideology and rupture opened space for Chinese finance, but Bolivia's state-led lithium model and political instability blocked Chinese (and German, Russian) deals; China's role remained secondary to regional lenders (CAF 30.9%).

countries.name: Brazil
countries.politics: Lula (2002) → Rousseff (2010) → Temer (2016) → Bolsonaro (2018) → Lula (2022) → runoff 25 Oct 2026
countries.china: China became Brazil's largest trade partner in 2009; iron ore, soy and oil; largest recipient of Chinese FDI despite not joining the BRI (2024 'synergy' agreement instead); State Grid transmission (Belo Monte), BYD Camaçari (2025), CDB loans to BNDES (2023).
countries.us: Temer and Bolsonaro aligned with the US politically; Trump II imposed a 50% tariff (Aug 2025, partly rolled back Nov 2025) and sanctioned a Supreme Court justice.
countries.assessment: Clearest case of cross-ideological continuity: China ties deepened under PT and persisted under Temer and Bolsonaro; US coercion in 2025 targeted domestic politics rather than China ties.

countries.name: Chile
countries.politics: Lagos (2000) → Bachelet (2006) → Piñera (2010) → Bachelet (2014) → Piñera (2018) → Boric (2022) → Kast (2026)
countries.china: First LAC FTA with China (2005/06); copper and lithium exports; Tianqi's 24% of SQM (2018); State Grid / CSGI control of electricity distribution (CGE, Chilquinta) and stake in Transelec.
countries.us: US–Chile FTA (2004); Albemarle as lithium incumbent; 2019 submarine cable switched from Huawei to Google after US pressure; F-16 upgrades.
countries.assessment: A 'trading state' that engages China pragmatically across governments while keeping US security ties; the Codelco–SQM lithium arrangement (2023–2026) and the cable case show limits to Chinese strategic penetration.

countries.name: Colombia
countries.politics: Uribe (2002) → Santos (2010) → Duque (2018) → Petro (2022) → de la Espriella (2026)
countries.china: Coal purchases; little Chinese finance; joined the BRI in May 2025 under Petro.
countries.us: Closest US ally (Plan Colombia; FTA in force 2012; NATO global partner 2018); 2025 tariff threats over deportation flights and US Treasury sanctions on President Petro (Oct 2025).
countries.assessment: Low Chinese state finance throughout (pro-US government); Petro's 2025 BRI entry under US pressure is a late hedge whose durability under the 2026 government is uncertain.

countries.name: Costa Rica
countries.politics: Arias (2006) → Chinchilla (2010) → Solís (2014) → Alvarado (2018) → Chaves (2022) → Fernández (2026)
countries.china: First Central American switch to Beijing (2007); FTA (2010/11).
countries.us: CAFTA-DR ratified soon after the switch; strong security and normative alignment with the US.
countries.assessment: Puzzle case: recognition switch without realignment, showing that diplomatic recognition and economic opening do not determine strategic alignment.

countries.name: Ecuador
countries.politics: Correa (2007) → Moreno (2017) → Lasso (2021) → Noboa (2023, 2025)
countries.china: Oil-backed loans and seven Chinese-financed dams (Coca Codo Sinclair); >US$18bn in 24 Chinese loans 2008–2019; FTA signed 2023 under Lasso.
countries.us: Correa closed the Manta base and expelled the World Bank representative; Galápagos debt-for-nature swap with DFC guarantee (2023); critical-minerals framework (2026); voters rejected foreign bases (Nov 2025).
countries.assessment: Archetype of the rupture-gap mechanism: China's share of new loans fell from >80% (2008–13) to 53% (2014–19) as Western access returned, yet ties persisted under right-of-centre governments (FTA 2023).

countries.name: Mexico
countries.politics: Fox (2000) → Calderón (2006) → Peña Nieto (2012) → López Obrador (2018) → Sheinbaum (2024)
countries.china: Competitor rather than complement: lost US market share and maquiladora jobs to China after 2001; little Chinese FDI; BYD plant stalled (2025); Congress approved tariffs up to 50% on Chinese imports (Dec 2025).
countries.us: NAFTA/USMCA lock-in (USMCA art. 32.10); top source of US imports in 2025 (US$534.8bn); 2025 'fentanyl' tariffs.
countries.assessment: Main counter-case to the premise: in the USMCA space US market leverage and Mexican trade policy limit Chinese economic expansion.

countries.name: Nicaragua
countries.politics: Bolaños (2002) → Ortega (2007–)
countries.china: HKND canal concession (2013, revoked 2024); recognition switch (Dec 2021); FTA (2023/24).
countries.us: Sanctions on the Ortega government.
countries.assessment: Shows the gap between announced Chinese megaprojects and realised outcomes.

countries.name: Panama
countries.politics: Varela (2014) → Cortizo (2019) → Mulino (2024)
countries.china: Recognition switch (June 2017); first LAC BRI signatory (Nov 2017); 47 bilateral agreements by 2018; Chinese contractor on the fourth canal bridge.
countries.us: Growth in the Americas, DFC, Clean Network invitation, APEP; Cortizo dropped the PCCP port, northern railway and Amador embassy site; Mulino withdrew from the BRI (Feb 2025); CK Hutchison port concession annulled (Jan 2026); US rotational presence MOU (Apr 2025).
countries.assessment: Strongest evidence of US denial capacity in a high-leverage setting — yet Panama's trade with China grew after 2019 and Chinese contractors kept major works.

countries.name: Peru
countries.politics: Toledo (2001) → García (2006) → Humala (2011) → Kuczynski (2016) → Vizcarra/… → Castillo (2021) → Boluarte (2022) → Fujimori (elected 2026)
countries.china: Copper (>60% of exports); FTA (2009/10); Las Bambas, Toromocho; Chancay port (2024); Chinese SOEs control Lima electricity distribution and Chaglla hydro.
countries.us: US–Peru TPA (2009); critical-minerals framework (Feb 2026).
countries.assessment: China's footprint deepened under governments of every orientation, shifting from trade to strategic-asset ownership (port, electricity).

countries.name: Paraguay
countries.politics: Lugo (2008) → Cartes (2013) → Abdo (2018) → Peña (2023)
countries.china: Recognises Taiwan; trade with China via soybean exports and imports.
countries.us: Critical-minerals framework (Feb 2026).
countries.assessment: Taiwan holdout: economic ties with China persist without diplomatic recognition.

countries.name: Uruguay
countries.politics: Batlle (2000) → Vázquez (2005) → Mujica (2010) → Vázquez (2015) → Lacalle Pou (2020) → Orsi (2025)
countries.china: China first export destination (≈26% in 2025); agri-food complementarity.
countries.us: Long-standing security ties.
countries.assessment: Hedger leveraging Chinese agricultural demand while anchoring security with the US (Sims and Lee).

countries.name: Venezuela
countries.politics: Chávez (1999) → Maduro (2013) → US capture of Maduro; acting president Rodríguez (Jan 2026)
countries.china: Largest recipient of Chinese policy-bank lending (≈US$58.8bn, 49% of LAC total 2005–2023); no new loans after 2016; US$10–20bn estimated outstanding.
countries.us: PDVSA sanctions (2019); recognition of Guaidó; Jan 2026 military operation; July 2026 oil-revenue arrangement barring payments to China.
countries.assessment: Ideological alignment produced the largest Chinese exposure — and the largest losses, prompting China's retreat from sovereign lending; US coercion in 2026 directly redirected Venezuelan oil away from China.

countries.name: Honduras
countries.politics: Zelaya (2006, ousted 2009) → Lobo → Hernández → Castro (2022) → Asfura (2026)
countries.china: Recognition switch (Mar 2023); Patuca III dam (Chinese contractor).
countries.us: US Joint Task Force Bravo at Soto Cano; Asfura government reviewing China agreements (2026).
countries.assessment: Switch without security realignment; possible reversal under a US-aligned government illustrates the reversibility of diplomatic gains.

countries.name: El Salvador
countries.politics: Flores (1999) → Saca (2004) → Funes (2009) → Sánchez Cerén (2014) → Bukele (2019, 2024)
countries.china: Switched recognition from Taiwan on 21 Aug 2018 under the FMLN (X-E054). Bukele's 2019 Beijing visit produced a ~US$500m grant package (X-E1018). Delivered: National Library (US$54m, Nov 2023, X-E759) and La Libertad pier (>US$18m, Nov 2024, X-E760). Advancing: Ilopango water plant (US$40m, 90% in Apr 2026, X-E761) and National Stadium (>US$100m, 75% in Oct 2026, X-E756, X-E762). FTA talks launched Apr 2024 and near agreement, unsigned (X-E752–X-E754). Chinese FDI is negligible (US$0.33m in 2025, X-E766), and no Chinese loans were found (X-E767).
countries.us: Washington threatened to reevaluate relations and recalled its ambassador in 2018 (X-E757, X-E758). Under Trump II, Bukele became a key partner: CECOT detention of US deportees for ~US$6m (X-E261, X-E763) and the first Western Hemisphere reciprocal trade agreement (29 Jan 2026, X-E755). The US takes ~US$2.34bn of exports (2023) and sends 92.4% of remittances, worth ~27.5% of GDP (X-E764, X-E765).
countries.assessment: China's position was kept and expanded through grant-financed showcase projects and FTA talks, despite US objections in 2018 and Bukele's close alignment with Trump. But these are mostly diplomatic and symbolic ties. In trade (except imports), investment and remittances, El Salvador remains a US economy, so the case qualifies rather than supports the pattern (X-E768).

countries.name: Cuba
countries.politics: Fidel Castro (1976) → Raúl Castro (acting 2006; 2008) → Díaz-Canel (2018); Prime Minister Marrero (2019)
countries.china: Long-standing PRC ally. Xi's 2014 visit brought 29 agreements (X-E323) and party-to-party ties continued (X-E1022). In 2026, under US blockade, China provided US$80m and rice (X-E376), political backing (X-E381) and 10,000 donated solar PV systems in Nov 2025–Aug 2026 (X-E771).
countries.us: Trump restored terrorism designation (X-E260), tightened policy (X-E268), imposed tariffs on oil suppliers (X-E135), indicted Raúl Castro (X-E381) and sanctioned Cuban military procurement, including the attaché in Beijing (Aug 2026, X-E770).
countries.assessment: China keeps and expands support under maximum US pressure, but the support is grants, donations and political backing to a sanctioned, insolvent state, not commercially driven trade or investment. It fits the 'keeps ties despite US discourse' half of the pattern, not the 'economic expansion' half.

countries.name: Dominican Republic
countries.politics: Mejía (2000) → Fernández (2004, 2008) → Medina (2012, 2016) → Abinader (2020, 2024)
countries.china: Switched recognition to the PRC on 1 May 2018 (X-E051); Medina met Xi in Nov 2018 (X-E1016). Exports to China reached US$325.8m in 2024 (+34.9%), and ProDominicana courted Chinese investors in Beijing in Sep 2025 (X-E774).
countries.us: The US recalled its ambassador over the switch (X-E758). Abinader (from 2020) chose a 'strategic alliance' with the US and barred Chinese investment in ports, telecoms and airports (X-E775). Later steps: CBP MoU (X-E1032), Minerals Security Partnership (X-E257), military access agreement (X-E276) and a rare-earths framework (Sep 2026, X-E773).
countries.assessment: Commercial ties with China continue and grow in non-strategic sectors, while strategic infrastructure and critical minerals are channelled to the US. This is a screened coexistence that qualifies the pattern. The link between US pressure and the screening is plausible, not documented.

countries.name: Guatemala
countries.politics: Portillo (2000) → Berger (2004) → Colom (2008) → Pérez Molina (2012) → Maldonado (2015) → Morales (2016) → Giammattei (2020) → Arévalo (2024)
countries.china: Still recognises Taiwan (Taiwan MOFA, Oct 2026, X-E779; X-E143). No PRC relations. Arévalo signed supply-chain and semiconductor letters of intent with Taiwan in June 2025 (X-E778).
countries.us: Safe-third-country deal of 2019 (X-E237) and 2025 deportee and border commitments (X-E1031). Reciprocal trade agreement of 30 Jan 2026, with 70.4% of exports at 0% (X-E777).
countries.assessment: No sign of China expanding ties at state level. Guatemala deepened both Taiwan and US ties, so it challenges the pattern. Imports from the PRC (not collected here) may still be large, so the economic side is open.

countries.name: Haiti
countries.politics: Aristide (2001) → Alexandre (interim, 2004) → Préval (2006) → Martelly (2011) → Privert (interim, 2016) → Moïse (2017) → Henry (PM, 2021) → Transitional Presidential Council (2024) → Fils-Aimé (PM, sole executive from Feb 2026)
countries.china: Recognises Taiwan; 70 years of ties marked in May 2026 (X-E783, X-E143). The PRC's role is visible mainly at the UN Security Council, where it abstained on the US–Panama Gang Suppression Force resolution (X-E781).
countries.us: The US backs PM Fils-Aimé (X-E780) and led the Gang Suppression Force, which had >US$200m pledged by Apr 2026 (X-E782). Aristide left on a US plane in 2004 (X-E508).
countries.assessment: Security-dominated relationship led by the US and multilateral actors. No Chinese economic expansion was documented, so Haiti challenges the pattern (or lies outside it).

projects.name: Venezuela loans-for-oil (China–Venezuela Joint Fund / CDB–BANDES/PDVSA)
projects.announced: 'more than US$32bn' announced loans by c.2011 (D27); US$44bn in six loans-for-oil (D01 text)
projects.disbursed: n/a in sources; US$10–20bn estimated still owed (2026)
projects.status: repayment arrears; no new loans after 2016
projects.note: Largest single exposure; losses and arrears are a key reason for the post-2016 retreat of Chinese sovereign lending.

projects.name: Ecuador oil-backed loans and Coca Codo Sinclair hydropower (1,500 MW)
projects.instrument: policy-bank loans; EPC; oil advance payments
projects.approved: Coca Codo loan US$1.7bn (D01); >US$18bn in 24 Chinese loans 2008–2019 (D03)
projects.status: operating since 2016; defects, erosion; 2025 settlement (US$200m compensation); final acceptance April 2026
projects.note: Flagship of the 'infrastructure-for-resources' model and its technical risks.

projects.name: Argentina Santa Cruz dams (Cóndor Cliff / La Barrancosa)
projects.actor: China Gezhouba with Argentine partners; Chinese bank finance
projects.note: Survived three changes of government (Kirchner, Macri, Fernández, Milei) with renegotiation and delays.

projects.name: Argentina Belgrano Cargas / San Martín freight rail
projects.instrument: credit line tied to Chinese equipment
projects.status: financed tranches (≈US$2.47bn Chinese finance reported); completion status unclear
projects.note: Large gap between the 2010 announcement and later financed tranches.

projects.name: Argentina Atucha III nuclear plant (Hualong One)
projects.status: cancelled (provisional): Nucleoeléctrica shareholders' meeting annulled the project on 23 Sep 2026, citing lack of funds; single outlet, no official comment [X-E808]
projects.note: Round-3 update (Oct 2026): see X-E808; status rests on one outlet.

projects.name: Espacio Lejano deep-space station (Neuquén)
projects.note: Cited by US SOUTHCOM and Congress as a security concern (D20).

projects.name: Argentina–PBoC currency swap
projects.status: maintained under Milei but usage reduced
projects.note: Contrast with US Treasury swap (PM08).

projects.name: US Treasury (ESF)–BCRA stabilisation swap
projects.note: Key counterexample to a structural US 'instrument gap': state finance deployed selectively for an aligned government.

projects.name: Chancay multipurpose port
projects.note: Flagship of post-lending Chinese strategic-asset ownership.

projects.name: Lima electricity distribution (Luz del Sur; Enel Distribución Perú/Pluz)
projects.actor: China Three Gorges / China Yangtze Power; China Southern Power Grid
projects.note: Chinese SOEs now control Lima's metropolitan distribution.

projects.name: Chile electricity (Transelec 27.7%; Chilquinta; CGE 97.3%)
projects.actor: State Grid (SGCC); China Southern Power Grid
projects.note: CGE agreed Nov 2020, completed July 2021 (correction to D15).

projects.name: Brazil Belo Monte UHVDC transmission (Bipoles I–II) and CEEE-T
Tianqi stake in SQM / Codelco–SQM lithium venture
projects.status: Codelco–SQM venture closed after Chile Supreme Court rejected Tianqi (26 Jan 2026)
projects.note: Counter-case: Chilean state-led consolidation limited Chinese leverage.

projects.name: Bolivia lithium: TBEA-Baocheng JV (2019); CBC (CATL-BRUNP-CMOC) DLE plants (2023); Uranium One (2024)
projects.actor: TBEA; CATL consortium; Rosatom's Uranium One
projects.approved: contracts signed, never approved by legislature
projects.status: stalled; under review by Paz government
projects.note: State-led model and political instability stalled both German (2019) and Chinese/Russian deals.

projects.name: BYD Mexico assembly plant
projects.note: USMCA context; causal attribution contested.

projects.name: Tesla Gigafactory Mexico (Nuevo León)
projects.note: Friend-shoring announcement not realised.

projects.name: Panama Colón Container Port (Landbridge) and northern railway
projects.note: Denial under US pressure.

projects.name: Balboa and Cristóbal ports (Panama Ports Company / CK Hutchison)
projects.status: concession annulled by Supreme Court (29 Jan 2026); ports occupied (Feb 2026); sale stalled over COSCO stake demand
projects.note: Flashpoint of the 2025 'take back the canal' rhetoric.

projects.name: Fourth bridge over the Panama Canal
projects.note: Chinese contractor retained despite US pressure.

projects.name: Chile trans-Pacific submarine cable
projects.status: Huawei route not chosen (2020; Chile cited route economics after Pompeo's 2019 warning); Japanese route announced, not built; Google Humboldt cable as alternative (operation expected 2027) [X-E803]
projects.note: Denial success cited by Leiva Van de Maele (2026); round-3 check (X-E803): the causal link to US pressure is plausible, not documented, since the government gave a financial reason.

projects.name: Nicaragua interoceanic canal (HKND)
projects.note: Archetype of announced-but-never-built.

projects.name: US initiatives: America Crece (2019), B3W (2021), APEP (2022–23)
projects.announced: no dollar totals given in corpus
projects.note: Symmetric with Chinese announcement inflation.

projects.name: Ecuador Galápagos debt-for-nature conversion (DFC guarantee)
projects.note: One of few large US official finance operations in South America in the corpus window.

projects.name: Huawei Safe City / ECU 911 surveillance systems
Ecuador oil assets (EnCana purchase → Andes Petroleum)
CDB loans to BNDES (2023) and Bolivia Oruro zinc refinery (2024)
projects.note: New, smaller lending pattern after 2020.

gaps.gap: Disbursement and completion data for Chinese and US official finance in LAC (most corpus figures are commitments or announcements).
gaps.source: Analyst (from D01, D04, D09, D20 limitations)

gaps.gap: Effect of the 2023–2026 right turn (Milei, Noboa, Paz, Kast, Asfura, Fujimori, de la Espriella) on Chinese trade, FDI and project status.
Outcomes of the 2025–2026 US coercive turn (tariffs, Venezuela operation, Shield of the Americas, minerals frameworks) on Chinese economic presence.
gaps.source: Analyst; D18 is the only corpus document covering Trump II

gaps.gap: Firm-level data on Chinese private firms (renewables, EVs, lithium) under the post-2018 model.
gaps.source: NotebookLM synthesis (N28), consistent with D15-C16 and D05-C22

Delivered vs promised rewards after Taiwan recognition switches (2007–2023).
gaps.source: Analyst; D09-C15 asserts countries were 'amply rewarded' without figures

Hedging indices that include finance and FDI, not only goods trade and arms imports.

audit.synthesis_claim: Western FDI is predominantly private capital; Chinese finance is state-coordinated through policy banks and SOEs.
audit.note: Stallings (2025, pp. 316, 326, 328). The synthesis adds that Western FDI seeks 'short-term' returns; Stallings says SOEs prioritise short-term profits less, which is a comparative claim, not a characterisation of all Western FDI.

audit.synthesis_claim: Policy-bank lending absorbs high political risk and embeds collateral and tied commercial clauses (loans-for-oil, tied purchases).
audit.note: Corpus also shows these features LOWER China's risk (Gallagher and Irwin 2015, p. 117) — i.e. risk is managed rather than simply 'absorbed'.

audit.synthesis_claim: 'Developmental State / Commercial Profit' paradigm attributed to Gallagher & Irwin (2015) and Kaplan (2021).
audit.note: Kaplan (2021) is not in the corpus; it is cited second-hand in Albright (2025) and Stallings (2025), where it is associated with 'patient capital' rather than a commercial-profit thesis. Gallagher and Irwin call China a 'globalizing developmental state' with mainly commercial motives.
audit.action: cite Kaplan only as cited in D09/D03/D24

audit.synthesis_claim: 'Geopolitical contestation' paradigm attributed to Urdinez et al. (2016) and Albright (2025); Albright also placed under 'Systemic/Neorealist contestation'.
audit.note: Urdinez et al. do read Chinese state-linked finance as contestation (with accommodation as an alternative reading). Albright (2025) argues the opposite emphasis: borrower interests and both political and pragmatic determinants; 'alignment with China is not the key factor'.

audit.synthesis_claim: 2005 Chilean copper JV (US$2bn) guaranteed China 836,250 t over 15 years at US$2.07/lb; with copper >US$4/lb in 2011 China obtained copper far below market; presented as a 'loans-for-oil & resource-collateralized contract'.
audit.note: Salinas de Dosch and Dosch (n.d., p. 6) report the deal and the 'far below market prices' inference citing James (2011) — a second-hand estimate. It is a supply joint venture, not a loan or collateralised credit. Corpus does not name the parties.

audit.synthesis_claim: Offshore escrow accounts in Western financial hubs give Chinese policy banks senior-creditor status.
audit.note: The corpus only describes CDB withdrawing debt service directly from the borrower's oil-sales account (Gallagher and Irwin 2015, p. 113). 'Escrow', 'offshore hubs' and 'senior creditor status' do not appear in any document.

audit.synthesis_claim: Since 2018 a 'Small is Beautiful' paradigm replaced sovereign megaproject lending with M&A, equity JVs and greenfield in 5G, power, renewables and minerals, driven by debt distress and defaults in Venezuela and Ecuador.
audit.note: Gao (2026, p. 167) uses 'small is beautiful' for small/medium concessional energy projects, motivated by BRI sustainability demands and the risk of sovereign over-indebtedness. The M&A shift is a separate (2015–2021) trend in Gao (p. 169). Gao does not discuss 5G or attribute the shift to Venezuelan/Ecuadorian defaults.

audit.synthesis_claim: Equity in utilities produces 'structural dependency' on Chinese technology and operations rather than debt-trap exposure.
audit.note: This is Gao's interpretation; Sanchez-Lopez (2023, p. 26) cautions that Chinese ownership 'will not necessarily secure' future dominance.

audit.synthesis_claim: Leiva Van de Maele (2026) uses neoclassical realism; US response filtered by Congressional polarisation and electoral cycles.
audit.note: Leiva Van de Maele applies Kingdon's multiple-streams framework (problem, policy, politics) and cites neoclassical realism only in a footnote as other work. He shows Congress identified China as a bipartisan problem from 2005; the missing elements were national mood and elite consensus.
audit.action: excluded; paper follows D20's own framework

audit.synthesis_claim: Chinese policy banks deploy non-conditional, state-subsidised, concessionary capital with low return thresholds.
audit.note: Gallagher and Irwin (2015, pp. 106, 109, 115) find commercial rates, concessional loans only 1.2% of the total and shorter maturities; Albright (2025, p. 92) finds Chinese loans carry higher interest and shorter grace periods. 'Non-conditional' holds only for macro/governance conditionality.

audit.synthesis_claim: America Crece was bottlenecked by reliance on risk-averse private equity lacking state underwriting.
audit.note: The corpus documents that America Crece and related carrots 'remained only promises' and gives no financing figures; the private-capital bottleneck is plausible (Correa da Cunha et al. on US MNC risk sensitivity) but not shown for America Crece.
audit.action: treated as analyst inference in M3

audit.synthesis_claim: ITSI Fund / CHIPS Act frameworks in Panama offer institutional integration but fail to match Chinese port, telecom and transport investment.
audit.verdict: partly in corpus; comparison not in corpus
audit.note: Zelicovich and Yamin (2024, p. 69) record only the announcement of a partnership 'to explore' the semiconductor ecosystem under the ITSI Fund; no scale or comparison.

audit.synthesis_claim: Correa da Cunha et al.: governance +0.147/+0.453 on US FDI and −1.086/−1.606 on Chinese FDI; BRI −0.243 total, −0.048 US, +0.308 China; USMCA +0.011/+0.013 US, −0.065 China; under high UCT −0.112 (US GPR), −0.035 (China GPR).
audit.note: Coefficients match Table 3 (PDF p. 9) and Tables 5–6. The synthesis calls them 'empirical proof'; our reading records serious data problems (reported N of 154,400 for a 7-country, 23-year panel; implausibly small SEs; interaction-sign inconsistencies). It also misstates the low-UCT result: effects are positive (US 0.193; China 0.573), not 'neutral or minor'.
audit.action: confidence on P18 kept at low-medium

audit.synthesis_claim: US sticks without carrots create a 'geoeconomic vacuum' that host governments fill with Chinese capital.
audit.note: Supported for large infrastructure needs (Albright) and for the 2003–2014 inverse relation with US influence (Urdinez). Qualified by Albright: borrowing from China also reflected leftist government preference and Ecuador returned to Western lenders once possible.

audit.synthesis_claim: 'Silent monopoly' attributed to Sánchez-López (2023), Gao and Gulley (2024).
audit.note: Only Gao uses 'silent monopoly'. Gulley documents Chinese control of cobalt chemicals; Sánchez-López documents processing concentration but warns ownership does not guarantee future dominance.

audit.synthesis_claim: Three-tier vertical integration forces ores worldwide through Chinese refining.
audit.note: Processing concentration is well documented (lithium refining mostly in China; 95% of cobalt chemicals). 'Forcing' all ores through China overstates it: Chile exports most lithium to non-Chinese Asia and Europe (D14-C12).

audit.synthesis_claim: Ganfeng's Cauchari-Olaroz output dedicated 'exclusively' to Chinese EV manufacturing; Tianqi stake grants 'state-backed' boardroom access and off-take rights.
audit.note: Corpus records the projects and the 24%/US$4.1bn stake but not exclusivity, off-take rights or state backing of Tianqi.

audit.synthesis_claim: Bolivia: state-to-state CBC/YLB agreements deploying DLE in Uyuni and Coipasa.
audit.note: Corpus mentions a 2019 TBEA-Baocheng JV (Coipasa, Pastos Grandes) and that 'a Chinese consortium will partner with YLB'. External verification (X-P007): CBC contracts were never approved by the legislature and are stalled.

audit.synthesis_claim: Ecuador Corriente Copper Belt: US$3bn by CRCC-Tongling at Mirador; 600,000 t deposit; 30,000 t first-year output; 6.03bn barrels reserves; 486,000 b/d in 2010.
audit.verdict: figures supported; names not in corpus
audit.note: Salinas de Dosch and Dosch (n.d., pp. 7–8) give the figures and describe 'a venture of two Chinese firms' that 'plans to invest'; the firm names and the Mirador mine are not in the text. This is an announcement, not a realised investment.

audit.synthesis_claim: Re-primarisation and Prebisch-Singer thesis attributed to Salinas de Dosch & Dosch (2011).
audit.note: D27 raises 'primatisation' and centre–periphery risk; it does not mention Prebisch-Singer. Re-primarisation evidence is stronger in Stallings (2025) and Bibi et al. (2026).

audit.synthesis_claim: Trade grew from US$13bn (2000) to US$180bn (2010); Hu's 2004 US$100bn target for 2010 was exceeded in 2007.
audit.verdict: supported, but contradicted elsewhere in corpus
audit.note: D27 treats the US$100bn as a TRADE target for 2010; Domínguez et al. (2006, p. 2) report it as an INVESTMENT pledge by 2014. External reporting is mixed (X-K002).

audit.synthesis_claim: Conservative 'Blue Tide' governments (Chile, Peru) signed FTAs with China and keep pragmatic ties.
audit.note: 'Blue Tide' is Bibi et al.'s term. Cross-ideological continuity is well supported, but Chile's FTA (2005) was signed under the centre-left Lagos government and Peru's (2009) under García; Ecuador's 2023 FTA under Lasso is the clearer right-of-centre example (external X-E086).

audit.synthesis_claim: 'Strategic exit' from Western conditionality and 'multidirectional diplomacy' attributed to Domínguez et al. (2006).
audit.note: 'Exit' language is from Albright's interviewees (2025, pp. 80, 92); 'multidirectional diplomacy' is Salinas de Dosch and Dosch quoting Shambaugh. Domínguez et al. speak of 'soft balancing' and cross-ideological support.

audit.synthesis_claim: Civil society, indigenous and labour mobilisation against Chinese projects; public rejection of the authoritarian model (Feng & Zeng 2020; Salinas de Dosch).
audit.note: Feng and Zeng is 2022 (online 2021). Evidence of backlash exists (FDI lowers China's image; online negativity; environmental damage; socio-environmental scrutiny of hydro) but corpus has little on labour unions. Useful overlooked mechanism: backlash changed the FORM of Chinese engagement (shift to smaller projects, Gao p. 166) rather than its persistence.

audit.synthesis_claim: 'Cyclic ideological reinforcement' thesis attributed to Ganchev (2020) and Bibi et al. (2026).
audit.note: Cyclic reinforcement is Ganchev's. Bibi et al. analyse subordinated integration in trade and the US-dollar financial system; they do not analyse Chinese integration by wave and disclaim causality.

audit.synthesis_claim: Hedging thesis attributed to Sims & Lee (2025) and Correa da Cunha et al.
audit.note: Correa da Cunha et al. only observe 'balanced relationships' in a policy discussion; hedging is Sims and Lee's construct.

audit.synthesis_claim: Debate: commercial profit vs coordinated geopolitical strategy (strategic equity in grids indicates coordination).
audit.note: Alami and Dixon (2020) contest the 'coordination' reading (provincial autonomy, weakly regulated SOEs) — a counterweight the synthesis omits.
audit.action: B5 (C01); D24 claims added to P27

audit.synthesis_claim: Research gaps: firm-level data on private Chinese firms; USMCA rules-of-origin diversion of Chinese FDI; governance moderating GPR spillovers.
audit.verdict: reasonable gaps; partly flagged in corpus
audit.note: Gao notes private firms' growing role; Correa da Cunha et al.'s models explain only 50% of Chinese FDI variation. Added to the gaps register.

audit.synthesis_claim: Evidence against asymmetric statecraft: shift to 'small is beautiful' reflects Chinese risk aversion after default losses in Venezuela and Ecuador.
audit.note: Gao cites over-indebtedness risk and sustainability; corpus does not document Chinese default losses in Ecuador (Ecuador's 2008 default was on bonds). Venezuela arrears are documented only externally (X-S034).

audit.synthesis_claim: CHIPS Act friendshoring is designed to build alternative midstream mineral processing.
audit.note: CHIPS/ITSI concerns semiconductors. Mineral-processing measures in the corpus are the 2022 Defense Production Act invocation (Sanchez-Lopez 2023, p. 28) and IRA FEOC traceability (IEA and OECD 2025).

audit.synthesis_claim: Bibliographic labels: 'Feng & Zeng 2020', 'da Cunha et al. 2025/2026', 'Salinas de Dosch & Dosch 2011', 'Ge Gao 2025/2026'.
audit.note: Register uses Feng and Zeng (2022); Correa da Cunha et al. (2026); Salinas de Dosch and Dosch (n.d. — year not printed in the copy supplied); Gao (2026; online 2025).

admins.name: George W. Bush
admins.summary: Latin America moved to lower-level officials after 9/11 and was handled through counter-terrorism and counter-narcotics (Leiva Van de Maele, 2026, p. 911). China was first recognised as a problem in Congress and by SOUTHCOM from 2005, but there was no US response (pp. 915–916). Trade policy went bilateral: FTA with Chile, CAFTA-DR, collapse of the FTAA.

admins.name: Barack Obama
admins.summary: 'Re-engagement' rhetoric and the Cuba opening, but no balancing measures against China in the region. In the second term Latin America lost priority to the Asia pivot (Leiva Van de Maele, 2026, pp. 903, 917). Officials framed China cooperatively; Kerry declared the end of the Monroe Doctrine era in 2013.

admins.name: Donald J. Trump (first term)
admins.summary: The policy window opened: China became a top priority, with hard-liners in every major post (Leiva Van de Maele, 2026, pp. 918–922). The administration used warnings, Huawei 5G pressure, the Chile cable case, America Crece and the CEIEC sanctions; carrots were mostly promises (Zelicovich and Yamin, 2024, p. 65).

admins.name: Joseph R. Biden Jr.
admins.summary: The threat framing was kept but softened to 'competition' (Leiva Van de Maele, 2026, pp. 918, 923). The administration offered B3W, APEP and the Minerals Security Partnership; the IRA tied EV credits to US FTA partners. Counter-narcotics cooperation with China revived in 2024 (Felbab-Brown, 2026, p. 8).

admins.name: Donald J. Trump (second term)
admins.summary: A coercive turn: pressure on Panama, a 50% tariff on Brazil, the US$20bn swap with Argentina, strikes in the Caribbean, the January 2026 Venezuela operation, a National Security Strategy that reasserts the Monroe Doctrine, critical-minerals frameworks and the Shield of the Americas. Capacity-building and anti-corruption tools were cut (Felbab-Brown, 2026, pp. 9, 24–25). The corpus barely analyses this period; most evidence is external.
